I would highly recommend this for any serious fighting game player, though if you are a serious player then you probably already love it or hate it. I have an Xbox 360 Madcatz TE2 fight stick that works flawlessly, but check your favorite forums to see if your stick is compatible because I've heard of issues. Frame rate is great even on minimum specs and the game is compatible with mods that are pretty easy to install. You can check
to find/request mods as well as a wiki with links to important mod tools.
The launch version was weak, not much content and no story mode. We've since had lots of updates, we now have a fully fledged story mode with cut scenes, we now have all the DLC characters as well as new Halloween costumes and beach swim wear costumes. There's also challenges that rotate every week which allow you to earn Fight Money (in-game currency) to make purchases such as DLC characters, stages, colors, etc. SP content is much better now, but it's still missing an arcade mode for some reason. Capcom really loves their waifu's, you're guaranteed to see lots of costumes for female characters in this game.
MP is fun if you like playing anonymous players in ranked match and grind away meaningless points and titles. There are "unranked" and "lobbies" but they are very limited in terms of socializing. The actual game play is great once you get into a game as it plays flawlessly and that's what I enjoy most. If you are a more casual player and you really like Street Fighter, then I recommend going to
to find players to play with in lobbies and use a 3rd party app to chat about your matches. I always have more fun when I play and socialize with other people rather than grind through ranked anonymously.
Would I recommend the season pass? Yes and No. I bought the season pass because I wanted every character, I also wanted to use the Fight Money from those characters game modes to purchase content, so I felt that it was worth it to me. Characters are 400k each, you can make that amount up pretty easily by playing through the SP content but don't expect to get 2.4 million FM to unlock all 6 without using 3rd party hacks (which you can get away with but be careful). Then again, the season pass at $50 is definitely high and you'd be supporting a company which has had questionable business decisions in the past. I'll probably purchase the season 2 DLC depending on the characters announced and the price, but so far there is no word on what the DLC will actually be.
Another thing, Capcom thought it would have been a good idea to install a rootkit on your computer to detect hacks... thankfully it’s gone now so no need to worry but I feel that anyone who purchases this game should be aware that this company was willing to install a rootkit on thousands of PCs without telling anyone.

When I heard about this game, I was hesitant to get it due to the fact that it wasn't as hyped as a GTA or a Saints Row and I didn't want to be disappointed. However, I knew I liked these types of games so I took a chance on it while it was on sale. I gotta say, I wasn't disappointed.
You assume the role of Wei Shen, an undercover police officer sent to infiltrate and take down the Sun On Yee, a traid organization based in Hong Kong. Wei deals with the inner conflict of being a cop, while proving himself to the Triads in order to gain their trust and complete his mission. Unfortunately, in order to gain the trust of the Triads, Wei must go against his moral code. It's only a matter of time before Wei gets in too deep.
Sleeping Dogs isn't just a GTA or Saints Row clone. It brings something different to the genre. It doesn't feel like a generic recreation of the previously mentioned, more established frachises. This game stands out on it's own with the addition of kung-fu melee fighting, parkour, chase sequences and a conflicting story. Other than the main story, there's side missions, races, drug busts, fight clubs and more. There's also an abundance of collectibles to find throughout the map. On top of that, there's four different skill trees that allow you to upgrade your abilities as you complete missions and activities. The melee fighting is really fun. You're not just blocking, reversing and throwing punches. You can use your environment to your advantage. Some of the environmental kills are brutal. Throw your opponents off a roof, or into an eel tank or impale them onto some meat hooks. There's also several types of melee weapons to use such as crowbars, machetes, tire irons, etc. If the use of guns in these types of games are a necessity to you, this game may not be for you. There are certain missions that will require firearms, but the majority of combat is melee fighting. I would estimate the melee-to-gun combat ratio is about 70/30. Guns are somewhat uncommon. This is even mentioned in the story. However, that's something I actually liked about the game. You had to play differently than you would in a GTA or a Saints Row.
I only have two complaints with this game. Firstly, the main story is a bit short. There's only about 30 main story missions. Once I beat the game and watched the ending cutscenes, I thought they could have milked out two or three more missions. Instead, they seemed to rush the end of the story and summarize it in cutscenes. The other complaint I have is the driving. It feels very stiff. I remember when I played the first Saints Row after playing nothing but GTA games and the driving felt so stiff in comparison. Well, I felt that way again with Sleeping Dogs. It feels even more stiff than Saints Row does. This isn't that much of a deterrence since the game offers so many other things, but it is something I think they could improve on for a sequel.
Overall, this game was worth every penny. If you enjoy games like GTA or Saints Row, I think there's a good chance you'll enjoy this as well. The graphics, the gameplay and the story are all excellent. There's a lot of things that will keep you busy. If you're hesitant, I would still wait for a good sale like I did. It's definitely worth a try.

The Binding of Isaac is on it's surface a rather childish narrative of poop jokes and weird body horror, but upon further reflection and piecing together of the non-linear story, one comes to realize that Isaac is a wholly unique, fairly depressing, and highly important narrative. Isaac is a child with everything stripped from him, his ability to choose, his ability to move around, his very humanity is offered up in the name of sacrifice. But unlike so many other narratives about child abuse, Isaac is a game that does not end with a child falling to the knife of his authoritative figures, but rather making his own choices, whether to live or to die.
Isaac's struggles are given serious attention even amidst all the giant poop monsters, and I truly believe this game can absolutely be a cathartic experience to some of us out there who maybe didn't always have the chance to make our own fight in life.

Northgard
Early Access
Shiro Games
Shiro Games
3D Real Time Strategy
8th of March, 2017
Singleplayer
You might say I’m a bit biased in Northgard’s case. This title fondly reminds me of The Settlers IV, one of the first strategy games I ever played. The game I’m reviewing today is still in Early Access stage, but it is a stable and entertaining experience nonetheless. The dev team have already proven their creativity on Steam with their successful Evoland series and even now with their third project, they still seem to focus on fusing two or more gaming genres into hybrid titles with few flaws between them. Northgard attempts to revive not just the long lost glory of the Settlers franchise but also Cultures, among other similar titles.
Sadly I cannot discuss about a storyline since it hasn’t been implemented yet in the Early Access version. From what I could gather in-game and by examining the game’s Store Page, I’m sure we shall have a captivating story filled with danger and adventure. We are talking afterall, about Norsemen. Scandinavian colonialism is uncontestedly accurate as both Iceland and Greenland were settled centuries before other European cultures would set foot on them.
Vikings or not, Norse explorers such as Erik Thorvaldsson and his son, Leif Erikson have left their mark upon history and their exploits most certainly deserved to be adapted for video gaming. So Northgard can currently be played in sandbox/skirmish mode and doesn’t include a campaign or a set of individual scenarios. Once it gets fully released though, expect a coherent plot and a natural scale of progression. Evoland I and II haven’t disappointed in that regard and I have no reason to doubt Shiro Games now.
The game looks great, with diversified assets and the option to zoom in, quite a lot. Fully 3D graphics that show clear signs of attention to details, from animation and even the dynamic weather effects. I do wish the dev team might also include a day/night cycle eventually. One thing I noticed and bothered me a bit (not enough to count it as a weak point) is that all the settlers are male and once they get assigned to a certain profession, they look like clones of one another. 2002’s Cultures: Northland had female settlers too and even children since it fully simulated the family life as well. And they didn’t look exactly the same.
It’s a game design choice, I know, but when addressing the topic of colonial life at least aim for a bit more realism, ok? The current building roster and the jobs they imply, offer sufficient variety for now but there is always room for improvement. The islands players get to settle could sure use more terrain diversity and perhaps more wildlife as well. I think that most of the minor issues I mentioned above can be ameliorated within several more months in development.
Both the soundtrack and sound effects are nothing spectacular yet they alternate pleasantly between a relaxing tone and a more alert one, once combat is being initiated by either the player or AI opponents. Honestly, very few strategy titles I played over the years could rival the sound scores of the Age of Empires or Blitzkrieg series and unlike action-packed shooters or role playing games, I know that real time strategy doesn’t need music to “assist or further the plotline”.
I already mentioned The Settlers and Cultures, as clear inspiration for Northgard’s gameplay, yet the title uses one of its most crucial mechanics in an entirely different manner from the aforementioned models. Territorial expansion is more close to the Civilization series, with (non-hexagonal) plots of land which first need to be individually explored and only afterwards, colonized if your settlement can afford the ever growing Food requirement.
Since Norsemen were known as both ambitious and resilient people, it should come as no surprise that the ultimate goal in Northgard isn’t simply to annihilate your rivals but to outsmart and especially, outlive them. Survival plays center stage, in a game which simulates some of the harshest winter conditions seen in strategy titles. The kind of unforgiving weather which will deplete both Food and Wood stockpiles if you weren’t paying enough attention to the rapidly shifting seasons.
If you think you can win in this game by mustering a large warband and swarming your opponents as soon as you see the window of opportunity, I have some bad news for you. Northgard is more static than it seems at first glance. You need to “turtle” not Zerg Rush the other clans which might not even offer a stiff resistance if you learn to properly defend before trying to attack them. Trade shall offer you both the ample supply of goods to survive and prosper, so long as you focus on the resource gathering closer to your Town Hall (the HQ, if you will).
Land patches offer different opportunities as some may contain rich soil (which could enable wheat harvesting) while other colonized parts might host the type of woodland which shall never leave you short of timber for construction, survival, and even trading with the other clans. A skill tree handles the unlockable perks which can considerably decrease the challenge, so I rarely bothered with them.
I keep mentioning rivals, but it’s time I explain the strengths and weaknesses of each “faction”, so to speak. The current game stage features four not-so-distinct clans so far. The combat-oriented Clan of the Wolf, prefer the aggressive approach and shall gain bonuses to their warrior training and damage they can inflict. The more balanced option is being represented by the Clan of the Stag, which prefer the more peaceful way of Fame towards the ultimate Victory. The “easy mode” appears to materialize within the Clan of the Goat, which have very useful bonuses to food production and consumption. Lastly, the Clan of the Raven represents the master traders of Northgard and can hire mercenaries to bolster their armed forces.
Indeed, I have won on Normal difficulty on a randomized scenario (procedural generation is implemented every time you start a new game) with the Goat Clansmen by trading food to the Jötunn (Giants) tribe in exchange for kröwns, the monetary resource in Northgard. Not all in-game creatures from the Norse mythology are as friendly and open to trade as the Giants though. Draugr (undead), valkyries and wyverns can lay waste to your warbands unless they have received adequate training and the leadership of a warchief unit.
Northgard’s a promising and polished game already, while it also proves that Steam didn’t fail completely with the implementation of the Early Access program. Being a hybrid of multiple genres and with an equal number of inspired gameplay mechanics, the title I had the chance to review today couldn’t have failed. I consider its price tag justified and I urge all strategy fans who prefer slower paced progression, to purchase Northgard even in its current stage. I personally can’t wait to see the campaign, Shiro Games has in store for us!
EDIT: Trading Cards have been finally added.
+ Pleasant graphics and relaxing sounds.
+ Steam Achievements & Steam Trading
+ Interesting mix of RTS combat with colonial settlement & survival.
- Not enough cultural/technological diversity between the rival Clans.
- No campaign or story missions in this Early Access stage.

The straight away answer I would to give to anyone who asked me if I enjoyed the game would be yes. But do I recommend it to others? The game comes with DOOM and DOOM II, two of my favorite games of all time. I would HIGHLY recommend you purchase both of those titles, even if you decide not to buy DOOM 3: BFG Edition. The DOOM 3 part of DOOM 3: BFG Editon is DOOM 3, but with minor gameplay and graphical updates implemented. It additionally includes the two expansion packs for DOOM 3, Resurection of Evil (RoE) and The Lost Levels, and the expansion pack for DOOM II, No Rest For the Living. To allow the game to sell in Germany, the Wolfenstien 3D levels in DOOM II were additionally censored to remove the Nazi enemies and pictures of Hitler and Swastikas.
DOOM 3 is a very fun game in my opinion. The games difficulty ramps up at a bit of a slow pace, but the game picks up near the end. It took me around 30 hours to complete the entire game of DOOM 3 (Not including any of the expansions or DOOM and DOOM II). The game offers a ton of enemies and weapons, and many people will try to compare it to the original DOOMs, saying that it is "bad in comparison". DOOM 3 is very similar to DOOM and DOOM II, but has a large change in pacing. Enemies are stronger and come in smaller quantities, you run and walk slower, with a stamina meter implimented to prevent you from always running, and enemies attacks are slower to compensate. Areas are smaller in size, with less dodging room, and the game encourages exploration at a slower pace to spot details in the environement. Whether or not this change was good or bad is up to you, but I feel it didn't kill the experience.
At several points in the game I got lost (the game has no map system) or stuck doing a time-wasting "mini-game" (such as using a crane to remove toxic barrels), which dissapointed me somewhat. Additonally, the final boss fight was way too easy, and some of the enemies had bad visual changes, such as the Cacodemon, or were weakened, such as the Arch-Ville, who no longer charges up a fire attack when you are near him and summons new monster rather than reviving dead ones. If I was able to change DOOM 3, I would in a lot of ways, but the experience to me was still enjoyable.
I would recommend this game to someone who likes first person shooters, games that encourage exploration, scary games, and both casual and hardcore gamers.

Supported this game from Kickstarter. I do not think it's worth $44CDN. Not even sure if I'd pay $22 for it now. I love how it looks, but not how it plays.
Pros:
- Cinematic moments that just look great, with clean graphics and lots and lots of robots! Imagine seeing the moon rise up over the horizon with massive jets of flame behind it as it propels itself into a another planet. A visual expierence not achieved in many other games that I know of in a full 3D engine; with real in-game consequences no less
- Love many of the things they brought from the Supreme Commander Series such as emphasis on sarger strategic decisions instead of micromanagement (for example the bulk building of power plants and metal mines by click-dragging)
- Orbital layer and multi-planet combat add 2 new dimensions most RTS games ignore
Cons:
Do you have land, air, and orbital units? Good luck making heads or tails of the hundreds of little things zipping about everywhere. The amount of clutter on screen is... not very usable. Zooming out, my favourite feature in Supreme Commander, allowed me to see the ENTIRE map on a single screen where I could overview, select, give orders, and manage my army using only symbols. Now, due to the very nature of the sphereical maps and multi-planet games, at no point am I able to do this for even 1 planet let alone all of them. And my units that are traversing the map are constantly appearing and dissapearing as I can only see half the planet.
I've seen rebuttles "But you can use the PIP system and this and that and and" and no, it just isn't intuitive. In fact I would describe it as disorienting at best. I appreciate that this system adds a certain level of complexity by requiring a person to be able to crazy multi-task by splitting their eyes and watching 3 or 4 cameras, or taking the time to memorize all the locations that are relevant to them on 5 planets. Not to mention that traversing the map constantly rotates your camera so you never have any relative position to work with (unless you lock your camera to the poles and cripple your ability to move it effectively).
To sum up, the ~10 hours I've played were fun and looked good. The number of times I would finish a match with a content "meh", when I'd hoped I'd be inspired to have a thrilling maniacal laugh, makes me wonder whether all the inconveniences of the new 3D space were what we really wanted.
I think the numbers that I can see speak loudly; with ~42,000 original backers (plus any and all purchases since) and less than 400 active users as of typing, people have moved on even if they liked the idea.
EDIT: Checked Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance on Steam; active players is also about 400. That game is 10 years old. Numbers speak.

CHKN is a nice little Voxel Survival (Co-op?) Sandbox game with crafting menu and a builder mode. It is Early Access on Steam and also on a very early state of development (V0.1.1). That means the game engine works quite fine, but some basic mechanics, the unit balancing and data safety still have to be improved.
The game simply makes fun and it is amazing how creative the ideas are implemented by the devs. You start on an island in the ocean. A small beach with chicken and eggs. So far so good. But then you breakup one of the eggs and it drops you all pieces of a new chicken scattered on the floor. You'll see a bumping heart in the air and a laserdome. That's the lifeform creator! Now you can puzzle together your own animals out of blocky pieces. And after exploring the island I can say there are many different kinds of animals. They're all cutely chickonized, like Chickenphants, chickengiraffs, chickenbulls, chickenpigs, chickensheeps aso. Lateron they even get mutated by themselves with all different kind of block pieces.
The game also offers features like crop farming, daylight-night circle, taming and riding animals and at last new alien invaders. Not all keybindings are explained entirely. So you must testout many things. Gathering metal, stone and wood is a pain in the CHKN since every tool breaks within 10 times of use. Another freaking thing is the poor pointing abilities of the crosshair. Even if you point at a chest it snaps back to the last thing you pointed at (tutorial mode). I wish it was more precisely.
Btw if you zoomout with key C your character looks like an assassins creed chicken. In conclusion I'm amazed by the potential that is in this game but they must do work on the stability and polishment. Otherwise the ppl get fastly frustrated if hard gathered resources and buildup bases suddenly disappear. Just because of saving issues.

It's kind of fun just building and interacting with your band of freakish mutants.
Is it worth $15? I don't really think so. It's Early Access, so I'm trusting the developer to add more things to do on the adventuring side, but at the moment it's essentially the Spore Creature Creator except attached to a game that's still more fun than Spore. I've seen a lot of goth Alice In Wonderland games, and Fran Bow isn't one of them, which is why it's cool.  Instead, this is a story like Alice, with a main character who has the same combination of sensibility, curiosity, friendliness, and straightforward acceptance of the fantastic that Alice had.  It makes no attempt to be Alice, or refer to the original particularly.  It just has the same spirit, but much, much darker.
Except it's not even as dark as it looks.  There's no shortage of gore, and death and insanity are major topics, sure, but there's also sweetness and a beautiful land of innocence and talking roots, and just when you expect to be murdered by a skeleton, you get birthday cake!  The story is non-standard, not going anywhere you would think, and even now I'm not sure what actually happened - rather like the original Alice.
I have done my best, but Fran Bow is hard to pin down and describe.  It is different, its own thing.  That is why if you have any fondness for point and clicks, and for dark themes, you should play it.
(Oh, and when you get to the season changing part, if you click fast you can change multiple seasons without going through the ones in between.  I feel like a doof getting stuck for so long because I didn't know that.)

If Minecraft and Spore had a baby, CHKN would be that baby. A pretty great baby.
Start by creating creatures. They're made of lifeblocks (which you get from other creatures) so you can arrange them however you like to make cute stuff or cool stuff or horrible abominations that have you questioning your own sanity.
Then command them to do things, like gather resources. Gather enough resources and build yourself a sanctuary. Create more creatures to grow your army and protect your sanctuary. (Two octo...things -- they had octopus legs but also horns and a beard -- attacked my meager abode and ate my walls. I learned a valuable lesson that day.)
Go out exploring to find more stuff, to build more stuff, to make more creatures. Also, DON'T DIE.
It's still early access so there are improvements to be made, bugs to find, and multiplayer isn't ready yet. But, there are lots of updates posted and it's being worked on constantly (which is always my biggest concern with Early Access), and the stuff being added in the future looks cool (there's a link to the roadmap on the website).
So yeah. If you like open-world sandbox survival, and also admire Dr. Frankenstein, you'll probably like CHKN, too.

Sanctum 2 is the sequel to the world’s first Tower Defense/FPS hybrid game. Pick from four unique character classes and embark on a mission to protect the oxygen-producing Cores from hordes of deadly aliens who are threatened by their existence. Outfit your character exactly the way you want through the new and extensive customization system. Choose your own loadout of towers, weapons and perks, but choose wisely because you are humanity’s last defense against the unrelenting hordes set out to destroy it.
Sanctum 2 is a new game completely rebuilt from the ground up using community feedback and innovative design to really push the bar of what an independent studio can do.

A lot of broken development promises during beta, a serious lack of depth for a 4X such as pathetically stunted tech trees and gimmicky planetary micro-management, and lacking any charm outside of faction comm screens (Which, I must say, are at least pretty) make this a very deflated experience. Maybe some day the developer will actually do something interesting with the potential of ideas, but with reports of game breaking bugs in launch, it's unlikely. The most fun you may have is with the modular ship design system, but that's it. Avoid.

Pros:
Fun blend of shooter and tower defence
Tower defence needs a decent amount of strategy
Shooter keeps you on your feet between building phases
Monster variation, weak spots and bosses keep the game interesting and challenging
Multiplayer with friends really gives that "teamwork" and "divide-and-conquer" feel
Good variety of weapons, perks, towers and skills
Towers sell for full price, allowing flexibility
Brilliant and fitting graphics
Absolutely awesome (fun and funny) text-to-voice chat
Friendly fire doesn't damage allies (technically)
Friendly fire can 'accidentally" push your friends off ledges and to their deaths (oops!)
Cons:
Friendly fire can accidentally push your friends off ledges and to their deaths
Difficulty varies, and the space for mazing are extremely limited on some maps
Bosses are really really tough and may destroy towers
Losing at late stages in a game really sucks
There's a stage where (depending on which paths you block) ranged units can hit (and likely destroy) your core even before they enter your maze, due to the map layout.
Tips:
Play with friends
Always prepare for air/final line of defence
Beware ranged units
Have one person take the core-healing perk
Kite bosses
If the round has a timer: build first, redo later
Don't rush monsters and end up in your allies' line of sight
Most Importantly:
Press "T" in-game and type something. Do it.

TL;DR: dont pay for this game, there are pages that give you its steam key for free every once in a while, and even so, i wouldnt really play it.
So this game is a Space Hack, or how one would say, a Space "Diablo"; that sounds very cool and at first it is! but then you realize that the game doesnt adds that much more into the mix, everything about the game is standard or sub-par.
The game in general is lackluster, it doesnt brings anything new to the Dungeon Crawl or Hack & Slash genre, the story is confusing at best, and the ending is VERY dissapointing and anti-climatic
to which the game takes FOREVER to get to. (take into account the 44.3 hours i invested on this game... on a single playthrough, with no restarts... that's how long the game takes to beat)
I would recomend against taking the "Knowledge" path, sure, get enough knowledge to be able to use Auto-doc, freezer, item scanner and base teleporters, those were the only techs i reliably used during my game, but dont expect the guns, rifles and launchers to be energy-cost-effective
.
I would also advice against going melee (although i do recomend spending some points in strength to be able to use better armor) as the enemies will eventually escalate into a whole world of pain, which with ranged weapons you can mitigate by picking them off as they close in.
Also dont attack all-in on clusters of enemies, advance cautiously and aggro-kite one or two of them away from the herd for easy pickings. Items run out of durability infuriatingly fast! so dont break any containers with your main weapon (or do it with your fists) only after clearing the immediate area of threats.
Sooner than later. enemies will begin to take a lot of damage before going down, and also dish out a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of damage also before going down, so investing heavily in endurance and resistance items and biochips is a good plan.
Near game-end (around hour 40... JESUS!), it gets unforgiving, you start to fight BOSSES as regular enemies, i must have fought around 10 to 12 bosses on the last two maps... imagine having to kill 12 Diablos in level 16 of Diablo 1.
In sumation, i wouldnt recomend this game, not even to my worst enemies.

Mindnight is a game about deduction, strategic thinking, psychology, deception and the skill of lying and convincing others.
If you've ever played the party game Mafia (aka Werewolf, or its video game offshoot Town of Salem) or perhaps the card game The Resistance, you'll feel right at home.
This game presents the core mechanics of The Resistance in an interesting cyperpunk setting with slick pixel art and solid music. It also is very polished (unlike Town of Salem... >_> ), and the developers are working hard on bringing more content to the game, including a voice chat system. They also are very open to feedback and suggestions, and active in their community.
The biggest weakness of this game is that, of course, being an online game, it needs a lively online community. However, unfortunately for Mindnight, the community for this game is very small. You can't really just jump into the game and play, but have to coordinate with other players of the game on the Discord server in order to set up even 5 (let alone 8!) players.
Despite that big issue, I do recommend getting this game. Mindnight deserves a healthy community to play this game. It really does. And perhaps if more people are willing to give it a shot, we will be able to get a proper community playing this intriguing game.

My recommendation goes to those with slower computers that want something that plays like Diablo 2, or for those who want a good "break game" that's engaging in short play sessions.

MINDNIGHT is an absolutely incredible game, and it looks like it'll only get better with time. The developers are active and open to feedback and suggestions, the playerbase is currently small but will grow with time, and the community is wonderful.
The game is simple to get into. Unlike some of the more complex variations of games like Mafia, there are only two roles: Agents, who comprise the majority of players, and Hackers, who form the minority. Agents aren't aware of who their teammates are, but hackers are. Teams of variable size are proposed to go on missions, with Agents wanting to secure the mission node, and Hackers wanting to hack it. Hackers do not have to hack the node, however, they can choose to secure it just like an Agent. Also a welcomed departure from more Mafia-esque games is that there is no system where players are eliminated from the game. Everybody plays the entire round, no getting assassinated at the beginning of the game and having to sit back and watch the rest passively due to bad luck.
The various game elements combine to form a game centered around the mind, appropriately. Records of who went on what mission as well as who voted for what teams help provide a look at who you can trust and who you can't, but the best Hackers will seek to blend in with the Agents while sowing doubt. Pure logic won't take you all the way, you need to engage.
But enough rambling. The game is quite fairly priced, has an active and growing community, the potential for even more styles of gameplay coming in the future, and is devastatingly fun. Stop by the discord channel to say hi if you'd like to learn more, and I hope to see you soon in MINDNIGHT!

The game consists in two types of teams: agents and hackers.
There are 5 nodes. As agents, you must secure 3 and as hackers, you must hack 3, in order to win.
Each round consists of a talking period, which is the main one, where you chat with other players in-game:
- as an agent, you try and convince other players to trust that you're an agent and try to weed out the hackers;
- as a hacker, you know who your other team-mates are, and try to trick agents into thinking that you're clean.
Each player, in turn, selects a certain amount of people to go on a mission at the end of each round.
As a hacker, you want to have hackers selected, so they can hack the node of that round (you can also bluff, so people think you're clean) and as an agent, you want to select only agents, so that there's no chance of nodes being hacked.
You must use your wits in order to weed out the hackers, as an agent, or fool the agents into thinking you or the other hackers are clean, so that you can hack the nodes.
It's very fun and I recommend it.

So after playing a 3hr match against A.I I enjoyed my self. After learning what everything does in the game I soon got ahead of my economy and then the real war began and ended up dominating the three A.I I went against.
Gameplay: You have small territories that have a limit of 4/4 or 3/3 buildings that can be built in that area. You can research for an extra building in your territories and on top of that also make the watch towers not take up a building slot.
The challenge at the start of your game is not the A.I it is the but the weather, my advice would be to get your food productiong strong and wood as you will lose 30% production during the winter.
A training camp will be needed to get a warrior or two for NPC's that invade into your territory every now and then and then you can retrain you warriors to gathering a resource again after the threat is done. Taking over territory requires you to have a scout that will run around exploring territory and then you take your warriors to take it over and buy it with food.
Is this game worth a buy? I would say wait.. Though I like it so far I would want to see how Multiplayer goes and Campaign.
$20 USD is not a bad price for this game and lets hope it stays at that price when the game is released.

This game does a fantastic job combining the enjoyment of strategizing in a tower defense with the fast-paced action of a shooter. Unlike a lot of games that try to combine TD with another genre, one style tends to fall short of the other in terms of importance to game content and/or quality. That is not the case in Sanctum. I saw it as a bold move combining the slow meticulous strategy of tower defense with the fast-paced twitch style of FPS but this game knew what it was doing. The tower defense aspect is fun and engaging and not as slow and monotonous as it often is in games like Dungeon Defenders, while the FPS aspect is diverse and rewarding with a multitude of weapons and augmentations.

A brilliant Isometric Action Platformer subtly masked as a narrative story where your actions build the world around you.
The music is deep and soulful adding a lot to the player immersion.
If you're a fan of voice acting and active narration (Battleblock Theatre) then this game will be a treat- the story is told aloud as you progress and changes when you make choices.
There's a lot of difficult battles, not quite a Gauntlet style Battle Arena, more like Robotron/Smash TV's dual stick movement and firing system and several augments and weapons to choose from to customize to your play style.
Can be difficult to pick up without a controller though playing with M/K is not impossible. Played through my first time with M/K and would not go back to them after using a 360 controller.
Varying difficulty settings and optional weapon mastery challenges make it so this game has a lot of obstacles to overcome for us players. The difficulty ramps very steadily from the beginning to end and is completely possible to master the game with a little patience and practice with the weapons that suit your playstyle.
Definitely an achievement hunter friendly game.
Worth playing, worth beating, worth 100%ing.

I’m not sure whether this game is honestly enjoyable or if my expectations going into it were were so low that I was able to enjoy it. The story is based around 3 campaigns(that may or may not be interlocking, some parts seem that way while others don’t), one for each race and each with their own separate playstyles. The human campaign started out really creepy, like something taken straight out of Alien, but then quickly became a really fun shooter but whoever decided to add a thump sound to the radar is dumb.  The alien campaign was the least enjoyable of the 3, in theory it should have been really fun because it has you climbing up walls and running on the roof but it is really disorienting. The predator campaign was also enjoyable but the stealth elements were pretty much useless so good thing the melee combat was enjoyable. It flirts with outstaying its welcome and it is almost too tedious but it ends at a good point and it’s not too dragged out. Overall I feel like this was a fun game, nothing amazing or anything but enjoyable.

The game is good. The development progress is slow, which I would say is good. It is far from abandon, far from stripped down, and far from being a waste. Interested in supporting a bright prospect of a game? This is a good choice. Want a 100% complete game that lays everything out for you, from A-Z? You'll probably want to move on. Even in this unfinished, beta-stage that Starbound is, it's still a pretty decent game. Want the survival part added back in? I haven't personally checked in a while, but I'm sure the community (which appears to be active, again not much personal experience in that particular area) has a mod for that. I will say my only gripe is that, as with any sandbox, the game gets very empty and very lonely, very quickly. So even though I've never personally visited a server, I can pretty much guarantee from experience on other games that a good community to play this with will fill that hole and enrich the experience a hundred-fold.
In short? Unfinished, but very promising. And try playing with some good company. Mayhem loves company.

Sleeping Dogs started out life as the third game in the critically-panned True Crime series. The first game was an underrated open-world game featuring a somewhat unlikeable protagonist. True Crime: Streets of L.A. boasted a realistically-mapped Los Angeles, a variety of side activities, a decent melee and shooting system, and a memorable soundtrack. The sequel, set in New York, fared even worse with critics and was known mostly for the presence of the artist then known as Snoop Dogg as a playable character. Because I was a fan of the first game, I’d been keeping tabs on the development of this title and was somewhat dismayed by the name change. Fortunately, Square Enix, having picked up the property from Activision, improved on almost every aspect of the original, making a terrific action game that plays like a John Woo film.
The player takes the role of Wei Shen, a young man who was raised in Hong Kong but whose family moved to America after the tragic death of a sister resulting from a drug overdose. Shen has returned to his birthplace and is recruited by the police superintendent for a deep cover assignment with the triads. Shen’s initial assignment is to collect evidence against the Sun On Yee lieutenant Winston Chu, but he soon finds himself embroiled in a nascent gang war that threatens the stability of the city. The story is interesting even if many of the beats are telegraphed well in advance (like a certain tragic occurrence that takes place near the end of the game) or are simply so obvious as to border on the cliche (it wouldn’t really be Hong Kong police story if Wei didn’t end up getting in over his head and defying his superiors in the police force).
Sleeping Dogs is primarily a martial arts combat game. The melee mechanics were heavily influenced by the Arkham games. You will usually face multiple opponents, enemy combatants signal impending attacks by flashing so that you have an opportunity to counter, and you can make use of combos to quickly take down large numbers of foes. By returning stolen statues to your former martial arts instructor, you will unlock new moves for Shen to use.
The game also incorporates two other upgrade systems: cop/triad experience and “face” experience. As you complete police missions, such as busting street racers that have turned to murder, and triad missions, such as intimidating shopkeepers into paying protection money, you gain cop and triad experience respectively. On most story missions, there is a chance to acquire both, depending on how you play (running over or shooting civilians hurts your cop rating and performing poorly in combat hurts your triad rating).  Completing “favor” missions gains you face experience, which unlocks performance boosts for Shen; these include things like increased duration of food and drink effects and increased durability when the face meter is filled in combat. Shen can purchase items like pork buns to give increased health regeneration and energy drinks to enhance his melee damage. Further bonuses accrue to Shen by the use of various articles of clothing that are either purchased as DLC or at in-game stores.
In addition to the story missions, Shen has access to a variety of side activities, including street races in cars and motorcycles, cockfights, mahjong poker, karaoke, and fight clubs. While the story races are deliberately not too challenging, the other in-game races can be very tricky. The cockfights and poker games seem to have somewhat random outcomes. Karaoke is amusing because it’s controlled by a Rock Band-like interface using the controller or keyboard and the vocal tracks are actually the Shen voice actor singing the songs in question. The fight clubs are pretty much what they sound like and are a great way to earn face experience.
There are a number of interesting mission DLCs available for Sleeping Dogs. “Wheels of Fury” has Shen safeguarding Dr. Tang’s new prototype DZS-90 supercar. After Shen has secured it across the DLC’s five missions–over the course of which it gains incredible abilities such as twin machine guns and a vehicle-stunning EMP device–he unlocks it for use in the main game. “The Zodiac Tournament” has Shen entering a suspicious martial arts tournament on an offshore island controlled by a madman. The setup and atmosphere deliberately invoke Bruce Lee’s Enter the Dragon, although the story ventures somewhat far afield from that film. The cutscenes alone are practically worth the price of admission for this one. Both of these packs integrate seamlessly into the main game.
On the
site, I’ve read that others feel that having mission DLCs outside of the main game and accessible directly from the main menu is a superior approach. I’m not convinced, especially after having played “Nightmare in North Point” and “Year of the Snake.” In the former, Shen must save one of his romantic conquests from an undead gangster known as Smiley Cat (for amusing reasons I won’t reveal here) and his army of restless souls. Most of Shen’s opponents in this DLC are jiang shi, a kind of hopping Chinese vampire, and yaoguai demons. The extended fights with jiang shi, especially the final encounter, have a certain artificial level of difficulty because the need to bodily toss the vampires into a gateway in order to seal it leaves Shen vulnerable to being grabbed and drained of his lifeforce (the vampires’ grip is preternaturally difficult to loosen, probably due to wonky controls more than anything else). In “Year of the Snake,” which is set after the main story, Shen has been busted down to a beat cop, and you have access to none of the unlocks and equipment that you gained during your playthrough of the main game. While the story is interesting enough on its own, the fact that you go from being a supercop to Joe Uniform in the blink of an eye tends to drain the experience of much of its color.
The latter two DLCs and the main story each have a number of collectibles to find and minigames to play. In addition to the statues previously mentioned, there are Buddhist shrines which give Shen a health boost, CCTV cameras (some of which are used in cop missions and some of which are just there) that must be hacked, and lockboxes containing clothing or money (some of which must be hacked and some of which can just be opened) that are usually guarded by hostile enemies. The hacking minigame involves guessing a four-digit sequence in six tries. The game provides you with clues by telling you when you have a digit that is correct and whether it is in the right location or not.
This is first and foremost, like the second game in the series, a console game. However the developer has created a fantastic PC port that controls very well by-and-large. However, the melee combat and most other aspects of the game control much more smoothly with some kind of gamepad and the shooting is (as one might expect) much easier with the precision of a mouse-and-keyboard setup. Fortunately, the game supports essentially on-the-fly switching between the two, making it easy to choose your control scheme of choice even for specific parts of individual missions.
Pretty much every aspect of the game is great, which is why the weak soundtrack is all the more disappointing. I’ve played a lot of these open-world action games and most of them have at least a few catchy tunes on the radio stations you listen to in vehicles while you’re driving around. Shen’s choice of stations is woefully limited and most of the music is neither memorable nor even very interesting. I actually found myself playing my own MP3s instead of listening to the game’s music during several play sessions. Nevertheless, if this is the worst aspect of your game, then you’re doing a hell of a lot of things right, and you should definitely wake this dog

Now that it's been officially released, I am going to recommend to everyone who sees this and enjoys 4X games to give StarDrive a test.
StarDrive is a game of immense depth. You are provided the option of designing your entire fleets to your specifications -- you can create ships using a variety of weapon types and defenses. The game even facilitates some very interesting and not inherently obvious strategies surrounding your ship construction.
The gameplay itself is basically a 4X RTS/TBS hybrid. "Empire" related things, such as economy, diplomacy, and colony management are done in timed turns where each turn is something like five seconds. "Ship" related things, such as flight, combat, and eventual destruction are handled in real time.
This game sucked away more than 100 hours my play time before it was even released. It can do the same for you, too, if you would like it to.

I walk through a corridor in Mars City, what was once a bustling hub for Marines and Scientists, now a blood soaked hell hole. I approach a door, after scrambling through the dark with the flash light on my gun showing a path, and quite literally shout in terror and fright as an Imp pounches through. This is the same type of terror you should expect all the way through the game.
DOOM 3: BFG edition is a graphically enhanced remake of the popular third game in the DOOM series. The game took a major turn from being the classic pixel-arcade-style game where a full on kill fest was expected into being a fully fledged horror spectacular.The enemies spawn in very jumpy ways, the sounds keep you on edge and well lit areas are very scarse and scrambling with your flash light activated happens often.
The flash light was a part of the original DOOM 3 that was near being contraversial. It was what REALLY pushed the game away from the older games. The idea of having to equip a flash light instead of a weapon added an extra level to the horror idea, when fighting creatures became a battle of 'predict the movement'. It was, however, both a point of praise and complaint. In the BFG edition, the flashlight is attatched to your weapons. This makes combat easier and subtracts from the fear of fighting in the dark... but only slightly.
The graphics overhaul is great. At times, there are moments you can tell that the game is old and has just had a new coat of paint. But at it's core, that paint looks like a canvas decorated with graphics on par with Quake 4. The blood looks realistic and the guts look lke they have indeed just been wrenched from the bowels of a marine, who now wanders the halls... his dead flesh fully animated into a basic enemy that still terrifies you.
The enemies over all are well varied and very well animated and thought of. Classic DOOM enemies return, reimagined and absolutely terrifying. I still remember my first battle with a Pinky (think over grown bull dog with two robotic legs), pointing my shotgun at the door only to... I won't give the spoiler. Even zombies can seem terrifying... taking multiple pistol shots to bring down. AND THEY ARE ONLY THE BASIC ENEMIES. Every enemy is scary in it's own right, even when you're wielding a chain gun and can rip demon hearts out like they're being served for breakfast.
I personally loved the game. I managed to purchase it on CD, for half the steam price, and it links to steam. To top off the deal, you get the core game, the expansion, an extra campaign and the two original games ontop. It's a great deal.

Normally I am not a fan of point and click games and rarely do I feel horror games present themselves in a fashion that grabs attention and keeps me playing. This games had only one thing that interested me, a quirky surreal story I had heard little about.
And oh boy was the story quirky. It was a very strange games with beatiful graphics and weird interesting characters. The point and click was not annoying in the slightest because you did not need to constantly look for items in the same area over and over. It kept the game moving and advanced the story into amazing areas. The universe that this game created was one of the most thought out ones I've seen in any surreal horror game. With this game being Killmonday's first game out on Steam I am quite impressed and I do hope that they make more games like this, because they can actually pull it off. No jumpscares, just the sinking feeling that something is going to go very wrong.
With all that said I'd give this game a strong recommendation for the amazing story writing, the beautiful graphics, and the overall immersive gameplay. One of my favorite surreal games indeed.

At the same time it's scaring the crap out of me, I can't stop looking at this huge piece of artwork.
Then I fell in love with the story. I'd hate to say too much, just in case I spoil it, but it did seriously mess with my emotions. Poor Fran Bow needs a hug! And after I finished the game, I needed a hug.

A must-own for any sort of DooM fan. Quite simply - it's a remastering of the third installment, DooM 3, with it's add-on content - Ressurection of Evil, and an extra short campaign entitled "The Lost Mission". It as well comes packaged with it's two original predeccesors, DooM 1 and 2, so that old fans can be nostalgic and newcomers might be able to taste the grandfather games of First Person Shooters.
In detail - the "Remastering" isn't a huge hype. The original DooM 3 already looks fantastic - at least considering it was born of the early 21st century - 2000 - 2004 being it's development time, and 2004 being the release year. This era had some great game production, but nothing as technologically advanced as this. Of course, the character models and anti-aliasing could do with a tune-up, but that's exactly why it helped bring along the success of newer games, such as Dead Space - that bring it's same isolated, dark storylines --- something very reminisint of the (Surprisingly) unheard of System Shock 2.
Even being a bit aged, it still brought innovation and a sort of "Breath of fresh air" to the FPS Horror scene, and helped carry farther what System Shock 2 started, with it's dark, tight corridors, it's feeling of isolation, and the sense that deep-space shall indeed be you burial ground --- except that you have a lot more ammunition with which to kick the seven shades of crap out of those pesky hellspawn.
Anyway, I digress. The BFG edition simply smoothed out some edges, changed the PDA menu, adjusted some textures and models to a higher resolution, and changed the flashlight into a shoulder-mounted flashlight instead of one you have to take out seperately (Which I believe removes some of the fright of the game coming from it's dark enviornments).
All in all, a great game package. 20$ - great value for what you're getting. If you haven't played DooM 3, or simply want a slightly better-looking version with simplified light-management that bares with it it's bloody, run-and-gun, demon-butt-kicking predeccesors, this is for you.

Although I never really paid any attenttion to the series along the years, seeing a proper fighter game come on Steam and remembering what defined this series made me buy this game. Gruesome Fatalities and now the new bone chlling X-ray attacks in a still simplish, but visually impressive arcade fighter world. Despite having been released on the console two years before the PC release, the feel of being a dated game is nowhere to be found. Or then I'm just enjoying the glorious gore galore too much. Having mastered the keyboard with this game to some extent rather than using a controller that most people prefer to play the game with I must say it is challenging. Kombos are sometimes much more complicated to perform than on a controller. However I found these issues to melt away with experience. Early on I had my♥♥♥♥♥royally handed over to me multiple times before I got the hang of the game. After pouring 20 hours in to the game I felt the change. The feel of defeating a pompous controller user with a keyboard is incredible. There's nothing more I love in the game (apart from the gore) than hearing the whiny cries of russian players, often following a rapid rage quit.
There are, of course, some flaws to the game. Single player and local multiplayer are very much playable, but the same cannot always be said about multiplayer. The game can often drop players from a match because of a poor connection, which leads to frustration of losing your opponent midgame. One other issue is the lack of players in the multiplayer. You'll be lucky to find more than 150 players in the multiplayer at once, making finding proper opponents a little difficult at times The other, more irritating con (to me at least) is the overwhelming amount of russians in the multiplayer. I'd estimate around 75% of the players to be russian when playing online. Hopefully in the future that will change. Those are the only major cons I*ve discovered about the game.
Aside from those flaws, this game is perfect for someone who (like me) loves vast amounts of gore and has had a thing for fighter games, but hasn't gotten the chance to play because of the pathetic amount of ports to the PC. If you fall into this category I highly suggest the purchase of this game.

Saibot Studios released 3 games titled Doorways between 2013 and 2016. These are atmospheric horror FPS games with particular emphasis on platforming and puzzle solving.
Old Prototype is a free version that shows us sections that were created before the above-mentioned games. Some eventually got to be part of the final product while others never did so. Gameplay mainly consists of running and jumping - the soundtrack tries to be as atmospheric as possible indicating what direction the developer went into in later stages of the development.
There are 2 main sections in the game - the first is the atmospheric one while the 2nd is a black and white section that I did not particularly like. Areas are introduced by notes that can be interacted with - we get information on the development of mentioned areas (too bad the creators did not pay much attention to correcting the grammar).
In any case, this is a no-brainer: an approximately 30-minute long ride that can make you purchase the already released episodes or deter you from doing it.

A very atmospheric little tech demo which seems to have its heart in the right place but everything else slightly off. I don't think a fast-paced platform game suits itself to be called an "adventure" as it claims to be and the beauty and depth of the environment (the first thing you'll be greeted with after the minor "intro" level) also would support better a slower game instead.
The platforming plus light puzzle aspect reminds me of the first generation of 3D games to come out, which isn't a very big honor to mention since most of those were clunky and cheap. "Doorways" seems to suffer form the same problems: uninspired, relying on concepts everyone has seen manyfold in games from the last two decades, lack of cues and a non-smooth difficulty curve. The only thing that it's got going on for it is the immersive-horror theme but, as stated prior that doesn't fit very well with a fast-paced platformer game, especially when it's not even well designed as one in itself.
Unfortunately, I could not even get myself to finish the demo after getting stuck and just not being that interested in grinding through the end. Even though I knew what I had to do to proceed, five deaths in a row were enough to get me to close the game - which doesn't offer an ESC menu so you're stuck with restarting your computer if you don't know how to kill a process manually.
Definitely won't be checking the official game - even if I can sense a lot of potential here, from what I have seen so far it is mostly not very well followed through on. However if you like platformer and / or immserive games, give this free-to-play short demo a try. If somehow you've waiting for a psychological horror 3D platformer all along, and you don't mind it being a tad amateurish, I imagine you'll enjoy the official release a whole lot!

Many people play this game, so it's takes a millisecond to join a full lobby. It's apparent that "classic" mode is filled with morons. Play it 20-30 times, and then head over to "Ranked Practice" where the mature people are. This is where ALL roles are available.

- More incentive to play other than it being fun. Ex: Progression system. Character skins, houses, pets, etc. isn't enough. In fact, it's useless. Perhaps a level system to show off to people. How hard could it be to implement if it is based on wins, or points gained?
- Option to return to menu if you die.

HONEST INSIGHT ON THE MAJOR ASPECTS OF THE GAME FROM AN EXPERIENCED PLAYER
I have been playing this game for quite a while  and played it quite a bit before I even linked my account to steam and started logging hours,(420 hours on steam at time I wrote this XD) you can say ive seen just about everything. I strongly reccomend this game to anyone who likes high risk/high reward playstyles or just having fun with freinds. There is so much to do and master in this game, that it's incredible that it is so simple at the same time. All the classes have a unique role, (accomplished by individual stat caps as much as the unique ablities so this is less prevalant at lower levels) and are geared toward encouraging teamwork. As a result, the community for this game is one of the best ive ever seen. Trading is structured, massive and diverse. Trolls and toxic people are few and far between. The third party site
which also hosts the wiki is even more condusive to this. There are many dungeons for low, mid, and high tier players that all have unique themes and required playstyles to them, many of them hosting epic and challenging bosses that reward players with unique loot and garuenteed valuable drops. It has very revcently gone under new ownership and lots of new content is on the way. To be honest there are a few pay-to-win feautres in this game, but that will only get you so far. There is a certain element of skill and expeirence required to really excel (only a little bit needed to have fun), and therefore those bought out charecters in a noob's hands WONT outdo everyone free to play who are around them, but instead will most likely perish. I won't lie, there is something a little broken in this game, the pet system. Pets in this game can be super powerful, and to get them from a medium to their maximum extrodinary strength requires spending some cash or MAJOR dedication and grinding. They are still very valuable at the medium level, because they are permannat and dont die. They still are a fun and cool/cute companions either way. All together, this is an incredible game that makes for a truely unique experience. Definitely worth taking a few hours to get into.

People are saying this game is slowly dying, due to hackers and the pay to win status this game is currently in. However, I feel that this game has so much potential. I have been playing for quite a few years now, and started even after Kabam brought upon us thier terrible rule of the game, and I still haven't seen the end of it. However slowly it is evolving nowadays, there is still the glimpse of WildShadows's light they shone upon this franchise at first, still there for you to enjoy.
Hackers may be a nuisance, but multiboxers, as a contradiction to current beleifs, are actually fairly unlikely to steal your loot from a dungeon, purely because of thier devastating over damage. Other downsides such as hackers ent sitting or just legit trollers scamming and dragging can all be countered with little care. Only teleport if at least 2 people call, always leave your afk character paused, and check the trade box before confirming. I don't see why so many people are making such a big deal out of it.
Quite recently, one of my friends posted a  dislike comment of how much of a grindfest maxing a character is. But the whole point of the game is that its a mmo co op. Friends can help, and if a certain dungeon is getting repetetive, find another one to solo out of the many that appear in this game, for instance, maxing speed is usually done in a snake pit, but a perfectly fine alternative is a haunted cemetary. Wis can be found in both UDLs and Mad Labs, so no-one needs to repeatedly do udls, unless they want to reach the unreachable and acheive the dbow drop.
My point is though, with all the almost infinitely large amount of content in this game, I don't see how a once convinced realm player quit due to just pure bore. Try soloing an Avatar with its Shatters if you feel too overpowered, and if you still feel unconvinced, try doing it petless, abilityless or even both. The possibilities this game creates are near endless, and this game will definitely not fade out of existence any time soon.
Edit: Ever since Deca has bought this game, it has gotten a lot better, and they have only had the game for less than a month, and they have already had countless events that Kabam could never dream of, many free packs (Kabam only gave us 2 backpacks) and a whole lot more hype for what could come next. 2 new skins have been added, 2 new boxes have been added, and this just leaves players wondering what Deca will add next. I would like to show my gratitude to Deca Games in this review for the game. Thank you Deca. ᶘ ᵒᴥᵒᶅ

This game was released back in late 2005 but it aged very well.  You will enjoy hacking and slashing your way through hordes of bug-like aliens, finding new items to become a better slaying machine and ultimately saving the lives of the people who crash landed on this strange world for some obscure reasons. The story is simple but well tought off, the music is repetitive but catchy and add to the ambiance, the level design is childish looking but challenging from time to time, the graphics are polygonal but artsy-looking (Set the resolution to the highest windowed one if you can't see it).
Monsters never respawn and once you've cleared a path the instances available on the map are yours forever. The feeling of satisfaction when you rid an area of a huge group of aliens is real. There are also events that occurs from time to time where you have to accomplish a few tasks and quests given by your fellow crewmembers who are stuck with you on this planet.

An open world racing game that's fun, but has its flaws. Let me start off by saying that I enjoyed this game and it was really fun, but it eventually got really repetitive. Much like other games that have one special gimmick/concept, something else will suffer. Despite taking place in an open world and giving you the idea that you can do whatever you want, you are limited to what you can really do. There are 3-5 different racing events and the only thing that really changes is how difficult they are and where in the city they take place. This concept almost reminds me of the first Assassin's Creed.
For the first few hours you're enjoying yourself, but then you realize you're repeating similar tasks over and over again. Along with the use of repetition, the compass/mini map system can be confusing. Since this game takes place in an open world, you're not really racing on a conventional track. Though the compass/mini map is there, you can essentially choose which route to take. What's confusing about this is that the compass/mini map is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to use. It wasn't until I was nearly halfway done with the game that I realized that the compass would guide you on which street to take just as you were nearing it. While this is helpful, it's also difficult to maintain a sense of direction seeing as how you're driving a car at ridiculous speeds and even the slightest turn can alter where you end up.
Though it may seem as if I completely hated this game based on what I'm discussing, I enjoyed it. It's not perfect, but it's a good arcade racing game that should keep you busy for ~15-20 hours. I give this game a 3/5 and I recommend it.

It is a great little game. What it does, it does well. There is currently only a single player skirmish mode. However, there are already achievements to hunt and I think I will have fun doing it.

After finishing my first single player match, I have to say that this offering has a lot of potential. The game isn't just fun; it's interesting. With multiple paths to victory ranging from trade to conquest to science/religion, you can pick what kind of Viking chief you want to be. The game's pace is slow at first as your village of Northgardlings struggles to gather enough food and firewood to last its first winter, but as your village grows (along with your rivals') the pace picks up and excitement builds quickly. The artwork and style of the game are beautiful and appealing, the music and atmosphere capture the Viking theme perfectly, and the concepts of the game are easy to pick up. Importantly, failure does not equal defeat in this game. If the Wolf Clan plunders your mining camp and slaughters your honest, hardworking civilians, go and burn his hunting posts and lumber mills to the ground while he replenishes his raiders. You'll see how tough he really is when the winter comes.
Pros:
Interesting and exciting gameplay
Beautiful audio and visual aspects
Numerous paths to victory
Many unique game mechanics, even within strategy genre
Cons:
AI-controlled clans are bloodthirsty, even for Vikings. They will raid your territory despite good relations and preexisting trade agreements. If there is an option for peace, they'll pursue war.

I've been looking for an RTS that rewards strategy over APM, basically a cross between Civilization and Starcraft, and to be honest I didn't know how that could be achieved.
Enter Northgard, besides the fact that I really like the viking setting, it seems to perfectly balance the strategic macro elements of resource optimisation and expansion with interesting combat elements. In this respect I definitely think Northgard is a first. When playing I get some of the same warm fuzzies I remember from playing Warcraft 2, Civilization and even a bit of Black & White.
In its current state the game is definitely playable and enjoyable, while some of the RNG considerations raised by others are definitely well-founded, I see them as a challenge. Its a singleplayer game at this stage, if you don't like your starting location you can reset easily, but I prefer to try and see if I can beat the odds, it actually lends a bit of additional replayability in my opinion.
Since its in early access there are some polish issues, strange behaviour when assigning combat units, map generation and unit clipping are some of the minor issues I've observed, none of which deterred me from enjoying the game. Since the developers seem to be very active and release regularly I'm sure these will be addressed soon.
My main gripe at the moment is that the game seems a bit simplistic due to being in early access, which will probably not be fair criticism of the final game but is something buyers should be aware of in the current state of the game. Lack of unit, building, map and music variety are my main issues, all of which I know will add a great amount of replayability and enjoyment once expanded. The developers have stated that multiplayer is a high priority and will make it into the final release which has the potential to expand an already great game even further.
Overall I am excited to see where the development team take Northgard and I hope that it reaches its full potential as it really has managed to bridge the RTS and TBS genres and expand strategy as a whole, truly a breath of fresh air in a market that seems to be increasingly just focused on TCGs and MOBAs.

This review contains Spoilers, so be warned
I really looked forward to this game, and when it was first released I found myself in utter disbelief of what I found. I was blown away by what has since become my favorite RPG/Shooter of all time.

A lot of people complained about this game, the lack of RPG elements, and the removal of the Karma system. Yet I think that there is something more to this game that goes beyond the need for those things. The RPG elements and karma system do not come from the points you invest in perks, or the arbitrary number that goes up when you do a good. Instead the character is made by the choices the player makes, and you hjave to decide what is good and what is bad without the supervision of the all knowing game. I find that the removal of these system have actually made the game a lot more interesting. In Fallout 3 and New Vegas I would often create characters for the sole intention of doing an evil run, getting negative karma, and siding with the enclave and legion respectively.
But now that the game isn't so black and white, and the lines are greyed out, it becomes less clear what sides are good and which are bad. Sure the institute appears to be the manifestation of pure evil, but it is conceivable that the player can influence them to a more noble path, especially since the player can give a speech indicating these intentions in one of the later missions. Furthermore, the institute is not an organization of pure evil like the legion who killed or enslaved anyone who came across them. Instead they are mostly self interested, albeit heavily misguided. Meanwhile, the other factions are also less obviously good or bad, as two of the other factions both have their pros and cons, and must be considered carefully before any judgement can be made, a stark contrast to NV and 3, where the lines were clear.
The gameplay is marvelous, combat has been drastically overhauled and now feels more alive and sleek. Weapon choice matters, and one can now diversify or specialize in a variety of interesting and unique weapons. The only complaint here is that legendary weapons are too easy to find and can become insanely overpowered way too early on in the game.
The story generally is pretty well executed, although a little obvious. I find this child-parent story telling very effective as one is forced to choose between what is ultimately good, and family. Which is not a choice I made lightly considering the consequences of losing a family, or doing the wrong thing.
The soundtrack is handsdown the best soundtrack of any game I have ever played, the opening theme is a masterpiece of music and Inon Zur deserves every accolade ever made. Graphically the game holds up very well, I found no isses or lag, or tearing, and the game looks very vibrant and pretty, a stark contrast to the previous monotoned games.
The basebuilding was a surprising but welcome addon and I have spent a good half of my time just building towns and collecting resources for building said towns.
I would absolutely recommend this game to absolutely anyone, newcomers or experienced gamers.
Lastly, all the outrage over the paid mods and the creation club is totally ignorable. Only some of the mods must be paid for, if one even wishes to play with mods, and all the paid mods are totally forgettable and can be left out. Honestly this is one of those situations where players are just mad at the principle, but in practice there is no problem at all. So buy this game, it'll do you a lot of good, and you'll spend hours exploring the Commonwealth.
So good luck, and have fun!

This game is a hell of a lot of fun, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise.  You just have to make peace with its flaws.
Like in previous AvP games, the campaign is split into three parallel mini-campaigns, which intertwine in a fun and interesting way, allowing each species to use common elements of the setting's colonies and ruins in different ways for different purposes, and to different ends.  This may end up dissapointing some who will see the campaign as lazily reusing map assets so they don't have to tailor make levels for each character, but I find this complaint falls flat.  The level design smartly builds a unique playing space for each of the game's three species in each game level, something which must have taken much deliberation and iteration, whether or not you agree with the design decision.
Each storyline is really successful in acheiving a different feel and imparting a unique importance to each character;  The marine campaign is a terrifying account of a human just trying to stumble his way through this whole mess alive, the Predator campaign is full of bravado, badassitude, and honor, and the Alien campaign is all about essentially trolling the other two species in a deadly way and undermining everything anyone else is trying to acheive.  Of the three, the Alien's campaign is easily the weakest, although there is still a lot of fun to be had terrifying marines and pinning scientists to the ground for facehugger implantation.
The campaigns themselves are surpisingly challenging, though short.  I found that the difficulty of the singleplayer game is mostly fair, harshly punishing stupid mistakes, though your mileage may vary.  A huge part of the game is a keen awareness of your own limitations as a human, Alien, or Predator, and also a smart but controlled exploitation of your own advantages, leading to an experience that can get surpisingly cerebral for what otherwise presents itself as a big, dumb action game (and the story IS big and dumb). The checkpoint system in single player is bizarre and terrible, unfortunately.  This meshes incredibly poorly with how difficult the game can get, leading to moments I just wanted to give up and walk away from the entire game.
Ultimately, on the single player side of things, expect a dissapointingly short, dumbly written, but absolutely exciting and relatively unique (at least, in this day and age) romp through the built up mythos of all three species.
Multiplayer, unfortunately, is a bit of a mixed bag.  At the best of times, Alien vs Predator's multiplayer is just huge loads of fun.  It's action packed one moment, tensely silent another, and totally empowering the next, just before you realize you're outgunnned or outnumbered and you start running away from other players in terror.  Unfortunately, people's complaints about rampant stupid garbage in multiplayer are SPOT ON ACCURATE.  The different deathmatch modes highlight this game's unfun nonsense way more often than other, more mechanically interesting and unique game modes; unfortunately, TDM is far and away the most popular game mode, drawing in players for its simplicity and action.
Be prepared to scream impotently at your computer as you, a slavering, 7 foot horror from outer space leap at a hapless marine from across the room, only to bounce off and land stunned on the ground as if the guy were made out of steel and bolted to the floor, simply because he saw you or heard you and blocked.  Prepare to occasionally see marines beating predators and aliens in melee combat.  Prepare for plasmacasters still being rage inducing, even 13 years after AvP2.  Prepare, even, for a stealth kill mechanic that encourages players to just run circles around each other to see who can get enough of a glimpse of another player's back to hit the "E" key and get an easy instakill.  At this point in the game's life,  players are obliged to play by their own made up rules about when it's okay to get an "E kill" or when weapons like the plasmacaster are permitted.
The matchmaking, additionally, is absolutely terrible (although there is a server browser), and at this point in time there are very few players, making it a chore to find a game running, let alone a game running something more interesting than Team Death Match.
That all being said, when you can get a good game going, the game is really good.  Even through multiplayer's bull, fun shines through.  The Hunt mode from AvP2 returns as Predator Hunt, featuring one Predator vs a team of marines, and is excellent and very evocative of the movies.  The Infestation mode is somewhat similar in set up; the entire team starts as marines, and one of them is chosen randomly to spawn as an alien.  When the alien kills a marine player, the killed player switches sides and joind the aliens, and this continues until the dwindling human group survives for long enough or is wiped out.  Aliens vs Predator also features its own co-op horde mode, Survivor, where marine players take on waves of alien bots. While tense and fun in its own right, Survivor is a bit too light on features compared to the horde modes of other games to really hold my attention.  These sit alongside the game's own point capture mode and three different rulesets for Deathmatch, adding up to a fairly large catalog of different ways to play.
All in all, Aliens vs Predator got an unfair shake, I think.  Huge hype combined with mixed reviews to convince the public that the game was a middling cash in, when in actual fact I think that the developers put a lot of thought and heart into bringing back the mechanics of an old multiplayer classic while still trying to innovate.  A lot of the moves they made in production are clear missteps and there's no hiding that, but if you can accept or work past the game's obvous problems, there's quality fun to be had here, and the game certainly offers an experience that simply can't be had anywhere else.
It's certainly more fun than Aliens: Colonial Marines, and manages to feel more authentic even with how much effort A:CM's team put into recreating environments and elements from the Aliens film.  I just wish AvP's Survivor mode was more like A:CM's Bug Hunt.
