► Game: Left 4 Dead
► Genre: FPS, Action, Zombie-Apocalypse
► Rating: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ 5/5
▲ Favorable Aspecps:
After watching, in the past 6 years, all that "boom" of Zombie themed games, specially those where you blow they head off, I can easily assure you that Left 4 Dead, launched in 2008, was one of the biggest responsible for that exponential growth, if not the main responsible. The zombie theme wasn't new at the time, but it never had a solid oportunity at the gaming world, much less in a FPS game. Valve used their best at the time to create this game, and what is it that Valve can't create and automatically become a classic?
Well, they did an excelent work again in this title, put extremely easy and soft controls, gave us hordes of zombies to kill, not only weak and rotten zombies, but special ones, with specific abilities, which guarantees different gamestyle, when you're trying to avoid them. Every character has it's own personality, line of words, thinking, and are at some point even funny to hear. For some, that may break some of the tension that the game can produce.
Other huge step in the making of this game is the addition of the Cooperative mode, which is undeniable required to survive. Any effort will be useless if you don't have on your side some good mates to release you when get caught by some nasty infected, for example. There are also some other game modes like Versus (player vs player) and Survival (player vs time).
Left 4 Dead is that kind of classic that can be played at any time, by any generation, and will always bring you that same joy and fun that you had when you played it by the first time. A real masterpiece. Without a doubt.
▼ Negative Aspects:
After giving that huge statement in favor of Left 4 Dead, it is hard to point out some minor imperfections, but they always exist. There are two things that I believe they could take better care on this game: the lack of weapons, by that I mean variety, there aren't many different guns to kill, specially melee. And the second is that they didn't launch a lot of official campaigns, or maps. Fortunately, L4D2 came out just one year later.

Originally on March 4, 2015, I achieved 100%. I felt really proud. Then they released DLC.
Finally today I got that last achievement, and I'm ready to review. Again.
I want to write a really good review for this game, but I really don't know what to say.
The game is hard, no denying that. There's plenty of characters to unlock and choose from, hundreds of items, (some number that I don't know what to round it to) of enemies, and an infinite number of randomly generated games. Nothing is as fun as finding a new item, and seeing what it did to your attack, or your defense, or passively, or whatever it did. The only thing more fun is seeing how it synergizes with your other items.
Some things in the game might be unfair, but the game is constantly getting tweaks and fixes to balance things behind the scenes. Having a game that gets small, unnoticed updates that can really fix a huge problem seem a lot better than large, glossy updates that have bugs behind all the new features.
The music, a lot of people have mixed feelings about. It's no Danny Baronowski, but it isn't bad. It does set the tone of the game well, but it definitely is a different tone compared to the old game. Good or bad, that's hardly something to worry about. If you want the old music, there's a mod for that. If you don't want the music at all, there's a mute button for that too.
Talking about comparing the old game to the new game, the graphics are for sure something to talk about. I remember this being a huge issue back when the game was coming out, and everyone was angry at the new art style. I stood on the middle ground. A full pixel art style game didn't seem right for a game like this, and I was used to the old style. Luckily they listened to this and added a filter option to make the art seem less "right angled", and that's what I love and use.
In the end though, I'm really glad they went for a new style, since it opened up opportunities to make the environments and enemies so much more detailed, and all of the effects and environments look beautiful.
Really though, if you like hard, rogue-like games and have never played this, it's a must. If you're not a person who handles hard gameplay and disappointing defeat well though, you might not have the best time with this game.
If you DO own this game, or are wondering if you want to get the Afterbirth DLC, I'd almost certainly recommend it.
Afterbirth, like the DLC for the original isaac, is basically a seamless expansion to the original game. It's not like how in other games' DLC where you have separate areas for the new things, instead everything new and old gets blended together into one new mess. New characters, items, areas, bosses, and secrets. If you're really enjoying the base game, or think you will, it's a good idea to pick it up.

First of all i must say that i got this game in a bundle for free, not even with that i managed to like this game. I wanted to like it because, c'mon, is you vs lots of monster aliens to kill. But the flaws are just to much for me to even enjoy it.
First, the curiosity is what makes you play the first levels. But after a while, you realize the game is just walk-kill, and is not even that rewarding, most of the time you will get items you can't even use, and most of your money will be spent in repairing. And when you got the money, there is actually not much to buy. There are not many weapons.
The mechanics of the technological weapons are not explained at all. And that reminds me, the interface is... not really good. You will be guessing what all those numbers and symbols on screen means in the first 40 minutes of play.
i didn't get as far as 3 biospheres or whatever they are called, not a single boss. Pity.
The mouse interface is a pain too, sometimes you will be fighting to get a tiny pistol or med kit that was droped on the floor.  And that reminds me that if you are not carefull, you will be missing some items on the floor because they are hard to spot most of the time, i wish the had left the "alt" key as a toggle key.
No stashes, no place to keep things stored, no secrets or hidden places.
Story is not good, if there is any.
Music goes with the mood of the game but is not good either. i belive there is only two background music pieces.
After a while of playing it, you will be playing with some kind of strategy using run/walk, hiding behind objects to ambush the aliens coming for you, but after a while of doing it, it gets awfully boring.
I know the developers put a lot of effort in this game, it can be noted, but is just a big "no" for me. The graphics are probably the best thing here. And for me, thats exactly the problem. It lacks good gameplay, good story, good music, even good ambient, i didn't feel inside a spaceship, neither a biodome.

3) It comes with The Ultimate Doom, Doom 2 and the previously Xbox Live exclusive episode, No Rest for the Living. Take in consideration that absolutely _nothing_ prevents you from simply copying the .wad files off the install and using them in your favorite modern source port. No Rest for the Living is simply
as far as doom wads go. It was made with modern computer capacities in mind.

Short Version:
For a VERY new, early access game, Northgard is very well polished and very free of bugs. While the gameplay is very repetitive, that's the nature of an RTS. The only issues I have with the game in its current state is that the different Clans you can play as are too aesthetically similar, and they both have just one single offensive troop type, warriors. The last RTS I really took seriously was Warcraft III, so I'm subconsciously comparing everything in Northgard to certain things from Warcraft (in the long version). Additionally, while the game does designate an icon to reflect 'Diplomatic Relations' with other clans, I haven't found that to cause any clan to not attack me - which needs to be fixed imo. Lastly, I find that the Stag clan is tremendously underpowered, while they function well at the start, they suffer HORRIBLY from early aggression.
Is the game worth a buy?
- Honestly, yes. While I do think the $21.99 CAD is steep at this moment, considering how well this first release is, I wouldn't doubt that this game will be worth it in the very near future, since the developers have already shown previews of an upcoming update (adds a fourth playable clan into the game).
(Actually worth reading, I think I covered quite a bit.)
Like your typical RTS, many things in Northgard repeats itself over and over. That's to be expected, but unlike the classic RTS (using Warcraft 3 as a reference), Northgard looks the same each time. While I believe this is a straight-forward fix, I think it is one that will take time. There are three clans, and they each have one thing that is different, 2 of them get a unique building and the other gets an additional hero to fight with. Otherwise, each clan has the same buildings, same troops and same victory conditions, each with just different colours. ALTHOUGH there is a talent-tree type thing (called Lore) that does vary a satisfying amount between Clans.
This issue wouldn't really matter if, at release, there were over a dozen clans, since all the devs have to do for each clan is change colours and change talent tree (which is just game balancing and programming, very little tedious art creations, not to say that programming is easy by any means). If each time you played a battle you'd face a selection of a dozen or more clans, I wouldn't really care that they looked the same at a glance, because the game would have such a different challenge each round.
To my surprise, the gameplay was actually quiet smooth and satisfying, although I thought the brute force method of winning seemed too linear. There is only one troop type (warrior) and one hero (Chieftan), with the Wolf Clan getting a Berserker, and an opportuntiy to befriend an NPC clan called Jotunn, that grant you a VERY powerful hero at the cost of lots of food and lots of time (passive time nonetheless). There is also just one defensive structure, a simple tower that shoots arrows, and you can only have one per map tile (which seems fair), although the Sheep clan is capable of building defensive towers that do not consume building slots.
Literally haven't found one. I have, however, found some things that could be polished out but I wouldn't call them bugs.
This is one thing that Northgard has down perfectly, the game is very beautiful, even during the arduous Blizzard map event (the weather pattern, not the company). The music is also appropriate and nothing really seems untoward in this category.
This is definitely the most concerning area for RTS fans, the ability to play the game over and over without getting bored of it, that's what this genre was built for, but that is not quite where Northgard is yet, but if this is the do all or end all, keep reading, that's not all.
I use a simple formula to determine if my money was worth spending on a game: 1 Hour of directed gameplay (This can be a campaign, or if the game doesn't need a campaign, then this would be progressional gaming time - before you knew everything there was to know .) per $1 spent.
Northgard (keeping in mind that it's an early access game) is currently worth about 75% of what you pay for it, I've played about 10 hours as I am writing this, am starting to feel the reptition, but I still will play more after I'm done this review.
BUT. Northgard still has no campaign and no multiplayer (yet. Both listed as "Coming Soon..."). So, when you consider that this game manged to deliver at least 10 hours of gameplay from just Single Battles, and it's been released as early access for less than a month, that's pretty freaking great. This means that the campaign really only has to be 8-9 hours long (not factoring potential multiplayer time) for Northgard to be worth $21.99 CAD by my personal formula. From the impression the developers give, I think this game will be worth a buy, without a doubt, VERY soon.

I am one of the most forgiving critics I can think of. Knowing how difficult game development is, I am quite willing to admire what a game does right over complaining of what it does wrong. As long as the developers have put evident enthusiasm and heart into the title—think Deadly Premonition or Sanitarium for instance—I find it much more gratifying to exercise a little patience and sift the gold out of the muck.
In the growing category of deeply personal indie games, though, I find this practice increasingly difficult. See, in creating a deeply personal game developers tend to make the narrative overly metaphorical and obtuse. I encountered this most recently in the RPG Maker phantasmagoria Stray Cat Crossing. Here the metaphors and the vague story took away from the experience, made it more difficult to connect to on an emotional level. As connecting emotionally ought to be one of the key ambitions of these personal indies, making it purposely impenetrable seems a self-defeating design choice.
In short, I am apprehensive when approaching narrative-driven games with an ambiguous plot. Killmonday Game's Fran Bow is certainly one of these. The feelings, as always, are mixed. By and large it is a great game, but whether or not it would be improved by a clearer story is a question that has been at the forefront of my mind since completion.
Fran Bow is the story of the titular character, a young girl who is shipped off to a children's mental asylum after her parents are brutally murdered. And without even getting the chance to say goodbye to her cat! Deeply unhappy, lonely, missing her feline friend and experiencing strange hallucinations from the drugs she is ordered to take, Fran sets out to escape the asylum. From there her journey features—but is not limited to—creepy forest animals, malicious conjoined twin sisters, a charming skeleton man, abominations beyond the ken of humanity and talking root vegetables.
Now, Fran Bow takes an Alice in Wonderland turn after its first chapter. This was jarring to me as a player, I was expecting something much more grounded in reality. Yet I have never been one to let my expectations get in the way of my enjoyment of something, so I went along for the ride.
From the outset, Fran Bow is full of beautiful visuals, ranging from the horrific to the quixotic. The Tim Burton-style art is charming and varied, showcasing a talent as qualified for saccharine-sweet scenes and Silent Hill-tier grotesqueness. Fran Bow is at its heart a visual experience, a sort of interactive storybook with clever puzzles. Certain brief interludes (one a platformer, one a maze and another a Frogger clone) take advantage of claymation—the original presentation style of the never-completed film Fran Bow is based upon—and other art styles. It is all a hodgepodge of settings, themes and styles, both dark and childlike—a sort of smorgasbord for the artist's talents. One genuinely gets the sense of joy in each scene, whether it be pretty or creepy—the joy of an artist making something they want to make.
Yet the problem with these varied settings is this: How do they come together in a plot? Well, I have been building up, the execution doesn't quite give everything the player needs to really experience the story. There are common themes among each location—everywhere you travel is, for instance, located on small islands—but the narrative makes great stretches to achieve continuity. An entire mythology is introduced to explain the greatly disparate nature of each location. The lines between reality and fiction blur.
While it does make an acceptable amount of sense by the end of Fran Bow, the game begins to lose its focus on Fran Bow herself. In crafting all these brilliant worlds, getting lost in their terror and wonder, Fran herself gradually gets pushed into the background. Her story, the story we set out to experience, gets muddled by so many other elements that the game introduces after we first leave the asylum.
In the end, Fran's story becomes deeply ambiguous. What is real and what is fiction? This reality-screwing is a purposeful theme for Killmonday, yet it doesn't quite reach the coherence it needs to be fully fleshed out. Fran Bow perhaps bites off more than it can chew—introducing many wonderful elements but never combining them satisfactorily. After a few chapters, Fran Bow starts to feel patched together. Her story is a network of psychological horror, children's fantasy, V.C. Andrews and surrealism.
I don't believe that Fran Bow is one of those games who tells an ambiguous plot just because the developers couldn't find a way to tell it clearly. No, there was clearly more heartfelt intention behind this title. For that it earns a great deal of respect, for it is rare for a developer to create a game with such a personal and emotionally-charged vision in mind.
The main problem here is that this vision branches in many directions. We've got Fran's character development branch, her connection to her cat branch, the mystery of her parents' murder branch, the "What's the deal with these drugs they prescribed to Fran?" branch, the mysterious new worlds she visits branch... All of them are good. None of them are given enough attention. By the end the player isn't quite sure which branch we've finally landed on, or indeed if these branches work together at all.

Arthur Morris (1922–2015) was an Australian cricketer who played 46 Test matches between 1946 and 1955. He is best known as a prominent member of the "Invincibles", a team that went undefeated on their tour of England in 1948. In his teens, Morris became the first player ever to score two centuries on his first-class debut. After serving in the Australian Army during the Second World War, he made his Test debut against England. He scored a century in his third match and two more hundreds in the following Test, becoming only the second Australian to score a hundred in each innings of an Ashes Test. By 1950, he was Australia's vice-captain and had amassed nine Test centuries with a batting average over 65. Thereafter his form declined, and his career ended after his first wife became terminally ill in 1955. In later life, Morris served as a trustee of the Sydney Cricket Ground for over twenty years. Selected in the Australian Cricket Board's Team of the Century in 2000 and inducted into the Australian Cricket Hall of Fame in 2001, he is widely regarded as one of Australia's most successful left-handed batsmen.

Sleeping Dogs is a Open World combat game. it takes pages from Grand Theft Auto and Batman Arkham Asylum. While guns are a big part of Grand Theft Auto in Sleeping Dogs hand-to-hand combat is the most used weapon, with Knifes/bars coming in second. you can get guns, but not by buying them. you have to take them from the police or the elite thugs. this is the first thing about Sleeping Dogs i dislike. i would have liked to been able to buy guns at a store or something, but i understand that the games core focus is the hand-to-hand fighting.
Gameplay in Sleeping Dogs is like i said very hand-to-hand combat focused but there are elements of hacking, and just like Grand Theft auto, following missions. but just because the game is focused on the hand-to-hand combat does't mean its not fun. in fact its a lot like playing Batman Arkham Asylum, but with added mechanics. you can smash people into environmental objects and watch a little animation of you beating the heck out of the poor guy. you can throw them into giant speakers, drown them in a public toilet, beat them with a public phone, and more.  Sleeping Dogs also has a strange mechanic called "face". Face is a lot like reputation or renown in other games. you get face for completing missions and doing other activities. the Face mechanic is at most a hamper in your quest for freedom and at least an annoyance. without the proprer level of "Face" you can't do certain things like buy the really cool cars. so even if you have the money you have to have the Face to get it.
Cars in Sleeping Dogs are great looking and fun to drive. they are a lot better than the cars in Grand Theft Auto. and they look better than Grand Theft Auto cars. once you buy a car you can get it from any parking area in the city. the amount of cars you can have are unlimited. if you have the money and face you can have the car. unfortunately Sleeping Dogs has no car editing or customization whatsoever, other than changing the car color. the cars are everywhere on the streets and you can grab any car you want, but you can not save that car to use like in Grand Theft Auto. Sleeping Dogs is also riddled with annoying quick time events. if you get hand-cuffed QTE! if you get grabbed QTE! if you get knocked over QTE! they are everywhere in this game, and they are really a quick time event, fail to do it on time and you will pay for it. even with the QTEs sleeping dogs is fun. i just wish there weren't so many of the dang things. Sleeping dogs also has skill trees and perks. you can get upgrade yourself to get more health, easy access to weapons, or new fighting moves.
The story in Sleeping Dogs is that your character Ricky Wong a would be drug dealer, is forced to become a undercover cop when he is threaten with lock up time in prison. he then must dive into a dangerous world of drug lords and turf wars. all the while working for the police to catch them. it is of course not easy. the story of Sleeping Dogs is great, while its not the best story ever it is a good story, it feels nice to be on the good side, and yet still be a kinda of "bad guy". and that is another great thing about the game, you can be a rouge/ends justice the means kind of guy or a good/nice cop. playing by the rules will give you more perks in the Police skill tree while being a rule breaker will give you more perks in the Criminal skill tree.
one more thing that Sleeping Dogs does better is that the game runs good. remember how Grand Theft Auto crashes and lags up so often? Sleeping Dogs rarely has any of that. granted Grand Theft Auto's world is bigger that Sleeping Dog's, but at least Sleeping Dogs runs like it was made for PC. in the end i would recommend Sleeping Dogs for anyone who likes games like Grand Theft Auto,Saints Row, or Just Cause 2.

What can be said?  It's Doom.  Through and through, it's an ID Software Doom game.  Over-the-top represenation of the UAC and what Hell looks like, right down to the name of the monsters.  A word to any AAA developers, this is how you're supposed to make a very immersive FPS with scary elements.  Yes, there are jump-scares, but a lot of the atmosphere is just as scary as well (the sounds are absolutely amazing).
My only grip with the game is the gun order is not the same as the original Doom.  The original Doom was:
1 - Fist/Chainsaw
2 - Pistol
3 - Shotgun/Double-Barrel Shotgun
4 - Chaingun
5 - Rocket Launcher
6 - Plasma Rifle
7 - BFG 9000
I guess they were out-of-order since a few new weapons were introduced (hand-held grenades is one of them).  Regardless of that small gripe, this game is totally worth every penny.  A total steal when on sale.  So turn down the lights, throw on some headphones, crank up the volume and prepare to enjoy the Doom universe through and through.

I debated with myself for a long time to buy this game. My favourite game is TF2. It was a really fun game to just mess around in. I could lobby up with friends and have a really good time. After TF2 updated and became an unpolished overwatch, I decided I needed a good game to play while I decided what to play next. I heard about Burnout Paradise and how it was a racing game with a well made open world. That peaked my interest. I looked at the store page and some reviews online and it looked like fun, and for only £10! I had high expectations for this game, considering it is supposed to replace my favourite game for a while, and it blew all of those expectations out of the water!
It is a game that is engaging from the start. After you get your first car, you quickly get your second, and then the upgraded version of it, and then your licence gets upgraded. It also gives you a wide variety of cars to suit any drving style, whether you like taking down your opponents to finish in first or just driving around the densely packed open world trying to pull off the coolest stunt. After starting off with about 3 events, I often just find myself driving passed the next one I planned on going to and just drove around for the next half an hour.
The only problem that I have for this game is that the data doesn't sync to the steam cloud, but that is only a problem if you are going to be playing this game on multiple computers. This is my first introduction to the Burnout series and I am hooked. I hope to be coming back to play the other games in the series!

It had been a hard winter. I went off to work alone, but Ulaf found me by the cliffs gathering stones for our new silo.
"
" he reported. "
", he trailed off, staring distantly into the cold grey sea. "
" I added, finishing his sentence. "
" He gave me that crooked grin that always filled me with hope. Next year really would be better. Hell, if it hadn't been for those three sheep we brought with us in the longboats, we wouldn't even be here talking about next year.
Ulaf leaned over to grab a hefty rock when the sound of horns forced him upright again. Both of us turned towards the direction of the village, our view obstructed by the hillside leading down to the cliff edge. Black smoke was rising high over the crest into the ashy blue sky. We bolted, bounding upwards over boulders and brush. Ulaf got to the top first and shuddered before howling like a wounded animal. I scrambled up beside him and saw the source of his,
, agony. The farms were ablaze. Hildred's banners danced alongside the flames. He must have been waiting all winter for this. My pain sharply gave way to fury. "
"
Ulaf and I arrived at the great hall just as the jarl's warband was departing. The warchief bellowed, his voice shaking the ground between us, "
" I snatched an axe gracefully tossed my way. "
" the chief roared, sprinting headlong towards the farms. "
" we echoed, sprinting after him.
That first clang, the initial strike of steel against steel. It's a note in a horrible symphony conducted by madmen, followed not by applause, but the buzzing of flies. Still, it's better than nothing. if you could hear the flies... it meant you were alive. My thoughts snapped back just in time to hear that note. Another followed. And another. Soon all sights and sounds were overwhelmed by a maelstrom of flesh, wood, and steel. I glanced over to see Ulaf beside me, his crooked grin beaming more and more wildly as he spun and slashed. We fought for what felt like hours, but must have only been minutes. Hildred's men pulled back, withdrawing into the treeline, just beyond our sight. Immediately, we set about dousing fires and bandaging the wounded. There's no way that was it. This wasn't over.
No sooner had we triaged the worst among us, the trees themselves started quivering. Before we could venture a guess as to what lay in store, the foliage burst apart and out lumbered 4 gargantuan men wielding clubs and mammoth tusks strapped to their wrists. "
" someone shouted. We braced ourselves for the attack. A sound like a bullroar buzzed loudly and a colossal handaxe zipped by me, missing and landing mere feet away, the impossible thud shaking me to the bone. I looked at it and saw it had actually found its mark after all. Ulaf. He was lying neatly beneath it, hewn almost in two under that crescent granite blade. I began shaking and lost awareness of everything. I thought of Ulaf's grin. I thought about how next year was going to be better. The jötunn began lumbering towards our shield wall. "
", I muttered... it seemed so far away. "
". A guttural moan evolved into a beastly lamentation as I started stumbling forward, my grip tightening on my axe.
The last thing I remember is grinning at those deadly giants, certain that next year was going to be better.

I honestly am a sucker for RTS games and when Northguard popped up in my store recommendations it caught my eyes immediately, I bought it and started playing. My first game I didn't do so good because they really don't give you any tutorial on how to actually play the game you kinda just play and figure it out on your own but once I got the hang of it I was doing pretty good. There are multiple ways of winning a game and you can even choose certain ways that you want to win. They also have a winter system where when winter hits you use more resources so it makes you really have to keep an eye out on how your resources are doing. As of this review I have been playing it for about 2 hours. And this is what I have seen from the start.
Gameplay
The game is fun. It's challenging and on hard difficulty it really makes you think about what to push for. Do I gun for a trade victory, or can I beat the lesser clans in the methods of war. Is it worth getting wood early or could there be deer in the next area. Is it worth investing money into a military unit that eats food but in the long term I'm defended and can conquer territory. It sounds like small decisions but there's one big difference. The game doesn't hold your hand. It's randomly generated, which means you haven't got a single clue what's going to appear. Iron? deer? Or valkyrie? Or even worse, could I appear next to a lesser clan?
Storyline/Campaign
There is currently no storyline or campaign as of this review, but in the future I would hope there is one, and I will amend this review upon the inclusion of a storyline.
Multiplayer
There is currently no method of playing with other people, be it friends, random people online or your friendly neighbourhood game critic.
Final opinion
The game is fun right now, if a bit low on content. You can't do much besides battle it out against the AI over different islands, with about 5 enemy variants and only a couple warband units. Hopefully the updates and new content in the future help pad out the game, but right now it's a good, functional baseline with which to expand the game from.
6/10 for early access

The payment model for this game is disgusting. DLC costs are insane for no more than what you get; i.e. Capcom Pro Tour DLC and locking DLC to Steam Wallet purchase only (minus Season Pass and OST) reducing any chance to get this content on Steam sale or within a bundle. The fight money has gotten only slightly better and this was only after multiple complaints from fans happened.
The 8 frames of input lag is down right horrendous. When you load up USFIV on PC it feels like a miles better game in comparison. The clipping with the character models is very distracting and wasn't really in or noticeable in other Street Fighter titles, but in this one it happens often. Still no Arcade Mode. Survival Mode does not have a continue/checkpoint system which it needs, because no one wants to play the game for x amount of time then get one or 2 fights from completing, only to lose and have to do the WHOLE THING OVER! Censorship, while it can be put back in with mods (until they patch mod support out of the game) is just insane. Look at past Capcom games, even Street Fighter games. Hardly any censorship if at all in the past games. This game is full of censorship which isn't even that bad and really did not need to be removed.

I believe this is an issue with the optimization with the Unreal Engine 4 because every other game I have I can run fine, but this runs fine for a bit then sudden lag spikes out of nowhere for a few seconds then the game is fine. GPU wise you might be fine but CPU wise, anything less than an AMD FX-6300 or i5 equivelant might as well just not play the game to avoid running into issues like this because it will happen.
Consider buying this game when it's on a Steam Sale and be sure to get it with the Season Pass bundled as well, for your own sake. The free-to-play early prototype version of Doorways really shows the platforming roots of the series, which is something even the in-game narration likes to point out.
Its two levels feature a fully developed stage of hellish scenery (with elements familiar from the last episode, Holy Mountains of Flesh), and a series of large white (placeholder-modelled) corridors, also displaying some of the enemy mechanics from The Underworld.
So, in the end, is it worth 30-60 of your time to play some prototype stages? If you are interested in the roots of this first-person horror platformer game, then definitely, they show some interesting game design moments. But if you are afraid of heights, then I suggest to stay clear: the lack of user interface creates quite an immersion, and staring straight into the abyss, especially on the second stage, can be pretty scary.

Aliens vs. Predator is a reboot of the extremely successful Aliens vs. Predator PC-game franchise, whose only 2 releases were in 1999 and 2001.  The 2010 release is made by the same team as the originals and features much of the same gameplay and features. I played through the Predator campaign and tried some of the Alien and Marine levels for my first impressions.
* This game features three separate campaigns, each with completely different control schemes and game mechanics. Although they are all FPS-action, the similarities between the three campaigns sort of end there. The Marine campaign plays a lot like a horror FPS game, you are stuck in dark hallways with a flashlight and loads of weaponry. The predator game is a bit more stealth & platform-based: the predator campaign gives you control of a character with super jumping power, the ability to go semi-invisible, and the ability to perform stealth takedowns. Finally, the alien campaign allows your character to walk on walls and ceilings, run extremely quickly, and also regenerate health over time. The alien campaign also features stealth elements but has a remarkably different feel from any other FPS game due to your avatar's low viewing position and extremely fast speed.
* The jumping mechanics for the predator are excellent: fun and intuitive. The game is fair in its level design regarding the implementation of a playable character that has super-human jumping abilities.
* The game's plot is interwoven across all 3 campaigns. You can experience the same story from 3 different perspectives.
* Great "kill" animations, but there are too few of them.
* Field-of-view is locked at around 70 degrees or so. Not the worst, but annoying.
* Inconsistent graphical quality. Some things look amazing, other times I felt like I was playing a Half-Life mod.
* The predator gameplay, which I was most looking forward to, is lackluster. The stealth technology hardly seems to work on the Marines, and it does not work at all vs. Aliens.
* Melee combat never really does well in FPS games, and 2/3rds of this game is melee combat. The developers needed some sort of gimmick or game mechanic to make the combat interesting, rather than just repeatedly mashing down the LMB.
* The auto-save checkpoints don't work if you're trying to play all three campaigns at the same time. For example, your savegame in the predator campaign will get overwritten if you try to go play the marine campaign. This problem can be fixed by manually saving your game, or restarting levels from the very beginning.
* The single-player game is essentially three long hallways with objectives clearly pointed out for the player with plenty of hand-holding. I am getting sick of games like that.
* The wall-climbing aspect of the alien is unintuitive and seems to only work half the time. Rather than giving me a button to click to go on a wall, my character should just automatically start climbing it. But that is not the worst part: the game puts in things like computer banks and bookcases against walls to purposefully restrict you from using certain walls. It is incredibly annoying that a super powerful alien can decimate an entire spaceship of marines but cannot climb on walls that happen to have computer banks at the bottom of them.
* Multiplayer, which is supposed to be a large chunk of the game's playability, is completely dead.
Although Aliens vs. Predator is a solid FPS with some innovative game mechanics, it does little to enhance gaming as a whole. The game will not be remembered five years from now and will most likely never make it onto anyone's top 10 list for anything. But the game is a fun diversion worth checking out if you can find the game on a deep sale. However, I don't think you will make it through any of the campgaigns before getting bored so I cannot recommend it.

I am forced to update my review after playing the latest version for many hours.
This is no longer the game that we were promised.  Instead of many procedural aspects and no artificial progression walls, we have been given just the opposite.  You need to kill Boss A to go to tech level 2...rinse, repeat.  You can no longer build an "arena" or alter the landscape in any way during said boss fights.  The enemies are less frequent.  You no longer need to worry about food for hunger (this one I believe will be readded later from what I have read).  You do not seem to be able to progress in your own way compared to what we were promised.  Even though we have the option to explore many planets, everything still seems to have a somewhat linear progression.  When farming was introduced, we were told there was going to be a way to progress using farming to continue further within the game as its own mechanic of sorts.  I have seen nothing that lets me to believe this will ever be the case.
Weapons continue to get additional attention/content.  This area is progressing in interesting ways, but with the lack of survival elements, you really don't get as many of those "wow I needed that!" moments.  Life seems to be more common on the surface compared to when Starbound first started.  It seems there is a village of some sorts on the majority of planets now.  With each one having its own store, this really takes away from the need to craft anything on your own for survival.  Then again, you are FORCED to equip a full set of top tier armor before you can be given the quest to kill the next boss (which allows you to progress into the next tech level.)
This game has been under so much hype since it started in Early Access, that I believe the developers felt free to change things in whichever way that they wanted.  The biggest problem has to do with a new community/player base that knew nothing of the previous versions of this game.  So they enjoy the new features not knowing what was sacrificed in the process.  What they have done would be considered bait and switch.  Which is highly illegal in areas of business outside of Early Access games it seems.
Going from a fairly good sandbox to a handholding/linear game is not what I paid for.  I may revisit this review in the future.  At this point, I highly doubt it.

This game has many of the same formulae that made Terraria successful.
--Resource gathering
--Crafting System
--House building
But Starbound took things a bit further by adding space aspects.  Instead of always relying on reloading new game maps for extra resources or fighting the same boss over and over for loot,  they have a large amount of additional worlds upon which you can exploit to your heart's content.  Some hostile.  Some not so hostile.
As usual, you decide how to play your game.  Do you want to be a farmer? Miner? Bounty hunter?  Or, maybe just continuously build onto elaborate colonies as you gain more resources.  The limits in this game are far greater in Starbound than in Terraria (imho).
For an Early Access game, Starbound has come a VERY long way since it first appeared on Steam.  I have been along for the ride through many character wipes (understandable but it still sucks!), seen entire overhauls done to various mechanics, and been there for the new additions that the community has asked for.  Speaking of the community, it has a fairly positive player base, that is willing to help you more than most.  Considering how long this has been in Early Access, to remain positive THIS long before it ever officially releases, takes a hefty amount of content development to be witnessed.  We have all seen Early Access games that flop hard due to devs neglecting to listen to their player base, and/or just never doing much with their game after they took our money.
Kudos to the development team for trying hard to give us the game that we really have asked for in Starbound.

Sleeping dogs is an excellent installment into the open-world sandbox genre. with a great storyline, memorable characters and excellent graphics, Hong Kong feels vibrant, exciting, dangerous and alive. There are many activities to keep you busy, and fun mini games that keep missions and side quests from getting tedious. Playing an undercover cop infiltrating the Triad comes with lots of opportunities for mayhem, betrayal, heroics and excitement Give yourself a treat and get the high res texture pack, with it the game looks gorgeous, from rain slicked streets to excellent character models with just the right visual effects The combat system is the best I have experienced in this type of game, with many melee moves and a fighting system that rewards timing and allows you to take on several opponents at once.
However the game is not perfect. the biggest weakness is the animation quality. Wen Shei (protaganist) looks like a robot when he runs, and if they had only made the fighting animations a bit more fluid, it would have added so much more. I am only a couple of hours into the game, but so far side quests are excruciatingly easy, and you are hand led through them. this can sometimes be nice when you just want to get to the story/fighting but it also takes away from much of the challenge.
Overall I would highly reccomend this game, as the story, graphics, excellently realized sandbox style, and beautifully crafted city far outweight the poor animations and relatively easy missions.

I hadn't played Doom 3 in ages, so I decided to buy this on sale and give it a whirl. I didn't see the comments regarding issues on AMD systems, but I've played for a couple of hours now and I haven't run into a single glitch, bug or crash. Not even a stutter in framerate. This is on a 100% AMD build (FX-8350 and Radeon 7950). I'll update my review at a later date once I've done a full playthrough of this version, but so far no problems.
So it runs fine, how does it look? Well, Doom 3 holds up pretty nicely, actually. I don't mind playing classics with dated graphics (I play through the original Doom games once a year) but this still looks nice even today. I think it's down to the hard shadows and the moody lighting. They've tweaked things in this BFG Edition, making things less dark, but it isn't bright, it's just... well, less dark! It's still dark as hell though, so don't think for a moment that they've ruined it by turning all the lights on, they haven't, it's still Doom3 and you'll still use your flashlight a lot.
Gameplay wise it's solid. If you like old school shooter action you'll probably love Doom 3 BFG. It's cramped and dark and things jump out at you regularly. At first it's simply a case of turn and shoot, but things soon amp up and you'll quickly find yourself ducking and weaving around fireballs, crouching behind cover and running around pillars to get that all important point-blank shotgun kill. In many ways it's just like the original Doom, only now you can't strafe from a safe distance, it's all up-close and personal - the hellspawn are rarely more than 10ft away from you in this game and your reaction times will be tested more than they ever were in the original.
Downsides? There have been couple of times where I found myself wishing I had a melee button to knock enemies back, but I know that would change the gameplay siginficantly. Not having a melee means even slow, lumbering, unarmed zombies can do damage if you let them get up close, and if you don't keep your wits about you, that can happen easily. You need to check every corner, keep your flashlight juiced up, keep your ears open. It's what makes Doom 3 Doom 3.
Do I recommend Doom 3 BFG Edition? Yes. The core gameplay is solid and the game still has the ability to put the ♥♥♥♥♥ up you. Don't expect a sweeping, epic storyline. Don't expect to see huge awe-inspiring vistas that stretch for miles - this is Doom 3 and everything is within spitting distance (not what you'd want when the minions of hell are after your blood).

Back when this game came out in it's unfinished state,(i was one of the first open acess players),it was great,nay,it was amazing. An absolute joy to play around,i would waste hours just building large towers on my "plot".
It's been over a year since i stopped playing,but i felt like i should make a review.
My first 300 hours spent playing this game were nothing short of legendary? Incredible? It sucked me in with it's large open worlds,clubs,FREEDOM. I even reached max mastery which was around 100 at the time,i believe? Point is,i had a lot of fun.
I would join their twitch streams everytime,i would watch people stream,i would LIVE for this game.
But,as new content began to emerge along with dragons (which were amazing,in their own right),so did some p2w elements. In a way,the game was,at the same time - both P2W and the least P2W ever. You had a very well done trading system which allowed you to use the main currency - Flux (which is gained from many different sources) to buy mounts,gear,etc,even the cash-only mounts/gadgets. The game was straight up - FUN! But then,difficulties and max levels began to increase (which was good),but getting gear became a grind,along with getting anything new,things became "randomized" and loot was mostly decided through RNG. Also,to even get into the harder "dungeons",you needed better and better gear,which required hours upon hours of grind,i went through those hours,even so.
People started to leave the game,i had literally hundreds of friends that had not even TOUCHED the game for MONTHS. I met people who had the rarest mounts that i didn't have through PAYING for them indirectly. I even had a person tell me he managed to get everything in the game in a day by wasting more than a thousand dollars,something that i wasn't even NEAR to for my hundreds of hours of gameplay. I saw my old friends leave and be replaced with people who paid their way to the top,and slowly the endless grind and RNG based loot withered my enthusiasm away. I had stopped playing for a week at first,came back to see my old club (which i built myself with a few friends that had their last logins 8+ months ago),and i stopped forever since then. It's a fun game,but it's very grindy and RNG based (and not even in a fun way,such as the adventure boxes,which were there from the beginning). I'm not going to recommend the game because it has become just like all the other F2P MMO's on the market,a grindy,RNG based,pay-to-progress life sucker.

It's startling, fast-paced, well-written, and the atmosphere, in my opinion, you can really feel (until you get used to it of course). The shotgun is satisfying, I never found myself scavenging for ammo (There was always something you could shoot out of to make something die) and although the gameplay is about 10-15 hours in length, going through the game and all the levels feels like a long time. I felt that I definitely got my money's worth and this was a solid purchase. I would recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of space horror, FPS, and / or loves the original dooms. Doom 3: BFG Edition includes the best verison of the original doom that you can find (again in my opinion) and although they're fairly old (1993-1995) they still are so replayable, the levels never get old, killing things never gets old, and the satisfaction of the shotgun's noises is like no other. To this day, I still find myself playing the originals over and over. Doom 3 itself is very different from how Doom 1 and Doom 2 are, because the original two were meant for shooting as many things as possible, whereas Doom 3 is meant to startle and capture you in its science-fiction grasp; still all are great games.

Many games in their Early Access stages aren’t worth the money that’s being asked for them. Northgard however, in my opinion, is worth the asking price already. That isn’t to say that it can’t be improved. Absolutely every game in existence could be improved in some way and Northgard is by no means an exception. However it’s already got the same level of content as many larger, fully developed games have. In some ways, I actually prefer this game to a fair amount of Triple A games out there. Northgard opened up and the first thing that I noticed is that it looks very professional. It looks like a fully finished game that a large company could have designed. The menus are easy to navigate, and everything is clear. It currently has no way of customising key bindings that I can find, but that isn’t an issue for me as the controls seem pretty standard and were what I was expecting. It’s not very demanding for my computer to run at all I get a solid 50-60fps. The graphics are minimalistic, but that works in favour of the game. Most RTS games are fairly cartoon-like and their graphics are meant to be a bit fun. This is definitely something accomplished in Northgard. I think the art style is incredibly fitting for the game. A lot of people go for hyper-realistic when it doesn’t greatly suit the game however they know what they wanted with this and they got a good result. I like the music in this game. It adds something that improves the gameplay a lot.
As far as the setting goes, it’s quite refreshing to see a game based on Norse mythology. There aren’t many out there and there are even less of them that are Real-Time Strategies. I think there is still a lot to be desired in the gameplay though. A lot of the time, it’s just luck as to whether you’ll do well or not. If you start off nearby to 2 enemies, you are going to be destroyed fairly quickly and even if you don’t get taken out, you’re other enemy has spent time building a stable system and has likely gotten halfway to a trade victory or wisdom victory. I think spawning needs to be a bit more balanced because sometimes you have an unfair advantage/disadvantage and that makes the match less fun. The tile system can sometimes be a bit of a pain as well. The entire match is set on tiles which make the game interesting because you have to scout ahead to be able to expand at all, but they also add an element of annoyance into the game. You can only place a set number of buildings per tile and I’m pretty sure it’s a near-random number between 1 and 5 that determines the building count. This was likely added as a way of forcing expansion to stop people from turtling, so it’s a good idea for that reason, but I was taken aback by it when I wasn’t able to place buildings without spending a large amount of food on a new bit of land.
I really like the fact that domination isn’t your only route to victory, but rather you can have wisdom, trade, fame, and whatever appears on the map help you to achieve victory as well. Not only do I think that’s a great idea, but you can enable and disable them for the different matches so you can make more interesting games.
Overall, I think this game is great because it hasn’t tried to do too much too quickly. It’s a nice economy-building game and it gives you a fair amount of choice as to what sort of match you want to have. I like that no unit is less important than any other so there’s a lot of balancing involved in unit assignment.
In the future, I’d quite like to see the game progress so the matches don’t take place on an island, but instead maybe have Viking Longboats to take units between different lands.
I’d give this game a 9/10 as an Alpha, but in comparison to fully developed games, I’d award a 7/10.

for fans of sandbox games, or people looking for a new time-waster. Between incredible mod support, a very dedicated dev team, and the incredibly expansive vanilla content, there isn't much not to love.
Starbound is a brilliant sandbox game where you explore space with no real goal. It's been compared to games like Minecraft and Terraria, but doing so doesn't do it justice.
Originally there were survival elements to the game, namely hunger and temperature among others, but these were ultimately removed, for better or worse. If you want them, there are most assuredly mods for them.
Speaking of mods, there are a metric ♥♥♥♥ton of great ones out there on the official forum. There's enough vanilla content to last you basically forever, but with things like Frackin Universe, the Avali Race Mod, and XS Corporation Mechs, it's hard to resist modding it anyway, especially when it's such a simple process to install and uninstall mods. Drop them in the folder and be done with it.
The only real "Problem" with Starbound is the infrequency of updates. The game isn't abandoned, and they are working on it... But for reference, it took over a year for them to make the last "Big" update--But like I said, it's not that the game is abandoned, or seldom worked on. In fact, you can download the "Unstable" version of the game from your library and enjoy nightly updates, allowing you to play with all the new stuff before it comes out/before it's stable.

I'm sure whoever thought putting in the mechanic "the longer the monsters are out the stronger they get" thought they were being clever, but one of the staples of tower defense games is making mazes to keep the monsters out as long as possible, so it started getting counter-intuitive.
I recommend this as a multiplayer game, but the single player experience got sour.

AvP offers a blend of interesting gameplay, from the gun-toting hardass Marines, to the swift and brutal Xenomorphs, to the stealthy and tactical Predators.
Marines: The marine campaign takes the Doom 3 route, and relies mostly on jumpscares to frighten you. Don't be fooled, because it does it well. It also knows when you've grown from the jumpscares, and turns itself into a proper FPS with enemies that are both easy and difficult to kill.
Aliens: The alien campaign is also a good one. The running on ceilings and hiding in vents, while one by one eliminating every single enemy in the vicinity. Also, seeing civies running in fear is fun.
Predators: The predator campaign, my personal favorite, is a blend of the two. You have both lethal melee and ranged weaponry at your disposal. But, the amount of times you can use these weapons are limited, forcing you to decide whether you should use your last four bars of energy to waste that marine and hope that you can recharge your reserves, or go up close and attempt to kill him that way.
The only complaint is that Rebellion have spread themselves a bit too thin. There's only six stages for the Marines and Predators, while the Aliens have to make do with a measly five missions. If they would give us more in the form of DLC, i would be satisfied. But, seeing as this is a four-year old game, i doubt it'll happen.

TL:DR- This is not a terrible game nor is it a great one
Fallout has been a favorite franchise of mine since playing Fallout 3 back on PS3 and finally on PC. From someone who's played majority of the fallout games (Fallout 1, 2, 3, NV), this is the weakest out of the bunch for me because of simplified mechanics, uninteresting main story, settlement building system, and many more. The originals (1 and 2) set a great atmostphere for a post apocalyptic game with limited but fun game mechanics for its time (1997). Dialog choices were numerous and gave players the opportunity to play a character and form the main protagonist to their liking. Fallout 3 and New Vegas expanded on those and created an open world sandbox to add more depth into an already great franchise. Fallout 4 further expands on this with more verticality and depth to ruined towns, cities, and areas for characters to explore and loot. Fallout 4 made some improvements from the originals but limited or lacked in others. The dialog system is broken down into 4 different choices good, sarcastic, quetioning, and a$$hole. This limits creativity, depth, and meaningful choices compared to the previous titles. Combat is better and not limited to certain playstyles and use of the VATS system. Fallout 3 noteably had terrible ADS mechanics but could be fixed with FREE mods, while Fallout NV slightly improved on Fallout 3's ADS combat. Fallout 4's main story is boring and unintersting making side quests and faction quests more interesting compared to previous Fallout games. Fallout 4 introduced settelment building allowing players to build thier own towns and supply lines. This idea sounded great but was poorly implemented because of confusing and frustrating building mechanics, lack of in-depth tutorial, and force in using this mechanic. Being forced to use the mechanic during non settlement building missions is dumb especially when it isn't fun to use. Overall the game itself has flaws, more than I feel like putting in this review, but Bethesda knows how to make an open world sandbox feel lively and engaging.
Bethesda allowed players to mod thier games adding more replayability and possiblities to franchises like Fallout and The Elder Scrolls. Modders would create mods and put them on a site like Nexusmods for players to download and use for FREE, but Bethesda decided to capatilize on this and make mods similar to thier free counterparts cost "points". These mods, according to Bethesda, were not "paid mods", but to get these points to acquire their mods required MONEY. This is not the first time Bethesda has pushed paid mods on thier consumers. They originally tried doing paid mods through steam on the steam workshop, but because the amount of negativity and hate for this business pratice steam removed it. Making mods paid content instead of free is shady marketing and business tactics, especially when the mods made by thier original publishers were orignally FREE. Its a shame the original developers of the Fallout franchise (Bethesda) couldn't make a better Fallout game then Obsidian studios (the developers of Fallout NV), yet resorts to greed by making mods cost money.
Even with Bethesda's shaddy business practices and dumbed down mechanics of Fallout 4 I still find this game fun and sometimes addicting. As of now I put in 255 hours into Fallout 4 and still plan on playing it in the near future. I would recommend this game on a sale not at full price because of the dumbed down mechanics and shaddy bussiness practices.

tl:dr: Wait until Starbound 1.0 is released. This game is very enjoyable if you like exploring, managing and crafting/building. The main idea is not to travel as much as possible, it's to explore for stuff that you need and, while at it, discovering new stuff that unlocks new ideas and new goals.
The story: It is being worked on... So far it feels a bit like super metroid. Which is a good thing, IMO.
The music: Some tracks are very immersive, sometimes you just want to stay longer on a planet because the music is just right.
Exploration: It feels repetitive when you do a lot of it (like grinding for everything, which is not the main purpose). But I think this is one of the main aspect the developpers are working on. Since the beginning, it has evolved at tremedous rate... meaning that exploration will probably get more and more interesting. You will get a good immersive experience If you stick to a couple planets or systems with a purpose, like building towns and gathering ressources for crafting. I played a lot of Terraria and I believe Starbound gets that part better than terraria because of the size of the exploration zone (infinite), the larger means to get around thoses places (spaceship, vehicles, movement mods, tools, construction entity) and the overall larger requisite to visit some of those places (heat, cold, poison, oxygen, darkness). It is the same feeling of when you are Samus Aran and you enter a room that burns your body just by standing still and then you go back to safety and think: ''Man I know I can get there, I just need to find how!''.
Crafting/Building: The crafting is, so far, separated by type like building materials, food preparations or tools (not exhaustive). All these types requires you to build their own crafting station, with a general crafting station only made for this purpose, which you can build with your own hands (the tier one version). These crafting station seems to be able to become more advanced with modifications, letting you build more advanced stuff to progress in the game (I haven't played lately but it seems like this is the case). The library of things you can craft is fairly big, and it gets bigger with each updates. Chucklefish also implied that this library will keep on growing after the release of Starbound 1.0. There is not much physics applied to the building so far, other than sand and sand-like blocks falling if the adjacent tiles are empty. But still, the building aspect is very interesting because of the giant library of things you can find, added to the one you can craft. So, if you like building stuff and have a big imagination... Starbound probably got the right block or object for you.
Management: You can also build entity (houses) for having people living in them. Those peeps will give you rent, in the form of money or other things, and they will give you randomly generated quests to do. These quests might get repetitive with grinding, but I believe their main purpose is to get you items that are hard to get otherwise. There is a merchant class of people you can get, which gives a purpose to the money you can acquire while playing. You can also have a crew in your spaceship that helps you in your endeavors. All this gives an extra purpose to your adventures: those guys can help you facilitates your exploration, but you've got to take care of them. Also, you can have the option of having the need to eat. This adds a layer of work to your adventure as it pushes you to concentrate a bit on building and crafting in order to survive, combined with the need to get better gears. It is a lot of fun and rewarding to progress in the game since you have to work on different levels in order to survive.
So far Starbound is my favorite 2D game. It is large in terms of content for building and exploring, the fighting is interesting and refining your skills is rewarding, the crafting is tiered in an interesting way and it efficiently pushes you to explore and interact with the content of the game and finally, the survival aspect is immersive and it touches many branches of the game, making you work hard.

-Feels like one of those games you would love to play on Flash sites like Newgrounds or Kongregate
Cons:
-Short, but enjoyable. You could actually ♥♥♥♥ the dev(s?) out of money by getting 100% achievements in less than the 2 hour refund period
Overall, I enjoyed these games enough to recommend them all.

The add-on packs are well done, but if you play everything back to back it might start to feel tedious. The inclusion of Doom and Doom II is nice if you want to replay them or see where the series had its roots. I had fun with my run through Doom 3, but it's just dated enough that I wouldn't recommend the full $20 price.

Space Hack is a sci-fi RPG/action, which was released in 2004. All players and even developers describe this game like Diablo-inspired gameplay mechanics clone.
All your walkthrough will consist of grinding alien monsters. All 40+ locations you will slaying hundreds of monsters. Sad thing is that your enemies differ from each others only in stats. With your way to "Mother" Module monsters become only fatter and hit harder. They have nothing something like special unique abilities. Just melee and ranged attack. Ranged attack can be one of four types. So all game you won't face any new creature, which has different fight mechanics you haven't seen in first 3-5 locations. I've completed this game on hard difficulty, cleared all locations. For 40+ locations I've met only 2 unique bosses.
There is no stash in this game. So all items you can't wear at current stats you need to carry in inventory.
At last locations when I tried to change locations with teleport game crashed a few times. Every biosphere had at least one location with  lightnings on my screen, I don't know - it was graphical bug or not, but it was disturbing. Steam version has no voice sound over dialogues and missions.
So if you are looking for interesting action rpg, better skip this game. Maybe Space Hack was good game for 2004. But in 2014 it was painful for me to complete this game. Yes, it has storyline, but you'll face 45 locations of grinding same monsters. Worth it?

CHKN is an amazing concept and it's pretty well executed, though buggy atm.
It's fun, it's cute -in that kind of horrific abomination kind of way-, and works decently well in the whole "create your own creatures" and survival ways.
The bugs hinder it though, and frankly, multiplayer is a fair way from being stable.

There's a lot of potential here, but you can say that about many things on early access. Overall though, given the fun to be had, and the price point for it, I'd say it's worth the money. And if not right now, then in the near future. If you can tolerate "roughing it" through the early access bugs, CHKN is a breath of fresh air in the survival genre that's getting all too stale lately.

Space Hack is a low budget, action RPG that well, is basically an old style Diabloesque game. It has a shallow plot that comes down to you playing the part of a veteran soldier named Hack, the colony ship you are on flew into a dark nebula and now you've got to fight the aliens that live in the nebula to free your ship. The game may not look pretty, or be all that detailed or interesting. It does however manage to be a pretty long game considering the price, and budget they had when making the game.
Now I have seen people argue that there is no fun in Space Hack, well I bet this game is right up many of your "alleys". I find this especially true for any of you who like playing classic games. Space Hack may not be old enough to warrant being called classic but it sure looks and feels like it. Overall though I can bet the majority of you probably wont like the game, but I can say that the game is not bad in and of itself. Plus its very cheap, so thats always a positive right?

Imagine if you loved marmite one day, then despised it the next, breaking all the rules. That's how Worms Clan Wars is for me.
On the one hand, the artistic maps with dynamic water provide a highly involving environment on which a remixed version of the classic worms gameplay can take place. Moving worms about with water - particularly small bodies of water released from high terrain, sweeping worms to their doom or at least discomfort - has proved very entertaining, much as it did in Worms Revolution. The weapons are exceedingly well balanced with just one major exception, though even that (the Concrete Donkey, of course) is more challenging to use now due to realistic interaction with the terrain. I'm impressed how tricky it is to make use of some of the most powerful weapons, for example it's rare to be able to get a lot out of the Old Woman unless on a very basic landscape with some long, gradually sloped or flat sections.
The darkside to the game involves somewhat dodgy physics when attempting to move about. For the most part, things are alright, but every now and then a worm will get caught on a small, pretty much invisible speck of land and this can ruin attempts to cross decent distances with a single jump or rope swing. Speaking of the rope, that really can be a nightmare, as for some reason it tends to get caught on bits of land very easily, forcing you to release and try another shot (if you have one). Not only that but it has a notoriously unreliable 'up and over' feature, which sees a worm that has pulled the rope all the way in to the land attempt to spring up from the rope to get into a ledge. It's about 50/50 whether the worm will make it or not, and if not - and this is the real troublemaker - the fact that the worm makes contact with land removes its ability to shoot out a new rope and save itself. All too often this results in a worm sliding into deep water or off the map entirely. Brilliant blow-by-blow standoffs have come to an unjust end as one player attempted to relocate just a short distance for a more strategic bazooka launching position.
Overall though, the game has entertained me enough to keep me coming back, despite a bit of lag due to the game's minimum requirements being a bit higher than the specs given in the store (trust me - I've tried turning all the options down to their lowest).
While I'm at this I may as well add that I feel the game would have greatly benefitted from the inclusion of a couple weapons in particular; the mail strike (a tactical wind-affected strike for which I always enjoy watching the different items of mail affect each others paths in Worms Armaggedon) and the Ming Vase (a cluster weapon dropped like dynamite that was good for blasting away several layers of land in W:A - making it a great tactical weapon despite being 'super'). This is, of course, a matter of personal opinion and does not affect the rating for this game that I am giving, which is:
7/10
So I do reccomend this game provided your PC/Laptop exceeds the minimum specs slightly (e.g. at least 4GB RAM) and/or you are willing to set the various game options to the minimum .

This game is delightful. I'm a big fan of strategy games and I like Northgard for it's accessability, and variety of maps and victory conditions. I think the biggest strength is the map design. Additionally, there are neutral threats in the land which I love. Some you can destroy for fame or to win, others you can befriend through trade. While the artist style of the game is unique, the game as a whole is fairly weak.
The combat system is overly simplistic and consists solely of attack-dodge-repeat mechanics; minimalism is great, but this is barren. The variety of weapons should make the combat more interesting, but they don't because the combat system is too simple. No matter which weapon you pick, the difference will only be how far away you stand from the enemies.
The design and introduction rate of the weapons are lousy as well: you bounce from weapon to weapon quickly and upgrading weapons is pointless. Sure, you can activate idols, which makes weapon upgrades a bit more useful, but you're still stuck in the same poorly designed combat system.
The story is one of the worst I've had the displeasure of following. It's a trope-filled story narrated in a discontinuous manner with character building ripped out. The writers failed to make me care about the world or any of the characters. For imagery, think of the story as macaroni necklace: it's strung together, but not cohesive.
The "narrative" expects you to be okay with the plot suddenly having certain elements; the turning point for me is when the line "We became fast friends" is mentioned. This is the kind of inept story telling I'd expect of inexperienced writers, of high-school students. You can't simply say a bunch of things: there has to be connectivity between story points. Why did they become fast friends? The calamity isn't a good reason, as the direction the plot goes afterward shows. Am I to infer all of the character building, relationships and details that are not provided to me? That's not my job; the writers must do their part.
If you're looking for depth, subtlety and cohesion in a story, I'd send you to Spec Ops: The Line, not to Bastion.
The dreams are bits and pieces of back-story for each character, and they at the very least tie the macaroni necklaces into a giant ball. This is still a failing on the game's part with blame lying squarely on the writers and designers. Why weren't these things part of the main story? Why do they never come up via character interactions? All these elements that bring the main strand of story closer to something legitimate are tucked away in optional iterative-round fights. This comes off as poor design, and ultimately looks and feels lazy. It's squirrelled away; swept under the rug.
What passes for story in this game feels like bullet points for the beginning of a story idea.
To say I'm disappointed in Bastion is an understatement; it's completely forgettable.

Street Fighter V is totally awesome. If you're looking to get into fighting games, I would definitely buy it. It's a simple fighting game, which isn't a bad thing. Street Fighter has always been one of the most popular fighting games, so it is easy to learn, easy to find videos online and easy to find players at all times.
It has a large emphasis on fighting game fundamentals and is very balanced. Besides one or two characters, you will not be "gimmicked" to death in this game. When you lose in this game, it is not because the character they were playing was overpowered in some way, because it is very well balanced.
The only detriment to the game is probably it's aggressive DLC system. There is SO much DLC for the game, and though they say that you can earn it all for free, it is nearly impossible to actually do. In a fighting game, cosmetics don't matter, but it's REALLY important to have access to all of the characters, which is why it's disappointing that it's so hard to earn all of those characters for free, and even worse than that, the game (like most other games with DLC) taunts you by having the characters appear on the loading screen, but be unselectable. If you are going to buy this game, I would definitely get the season pass with it. Another negative is that the game STILL doesn't have PS3/PS4 input support, so you'll need to look online for a 3rd party program if you want to use anything but the default keyboard bindings or an Xbox stick/controller.
If you haven't gotten into fighting games before, and you want a good starting point, especially if you're looking to play fighters on PC, get Street Fighter V. When it comes to fighting games on PC, there are not a lot of options, most fighting games on PC are released a year later than the console versions (Guilty Gear, Blazblue) or they are poorly made and drop PC support after a couple of months (Mortal Kombat X). Street Fighter V for PC will be continually supported and with PS4/PC crossplay, the online will not die soon.

Aliens vs Predator is a great game based on the Unreal Engine 3 focused on 3 main parts, 2 of them are 2 different types of stealth action and 1 survival horror (the marines, aliens and predators respectively). The game is always in the first person view, making it highly realistic but a bit confusing when running on walls and it takes some getting used to.
The sounds are highly emersive and very realistic, adding to the atmosphere of the game.
The graphics are very good (as already mentioned the game is based on the unreal engine 3 , so there isn't really a way to could look bad anyway ), naturally I found one or two places where the textures glitch out but those are random spots on the terrain where the majority of players wouldn't probably visit.
The gameplay is solid, the Marines campaign gets a bit tiring since it's pretty much a lot of the same. The aliens campaign is the best however the shortest, (you can't have your cake and eat it too) the predators campaign however kind of doesn't fit in... What I mean by that is that the entire battle between the aliens and humans doesn't really leave much space for the the predators story to develop, but then again I'm just nit-picking at a really solid title.
This game is an awesome game just like "Left 4 Dead 2". I totally recommend this game, but make sure to beat Left 4 Dead and then Left 4 Dead 2 to get the best experience out of these 2 games.

Graphics;

Youtube, people! Max settings! Gaming on the Pc Friday night with a bag of your favorite chips and some Mountain Dew, curtains closed, doors closed - absolute silence - absolute darkness. Only focus; The game, and surviving it, you'll try- ohoho! Anyway! Back to the matter at hand! The graphics are overall good, nothing too fancy-smanchy, nothing too... Ew. The game itself doesn't require your computer to be top notch - A decent computer will do just fine on high settings! This game is undeniably rubbish.
This game doesn’t bother with the two AVP movies and has its own story line.
The game consists of 3 campaigns, which sounds like a good idea, unfortunately they take place on the same 5 levels.
The marine campaign consists of a generic FPS experience, they seem to try to make the game scary for the first couple of levels and then just give up on that and throw it all out the window.
There are 67 audio logs that you can pick up and listen too, however if you are halfway through listening to one as you're playing through the story if a NPC makes any type of noise, the audio log will immediately stop playing, forcing you to start it from the beginning.
The predator campaign also starts off on a good note, it's what you'd expect from a Predator campaign, jungle level, stealth, stalking marines, but once again, for some unknown reason the developers decided that the predator would be better suited to walking around small grey corridors.
The Alien campaign is by far the worst, thanks to dodgy controls and a ridiculously short campaign, (I completed it under an hour on the hardest difficulty). The Alien latches onto every wall without you telling it too. There's a setting in the options menu that disables that problem, yet when you do disable it, it continues to do it anyway.
Overall the single player is pretty god awful.
MP:
Well, the game has it's bog standard multiplayer modes, deathmatch, team deathmatch and a few lesser used modes. However there's no point talking about them because nobody plays them anyway.
Team Deathmatch is the only mode people play. You choose between a marine an alien or a predator, there's no difference at all from their single player counterparts.
Unfortunately there's some severe balancing issues. There’s no point being anything other than the Predator for one reason, the plasma caster, impossible to dodge and will kill in 1-2 hits, if it doesn't kill you in the 1st shot, you'll be knocked over, unable to move and then they'll fire immediately to kill you again.
The stealth kill command is still in multiplayer, which just leads everybody trying to run behind your back and mashing the E key, because as long as the animation starts they get a kill. (Some cool animations though).
This game is filled with glitches and exploits, such as spawning out of the map, to instantly fall and die, no spawn protection so people often kill you as you spawn and the Aliens use an exploit to kill you nearly instantly.
Another thing this game does, you have to level up with an annoying EXP system (apparently every game needs this now. (I just hate it though)). The reward for leveling up isn't anything special and is indeed ridiculously pointless. You get skins for your character, on a first person game, Which obviously means you can't see them.
Overall, the game is pretty appalling, there's honestly no point in spending any money on this game and you are better off spending it on something else.
