Space Hack is a Diablo-esque ARPG made by RebelMind.  It was released pretty late in the whole Diablo hype, though, and is kind of lost in the many games that exist today.  The game may have been great in it's prime, but in the modern age of gaming, this game fails to impress, and I do not recommend it.  Though the game is a dollar, so the choice is up to you.
Space Hack claims to offer "50-80 hours of gameplay!"  Note that this is on the retail box.  While this does sound like a great reason to buy it, I was pretty bored within the first 5 hours.  The game does some pretty low-blow crap, like having to travel out for an objective, get severely hurt, travel back to camp, heal, head out, get hurt, return to camp, heal, ect, ect.  This system was obviously created to make the game longer.  And it's a ♥♥♥♥ing pain.  The music has no specific genre, and really never tries to create an atmosphere.  The visuals are pretty poor, even for the time period that the game was created in, and the game is very inconvenient to play on a modern computer.  The game runs at a really low resolution, somewhere around 720x600, and if you have a  second monitor, it'll ♥♥♥♥ around with it.  Even if there weren't these minor inconveniences, I still woulden't recommend this game.  While the gameplay is decent, it basically borrows 80% of gameplay from Diablo 1.  You might as well play that.
At the end of the day, I tried to enjoy Space Hack, but I just coulden't.  Since it's a dollar, though, the choice is up to you.  Maybe you'll enjoy it more than I did.

If you are fed up with Generic Shooter No2000, I would reccomend picking this up.
Sure, Doom 1 and 2 look really old now and Doom 3 isn't the most original of shooters, but even in their old age, they are still solid games worth playing.
Doom 1 and 2 are easily worth the price of entry and thankfully, Bethesda have made changes to the controls to make them more useable without having to seach for  a program like ZDoom. Of course, that option is still there if you still want to use extra programs.
Level design wise, they are a breath of fresh demonic air in comparison to all of the linear shooters of modern times. Exploration and thorough searching will net you much needed supplies which can mean the difference betweeen life and death in later maps.
The enemy variety is something to admire too. Gone are modern shooter's variety of 'Guy with gun' or 'Guy with slightly different gun' and in comes the armies of hell itself with basic enemies consisting of Zombies, Fire-throwing Imps and the mass-mobbing of 'Pinky' Demons, with the enemy selection getting bigger and nastier from there.
Doom 3 trades in the open level design for Sci-fi horror asthetics. While many did not like the change (and I can't blame them), I still find Doom 3 worth a look, especially now that they have fixed the flashlight problems of the original release.
If all of that still hasn't sold you; Wieldable. Chainsaws.

Space Hack uses the Diablo formula, but it is a lesser derivative that doesn't do anything other than provide a setting in space with alien creatures. The environment is situated in an enormous cargo ship transporting biospheres for planetary colonization.
There are some good things about the game; the science fiction environment and back story created are interesting. Graphically the game looks good and feels convincing. Also, the controls are quite fluid and the game operates smoothly (I loved being able to rotate the map with the mouse scroll wheel). No bugs or crashing to be found; overall, I found no technical reasons to dislike this game.
I played the game for 8.7 hours and finished 2 quests. To finish this game 100% one must visit 15 biospheres; all that time and I only fully explored biospheres A and B. I have a hard time with games that are too fast paced, but even for me this game is too slow. One would need to put in about 50-60 hours which is too long for a game that doesn't have much variety.
The maps are large but feel quite empty. There are too few scripted events, no special spots, or interesting extras, just hundreds of monsters to slay and a lot of space station objects that have no interactivity. To be blunt, after a few hours this game gets boring.
Despite the very reasonable price of this game is not recommended since they forgot to make it fun, This is not a bad game, but it is boring due to the lack of variety.

I already owned Doom 3, but I bought this version hoping it would be more bearable to play. Oh boy was I wrong.
Yes the always available flashlight is needed, but the same old Doom 3 bs gets you all the time.
Here's how the game goes:
You go to a mission critical area --> closet monsters come from behind and front of you, some may teleport.
You pick a powerup or a gun -->  closet monsters come from behind and front of you, some may teleport.
You pick your nose -->  closet monsters come from behind and front of you, some may teleport.
I do love Doom 1 and 2 and I do realize they had their share of closet monsters and teleporters too. But the closet monsters weren't so annoying or common. And there are no technological constraints to spawning monsters nowadays.
And then there's the issue with the weapons: Pistol = crap, shotgun from 1m away = crap (shoved up on an enemys ♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's ok), grenade = useless, rocket launcher = meh, BFG = not nearly as fun as in D1 or 2.
The biggest problem with weapons is that only zombies react in any way to damage. You can headshot a full clip to an enemy with chaingun and it just keeps shooting or charging at you.
And sounds: Weapon sounds are -really lacking punch-. Shotgun deserves a mention of really lacking a satisfying sound. Chaingun sound is surprisingly good and plasma ok, everything else is not. Your character doesn't make a lot of noise when hurt, if any. Imps make same screetching noise that was in Turok 2 and I don't think it suits them well. The fat rocket shooters and crawling wing babies make actually nice atmospheric sounds.
This version also dumbs down settings way too much. And I don't think the textures are even the 512MB ones that were available with original Doom 3 (even though they should be improved???). Some textures are really pixelated and I don't remember that being the case with the higher quality ones in the original. My LOD bias is was set to highest.
Well at least you get the Doom 1 and 2 wads with this version.

This game was offered for free for 24 hours but it might as well be free forever. It's a dated game for sure but it has a lot of issues with balance, gear, energy management and the actual element of a game being fun.
When you first start the game, you're given a club (a melee weapon in the game with degradability). I read a review here saying there's other stuff on the floor but I didn't see anything, maybe they meant the monster drops. The problem here is (at least in Normal difficulty), that monsters chop you down very easily, you swing, they hit, you swing, they hit, rinse repeat. Eventually, you will either run of HP or your weapon will break. If a weapon breaks in this game, it is removed entirely from your inventory which is a bit harsh.
Luckily, there's a free doctor at the base but running back and forth between him and to where you want to go is very tedious. You can get healing capsules but they cost about 150 cells (currency in the game) per one use, which is far too expensive as the payout from the first few areas is absymal. Monsters have a small
to drop cells or random gear. I spent most of my income on repairs and purchasing one helmet. The prices are set way too high and this encourages grinding except this quickly becomes a chore in a game with uninspiring enemies and locale.
Gear-wise, the club is a good option but lacks speed so it leaves you open to a lot of hits. The bow is pretty redundant as there is no stand-and-shoot option and the range is laughable. So much so that once you're in range, you'll deal only a small amount of DPS - might as well keep the club.
The energy guns are a much better option but unfortunately, they rely on energy which is spent very quickly. I think I found an energy refill item but that was when I stopped playing, the game just got a bit too boring after that.
Story-wise, there isn't really much to it. Wall of texts try to flesh out the characters but otherwise not a great deal to say here.
A much better free game is Path of Exile, similar game mechanic but overall, just much better in every department.
It's very difficult to use a Yes or No conclusion to this review, especially for a game that cost nothing but an hour to check it out but if I had a chance to take that hour back, it'd be spent elsewhere.

Alright. After getting every achievement in both Rebirth and Afterbirth, and with over 350 hours put into this game, I think it's time to review it.
I'll first start with the gameplay, which, overall is pretty fun. You collect items, slowly powering up and modifying your main way to attack, which is with Isaac's tears. Most of this game is based on RNG, which means you could get some pretty garbage items or you could become a literal god by the end. But don't get me wrong, it also requires some skill.
Most of the characters are pretty balanced overall and I find many of them enjoyable to play; my favorite character being Eve.
The story and graphics are also nice. The story is usually sprinkled through little details and music, but is obviously mostly found through the cutscenes, which look really great. The graphics overall compliment the game, and is definitely a lot better than the original The Binding Of Isaac.
The music here is just godlike. Every single track fits where it's played, and I find every single one of them enjoyable to listen to. My personal favorites being Sketches of Pain, Ascension, and Infanticide.
Overall, this is one of my favorite games of all time. Everything in this game works, the replayability is high, and I definitely recommend it to anyone who would want to try it.

I want to write a really good review for this game, but I really don't know what to say.
The game is hard, no denying that. There's plenty of characters to unlock and choose from, hundreds of items, (some number that I don't know what to round it to) of enemies, and an infinite number of randomly generated games. Nothing is as fun as finding a new item, and seeing what it did to your attack, or your defense, or passively, or whatever it did. The only thing more fun is seeing how it synergizes with your other items.
Some things in the game might be unfair, but the game is constantly getting tweaks and fixes to balance things behind the scenes. Having a game that gets small, unnoticed updates that can really fix a huge problem seem a lot better than large, glossy updates that have bugs behind all the new features.
The music, a lot of people have mixed feelings about. It's no Danny Baronowski, but it isn't bad. It does set the tone of the game well, but it definitely is a different tone compared to the old game. Good or bad, that's hardly something to worry about. If you want the old music, there's a mod for that. If you don't want the music at all, there's a mute button for that too.
Talking about comparing the old game to the new game, the graphics are for sure something to talk about. I remember this being a huge issue back when the game was coming out, and everyone was angry at the new art style. I stood on the middle ground. A full pixel art style game didn't seem right for a game like this, and I was used to the old style. Luckily they listened to this and added a filter option to make the art seem less "right angled", and that's what I love and use.
In the end though, I'm really glad they went for a new style, since it opened up opportunities to make the environments and enemies so much more detailed, and all of the effects and environments look beautiful.
Really though, if you like hard, rogue-like games and have never played this, it's a must. If you're not a person who handles hard gameplay and disappointing defeat well though, you might not have the best time with this game.
If you DO own this game, or are wondering if you want to get the Afterbirth DLC, I'd almost certainly recommend it.
Afterbirth, like the DLC for the original isaac, is basically a seamless expansion to the original game. It's not like how in other games' DLC where you have separate areas for the new things, instead everything new and old gets blended together into one new mess. New characters, items, areas, bosses, and secrets. If you're really enjoying the base game, or think you will, it's a good idea to pick it up.

I have always had a soft spot for the Worm's series, which it's crazy physics, bazookas, dynamite, super sheep and holy hand grenades and this game hasn't changed that opinion one bit. I took advantage of the package deal and got this Worms game along with several others. Note this is a first impression review.
Worms Clan Wars is an 2.5D artillery game where you control teams of Worms to defeat the other teams. You use a wide selection of weaponry and tools to secure victory. Sometimes in hilarious ways. Gameplay wise this is no Armaggedon but it comes close.
Even when you lose or do something daft you can always laugh about it. In one case, I was going to do a classic tactic of using a baseball bat to send an enemy worm into the water, only instead for the worm to catch onto a piece of landscape, I was still laughing afterwards.
Unlike most Worms games including Armaggedon, you have several classes of Worms to use. The Soldier is basically the standard Worm, but gains the ability to detonate grenades at any time. The Scout is a weaker, but faster Worm that doesn't set of mines. The Heavy is a slow, but tough worm that does extra damage. The Scientist is similar to the Solider but can heal itself and its teammate each turn whilst producing better tools. You can configure your team to adapt to this.
Online Gameplay is fun, and even when something daft happens you can still enjoy it and the clan features are nice.
The only criticism I have is the modded in cosemtic options, which with some items like that Master Chief helmet can really cause the lag in an online game to go theough the roof and with a rather low spec computer it has firced me to quit several times.
Definately recommend giving this game a shot!

This game has been such a colossal disappointment. It's a mess of broken promises (Linux support), nickle and diming (insane amount of costume and stage DLC / selling season passes without announcing what's contained in it), delays (multiple month delays for characters / patches), lack of communication (patch notes released hours before the patch as a non formatted pdf file filled with typos and incorrect information), and just a sheer unbelievable level of incompetence all around.
The fact this was released after US4 is really a kick in the teeth to any SF fan and is a detriment to the FGC as a whole. The game is severely lacking in content and the initial 60$ purchase is laughable, not to mention the disgusting amount of DLC the game has released since it's launch. Compared to Injustice 2 and Guilty Gear it's gross that they charged the same amount as these games given the lack of content this game features.
Pros
+ Return of fan favorite characters (Alex, Urien, Nash, Karin).
+ Tutorials are decent and help to explain fighting game concepts to beginners.
Cons
- Feels like a guessing game and you constantly feel cheated out of matches.
- Very rush down heavy.
- Completely lacking in defensive options (V-Reversal doesn't feel like enough).
- V-Skills are completely lacking and uninteresting for a lot of the cast.
- Neutral feels completely lacking due stubby normals and crush counters.
- Zoning is completely neutered and non-existent save for Guile.
- Combos feel very bland and don't allow for any creativity.
- Atrocious netcode that still isn't fixed.
- Constant server problems and extended maintenances which don't seem to fix anything.
- Player stat cards that had been in since launch were completely nonfunctional until around December of 2016.
Capcom is a shell of it's former self and I can't express how sad this makes me. I'm a huge fan of the franchise and it's my favorite fighting game series. I had so much hope for this game and at this point they have completely destroyed their reputation and any good will they had garnered previously. Barring a complete overhaul of the game and netcode I can't recommend the game in its current state.
Do yourself a favor and pick up any of the other great fighting games out there with developers that actually care about their player base and don't take them for granted.

Street Fighter 5
While I am somewhat bias towards it being the type of fighting game I like, however I still will attempt to be unbias in my explanation of the pros and cons of the CURRENT buy.
___________
CONS:
CAPCOM - Lots of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mistakes and concepts with reverted patches here and there and slow development time overall.
SMALL CAST - In comparison to something like MK9, guiltygear, or KoF it isnt a super BIG cast for the purchase price, even if the DLC characters add more variety, they arent available with the first 60$ purchase.
BAD STORY MODE - I mean its not Terrible, but its not at ALL worth buying for that.
HORRIBLE WAY OF GETTING COLORS "SURVIVAL MODE" - So now there are ways to buy colors you want, but to get them normally you have to do a mode called "Survival" which in concept could be fun but its very static and ramps difficulty really quicky while leading through WAY too many easy matches; You'll find yourself almost forgetting what "level" you are in the mode and get to 15+ and then the AI suddenly knows how to block and combo and you lose all your HP to the boring no blocking no attacking AI for the first 15. The mode unlocks colors for the CURRENT skin, not all skins too, and only unlocks 1-3 based on difficulty you COMPLETE. Its not fun in any way sadly.
THE COMMUNITY - Its a big pvp game, and for the past few years you probably know what that means already. People think they need to be a jerk to have fun, and need to completely obliterate newbies. The ranking system helps, but you will find you gotta grow a little tough skin to get through the childish teenage anger issues and trolling that happens. PROTIP: Take every taunt emote as a compliment and try to find people to play with who seem new as well, or are approachable and open to helping. Also, when it comes to fighting game communities, I've noticed some of the lower skill end really judge by character choice, take the flak with a grain of salt if someone starts flaming or making fun of you for playing a character you like, they are parroting what they think is right.
_____
PROS:
THE CAST - In the same right that its a smaller cast, the cast is also very unique to each other in gameplay, which can be very rare for fighting games. Each character has a decent variety of moves and has his own specialty. There isnt a lot of overlap in characters for how you play them in my opinion.
THE MULTIPLAYER - Crossplatform play with PS4 makes it so we always have people to play against, and the connection generally is good even with my poor internet. Not to say I have TERRIBLE internet, but its not great and the game holds up really well online.
LEAGUE SYSTEM - Its not "perfect" but for a fighting game, its one of the best, I always feel like when I get matched a league ahead of me, that I'm fighting someone Better then me, unless I'm ready to move to that league. Your experience may varry based on location, but as someone in the US, this is my experience with it.
ANIMATIONS - So lets be fair, Birdie's chain clipping through his neck chain in the character select is really bad, and the closeups arent the prettiest, HOWEVER in motion the game looks GREAT, I can tell what I'm being hit by easily and the characters move very cleanly with impact to make shoryukens feel really heavy and strong.
GAMEPLAY - With a high ceiling you can keep improving towards, you'd think it'd have a steep learning curve like other competitive games. The only thing a new player has to really get past though is general Fighting Game analog/stick motions. the classic Z motion which is Forward, Down to Forward. or Fireball Motions which cuts out the forward to just Down to Forward. Really there isnt any motion thats crazy though still and you can just start playing and enjoy your character after that.
(Disclaimer: There are still "Charge Motions" which have their own new player learning curve that can scare you off when you really want to play a character like Chun Li that uses charge motions, but it just takes a bit more time to get used to and you get the hang of it within a week or so of practice, maybe longer or shorter based on previous experience.)
THIS REVIEW IS FOR NEWCOMERS, VETS OF FIGHTING GAMES PROBABLY MADE UP THEIR MIND MONTHS AGO ABOUT THIS GAME.
______________
OVERALL:
The game is a solid package for Player vs Player gameplay, but the price is a bit steep when you add in DLC characters IF you buy them with real money.
For the players looking for a good competitive game to dump free time in to and feel accomplished and self successful as you improve your reflexes and understanding of characters and player habits, its great!
For the players looking to kill a boss, get fancy items/achievements/digital rewards, or feel like they are the best in the world when they press buttons without thinking about it? Not so great for that.

This game is a lot like Diablo.  You remember that part in Diablo where you went two levels punching monsters with ranged attacks with your fists while finding almost no loot?  Me either.
The thing is it is faithful to most of the Diablo design, but not gameplay or fun.  The little bit I've been willing to play has demonstrated two of the key strongpoints of Diablo are missing here.
First, gear.  Diablo is a game about gear and loot, and the same systems are here.  Except you don't start with weapons, and the ones you could buy are expensive.  As in, a simple club is worth more money than you will make in the first area.  You will find guns right off the bat, but they will have a limited use, that does not seem to recharge.  That is not a limit per gun, but rather that your energy doesn't recover any way I've found.
Second, in Diablo you could get swarmed.  You could die.  You could get in over your head.  But it wasn't difficult to try again, or retreat and try a different approach.  Right now I am at the first teleport going into the second area, and a brief exploration caused a huge army to park there.  I nearly die as soon as I enter the area.  There's no way around it.  And no weapons or decent armor because of the minimal loot and high prices.
Another irritant is the camera.  If you get too close to a wall, it causes the camera to move in odd ways.  Sometimes enemies can be obscured behind objects, so it is necessary to rotate the camera often just to be sure.
The thing is, whether or not this game will be good if I push through it, so far it is tedious.  I am getting hurt in fist fights with no easy way to heal except to return to the base.  I am literally doing hit and run attacks with my fists between the second area and the base.  Get three punches in, walk home to heal.  Over and over and over.  And that is not good design.  It doesn't bode well for the rest of the game.  I'm not saying it's hard.  I'm saying it's boring at this point.

Please be advised that I got this game when it was being offered for free for 24 hours (to keep forever) during the Meridian4 10-year anniversary. Also be aware of the very strong bias in this review, as the game I have played for the longest in my entire life was Diablo 2 (online and offline). I have also fallen in love with Path of Exile, due to the vastness of the metagame seen in the character builds (see my PoE review for more details).
This will be my 73rd review, and I must first admit that this has been one of the most difficult ones to review in a while - the previous most difficult review was Starbound. It has definitely made me think of a new, critical element when reviewing games and considering the readers, which I will explain near the end. This game also made me sincerely wish that you could only see the recommended rating at the END of the review, so readers aren't primed by seeing the huge thumbs up/down symbol while looking at reviews.
If you like isometric action role-playing games similar to the renown Diablo series, space themes, and challenging gameplay, then you may enjoy this game. If you happen to be a veteran of isometric ARPGs, however, you may also end up disliking this game in favor of other, better alternatives.
Before we start, I just want to mention that this game is not bad or horrible. It also, however, is not good, but somewhere in between (subpar, mediocre).
The aesthetics are pretty decent, but very dated. You can see all items you equip on your character, which is very nice. The detail in the levels and character models are good. The music and sounds are good, and add to the space theme of the game - I actually find some of the ambient music quite soothing. The feedback similar to most isometric ARPGs - health and mana vials located at the bottom of the screen, and you can hold ALT to display enemy health and any loot on the ground. Pressing tab brings up the map, which is transparent and fills up most of the screen. The number of enemies and your current money/ammo is displayed at the top of the screen - a really good feature.
The controls were a bit different from what I was used to, but easy to pick up. There is no in-game tutorial, so take a look at the key bindings before heading out into the world. The camera ONLY rotates - you cannot zoom. I have noticed that the camera can reorient itself into awkward angles if you push up against walls or buildings, however, rotating the mouse easily fixes this. The learning curve is moderate to difficult depending on your experience with this genre. In particular, the aggressive mobs and their ability to detect AND chase you at medium ranges means that you can easily find yourself overwhelmed - especially in the beginning of the game. Furthermore, the grinding is fairly slow, so it may take a while before you level up and can equip better items. I strongly advise you to save often, as you can die at any time.
Another critical mechanic of the game is the currency - you use "energy cells" to pay for all items, however, you also use those same cells as ammo for any energy weapons you may equipped. Since basic necessities like health shots (your healing item) cost 100 cells, the start of your adventure will require a great deal of planning and balancing of energy management. Using projectiles can make the game a lot easier, as you can get surrounded by enemy mobs very quickly. Ammo is given in batches of 100 (for every 100 cells you have 1 "container/clip" of ammo, and the vials on the bottom right will deplete as you near the next multiple of 100).
You can repair your items (they have durability) and identify unidentified items that you loot.
To use "skills," you have to first purchase them from the store. Initially, you will only be able to use the "base teleport skill." To use it, you can equip it to a slot (hotkeys 1-5), and press the right mouse button when the skill is equipped. You will automatically teleport back to base, and can click the portal animation to return to the same spot (using up the two-way portal). Each skill has a set number of "uses," and these must be refilled (costs energy) back at base.
This game was offered for free, and, while it is unfair to compare a dated game with more modern games, I feel that I have to. Path of Exile is also free to play (and forever, it is not "only free for 24 hours"). If you are new to ARPGs, try that game before/after this one, so you can see your alternatives. If you are a veteran to ARPGs, you may want to honestly avoid this game.
The gameplay for Space Hack simply do not survive the test of time when compared to alternatives, and reviewing this game made me consider something I haven't really looked at before - time investment. ARPGs have an extremely powerful potential to receive time investments from their players - I know, I've played Path of Exile (outside of steam) and Diablo 2 so much I have no idea what to estimate as total playing time.
As a serious reviewer, I advise you to try this game out - maybe as a short-term filler game for an hour or two every now and then -
. It IS and can be fun.
However,
Recommend you try it for the short-term if you are really interested; recommend you stay away for the long-term if you intend to invest a good amount of your time into an ARPG.

A very fun game that is a hybrid of classic RTS and city builders. Exploring and building makes this game feel like you're actually managing a budding colony.  Combat is pretty basic, but is forgivable since it is not the primary emphasis of the game.

Bastion is an excellent top-down brawler with an even better story.  The combat is simple but hard to master, and the variety of weapons allows huge flexibility.  The narration is really where this game stands out, your entire journey will be spoken out loud.
Combat starts out pretty straightforward, it's just the WASD keys and click to attack.  You start out with a hammer and a 'repeater', a ranged weapon.  The great thing is that these weapons remain relevant: all the weapons are balanced nicely, except for a couple of endgame cannon sort of things.  Your character has two weapon slots and an ability slot.  A great thing about this game is that no weapons are designated as 'primary' or 'seconday'.  Also, you are not restricted to having a melee and a ranged weapon.  You can have two melee weapons or two ranged weapons in whatever order you like.
There are not a plethora of enemy types, but Bastion still manages to suprise with its varied combinations of enemies.  The first few levels are mainly one-type-at-a-time, but after that you'll have to fight turrets while dodging 'gasfella' attacks while getting mobbed by squirts.  The boss fights are dynamic and unique as well.  Sometimes the bosses are simply just larger, recolored versions of other enemies, but at least their attack patterns are new and tough.
There isn't much since you are almost always in search of the next core, but there are world areas that consist of weapon based minigames.  There are prizes, usually crafting items necessary for weapon upgrades, but first place prizes will be powerful equipable abilities for the respective weapon.  These world areas are a nice quick break from fighting monsters and are worthwhile for the aforementioned abilities.
Logistics-wise, the game is very simple.  When you level up, you get more health.  You can also drink one additional brew to increase your stats or weapon abilities.  Once you are suffciently far in the story you may activate idols for different gods that make enemies more difficult in certain ways but increase shard drop-rate.  Your inventory is just all the crafting items yoou have picked up, and is essentially infinitely large, since yo can only get rid of your items by using them to upgrade a weapon.
The story is very good and makes the game so much more fun to play.  The narrator's voice fits perfectly with the game.  And you are responsible for some decisions at the end which will affect the ending.  Unfortunately the game is a little shorter than I'd like it to be, but its merits far outweigh this.  If I had to give Bastion a score, it would be 9/10.
Thank you for reading this review, I hope it was informative and helpful.

Steam suggested me to buy this game many times, but I always passed, since I heard bad things about it in early access. Now recently it was on sale, and I bought it, and dude, it's amazing.
All domains (Vehicles, Navy, Aircraft, Infantry, Spaceships) are viable, yet special, enabling you to approach the game with multiple different playstyles.
The game is set up for long matches compared to other Strategy games like Command And Conquer or StarCraft, however it never drags out too long, since there are lategame weapons with incredible firepower. It usually ends up taking less than 2 hours.
Occasionally the game freezes, or drops in performance. You will require a fairly beefy PC for maps with more than a few planets.
I would've liked to see more than one faction. There's no campaign, just a galactic conquest mode, but it's not really impressive at all, skirmishes and multiplayer is where it's at. The tutorial is decent and teaches you the basics very effectively.
At anything other than normal difficulty the AI is very powerfull. I think it does get an economy bonus, but it appears to be just a multiplier, not ridiculous cheats (like in Empire Earth, where it simply spawned in units), so any tactic against a human is also viable against an AI. I've seen the AI use all tactics and units, eventhough it appears to have a fetish for Helios Titans. Turtling up is very viable, since in the late game, you'll be confronted with Nuclear Missiles that can take out your commander in 1 or 2 blows in most circumstances.
I'd love to try this game at a LAN-party with buddies, you can even adjust an economy multiplier to balance the game when experienced players play with newer players

Part I: 8 February 2014
I remember my first contact with Left 4 Dead. Saw one of many (at that days) gameplays and walkthroughs on YouTube and after watching first 5 minutes I watched next video, and next, and next… After 2 hours I was sure: I'm definitely gonna buy this game. I haven't had good enough PC that time, but first thing I did after getting new computer was installing Steam and… meh, buying L4D2, what I regret. 3 weeks later I bought L4D1 and I couldn't believe that game could be so much messed up after just 12 months. The only bug I encountered in L4D1 is that Zoey's animation gets stuck in weird position after loading shotgun (but it's fine when it was empty or only one shell was loaded), and only if playing by Zoey. In L4D2 the most, huh, „critical” bug I got was having all Survivors invulnerable for a few minutes after I somehow managed to shove Jockey off my head (big shame I didn't record it then).
Besides this, L4D2 feels like it's just not polished – dumb Survivors animations, even more overpowered weapons, cartoonish feeling, annoying behaviour of Special Infected… L4D1 is free of this flaws – and that's why it's my favourite. Heh, in L4D1 I have only my own weapons sound mod in constant use, while L4D2 has about 1 GB of mods throw on it and I still can't get as much fun from it I get from L4D1. Big shame Valve practically dumped it in favor of money they get out of L4D2.
Part II: 18 November 2016
It appears after all these years I've been playing this magnificent game I'm one of the very few that still enjoy playing just a normal, casual game with bunch of known people in classic vanilla coop. Despite having pretty much only one friend still being around here and sharing my preferences, I am unable to forget about this game, even when I'm not playing it. It just had so big impact on my real life I just can't. Left 4 Dead gave me everything: great moments with good players and even better people, chance to meet really good people not only in game or as a voice in my speakers, but also in real life. It learned me how to treat people so they will be straight with you and honest, but also how to „read” them. How to love and how to hate. Gave me the only one opportunity to meet someone I cannot forget despite I've been trying and wishing to. It gave me depression and suicide thoughts. At one time in my life L4D was the only thing that was keeping me away from madness. I've seen in this game so many different stories and heard so many things about people I could easily write a small book about it. In my case Left 4 Dead was like a soap opera, except that I was one of actors in it. It really changed my life and me as myself. I guess I went too deep into this game and I've never noticed when it was too late. Maybe I'm too sensitive. But still, after all these almost 3000 hours I am a different person than I was before. The bad thing about that is that I'm worse, even though I know myself better than ever before. This may look like a joke, but I'm really f♥cking serious here. Left 4 Dead created and then destroyed me. And here I am now: alone, forgotten, having problems with almost every aspect of my life except my health – a bad thing never dies.
And I guess that's why there are still people playing this game.

(DLC opinions at the bottom)
On top let me just say that I'm a bit of a sucker for sandbox city based games.
Sleeping Dogs gets more right than it does wrong. I thoroughly enjoyed playing through the story, and while not as well acted and voiced as the GTA games I will say I found it far more compelling. Also the game seemed to feature just the right amount of collectibles and side quests for my taste. I didn't feel like it was just padding unlike say Black Flag which I felt was just disrepectful in the amount of junk they wanted me to collect.
Gameplay wise, the cars handle well, better than GTA plus the on road indicators mean you aren't driving by way of looking at the mini map constantly. Hand to hand combat is good, but it can get tedious in long play sessions. I still enjoyed it though, even on my second play through. There were a number of subtle innovations in this game I hoped Rockstar would appropriate, but sadly they didn't.
The graphics weren't top notch, even on release, but they're not bad either. On my second play through I used the hi-res texture pack and I can't say I noticed any difference. They're slightly stylised and I enjoyed that although I sometimes wasn't sure if the people making the art assets and the people making the story were quite on the same page. The game does look great in rainy weather cycles.
I enjoyed this game a lot. If you like open world with a coherent story that makes more sense than most this is the game for you. I don't think its gonna hold up well over time though. I'd give it 8/10.

Do yourself a favor and play with a controller or fight stick. The Xbox 360 controller mostly works alright, but the D-pad on that thing is god awful. It's so hard to just move Left or Right, it keeps making you jump or crouch as well.
The story mode is kind of bad, but next to story modes from other MK games, it's pretty good by comparison. The story has some low-res cut-scenes that look awful at 1920x1080, I much prefer the in-game cut-scenes. They look better and play at a higher FPS.
The fighters are pretty fun. The game has pretty much every fighter from every MK game, though not all are playable (Goro, Kintaro, Shao Kahn). I think my favorite is still Scorpion just because he has such a wide variety of moves that it makes it really easy to string together combos.
The game plays smoothly and actually looks pretty good for a 2 year old game. The one exception I've noticed is that there's one particular stage where the game plays like it's in slow motion. There's so much going on in the background that the game literally slows down. It's pretty annoying, but it does give me an edge over CPU players because I can see their attacks coming.
I don't know if it's worth $30 to be honest. $20 is more like it. Maybe wait for it to go on sale. But if you're craving some MK action on the PC, you don't have many choices. It's either this or the Mortal Kombat Arcade Kollection (MK1, MK2, and MK3 Ultimate).
Overall, MK9 is a pretty good reboot of the franchise. It plays like a high-polish version of MK2 with better graphics and more fighters. To me, that's enough because MK2 was one of the best in the series.

Now playing as the xenomorph may be disorienting for some, but once I got used too playing as one I found that sneaking around in the shadows and striking from the dark was extremely satisfying. Especially when I could hold someone down while a facehugger comes to impregnate them. I have not yet tried the multiplayer, which I hope still has some players. But I can't wait. All in all, I found this title as pleasantly surprising and with more substantial singleplayer content than most shooters out even today. If you are a fan of Aliens, Predators, Colonial Marines, or are just looking for a fun FPS to play, definitely check this out.

Very nice open world game and pretty polished. Some aspects do come off as gimmicky, like the face-meter. When you complete a couple of side-missions and you're wearing stuff that's giving you a bonus face percentage when completing these missions, your face-meter is already at max halfway through the game.
Graphics are very nice, espcecially when it's raining (and it's raining a lot!) the roadreflections look really cool.
Story is okay, but I tended to get out of the flow when doing all the other stuff that there's to do.
Side-missions can get pretty repetitive or tedious even, but I still got the urge to do every one of them, because there actually is a lot of gameplay on offer. For instance hi-jacking moneytrucks was a really cool thing to do (actually hi-jacking any car was), where the races actually could be kind of frustrating and hacking camera's was just addicting (and there's a lot more to do!).
Combat in this game felt reminiscent of that in the Batman games although not done as well imo. This was mainly because of the not-too-good camera-work. Being able to make use of the environment while in combat made up for this. It's really satisfactory slamming some bad-guy's head into a car door while seeing the glass shatter all around.
All in all if you like open-world games like GTA this is definitely for you. For 4 bucks or euro's you can't go wrong. It's sure to keep you interested for a couple of dozens of hours.

To those who-like me-crave the sort of top-down loot fest action that arpg series like the Diablo, Torchlight, and Sacred series have provided in the past keep looking further because this game won't provide it. Released as "Maximus XV: Abraham Strong Space Mercenary" in Germany it was released in the US under its current title. At first it seems like a no brainer-lot's of loot, lots of monsters to kill, and set in a futuristic setting but there's not much to write home about here.
The game is grindy as hell due to the energy bits required to fuel any weapon worth anything doubling as your currency. This means the game punishes you for mistakes rather than turning them into learning opportunities. Death is severely punishing as well. If you don't save frequently you will have to go through everything you did before all over again. A system such as the one in Fate or Torchlight (Pay gold to respawn immediately, pay less gold to go back to the entrance, pay nothing to restart back in town) would have been far more beneficial, and way less annoying.
While the graphics are OK what few animations exist are stiff. The sound design is almost non-existent, and the soundtrack is forgettable. There's very little enemy variety, very little loot variety, and even less appearance variety. The story is minimal-standard go here, kill this many of that, come back fare-and there's very little variety as far as areas go, too.
The Tl;dr of this is that this is a very disappointing game, and I wouldn't recommend it unless you (like me) crave DIablo in space so much that you'll play a game so deserving of the title 'Hack' that the developers made it part of its name.

Bastion is an excellent top-down brawler with an even better story.  The combat is simple but hard to master, and the variety of weapons allows huge flexibility.  The narration is really where this game stands out, your entire journey will be spoken out loud.
Combat starts out pretty straightforward, it's just the WASD keys and click to attack.  You start out with a hammer and a 'repeater', a ranged weapon.  The great thing is that these weapons remain relevant: all the weapons are balanced nicely, except for a couple of endgame cannon sort of things.  Your character has two weapon slots and an ability slot.  A great thing about this game is that no weapons are designated as 'primary' or 'seconday'.  Also, you are not restricted to having a melee and a ranged weapon.  You can have two melee weapons or two ranged weapons in whatever order you like.
There are not a plethora of enemy types, but Bastion still manages to suprise with its varied combinations of enemies.  The first few levels are mainly one-type-at-a-time, but after that you'll have to fight turrets while dodging 'gasfella' attacks while getting mobbed by squirts.  The boss fights are dynamic and unique as well.  Sometimes the bosses are simply just larger, recolored versions of other enemies, but at least their attack patterns are new and tough.
There isn't much since you are almost always in search of the next core, but there are world areas that consist of weapon based minigames.  There are prizes, usually crafting items necessary for weapon upgrades, but first place prizes will be powerful equipable abilities for the respective weapon.  These world areas are a nice quick break from fighting monsters and are worthwhile for the aforementioned abilities.
Logistics-wise, the game is very simple.  When you level up, you get more health.  You can also drink one additional brew to increase your stats or weapon abilities.  Once you are suffciently far in the story you may activate idols for different gods that make enemies more difficult in certain ways but increase shard drop-rate.  Your inventory is just all the crafting items yoou have picked up, and is essentially infinitely large, since yo can only get rid of your items by using them to upgrade a weapon.
The story is very good and makes the game so much more fun to play.  The narrator's voice fits perfectly with the game.  And you are responsible for some decisions at the end which will affect the ending.  Unfortunately the game is a little shorter than I'd like it to be, but its merits far outweigh this.  If I had to give Bastion a score, it would be 9/10.

I wrote a review based on the demo and now that I've played it I can give a proper review.
Fran Bow is based off of swedish folklore and you take on the row of the titular character: Fran Bow.
You're a young girl in a mental ward for children. You don't want to be there. You want to find Mr Midnight and get to Aunt Grace. That's how the story starts.
From escaping the mental ward to trying to find your way home, Fran Bow does not lose any lustre as you encounter new characters, new situations and various puzzles to keep you entertained and curious.
Although it is not always easy to work out some puzzles, Fran Bow's thoughts are more than enough to help you work them out eventually.
Upon finishing the game however, I've found myself deciphering it in countless ways as it's true meaning is not given a clear definition.
If Fran Bow 2 was ever put into production, I would definitely be amongst the first to buy it!

i have to say
so far Northgard is one of the best games i've played in a long time & it's not even fully released
it's not perfect but still lots of fun with high replayability value ːsteamhappyː
Northard's basic genre is RTS with settlement building
it combines additional features from other genres, turn based strategy, tower defense, survival
currently it contains "only" the skirmish mode
but since i play usually rather skirmish so for me the most important part is already included
features :
3 clans, a 4th is announced : Wolf, Goat, Stag & Raven
3 difficulty levels *(see below under negative points)
different win scenarios : Fame, Wisdom, Trade, Domination, Map Special (those options were included via update)
wonders : Wyvern, Yggdrasil, Gate of Helheim, Relic of the Gods, Magma Field to forge the Sword of Odin
a neutral trading partner, Jotun giants
maps are generated randomly
3 different area enemies : Wolfs, Draugr, Valkyries
seasons with harsh winters & elevated wood & food consumption
hunger & freezing causes illnes, Healers heal the populace
3 different difficulty events : Rats (causing food scarcity), Earthquakes (causing buildings damage) & Blizzards (causing extremely elevated wood & food consumption)
the entire map is disected in smaller areas, every area contains certain features (monster, AI enemy, ressources), often several combined
AI enemies & monster are agressively crossing borders forcing the player to interact & actively or at least passively defend the area with a tower
one has to build a functioning settlement io to get the military going
4 food ressources : gathering, hunting, fishing, sheeps (only Goat clan)
building & upgrading ressources : wood, stone, iron
all ressources can be acquired via trade
every area has a limited number of buildings which varies, the Goat clan has several Lore achievements to unlock allowing it to build additional buildings per area
announced is multiplayer & a campaign
the game gets updated often & the devs ask for suggestions from the players
negative points :
the game has difficulties with Intel graphics chips, causing black screen, not starting, visual distortions, the devs are working to improve the playability there, there were several updates already addressing those issues
balancing of the clans is somewhat off, Goat clan overpowered, Wolf clan underpowered
* as far i've played it, the 3 difficulty levels consist mainly of the different scarcity of ressources at the start, the maps generate purely randomly not considering the difficulty level & therefore easy mode is too hard & hard mode is too easy
few random crashes
but since the game saves regularly, it's not big of a drama
conclusion :
a fine RTS with some new twists to the genre
this review is not complete, it does not mention every feature included, there are some more & there will be probably added more with updates like eg female vikings announced after some players asked for that feature
review written after 100 hours played
all 16 achievements unlocked

Great game. I don't think I really need to tell you what Mortal Kombat is and what it's about, so I'm just going to briefly describe what it is before going into detail about how the PC port is.
Mortal Kombat is a solid fighting game with great gameplay mechanics. I'm sure everybody already knows how Mortal Kombat plays so I'll talk a bit about what's new in this version. MK9 introduces X-Ray moves, which are really powerful moves you can unleash when your special meter is maxed. You can also use that same meter to dish out amplified versions of your special attacks. The story mode basically encapsulates the events of MK1 all the way to MK3 and is quite humorous at times. You also have a few new characters and a ton of other modes, like ladder, challenge tower, and test your luck. Also, it should go without saying the PC version comes with all the DLC that was on the consoles. Honestly, if you like fighting games, you WILL love MK9.
Now onto the port. The graphics are much better on the PC version with crisper textures and higher resolutions, the framerate runs flawlessly with everything maxed out, and I'm not having any delays with my input when I'm playing with either my keyboard or my controller. Functionally, it works fine. The only thing that looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥are the cutscenes, the developers pre-rendered them on a 720p resolution (I'm guessing 1280x720 from the looks of things) so when it gets upscaled on a 1080p resolution it ends up looking like♥♥♥♥♥♥ developers really need to stop doing this but since this is a port of a 2 year old game it's to be expected.
Where it falls is in the Online mode. It works, but it's very crude. People's mics are always on with no option to turn it off, if you're pitted against someone with a crap PC the game slows itself down for both you and the guy you're fighting, and here and there you may have a disconnect issue from nowhere. I doubt any of this is going to get patched so if you're buying this game with fighting online in mind, I'd do more research before buying. Another possible flaw of the port is that I've heard reports that people will have FPS issues if they have AA off, so make sure you have yours on at least 2x.
Overall, if you like fighting games and have a controller, pick this up and have some fun! Just beware if you're buying this just for the Online mode as your mileage may vary. Highly recommended.

(Disclaimer:  I was a volunteer English proof reader for this game for the last four months of its development.  I also contributed as a backer to the Indiegogo campaign which funded some of the development of this game.)
I absolutely adore this game.  If you like point and click adventure games,  please give this one a whirl.  And if you've never tried a point and click adventure game, I think this one will make you love them forever.
The art is gorgeous, the animations are beautiful to look at, the sound effects are plentiful and well designed, and the ever changing music adds so much to the ambiance of the game.  But above all, the story of the game is so detailed and rich and keeps you interested to see what happens next.  If you're like me, when you finish the game, you'll definitely wish the story wasn't over.
Many people complain about puzzles in adventure games being illogical and that it's difficult to figure out what the game developer had in mind for a solution.  Well, the puzzles in Fran Bow are very logical, the items needed to solve the puzzle are always within a screen or two of where they are used to solve the puzzle, and solving the puzzles always gives the player a good sense of satisfaction when they are completed.  Solving puzzles without the need for a walkthrough is one indication that a game is well designed, and, in my opinion, this game meets that test--I think the puzzles can be solved by an observant player without a walkthrough.
This game has two major game mechanics which are truly original and inspired designs of the developers.  Both make the game a joy to play and allow the player to see even more of the delicious art design of the single artist who designed and single-handedly drew all the art and animations in the game.  There are so many little details built into the game, involving art, animation, and programming--the footprints made in the snow, which are made as the characters walks over freshly fallen snow, which then fill in as the snow continues to fall, with the sound of crunching snow as the character walks, for example--that absolutely show the level of detail and love the two indie developers of Fran Bow put into the game, all to make the story feel so very real for the player.
I believe that if you play this game, you will not be disappointed.  You will fall in love with the characters in the story, you'll root for the success of the main character, cheer for her, feel both happy at times, and sad at times for her, and boo and hiss at those characters who appear to be against her.  I both laughed and cried while playing this game, and I believe that you will too when you play.
It's clear to me that this is a very special game that makes you think about the things said in the game.  The two-person development team poured much love, time, and hard work into the game.  You will likely want to play the game more than once in order to absorb all the story told in it--it is that intracate.  The result is a wonderful story that you will remember for a long time, and Fran Bow just may become your favorite adventure game, like it is for me.  I highly recommend it.

A very polished experience, especially compared to the original! It improves on the original with a new graphical style, tighter controls, improved item combinations, new preset challenge runs, and tons of new items, pickups, dungeon layouts, bosses and more! It's a straight-up upgrade to the original!
Gameplay resolves around a very simple but well-executed formula: explore, collect items that incrementally improve your stats, kill the boss, progress down to the next floor, repeat. Nothing beats the feeling of getting all the best items and becoming an overpowered killing machine!
The game is very difficult and unforgiving. In true roguelike fashion, the game features perma-death: if you die, that's it - start again from floor 1! No second chances! You'll have to make do with a different dungeon and a different set of items on your next run!
Tons of replayability - hundreds of unlockables (including characters, items, challenges and additional bosses!) and thousands of interesting item combinations. 100+ hours of content - no exaggeration!
If you love pain, you'll love this.

===
Gluon is a space simulation sandbox game with management and building elements. This game is set in a rather distant future, where space colonization already took foot on many planets. One day, the Imperial forces, for reasons unknown, decide to attack Earth, manage to destroy its fleets and successively devastate the planet. You will impersonate Ares, the pilot of a modular transport which happened to not be near earth when the attack happened. Startled and confused by this sudden imperial attack, you will have to get your wits together and find a way to rescue people and then mount a counter-attack against the forces that destroyed your home planet. This game includes exploration, ship building and resource management elements, to create a feature-wise rather complete space sim, or at least this is what it seems.
===
Gluon's gameplay is divided mainly into three aspects, which are:
Management: You will have to manage a variety of resources and people in order to accomplish your goals and build a fleet: mine asteroids to get metals and rare ores, make deals with space stations to settle your colonists on planets and produce food for the fleet, get mining licenses or you'll have troubles. There are honestly many aspects to manage about your ship and fleet, too bad all these management operations are run via a very badly designed user interfacem that will make even the most simple operation very clunky and unintuitive, it looks like in this aspect, the game is coming right out of 1998.
Ship Building: Your ship is composed of modular sections of different types, each one can be modified to use a variety of tools, for example combat sections will be used to host various weapons, while engine ones will be used to, obviously move the ship. All sections are of cubical shape and will automatically snap to each other. Each section will have requirements in materials to be built and requirements of energy to work properly. All this is directed by your command module, an indipendent cube-ship that can detatch from your main vessel at any time and be indipendent, even if for a short time. what i noticed is that ship building is quite bugged especially when it comes to detatching the module, i personally had to replay seven times the tutorial sequence because each time i detatched my command module the ship exploded, because of bugs. This will happen more often than you think, just because the ship building system is bugged as hell.
Combat: when in combat you have your ship's weapon and your fighter ships at your disposal. Your ship is the main firepower out there, and fighters will only be good to divert enemy attention from you while you fire at them. Your weapons are automated, as your fighters are, you just have to move the ship around and decide if or if not to retreat. You can select which target to hit but that's it. Generally i noticed the combat is quite slow and clunky and generally does not give out that involvement sense that should be there in space combat games.
Read above
There are not many planets to explore, all are already charted on your starmap so forget about the sense of discovery that is an important part of space exploration games. The campaign will put you through a series of objectives, and there are secondary missions given out at space stations to get some money or resources. Missions are of few types and become quite dull after not long. content wise this game is not very large, especially for being a space sim, honestly it gets uninteresting very soon, also because of its clunkyness.
===
Graphics are 3D, but terrible at that. Even at maximum settings, there is very noticeable aliasing, textures are low quality espexially on planets, art and color palettes are few and of forgettable quality or craftmanship. Space looks static and dead, no effects or particles to get you that "aliveness" that is typical of space in modern space sims. Not good.
Sufficent, when it does not bug and a sound loops indefinitely until you restart the game. And that happens quite a lot.
For the amount of polygons and textures we have in this game, it should run well even on old machines.
Crashes were a few, still a major issue for a NOT early access game.
Very basic, will try to kill you but won't engage in complex fleet manouvers like you'd expect.
Absolutely disastrous. An apocalypse. The interface and the way menus and actions are designed is awful. To do even the simpliest thing it will be an endless pressing fof buttons and menus, interface is unintuitive, unresponsive and just uncomfortable.
English translation is terrible and probably was made with an automated program, i hope so at least. The storyline is a stereotype and very boring and uninteresting. The game is riddled with minor to medium severity bugs which take an heavy toll on experience enjoyment. There is no difficulty setting for AI. The game does not properly render 1920x1080 at fullscreen but will instead be an obscure resolution of like 1918x1060 or approximatley that, at least what resulted from screenshots was this.
===
This is a space sim you should avoid. With a few very mediocre points at its favor and a massive quantity of points against it, this game should really be an early access title, or rather IT IS an early access in disguise. do not waste your money and time on this and move along to better space games, because there are a lot.

I got it for free, and that's all anyone should pay for it. It's a ten year old sci-fi knockoff of Diablo II, probably produced on the cheap to profit off of Blizzard's success. The game balance is pretty off; it's hard to progress without abusing free heals. Nothing respawns, so you get a finite amount of resources, and given that there are enemies in the first area that can kill you in five or six hits, you either have to tank them and heal, or try (and probably fail) to sidestep their erratic attack patterns and plink away at them from range.
The "magic" system, Hi-Tech Devices, seems fairly interesting, but it's stat-gated such that you won't be able to use more than one or two of them in the first ten levels or so, or even longer if you're not putting most of your stat points into Knowledge, which will gimp everything but your energy weapons, including your ability to wear armor.
It also tried to implement a currency/ammo tradeoff, by making your Energy (which you use to fire laser guns and such) rechargeable only by spending 100 of your (finite) currency, which just ends up being incredibly limiting, especially in the early stages of the game.
It's nice for killing time, but nothing about it seems to have aged well. It might get better later on, once there are more options available, but the first few hours were fairly tedious, and really gave only one style of play a chance of progression. Pick up Path of Exile or Marvel Heroes if you really need an action-RPG.

A tremendous, perhaps even startling achievement, "Bastion" is everything great in gaming.
It starts with a tremendously accessible and altogether fluid control system that works beautifully on PC. It adds to that a number of "micro-customizations" that let you nudge the core mechanics towards your favored playstyle. These micro-customizations take the form of weapons, weapon upgrades, "spirits" that act as passive skills, and shrine idols that make things tougher.
On top of that, the game places very nicely crafted art. "Bastion's" visual stylings are highly distinctive, fun to look at, and also completely functional as a gameplay element.
The final layer is a wrenching, yet never overdone or melodramatic story. There are very rich, mysterious elements that get woven in to fire up your imagination, and those elements are given with the same sensitivity and subtlety as the character arcs. The story is told almost entirely through gameplay, which keeps the narrative entirely connected to what's going on.
...and that soundtrack. Goodness gracious, that soundtrack. A person could buy this game for the sole purpose of listening to it. The music is superb (especially the main theme and the blues/ Americana tinged tracks) and the narrator could read a phone book without becoming tiresome.
As far as I can tell, "Bastion" is flawless.

A game too smart for most of its players.
The game has a bit of a learning curve, but nothing too intimidating. Once you've understood what roles do what, you can start your own investigation based on the result of others.
People could lie or tell the truth. It's up to you to decide if the evidence supports the claims.
Unfortunately, this is too much for many people to handle. Those who take advantage of this game's features will love it and contribute greatly to their team. Those who are lazy or can't keep up will just jump straight to the most common question, "role?"
Asking someone's role will do 1 of 2 things.
1. They claim to be a town member. People who are against the town members will eventually target them and kill them.
2. They will lie and claim to be someone's role. That person may speak up and there will end up being 2 people who claim the same role. One will die in some way to reveal the truth. Depending on the unveiling, the other person will still die because the opposing team will discover their role.
This method is counter-productive and ignores the game's potential. Don't be THAT guy.
Nonetheless, the game is very fun and allows players to kill or be killed, lie or be lied to, or be the saint of the group and hope people take your word. Anything goes in the Town of Salem and although every ending doesn't end in complete shock, by the time players have figured out who is who, it's too late, so you must be quick, remember who said what, and sometimes trust your gut feeling to win the game.

The netcode is decent, ranked feels competitive and it places me against similarly skilled players, the moves and combos are satisfying. I guess Im part of the few that play this almost purely because of online for ranked, and for that this game is actually really fun and rewarding.

The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth puts you in control of the titular Isaac (or one of the many different unlockable characters), trying to survive the horrors of his basement, caverns, essentially depictions of Hell itself and more subtly creepy stuff, because the alternative is getting sacrificed by his delusional Mother, following the order of God to kill her son. It's way more open to interpretation, but that's the initial presentation of the plot.
The game is played from a top-down perspective, with pixelated, though impressively detailed and fluid sprites and models. It keeps a consistent, if mildly unsettling tone.
The sound effects are distinct and satisfying - from the growls and shrieks of enemies, to the subtle differences between picking up a penny, a nickel or a dime. Every level sequence has a musical theme attached to it, which gains a few more background instruments when there's a lot of enemies. Boss battle music is great.
This is a roguelite, so expect two things: permadeath (unless you have items which grant extra lives, your run ends when you're completely out of health) and random generation (levels are composed of random rooms, room sizes, designs, enemies, items and so on). The sheer unpredictability of any run is a contributing factor to its longevity, alongside the ridiculous item collection: who knows if, on this run, you'll get, say, Brimstone? And what crazy combo can you discover or make use of with it? And even if you don't find what you're looking for, the game expects you to push forward, weighing together chance, risk and opportunity.

SFV started off with a poor launch, continues to suffer numerous server side issues, lack of communication from the developers, overpriced DLC and still hasn't truely recovered from being an unfinished product that was clearly rushed out before it was actually ready to ship.
However, having spent nearly 500 hours & almost every day since Feburary 2016 playing the title, not including the beta a few months earlier, it's been some of the most fun & engaging time I've spent with any video game in the last 30 years.
Nearly a year later I'm still learning & improving with my main fighter, Zangief, after a brief dabble with both Laura & Claw. If I really wanted too, I could spend countless months getting to an equally proficient level with the other characters in the cast, many more who I presume are still to come in the years ahead with Season 2 trickling out another 5 over the next 12 months.
I've made some great friends in the fighting game community over at twitch & on discord channels thanks to this game & even started regularly tuning into the CPT tournament events to watch and learn from high level play. Something I never felt the desire too with games such as CS:GO & Hearthstone. I've become familiar enough with all the 'professional' players such as who they main, what their personal rivalries are etc to the point where if I was asked I'd claim that this was my 'sport' the same way others may follow more traditional games like football or hockey.
Despite the numerous negative posts you'll find about SFV's server woes - justified as they are still on-going, finding a game here online in the UK doesn't typically take longer than 20-30 seconds. Setting the match making options to 4-5 bars only & 'ASK' typically solves the laggy match issue 90% of the time but despite this the connection bar can still be misleading.
Due to the cross compatability with the Playstation 4, it also makes playing a fighting game on the PC more viable than ever in terms of player population which is the major problem with this type of game on steam and pc in general being a somewhat niche category in the world of MOBA's & team FPS's.
While it helped I had previous experience with both SFIV beforehand & the various incarnations of SFII back in the day, the amount of resource there is both in game with training & challenge modes along with unending online resource should mean anyone with a passing interest in fighting or competitive gaming should find it easy enough to get to a semi-competent level. The systems in game aren't as difficult to learn as KoF or a GG/BlazBlue & the removal of focus from IV makes the game far more beginner friendly.
Unlike other online competitive games your progression really is dictated by how much time you personally put into practising rather than having the quality of your team mates & RNG be a factor. While learning frame data, character specific MU's & optimal punishes will speed your ascent up the league ranking, it's still more than possible to have an enjoyable time just going by gut feeling and a basic knowledge of target combos and special moves.
Despite the positives there have been numerous & sizeable negatives since release.
The rootkit debacle which (thankfully) is now gone probably cut a sizeable chunk of the more casual player base away from the game along with the repeated & on-going failure for them to implement a proper rage quitting system. The single player story mode also took several months to be released and was frankly, quite rubbish.
I would say though that the people still complaining about a lack of single player mode are oblivious to realise that this was a game mode designed to compensate for a lack of online play in consoles back in the 1990's-2000's & now completely redundant. You don't get the same amount of negative feedback about Counter Strike or Overwatch not having a single player campaign, it's quite frankly ridiculous.
Overall SFV is a fantastic product & compared to titles like which despite phenomenal sales were completely broken in terms of netcode & framerate & ultimately abandoned by their developer after less than a year (cough nethersoft cough) it's definitely worth a purchase & what is by now quite often a bargain price.

Countless hours spent in this game just to learn and relearn the basics of the gameplay and how everything works in this randomily filled basement of hellbound monsters while having to kill your very own mother and beyond.
I've got to admit right off the bat, "Binding of Isaac: Rebirth" is such an improvement from the first game that it's hard to go back from the first one. The controls feel a lot more fluid and all of the items and upgrades have been tweeked and balanced. The addition of more enemies and bosses is also a big plus! The only nitpick I have is that the soundtrack is not as catchy as the first game, but even then... I got used to it after a bunch of playthroughs.
All in all, There is plenty of replay value in this pacakge that will leave you wanting more and more. This is the type of game I will be thinking and going back to, time and time again.

Clan Wars is probably the most innovative Worms game to date offering the same diversity of classes as Revolution albeit with some tweaks for balancing.
In case you're not familiar with them:
Weapons variety is largely the same as in Revolution from the traditional bazooka to some of the more wacky ones, many of which have multiple uses, like the Lightning Strike allowing you to heal worms, resurrect dead ones, convert turrets and activate inactive mines and magnets. Unlike classic Worms and Armageddon the Ninja Rope functions more like a rope than a mix between a rope and a ladder, meaning you'll weigh it down and have to use your momentum to swing around. Other mobility items, both old and new to the genre, include such items as Jetpack, Water Jetpack and Teleport Gun to name but a few.
As far as gameplay goes Clan Wars is an optimized Revolution meaning no lag when water sloshes about. However, both games are made in the same engine which limits animations to 30 frames per second regardless of what fps the actual game runs on. Note the game itself can run above 30 fps; only the worm animations are limited.
So all in all I think it's one of the freshest Worms games out there since Armageddon.

A substandard effort by Artifex Mundi still makes for a tolerable hidden-object game, as they normally uphold a high standard.  This is far from the best AM has produced, though.
The
series started weakly, improved noticeably in the second title, and now slumps right back again in the finale.  The HO scenes themselves are pretty good, and the other puzzles respectable, if unoriginal.  The storyline, sadly, is forgettable, throwaway garbage.
Even though HO games never offer branching paths, multiple endings, or any other element of meaningful player influence over story events,
did a pretty good job of creating an illusion of player agency. It cast you as an investigator pursuing a paranormal mystery, and events of the story involved actively searching for clues and following up on them.  In
the same character doesn't really investigate anything; she enters a creepy haunted mansion-type structure, and then marches through a standard array of HO overworld environments -- mostly decaying manor interior rooms and underground chambers, until she reaches a completely clichéd "close the Hellgate" scenario.  Along the way, she is gradually spoonfed the tale of her mysterious past.
The storyline never features the heroine making a meaningful decision, or formulating and executing a plan.  Cutscene events are always things done
her, never
her.  NPC interactions are abrupt, perfunctory, and rather implausible.  Remove the
name from it, and remove the expository kiosks that spew backstory, and all you have left is an assemblage of stock HO environments that could have been made for almost any game, bolted together in an arbitrary sequence.  The playtime is a bit short, too.
also uses the old "find the statue's missing eye" progress barrier at least four times, perhaps more, with the majority of those instances using identical statues, which no doubt offered some savings on graphic design.  In a title already suffering from blandness and appearing generic, finding the same eye for the same statue over and over again really didn't help to distinguish it.
There's an awful lot of garbage cluttering up the Hidden Object genre, and
is far from being the worst.  It's playable, and graphically nice.  It's completely forgettable, though, and doesn't manage to stand out from the pack in any way.
is an acceptable choice for the HO player who chews through games like popcorn and always needs another, but for those who only play a few, the same publisher has much better games to offer.

This is a little known point and click adventure game with a surreal horror edge to it. I felt I should give it my praise, as modest as that is, since it deserves more attention. The puzzles are quite challenging, but nothing that will make you tear your hair out. The mood swings in an almost bipolar fashion, between charming surrealism and truly disturbing horror. Perhaps the most notable aspect of this game is the art direction, featuring a number of different mediums of animation.
