Most excellent coming off of Aliens: Colonial Marines.  Overall a well made game whose minor gripes are far outweighed by the great ambiance it conveys and graphics/AI that holds up well several years later.
ATTN: This is mainly an explaination of my opinion of the Marine portion of the game and how it stacks up to the ill fated Aliens: Colonial Marines game.
To be clear:
I consider myself an avid Alien(s) fan and enjoy the Predator movies.  I did not care much for the AVP cinematic attempts.  I begrudingly accept Alien 3 and 4.  AVP 1 was the first game to truly terrify me and AVP to was one of my favorite examples of how a great story in a scary♥♥♥♥♥game can motivate playing through the fear.  Damn you Level 3 to this day.
Now, AVP 2010:
I first played this briefly on a rental on PS3 when it came out back in 2010.  I was playing in the afternoon in a sunny house.  I was not overly impressed with it then, but I also only played a few missions before returning it.
Time passed, Aliens:Colonial Marines E3 demo happened.  I saw that and declared "That is what AVP 2010 should have been like!!"
Now Aliens:Colonial Marines has come and gone and I very nearly spit on it, though I have managed to find a small amout of redemption in its DLC.  SMALL AMOUNT. But it had to be played.
After that unpleasent experience, I have returned to AVP 2010 with a new perspective. And I tend to play it at night, in the dark, with the sound turned up as it should be.
AVP 2010 is the younger brother of the game Colonial Marines should have been.  Marine mission-wise it excels at making you uncomfortable, remembering that hordes of slathering xenos are not so much terrifying as unpleasent when used to excess (CM), and using wisely the detailed environments and sound effects during well paced moments without combat that give you time to think about what's around the next corner and how low your ammo is.
Marine-wise, this is where you must go to wash the stench of Colonial Marines from you.
Alien and Predator missions are where it falls short of AVP2, losing some of the creativity and story telling excellence along the way.
I wish we could lose the HUD and I would rather a motion tracker you had to check more like CM, but as an experience, AVP has what I was looking for, and that is to feel like a PBI grunt in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation surrounded by nasty giant bugs wishing for a platoon of Ultimate Badasses that are never coming.

Despite its cons, this game is still a fine HO / Puzzle game. Being the sequel of Demon Hunter 2, this third installment can be played independently if you wish. Every Demon Hunter of this sequel shares 2 common things : fighting demons to save the world from darkness and the medallion you almost always have with you.

"Having defeated the Beast from another dimension, Dawn Harlock had hoped to spend the rest of her life in peace. However, circumstances have placed the life of a child at stake and brought her out of retirement to once again solve supernatural riddles and hunt hellish demons. Can the world's foremost paranormal detective muster the courage to follow the dark path and face off against an enemy from beyond? With you as her guide, she stands a chance."

Graphics are nice as well as the animations. Only the cut scenes aren't optimized for higher resolutions.

Sounds are find and the music is nice.

You will mostly hear the story at the beginning and at the end of the game. There is an additional story you will listen to, while recovering the parts of your medallion : a story from the past.

Like any Artifex Mundi game, the game have some common features :
3 difficulties
A diary for your objectives
A map mostly used to fast travel (if you are lazy to walk)
A game overview, mostly for the achievements
A hint feature
An inventory
The game has 4 gameplay parts :
Puzzle scenes
Hidden Objects  (HO) scenes
Items interacting / crafting parts
Fighting demons
For the puzzle scenes, you will have mostly the same one as you will find in any other Artifex Mundi game but most of them are so easy to solve.
The HO scenes are relatively easy and are one of the key point of the game because they are nicely done. You have the regular one where you need to find items according to the text list, the one with the shadow of the objects you need to find, the one where you need to find the same object several times and the story telling one where you need to find symbols.
Only the regular HO scene will have morphing objects, objects that morph to another a short amount of time. Mostly all the Ho scenes except the story one will need you to interact with the scene in order to find some objects.
The inventory is the second key point of the game as you will acquire many objects to help you in your journey. Some can be used as is and some can be interacted or combined. Interacting puzzles are interesting though I didn't know that throwing a glass jar of water would break a spell. And you will also need to craft some stuff according to a recipe or even repair things.
Finally you have a few fighting parts which you can't loose and don't have any time limit. It's a short puzzle where you need to find the unique symbols you don't share with the enemy’s spell.

They are easy and add a little challenge to the game. But like any Artifex mundi game : do not use hints and do not skip any puzzle or hidden objects scene.
Several achievements are collectibles related, so it's highly recommended that you follow a guide if you don't want to play the game twice. Mostly because you can't backtrack the first half of the areas of the game after you've reached a cut scene.

I got the full package (Main game and all DLC) whilst it was on special, thinking that it might occupy a few hours and expecting at sort of GTA-like. Boy.. was I ever suprised when I fired her up. Goodbye almost 3 solid weeks of gaming time as I found one of the most engaging and addictive games to ever hit my library.
The main hook for me, is the suberbly crafted storyline which engaged me immediately and kept me coming back for more in the best tradition of the saturday morning movie shorts (a la the old black and white Flash Gordon and Rocket man series). I just HAD to know "What happened next".
The gameplay itself is slick and well crafted (although I found it better by far when I abandoned mouse/ KB and switched to an X360 controller - almost heresy for me!). Combat is skillful and benefits from thinking about combining moves, rather than button mashing. However, if button mashing IS your thing, then not using combo moves and stringing together a chain of strikes is far from game breaking. The biggest thing for me was the removal of dependance upon guns. Not only did this add to the feeling of playing through a classic Hong Kong martial arts movie, but it made the appearence of weapons in missions seem all the more special.
The extra seek out content (health shrines, jade statues etc) add to the game and deliver a clever way of upgrading your survivablillity/ damage and so on that makes it far more worthwhile to seek out every little one. The way that you will encounter most through the main storyline however is a refreshing change from the go look in every nook and cranny method usually applied in such games.
The little boosts from clothing gave me a reason to use the in game money to purchase them (and to seek out the various shops for full sets) that I have never found reason to do in other titles.
At the end of the main game, I found myself hooked by the fun of the game to the point where for the first time in a very long while, I found myself determined to complete all the achievements and play all the DLC "just for the fun of it".. and on the subject of DLC "Nightmare in Northpoint" had me rolling around chuckling.. if you have ever had the pleasure of watching a classic chinese horror film like "Mr. Vampire", you'll know exactly what I'm talking about. Having a zombie/ ghost/ vampire add on that actually bases itself in traditional chinese interpretations of these things just added to the immersion factor.
Overall - 10/10 and worth every penny. (and a big kick up my own backside for not having bought the damned thing on release!)

I'm a little hesitant to recommend this one.  Doom 3 BFG Edition ties all three of the classic id Doom games together, with a dash of new content. Doom 1 is unchanged from The Ultimate Doom, and still comes with Thy Flesh Consumed.  Doom 2 on the other hand includes a new campaign, the formerly XBox 360 exclusive "No Rest For the Living."  However, the .WAD file has been slightly altered, making it incompatible with certain source ports.  The classic games don't run as smooth as a source port like GZDoom would, though you're free to take the .WADs and play them with your preferred Source Port if you so choose.
Doom 3 comes with the original Resurrection of Evil expansion, along with a new 8 level "Lost Mission" campaign, but has lost all mod support the original release had.  In addition to that, Doom 3 is rather taxing on your rig, even though the graphics haven't changed much.  The most you can do to tone this down is change the motion blur; pretty much all other settings are locked in place.  The whole game also refuses to work on certain GPUs without some fiddling as well, and if you use f12 as your screenshot key, the game thinks you're cheating and disables achievments.
All in all, this is a decent package for anyone new to the franchise and looking to get in, but weathered Doom veterans would be better off buying the original releases for the increased mod support.  You might want to consider getting this on your XBox or PS3 as well, since the PC port is a little unstable.

A tremendous, perhaps even startling achievement, "Bastion" is everything great in gaming.
It starts with a tremendously accessible and altogether fluid control system that works beautifully on PC. It adds to that a number of "micro-customizations" that let you nudge the core mechanics towards your favored playstyle. These micro-customizations take the form of weapons, weapon upgrades, "spirits" that act as passive skills, and shrine idols that make things tougher.
On top of that, the game places very nicely crafted art. "Bastion's" visual stylings are highly distinctive, fun to look at, and also completely functional as a gameplay element.
The final layer is a wrenching, yet never overdone or melodramatic story. There are very rich, mysterious elements that get woven in to fire up your imagination, and those elements are given with the same sensitivity and subtlety as the character arcs. The story is told almost entirely through gameplay, which keeps the narrative entirely connected to what's going on.
...and that soundtrack. Goodness gracious, that soundtrack. A person could buy this game for the sole purpose of listening to it. The music is superb (especially the main theme and the blues/ Americana tinged tracks) and the narrator could read a phone book without becoming tiresome.
As far as I can tell, "Bastion" is flawless.

Lots of strategic and tactical design making. This is the holy grail of RTS games. I played the original command & conquer series, warcraft before it was an MMO, starcraft, and even the original total annihilation.
This game took things up a notch and introduced orbital units along with multiple planets. Basically, the entire was once square playfield is not wrapped around a spherical planet. And, there can be multiple planets.
You have a lot of choices in how you can win or lose. You have the usual infantry (bots), vehicles, air, and unique orbital units. There is only one actual faction, but that is okay since it provides some uniformity to the game. Really allows you to dive down into the strategy and tactical aspects instead of having a rock, paper, scissors outlook to picking a certain factor with certain units.
Also, forget to mention the titan units or super units. These really help break open those tough games.
Its also a game that is all about expansion and aggression. If that play style is not for you then you might not like this game as much as others. However, you can still do successful turtling in certain games and situations. For example, you could create a custom game that prompted that style; but against other players and the A.I. you want to expand and get aggressive.
One aspect that is both negative and positive is the fact that you will find the gameplay overwhelming becuase of a need to manage multiple battles, bases, and planets in a single game. However, rest assured that you get better! It is not impossible to do it. It just feels unnatural because its... a challenge! And, fun to learn how as human to control so many different large seperated spatial areas in the game.
You do need to do some micro-management at the tactical to a large degree but there is also a giant need to do strategic big picture choices and ordering. For example, you might need to rapidly switch back and forth on a battle front to help keep your units grouped and moving properly, but at the same time, on the strategic level, you will have to be zoomed out looking for new metal sources, thinking about other planets, figuring out the best path throught the units.
The game offers the usual tiers of units. Of course, the higher tiers are quite powerful, but theres no complete abandonment of the lower tiers. They help soak up fire and are cheap to do it. Unless you are playing a weird turtle game you will usually find yourself in a fairly aggressive game where you do not have much time to build up a super sized army of the highest tier units -- unless your playing another human who lets you do it.
The best path to victory in this game is a quick death to the enemy before they can build more powerful units and weapons. Its a constant race to higher tiers and technology but this game gives a really awesome balance to it.

I'll start by saying that I have never played Sanctum 1, and write this review for other people like me who are new to the franchise.
As a tower defense game, it does little to reward creativity, and as a FPS it does little to reward skill.
Maps are typically open, allowing for a standard horizontal-maze style defense which is mathematically optimal in every scenario for creating the longest creep path. Different tower types are similar in damage and upgrade potential, making a choice in towers somewhat meaningless. Different styles of towers are geared towards different mobs, but one is nearly equivalent to any other against all mob types in many cases; at least for three of the most obvious choices in primary damage towers.
Character choice is extremely unbalanced, with the shotgun-wielding character capable of dropping the toughest creep in the game in a single shot, and all other characters being far less effective than a single tower. This makes the only important skill in the FPS side of the game being in the right place at the right time to drop the tough mobs.
Social aspects of the game are emphasized and facilitated well by the UI, with an effective (and kind of funny) text-to-speech program, and public matchmaking. However, addition of more players limits the ability for a group to think through tower defense design since build time is limited (loosely though, plenty of time for an individual to plan the field), and building resources are automatically divided amongst players.
Sanctum 2 may be a fun game for players who are playing with people they know, who can organize a well thought out tower defense layout in a relatively short amount of time, but other games such as Dungeon Defenders offer more potential for skill, creativity and character development.
No offense to Coffee Stain, but they should be spending more time with great (and hilarious) games like Goat Simulator.

A game too smart for most of its players.
The game has a bit of a learning curve, but nothing too intimidating. Once you've understood what roles do what, you can start your own investigation based on the result of others.
People could lie or tell the truth. It's up to you to decide if the evidence supports the claims.
Unfortunately, this is too much for many people to handle. Those who take advantage of this game's features will love it and contribute greatly to their team. Those who are lazy or can't keep up will just jump straight to the most common question, "role?"
Asking someone's role will do 1 of 2 things.
1. They claim to be a town member. People who are against the town members will eventually target them and kill them.
2. They will lie and claim to be someone's role. That person may speak up and there will end up being 2 people who claim the same role. One will die in some way to reveal the truth. Depending on the unveiling, the other person will still die because the opposing team will discover their role.
This method is counter-productive and ignores the game's potential. Don't be THAT guy.
Nonetheless, the game is very fun and allows players to kill or be killed, lie or be lied to, or be the saint of the group and hope people take your word. Anything goes in the Town of Salem and although every ending doesn't end in complete shock, by the time players have figured out who is who, it's too late, so you must be quick, remember who said what, and sometimes trust your gut feeling to win the game.
What more can I say about this game that already hasn't been said already? This game will make you ragequit and come back for more.

Everything about Demon Hunter 3 is pleasantly decent, like its hidden object scenes, story, or artwork… but somehow the result is still entirely forgettable.
When I finished playing Demon Hunter 3: Revelation, my impression was that it is insultingly short, but at least it did its job. If you buy it, expect around two hours of pleasant hidden object gameplay, but also something you will forget by the next day.
It seems like as if the main direction in the game’s design was to meet basic expectations but nothing more. The story uses the most common elements: you are looking for a kidnapped child through a set of usual fantasy scenery. The hidden object scenes feel more like a randomised asset collection than in most games, but at least this makes them challenging enough to be fun. The puzzles are the same we saw in dozens of other games on the SPARK engine. The only thing that really stands out is the art, which is better than in any of the previous games.
This game is pretty much the perfect bundle fodder: not worth the full price, but recommended when you get it cheap.

When it comes to hidden object games I admit to being a little bit picky. I enjoy a mix of a good story with good gameplay, quality audio and visuals also help but if a game lacks in that department I can forgive it.
is the third in this series and so far I haven’t been fully impressed with the titles. The first one I didn’t enjoy much and the second was fun but could have been better, I wasn’t sure what to expect from this title. Thankfully, I was pleasantly surprised, and I found it to be the best game in the trilogy. While the story is still the weakest point, the game is overall a good package. You don’t need to play the first two to enjoy this installment but it can’t hurt to be up-to-date on things.
The main character is once again Dawn Ashmore, an orphan with mysterious red eyes who works as a demon hunter. The story is set twenty five years after her first adventure and for the past five years since the second game she’s been living a peaceful life. This peace ends when Dawn's detective friend calls her to the scene of a murder where the victim’s daughter was kidnapped because the evidence pointed to the supernatural. Indeed, Dawn finds herself in another battle with demons in a race to save the child’s life. Along the way, she finds clues to her own past that have come back to haunt her on this very case. I enjoyed the how the story shed some light on Dawn’s past but she still doesn’t have much personality. What’s worse, the game ends with a lot of loose ends and the bonus chapter doesn’t answer any of them since it takes place before the main events in the story. Despite being a tad bit cliche, and the final demon being completely underwhelming, it was a good story for the game to cover.
What I really enjoyed, however, was the gameplay. It takes what worked well in the previous games and expands upon that. The hidden object scenes offer a nice variety of ways to play, using lists or even shadows and other gimmicks. Things were kept fresh from scene to scene and the you never had to play a hidden object scene twice either. The game also offers plenty of puzzles, most of which aren’t too difficult or frustrating to players. Your inventory system is there as well, with interactive items which almost like small puzzles themselves as you need to find and combine items to make new ones. The game has a useful map which allows teleporting and shows you areas of interest depending on what difficulty you play one; you have three to choose from as well as a custom option. There are also plenty of collectables to find hidden around the game and bonus features where you can replay certain hidden objects or puzzles whenever you like.
The visuals of the game are great, everything is dark and spooky fitting the tone of the story well. The characters are still a bit stiff when they walk and talk but there has been notable improvements since the previous titles. Despite having a darker tone, I found I had no trouble finding items while playing the hidden object scenes which is very important since I have bad eyes. The audio also wraps up the package, the music fits and most of the voice acting is just fine. There are no glaring issues with the audio or visuals that hinder how the game is played.
Aside from being a bit of a nitpick when it comes to the story, my biggest issue with
is that it’s rather short. I finished the main game and bonus chapter in under three hours. However, because I enjoyed playing the game as much as I did it really didn’t feel that short. I was surprised to see I had clocked in such a small amount of time, the game felt longer. And in the end that’s what counts, sure it was a short game but it was time well spent. If you’ve played the other two installments then I recommend grabbing this one as well, or even if you’re new to the
franchise. If you play the game on Steam you will be treated to trading cards as well as plenty achievements to hunt after. I personally look forward to more adventures with Dawn, her story is shaping up very well.

Here's the last chapter in Dawn Ashmore's story. After finding why her adoptive father died and defeating twice Ragnar, Dawn was called by her friend, Officer Brown (who was trying to arrest her in the previous game), to investigate a supernatural disappearance and find a little girl with red-eyes too. Revelation will give answers to Dawn: who were her parents.
Artifex Mundi is publishing this trilogy on Steam but remember how it began: the first game was plagued (and still is) with bad translation. But the second game corrected everything, apart that there were some plotholes.
Revelation is set 25 years after the first game and 5 years after the second one. Dawn lost her precious amulet but she's still good with magic. However, the story is badly written: while the idea of discovering Dawn's real past is nice, the rest is just non-sense. You don't know why Officer Brown was kidnapped, you don't know why Father Jones was murdered, the man that was scared in the greenhouse is just useless and the end is very abrupt: how come your ancient enemy is now willing to help you, like that, without even speaking together or something like that. Was it for the bonus chapter? But the bonus chapter is involving Brown before calling Dawn.
Besides, Dawn's appearance is always changing and not even sticking to her original design. I'm not saying that the graphics are bad, they're quite creepy and nice but for the cutscenes, Dawn isn't even close to what she should have looked. Even her portrait is different from reality, when the other characters have the same form than in the previous/current game. Why Dawn got a different treatment?
The gameplay is quite the same: pick items, use them, clear hidden objects scenes (with one that I've liked as it was finding items to move), solve puzzles. Minigames are easy, hidden objects scenes are good. The hunt for special objects is also interesting : scary dolls, coins that will open a chest, portraits with characters from the past and present and a biography.
But even the biographies are wrong: the priest is called Father Jones in the game but he has a different name in the portrait. Same for the doc inside the manor: he's called Hughes but is Andrew or Scott in the biography.
Anyway, the soundtrack is nice and voice acting is good.
But you bet that after a bad start with translation and a good second opus, Revelation is just... a big let down. The story has many plotholes, nothing seems coherent. I've still enjoyed it but yeah, the trilogy Demon Hunter is probably not the best in Artifex Mundi's publishing catalogue.

The difference between BFG and Doom3 with mods is:
--------------------------------------------------------------
You can pay Beth to upgrade Doom 3 to HD with all the nice bells and whistles and get BFG.

Cost: Time (how much is your life worth to you)
--------------------------------------------------------------

The Stock version with mods will give you the closest feel to the origional game but there are more drawbacks then the pro stock preachers will admit. Animation even with mods is off useing todays technology. Unless you have a system that was pulled from Doom3's day the game plays different and the animations, gameplay, feel, and preformance is just a bit off. For example the characters eyes are off pitch during animation causing some glances (like dievous gesture) to make the eye roll into the head.

You do however get to enjoy a quick and easy option to play doom3 in hd with high preformance. The upgraded design of the game and ability to set your video without having to edit cfg files is quite nice.
In the end its up to the player.

For a long time I've been waiting for Team 17 to release a working version of Worms World Party that was compatible with a version of Windows beyond 98. I don't really think thats ever going to happen because Team 17 insist that Armageddon reaches feature paritywith WWP before thats possible, and they no longer work on that game.
So, this game is pretty close. It doesn't seem to run that well on my ATI hardware (my computer is fairly rubbish anyway), but its pretty good in terms of being somewhere between the Armageddon kit and the WWP kit. The physics feel pretty spot on. I don't know if thats good or bad, considering the cartoonish tone, but as a whole it all seems to knit quite well.
Its true that the backgrounds confuse the foregrounds a little, but moving the mouse around tends to resolve the confusion. The museum set idea is cool, and the narrator is quite droll (funny), but the water (bottom border) is a really crappy texture/surface that is entirely unbelievable, particularly in context of the museum set.
I'd give it a 7/10 production value, but as usual, with a Worms game, the real value is in having someone to laugh at your incompetence in trying to kill them. The game seems to do that exceptionally well, and allows hot seat, so it gets atleast one more point for longevity. The online component is deserted, but LAN and hotseat is what this game as always done best anyway. Its an underated gem in the Worms series.

For an early access game, it is actually pretty good.  Obviously it is still somewhat bare bones in many aspects as they are still working on it.  Don't go into it yet expecting ridiculous amounts of content and massive replayability yet as it is clearly not a finished product.  That said though, the foundation is there for a potentially really good game.  It's Settlers/Banished/etc meets Vikings.  There are seasonal/weather mechanics as well as random events (for example earthquakes) that are legit and add to the difficulty of the game.  You can send out raiding parties to gain money as well as fame and lore.  Building and managing your economy actually takes some thought at the harder levels unlike some past games.  Combat is nothing impressive, but isn't terrible either.  Top everything off, the game currently runs pretty well.  I have yet to experience any issues with anything... (fingers crossed that continues).  Also, has a campaign that is in the works as well as more Clan diversity and a multiplayer mode are coming soon as well.  Again, there is a lot to work with here and could lead to a fairly impressive game if done right.
Not going to go into Cons as it's obviously not done, so I'll just add some things that so far I think would greatly help it.
Increased unit and building diversity would be a plus.  Same could be said for random map elements and enemies.  Adding random incusions from the sea on your coastal lands could potentially make things interesting.  More options during skirmish setup including increasing players allowed from 4 to 8.  Adding some sort of map editor or map generator with options such as resource quantity/quality, NPC strength, etc.  There are more, but these alone would be huge.  Fingers crossed, we will see what happens....

I had just finished this plethora of games, and i will give an evaluation of the product. Now, if you haven't played Doom before, but want to get into the series, this is the perfect stepping stone in getting your feet wet in the Doom universe. Now, the action is second to none, easily based on actual events so newcomers and fans of this series will rejoice at what Doom 3: BFG Edition has to offer. Now when I had first booted this game up and saw the intro, the amount of emotion, and the amount of detail that it managed to elicit from me, was nothing short of etherial. I truly felt connected to the Doom universe as a whole, but when you finally get through the intro and you remember you are playing a game, you see an abomination on the lower part of the screen that looks like a cross of Coop from Megas XLR and Max from the Blue Tax commericals. The nameless hero you play as has only 2 attacks, shoot and punch. The next thing I want to mention is how remarkable the backbrounds are, the computers bleep blooping in the background truly sells the atmosphere, and I can easily say that this game did not disappoint in the landscape and background design department. At the bottom of the screen you will also see a portrait of the face you are probably making, I know this was the face I made during this entire play session. Health is replenished by eating medical kits, as it took me a good hour to figure this out because instructions are non existant. There's billions of people in the world, but who wants to meet them when you can drink Mountain Dew and play Doom 3: BFG Edition. I have not played Doom 1: BFG Edition or Doom 2: BFG Edition, but I did buy a snapback with the money I had saved, hallelujah. So, in conclusion if you like Doom, you're gunna like this game, if you don't like Doom, you're gunna like this game, if you like video games, you're gunna like this game, if you like putting your hands in your pockets, you're really gunna like this game, you're gunna like this game, it's a good game.

For all the people who say this game has turned to a PTW or that the game is unplayable because of the lag are just down right wrong.
Trove is a grindy MMORPG where you will spend hours with your friends destroying well thought out bosses and traversing massive dungeons to reach the end boss all in hopes of getting better loot. You'll notice a lot of the negative comments speak of lag. YES, there is SOME lag, but if your game lags to the point where you can't play it, you should start looking at your computer and your internet connection. I've put in 185 hours and have never lagged to the point to where it was enough for me to want to quit.
As for the Pay To Win comments. Microtransactions can be made in order to purchase new characters, new mounts, new costumes but NOT WEAPONS OR GEAR. Weapons and gear has to be farmed and the microtransactions are more centered around cosmetics. One mission asks you to "purchase" something from the shop, but it is literally a free class token. Nearly everything in the game from classes to mounts can be crafted. Granted it would take hours to grind enough to craft the "advanced" heros, you still have plenty of choices from the basic free heros.
Pros:
Lots of people to play with
Building your own home
Tons of new worlds
Constant updates and events
PVP is entertaining
NOT PTW
Cons:
Can be laggy
Grinding can be a snore fest alone
Some missions require to kill an outragious number of enemies like 500
Crafting certain items and classes require a ton of crafting items
TL;DR give this game a go if you like open world, Voxel, MMORPG, crafting, building, PVP, etc, etc.

As someone who loves racing games, this one just never clicked for me. I sunk a good 50 hours into it back in the day on console and it was just okay back then. Any way you slice it, it is easily the worst of all the Burnout games (it's a shame the better games never made their way onto Steam). While a bit disappointing, Paradise was still a solid game at it's time, but it simply hasn't aged well. The city is bland, the cars handle very poorly and the takedown system gets really annoying over time. It seems we've had a deluge of open world racing games since this one launched, and with the exception of NFS Rivals, I'd say all of them are superior to Paradise in one way or another. Even The Crew, despite suffering dreadful gameplay, has a much more vivid and engaging world than Paradise. Not that this is a bad game, it's just the weakest in the series, below par when compared to more recent open-world racers, and for me, the “ultimate” kicker that turns this from a “buy during a steam sale” into a “no way”, is the fact that the game is blatantly falsely advertised. What EA meant by ultimate is a mystery seeing as it does not contain the DLC. Big Surf island, the most important piece of DLC released was never even ported to PC, and the rest of the DLC you have to purchase through Origin. How exactly is that “The Ultimate” edition?

Dont get misguided by my playtime, I only added it to Steam to write a review, I played a wholelot of this game for a couple of years.
Few months ago, I got back to this game (after like 5 years break), dragging my girlfriend with me for a whole fresh start. Two of us, new server, new friends, etc... I is much more fun than I suspected, to be honest. Judging by the past, the game got A LOT easier, and less pay2win. Leveling up is smoother, more casual, dungeon are simplified compared to their version from like 2008. Generally, very positive experience.
Short description Old-time grinding Korean MMO set up is some weird, magical, but also post apo, but also neo futuristic world. You can say whaaat but it actually fits together. Quests are boring, pvp is awesome, dungeons and bosses are dynamic and very fun, but it takes a lot of time to get to the level where you can actually ddo them... You get the idea. Down to pros and cons
PROS
+It's been getting progressively easier (in the good way) for quite some time
+Easy quests and first field bosses equip you with decent gear up to level ~130, so no need to grind early on.
+Classes are quite balanced and fun, different from the regular one class actually decent for dmg and the rest is♥♥♥♥♥♥but  buffs and heals approach in the mmos from that era.
+Music is very catchy and diversed, from slow and idyllic notes to techno and hard rock, but it fits the places and action perfectly.
+SOME of the maps and palces are very imaginative. Post apo with intelligent, mutated half animals-half robots Sure, why not. Lets also throw in laser bows that are also magical. IT SOMEHOW FITS
+Animations and skills are brilliant and still look great after all these years
+Game's dynamically developed and new instances, bosses, maps etc. are added quite frequently for MMO this old.
+Dungeons and bosses on high-level areas are super fun and challenging. Nothing beats the feeling of finishing the MO (dung) with only 3 people in the party, while also looting some quality drop.
+Frequent, fun events
+Since itroduction of vouchers, everything from CC shop can also be bought with in-game currency.
+ITS STILL ALIVE SOMEHOW.
CONS
-Graphics didnt get ANY better for the past X years.
-Still very poorly optimized. Crowded places kill framerate on low end PCs.
-Very repetetive for some periods of time.
-Game only starts getting fun after like 170 level, when u finally can get a decent guild and find party and start going dungeons.
-Very boring to play alone.
-Premium makes everything so easy, its hard to imagine playing without it.
-After some time, all necessary items are only available from CCshop (real money, or grind to buy vouchers)
-Grind isn't for everyone
-At first, you buy a new, stronger item every day and suddenly you realise that you need to start saving for a week to buy sht that you wont even feel a diffrence in using.
To sum up, I its a game for a nostalgic adventure, but it does deserve some newcomers nowadays. Sadly, it doesn't get too many, so I highly recommend you give it a chance. Dont get fooled by people saying u need to pay to respawn. The function to respawn on point of death is a mechanic introduced very late, as a mean for ppl in very difficult and long dungeons to not fall behind ticking clock. It's absolutely not mandatory and doesn't hurt at all until very late levels. Mission dungeons keys do not need to be bought with real money either, they actually drop very often in the fields and are super cheap on the market. If you loved this game at some point in your life, you'll love it even more now. If you didn't, well you might give it a chance now. If you never tried it, but have friends who play it, dont hesitate. With friends, it's fun for hours, and hours.
PS. Just avoid Atlas server and EU. They dont get any support and are aweful compared to Titan - official NA server available through official website client (not the steam one).

A fun game with tons of potential down the road, I can recommend the purchase easily especially when it will (and probably should) cost more in the future. The only complaints I have can be ironed out with maturation, but I may as well mention them.
-Upgrades to buildings only go up one tier, and ones with workers can hold one more. So not much to build on.
-Victory requirements are pretty easy to obtain, and just progressing naturally will get you to any of them.
-Combat is very overpowered, for one if you select the wolf clan I'd say it's a sure victory. There are no negatives to fighting (except for hurting trade prices, but those are pretty unnecessary) and you can only slow the enemy down unless you have a very small warband. If you wipe out a factions main force, you've pretty much dominated with no hope for them as they can't defend themselves. Also, if you take their area with say major food production they'll be scrambling. There either needs to be a penalty for war, or a better way of defending as the towers do nothing once the wolf clan techs up.
-Your map placement is everything. My first playthrough I was adjacent to the only two farming tiles as well as deer and a forest. From there, resources weren't much of an issue so I cruised through. Also as part of this, food is almost impossible to aquire WITHOUT these tiles, unlike woodcutting which can be done anywhere (without a boost) you can ONLY farm, hunt, or fish with the resource tile. You'd be screwed without a farm or fish or deer. This would be even worse in multiplayer unless map gen was even, but if it's even then who will win depends on whoever clicks combat the fastest (that and mob spawns) so depth needs to be added here.
-The "Map Victory" deserves it's own section over just map generation. When discovering the necessary tile, the whole map is alerted of it's EXACT location, so everyone can rush it. It happened to spawn next to another clan so for a moment I was worried. I don't know if the AI was dumb or they had no iron, but they didn't build the pieces. I went with a fairly basic warband, took the area, and built odin's sword in minutes as I already had iron. I beat the game in like half an hour. On easy, but still.
-Lastly, and this is very minor but I think the developer's may want to know, I selected to continue past all of the victory requirements just to see if I could capture the whole map, have the (irrelevant in game so far as I can tell) giants clan, and just build everywhere. I don't know if I had too much wood and that broke the stack overflow, or maybe the game can't handle you owning too much land, but it just randomly crashed. No warnings be it stutters or a pop-up, just straight to desktop. Now while my scenario may be outside of "normal" gameplay, this COULD be important in domination only multiplayer if only two remain and they're pretty evenly building and gaining land.
In conclusion, great game, no regrets on purchase, and be prepared for all of those issues to be ironed out!

Fran Bow is one of those games where you really have to play it yourself. You can't just watch someone LP it, or watch a review from a youtube personality, or look at screenshots. You will never, ever get a good idea of what kind of experience this is without experiencing it first-hand, and witnessing it in it's hand-drawn, creepy, atmospheric and on-the-edge-of-your-seat storytelling.
The puzzles in this game are some of the most interesting and well-thought-out I've seen in a Point & Click game. While I'm normally not a fan of the "inventory" sub-genre of P&Cs, the game doesn't fall into that tragic ditch of "rub X on Y until it works". Everything you have has a use and while playing the game, it's obvious as to which objects you can and cannot interact with.
The "dual worlds" mechanic helps to create a very uncomfortable vibe in the player at times. You will come to know that no matter how peaceful the area you are in looks, the moment you take that pill, your surroundings will change to the exact opposite. Every screen has it's own dark and disturbing twin, and the knowledge that sometimes you will have to pay good attention to every sickening detail will really keep you in the edge of your seat, and sometimes leaping back when you notice something out of the corner of your eye, or even in plain sight.
During the game, you'll come to love Fran Bow as a character. She's a little girl who's been thrust violently into a world she doesn't quite understand, and while it's a little unnerving as to how calmly she takes in most of what she's seeing, it really works to create a personality and a character whom you desperately want to succeed.
A cat is fine too.
I'd like to add that this game contains NO jumpscares, in the traditional meaning of the word. Yes, whenver you take your pill, it's quite instant, but nothing's going to jump out at you or scream in your ear, there's no random scary faces or evil beings leaping out at you. You can take your time as much as you want. That's because this game uses atmosphere, story and setting to keep you from feeling at ease. The game is at best stunningly eerie and at worst absolutely horrifying and disturbing. You'll really be frantically clicking on your pill bottle to return to normality, or at least Fran Bow's version of normality.
To conclude. Fran Bow is an experience that encompasses many emotions, fear, happiness, excitement, foreboding, childlike wonder and a sense of fulfillment as you solve puzzles that are never too hard or too obvious, discovering new characters, new places, and uncover the unsettling mystery of your family's murder, and the reasons as to why you are being stalked by a horrifying entity. At no point was I left unsatisfied, and at no point was I left angry or annoyed at a puzzle or a loose end to the plot. I would recommend this game to anyone seeking an emmersive and creepy experience. 9/10.

Don't buy this game.
(This review is based on an unpayed for copy, Steam sharing and lots of pain)
While it comes with free, convenient widescreen support, it is a very, very gimped version of the original Doom 3.
There is ZERO mod support, meaning you cannot modify the game in the least to deal with any given problems or wishes you might have, in stark contrast to many, many Bethesda and Id games in the past.
Not only is the difficulty severely reduced (your flashlight is now on a regenerating battery, permanently strapped to your shoulder), ammo is now far more plentiful.
There are no options to change any of these aspects.
If you were interested in a graphical upgrade to Doom 3, just look into sikkmod and wulfen's texture pack. They make the game look BETTER than this special edition asks you to pay money for.
Lastly, if you were interested in this for the supposed "lost missions", stop while you're ahead. Made for the BFG edition (lost is a major misnomer), they recycle entire rooms of assets.
This is outright ignoring how the original Doom games get massacred by censorship in this game, as well as horrendous shift pitching you can't turn off that makes every single sound in the game seem ridiculous.
If you're interested in a simple plug in and play avenue to play the Doom trilogy, this is the right buy, as the convenience of not having to set things up in HD is rather nice, and understandably so if you don't feel like setting up source ports for the original Doom entries or using console commands to run Doom 3 in 16:9.
Otherwise, you'll want to avoid this, and purchase the original Doom 3, spend some time to get it up to modern par, and find a better avenue for the 20 year old Doom games that you might otherwise be looking for.

Left 4 Dead is a first-person shooter game, an apocalypse survival game from Valve. The game is a zombie apocalypse game where you play as one of four survivors trying to get themselves to safety. These survivors are Bill, Zoey, Francis and Louis. They're trying to get themselves to safety as their story began two weeks after the infection. They themselves are immune to this virus while thousands of people already become hungry undead.
The gameplay is almost similar to any Valve game, you can play up to 4 players with friends or people from the internet and play together. The zombies in this game are also unique, you won't just meet regular zombies, there are special infected that has many special abilities which can get you some troubles. Hunters for example, likes to leap and then pinned the survivors by surprise. The most fearsome infected could be the tank or the witch, they are the worst. Witch can take you down with only single attack despite her pity appearance. Weapons are quite good here, there are pump-action shotgun, dual pistols, submachine gun, assault rifle or hunting rifle. If you're overwhelmed, simply toss a pipe bomb and that thing will attract zombies from you and then blow them up.
Graphics of Left 4 Dead is quite decent and impressive. The Source Engine has again prove its worthiness. Explosion effects, gore and blood effects, the sounds and the environment are all impressive, including the amazing ragdoll effects which makes the environment more chaotic. And still, the game runs pretty stable and smooth.
Overall, Left 4 Dead is a good game to play with friends. I recommend this.

People gave this game a bad rap, but I actually enjoyed it. I am traditionally not an FPS player, but I liked the idea of seeing the story from multiple perspectives and being able to play as marines, aliens and predators.
All of the different play styles were enjoyable, especially predators with their nifty abilities and they all played differently. One part of playing as an aliend that I didn't like was climbing on stuff upside down. At times, it actually got a little nauseating, but again, I'm not used to the first person perspective and for those who are, they may not find it as off putting.
I also dabbled in a few multiplayer matches and found them to be enjoyable. I would argue that multiplayer does not have a great balance between classes, but in the context of the fiction, I'm not sure it's supposed to. Predators seem to have the best ability to take down enemies and they are fun to play as, but I actually enjoyed feeling like the underdog in certain situations, it gave the match a sense of excitement and accomplishment when vanquishing a superior enemy.
This game will not win any awards for amazing innovation or technical prowess, but does that really matter? Not to me. I enjoyed the game for what it is; a fun trip into an enjoyable fiction.

Updated 3rd times on Nov.10, after beating the game for another 5 hours further:
After 20+hrs of gameplay I still have to say this game require some aggressive balance work.
The visual is pretty good, new alien models look nice, but what most Sigma franchaise players expect is AS3 not this tower defence style thing.
Leaving that alone, about the game:
1. Troopers, their required stars to unlock/crystals to purchage, their combat capabilities, are unbalanced in general.
Some levels are proven impossible to go through linearly. You simply can't choose easy difficulty and beat all of them till the end. You HAVE to go back beat earlier levels on higher difficulty till you get all the money and stars to unlock better troopers. This makes it a total slog fest.
Flamethrower, Shootgunner and Rockeeter - without unlocking and upgrading them at least once, it is hardly possible to go further with low tier gunners. Unless you beat the starting levels repetitively to upgrade them in a crazy manner.
Flamer replaces Soldiers readily. Rocket renders Sniper useless - they are way more capable to repel hedgehogs and spouts than snipers. The secondary ability also clean the mess more efficiently. Defenders may prove less capable as a frontline tank than flamer early on, but their upgrades outpower flamethrower significantly later and kater, plus their far more useful secondary ability.
Elites are too expensive. It may be fair if the cost could lower to like 700-800, but 1000 renders it a pale choice as a ranged high DPS.
In late game you find soldier and sniper useless. No need to upgrade them anymore, just bank a ton of miners for opening, transition to defender.
2. Some level designs are questionable.
Although I played the game for 20 hours I still doubt this game have way too many suicidal enemy roles. It has never been so many in AS and ZS series and AH1. The kamikaze units make the gameplay quite tedious. Explosions are everywhere on your way, on every planet, on every single mission. I wouldn't say it is a totally bad idea but this looks stupid after you playing for hours long.
Acid pools last too long and force you to step over them, losing hp and repaired by medics - I doubt this mechanics and personally speaking this is stupid. You can avoid such scenario in AS/ZS, but this game it is unavoidable. Regardless how little damage it actually does, it is discouraging and an unclever design.
3. Slot design is insufficient, providing limited gameplay choices, making it very boring.
4 slot is not enough. It is enough to beat the game, but NOT enough to allow variable gameplay tactics. You have to pick a tank unit, a ranged unit, bring your miner and medic - ALWAYS. This means it has no variable choices in late game.
I would suggest 5 or 6, so you can transition from midgame to lategame for more diversities of tactics.
4. Medic may should be allowed to heal the whole squad instead of just whom around him. I am not sure if it will make it OP but otherwise you will always have to bring 4 medics to heal the whole phanlex, and thus your tactical choices are reduced.

Buy it if you a Sigma fan and want to have a glance at what will it be like in AS3. Or don't buy it if you can't tolerate all these above.

Acceptable game for the price! Actually, it's fun!
This is not a pretentious game, the developersand designers give what they offer: a nice atmosphere, plenty of aliens to shoot at, upgrades  for weapons and for the classes of different soldiers you may use to achieve the missions' tasks, and...loads of shooting action.
Graphics are and look ok and the game runs smoothly. Music is good but quite repetitive. Controls are simple to use. Although your men shoot automatically in a more or less acceptable way, some extra aiming and a good distribution of your men's classes are necessary to get the best offensive-defensive performance possible.
AH2 doesn't have, nor pretends having, a solid story line, not even a shallow one. Before each mission, you have a breifing informing you what's going on, what your goals are and that's it. Equip or upgrade your attacking group as much as the collected money allows you to, and go to kick some alien butt...or get your men dead trying.
As one of the people who sent a previous review said: this is not a game to spend long sessions of gaming, just play the game as a time waster and having some fun at the same time. It's a good game to play before or after playing a heavier game, or when you have nothing better to do.
I recommend the game for those who are fans of non-stop shooting action.
Another good thing about the game is that every level starts with certain achievements with an easy rate of difficulty, after you complete the level, you may go to the next one or you may stay there in which case you will have to complete a set of different achievements but this time with medium difficulty...then you may repeat, if you want, the level with harder difficulty and harder tasks.  This repeat-the- level issue is useful in order to get more money to upgrade your men.

I know this system has nothing you may call "a novelty factor" but at least you are not going to suffer the frustration of getting stuck in a particular level having to repeat it forever.

I really like this game, though I do have one question/complaint: Why is there such a low limit on the number of towers I can have?
Essentially this game is the same as Dungeon Defenders or Orcs Must Die, with a first person perspective and more of a focus on the player as a weapon than depending on your towers to eliminate the opposition.  That last is probably why there is an arbitrary limit on towers, and while I don't think it hurts the game necessarily, it does make the game much more challenging.
If you like tower defense, though, this game is really good.
Essentially it is played like any other TD game; you choose the towers you want to use, create a channel for the baddies to run through as your towers attempt to obliterate their collective gonads, and you run all over the place throughout with the goal of finishing off anything that still HAS gonads.  It's very addictive, and a rather fresh take on the genre, what with the focus being evenly between the player and a good tower setup.
There's multiplayer, too, but more often than not that resulted in me banning the knucklehead because they decided to start taking down my towers.  Call me a noob, give me some criticism, heck you can just sit there saying 'wtf...' over and over - just don't mess with my build without asking.
Highly recommended.

A fun game with tons of potential down the road, I can recommend the purchase easily especially when it will (and probably should) cost more in the future. The only complaints I have can be ironed out with maturation, but I may as well mention them.
-Upgrades to buildings only go up one tier, and ones with workers can hold one more. So not much to build on.
-Victory requirements are pretty easy to obtain, and just progressing naturally will get you to any of them.
-Combat is very overpowered, for one if you select the wolf clan I'd say it's a sure victory. There are no negatives to fighting (except for hurting trade prices, but those are pretty unnecessary) and you can only slow the enemy down unless you have a very small warband. If you wipe out a factions main force, you've pretty much dominated with no hope for them as they can't defend themselves. Also, if you take their area with say major food production they'll be scrambling. There either needs to be a penalty for war, or a better way of defending as the towers do nothing once the wolf clan techs up.
-Your map placement is everything. My first playthrough I was adjacent to the only two farming tiles as well as deer and a forest. From there, resources weren't much of an issue so I cruised through. Also as part of this, food is almost impossible to aquire WITHOUT these tiles, unlike woodcutting which can be done anywhere (without a boost) you can ONLY farm, hunt, or fish with the resource tile. You'd be screwed without a farm or fish or deer. This would be even worse in multiplayer unless map gen was even, but if it's even then who will win depends on whoever clicks combat the fastest (that and mob spawns) so depth needs to be added here.
-The "Map Victory" deserves it's own section over just map generation. When discovering the necessary tile, the whole map is alerted of it's EXACT location, so everyone can rush it. It happened to spawn next to another clan so for a moment I was worried. I don't know if the AI was dumb or they had no iron, but they didn't build the pieces. I went with a fairly basic warband, took the area, and built odin's sword in minutes as I already had iron. I beat the game in like half an hour. On easy, but still.
-Lastly, and this is very minor but I think the developer's may want to know, I selected to continue past all of the victory requirements just to see if I could capture the whole map, have the (irrelevant in game so far as I can tell) giants clan, and just build everywhere. I don't know if I had too much wood and that broke the stack overflow, or maybe the game can't handle you owning too much land, but it just randomly crashed. No warnings be it stutters or a pop-up, just straight to desktop. Now while my scenario may be outside of "normal" gameplay, this COULD be important in domination only multiplayer if only two remain and they're pretty evenly building and gaining land.
In conclusion, great game, no regrets on purchase, and be prepared for all of those issues to be ironed out!

There's no doubt about it, Doorways has been a highly successful horror series that has just concluded with its third and final installment. With Doorways: Old Prototype, we get a rare glimpse into the world of a game while it's in its infantile stages. Consisting of only three short levels, it's truly inspiring to see where the series began, and reflect on how far it has come.
It's obvious by this prototype that the original mainframe of Doorways was platforming. You start off in a hellish level, and perform a series of jumps to traverse to the end of the map; sometimes avoiding fireballs and crushing pillars. There are even mobile platforms and a couple of areas that require extremely well-timed jumps. Most of the textures here are used in abundance, though the level feels extremely well polished and ready.
Continuing on to the second phase, you will find yourself in a mostly white area with giant pillars. The jumps and platforming in this section are filled with tight precision, though there are invisible checkpoints placed at just the right locations so that when (not if) you fall and die, it's not tedious to continue onward. This area is void of textures and assets, which is a stark contrast to the first level.
As you venture through this early demo, you will find notes left by the developer where they talk about each specific level, what names that the game almost went by, and the original ideas and concepts for Doorways that eventually morphed into what the game is today. It's a really wonderful inside perspective for gamers, but also incredibly inspirational for up-and-coming small indie teams.
Even though it only lasts about half an hour, Doorways: Old Prototype offers a unique perspective at a game in development, and what the series could have been. It's not afraid to show all of its rough design edges and flaws, while still being solid and playable. The platforming sections are challenging enough to be engaging to even those that may not care about the scattered notes that detail the game design and history. It's pretty much a win/win for everyone.

Let's get this out of the way: AVP2 from 2001 is still the best. So how does this 2010 reboot fare?
STORY: Barebones.
All 3 races share the same storyline, so mostly it's just perspective and gameplay that changes. There's some planet, another Weyland android tries to capture aliens to get their technology. Go kill each other. Yeah, story's pretty weak.
LEVEL DESIGN: Good variety but reused a lot.
Most of the maps will be the exact same for all 3 campaigns, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. Each level is actually designed to be navigated in different ways depending on your species: the Aliens will go around walls and through vents, the Predators will hop across distances and heights, while Humans will walk horizontally.
PREDATOR GAMEPLAY: Fun, but not many combat options.
You wish you could toy with your prey more, but the game encourages you to go fist-to-fist. You only get the diskus and the combistick (which can only be thrown) very late in the game, so most of the time, you're just trying to stealth and sneak behind for a quick dramatic kill. It also sucks that you get UNLIMITED CLOAKING, which takes away the suspense of running out of power at exactly the last second.
MARINE GAMEPLAY: Good atmosphere, but few weapons.
I love the level where you try to escape from a Night Club. You never see this in a space horror game: you're the last survivor trying to get out of a failed rescue mission, and then ... the music blasts, so you're fighting off hordes of aliens while dancing to the music. Unfortunately, you're stuck using the very basic autorifle or pistol most of the time, with the shotgun, flamethrower, and smartgun making an extrance very late in the game.
ALIENS GAMEPLAY: Short, and feels weak.
You don't have the "Press E for pounce" anymore. Instead, you have to hold SHIFT and target an enemy in order to leap onto them. Attacks also feel clunky, and not fluid. You only play as a regular alien drone, never a facehugger, praetorian, or predalien. I really thought you'd play as a predalien, but no.
OVERALL: Not bad, but nothing special.
Rating: 6/10.

Bought it for $4.99 on Daily Deal.  Well worth the purchase.  I am very surprised by how enjoyable this game is.
At first I thought this game would be the same old shooter with jump scares and hidden hallways, and I was right....
However, the way they carried the sub-par story through the game is spectacular, and makes all the difference.  Everything has its place, and the video logs and emails through your PAL bring a fantastic level of emersion.  I like how the game is able to poke fun at itself, at science, and even at something unexpected like work politics or D&D.  The levels are fun; fighting the creatures is fun; the game is fun.
What I enjoyed most is despite how far the game has come since Doom II, the game kept much of the spirit of its predecessors throughout.  It actually reminded me of playing a Doom II level.  I love the unique ways they make the monsters blind side you, and just when I thought I got the “jump scares” figured out, Doom 3 in classic fashion surprises you.  The game literally had me checking every corner of every room before I progressed for tucked away hidden monster waiting to ambush.  The darkness, although a bit much, was still extremely appropriate and well done.  I’m so glad they made the flashlight something you wear, rather than an item to switch in and out with like they had on the previous Doom 3 (TERRIBLE IDEA GUYS!!).  The use of light and space was masterful and suspenseful.
What I don’t like about Doom 3 is there are only a select few collection of monsters to encounter.  Once you’ve figured out how to deal with them, the only challenge left is managing an entire room’s worth of them.  I would love to have seen twice as many different types of monsters as was shown (especially since this is a reboot).  I also didn’t like the ending.  It didn’t feel “epic” enough.  It was very easy.  There weren’t too many side characters to interact with, nor were there very many puzzles.  Remembering a scrap paper’s-worth of Storage Container access codes does NOT make it a puzzle. :/  Finally, while the animation of the monsters was beautiful, the animation of the npc’s and yourself was abysmal.  Some of the worst dubbing I’ve seen with newer-generation graphics.  The character designs of npc’s were boring, re-used for multiple different characters, and distracting.  With the reboot they really should have upgraded the animation quality, if nothing else the speech animation.
Regardless of the above, I overall really enjoyed the experience Doom 3 has to offer.  I am happy with my purchase and my game.  I’d give it a 7.2/10.

By this point Bastion doesn't need another positive review to solidify its standing as a must have game. With only the most bitter and caustic contrarians providing negative feedback, Bastion has an approval rate of 98%. That should speak highly of the game's value but one should always strive to understand what makes something good rather than blindly following popular opinion like one more lemming in the heard and indeed one should highlight the strengths of a thing rather than simply using popular opinion to define something's value. Rest assured however, in this case, Bastion is one cliff you'll be happy to jump off of with the rest of us.
Bastion begins with a young child waking up to find his world falling apart, literally. An ominous and mysterious disaster, referred to as the Calamity, has caused the fabric of the world to collapse. Finding that only he and one other person survived, the boy must recollect the essence of the world and rebuild it. Narrated by one of the best voices on planet Earth, the boy's journey takes him through the ruins of a deep and interesting setting. Indeed Bastion has one of the most unique settings in video games, its indie origins contributing to the bravery of doing something new and interesting. The game is fairly short admittedly and to discuss too much of the plot would be to give it away but trust me in that it doesn't disappoint.
Mechanically the game is remarkably solid. The purpose of collecting the shards and mcguffins is to upgrade both your base and character. There are a wide variety of weapons and enough distinction between bonuses and weapons to fit a wide variety of play styles. Being of a short length, the difficulty ramps up quickly and you must choose which upgrades are most valuable to your play style. Committing is the crux of the matter as your investments need to pay off to complete later levels.
With story and mechanics blended this well, I never stopped feeling engaged. My drive maintained from start to finish which is tougher that one might think. Bastion walks a very fine line with not having any lulls in the action while at the same time not being overwhelming about it. My final analysis: Buy this game. It is great.

Action RPG with a pleasant story, art style, and memorable music.  There are plenty of weapons to master, challenges to complete, and things to see/hear that are well worth multiple play throughs.
It begins with the Calamity, a mysterious event that leaves the world nothing but floating pieces of land and the people ash.  A lone survivor, "The Kid", wakes up to his city undone and begins searching.  The Kid finds his way to the Bastion (a sort of bomb shelter in case the world ended) and meets the man who narrates his every step, Rucks.  Together, the two set about upgrading the Bastion.  The Kid visits individual areas of the world that remained intact to hunt for cores, power sources for the Bastion.  As players journey through the remnants of Caelondia, they meet other survivors, taste strange liquors, and discover the truth about what has happened to the world.
Bastion is an action role-playing game by definition but is played from an isometric perspective.  As The Kid, players will wield a variety of melee and projectile weapons against the creatures that inhabit the wilds.  Players can also equip one secret skill, a sort of ultimate attack that is usually specific to one of the two weapons you can carry.  In addition to the two weapons and the skill, players also have a shield to block/reflect attacks as well as a dive roll technique for dodging attacks.  Players start out at the Bastion, which acts as a travel hub in addition to housing the armory, forge, distillery, etc. once upgraded.  Levels themselves are all linear, though there are branching paths to explore for weapon parts, mementos, pets, and currency among other things.  Enemies come in a variety of types and behaviors, often attacking in large groups thus forcing an adaptive play style.  Health is replenished through manually drinking tonics that drop from dead enemies or are found in the world.  Health tonics can also be refilled at fountains in the world.
At the Bastion, players can upgrade their weapons, equip tonics that provide different passive/active buffs, change their loadout, shop for items, read about challenges, and turn on different mutators that make the game more difficult in exchange for a currency bonus.  There are also trips to Nowhere that have the player facing off against waves of enemies as they learn more about a particular character from the game.  Once the main game is completed, players unlock a new game plus mode as well as a score attack mode.  In about 10 hours, I have completed both the new game and new game plus modes, though I did spend time completing challenges.
An oil painting come to life, Bastion has a unique look: two dimensional background/foreground with three dimensional character models.  Everything is warmly shaded and weather effects help to enhance the mood of certain levels.  As you move through levels, the ground forms right in front of you like some kind of dream.  The screen will also change to reflect the environment: getting hit with a stink weed fuzzes the screen/muffles noise and cold environments produce ice crystals around the frame.  Every creature has its own sounds, looks, and movements.  Explosions and gunshots sound alright, though the gun reloads sound a bit toyish at times.  The soundtrack is excellent and the theme will stick with you long after you've heard it.  Voice work is great and the narrator has something to say about nearly everything you do.  It does not get old though since his delivery of the lines is amazing.
Blending simple gameplay with an excellent original story, Bastion is very deserving of your time.  While it may not take long to complete, the art direction, voice work, and gameplay will make your time in the Calamity rewarding.  Gamers of all ages should not miss this noteworthy game.

An very intresting point and click adventure that takes lots of inspirations in old fashioned fairy tales such as Grimm Fairy tales and Alice in wonderland, and anything horror related, such Ghosts, gore, creepy twins and so much more. But also some dark narrative themes like mental disorders, sucide and other things I wont spoil. Which if done wrong could have been really bad but I feel the game use those subjects respectfully and it does also even has it moments where the game lights up and shows happier sides. Even if that might seem unlikly at the very beginning of the game.
The game is about a girl named Fran Bow who escapes the mental hospital to look for her cat and hide from the monster following her. To her aid she has her stolen medicn that makes her able to see the world with diffirently. It's as wacky as it sounds, or maybe far more wackier than it sounds. Like Alince in wonderland, Frans reality shifts as much as it wants to.
The story starts of very feeling loose, and feels a bit too random, but it does develop and becomes quite intresting after the first part of the game. As a whole the plot is just as intriging it needs to be to make you want to play through the whole game and Fran, her pals and enemys grows on you as characters. The randomness of it all is forgiven for the spectatular creative setting and characters.
The game features an "world switching mechanic" similar to "Day of the tentacle" and "Lilly looking through" where you have to switch between diffrent version of a setting to find new objectives and puzzels, It's not anything ground breaking, but like those other games, it does work very well here, and makes the game show of it's wonderfuls settings. This games worlds might be the best thing about this game, they are so darn beautiful/disturbing to look at, and you just want to explore this rabbit hole deeper to make it show you more of its maddness. It starts of very dark and gloomy, but then makes a few twist into other directions but never strays away from it's own weirdness.
Things I feel could improv the game is that I wish it could highlight everything that is interactive in one area better. It's easy to miss stuff you was supposed to click on. Also the dialogues are a bit slow. Some textures could also have been in an higher resultion, sometimes things just seems blurry and low res, I'm not sure if it's intentional or just technical limitation.
If you're an fan point and click adventure games, and horror such as Grimm Fairy tales, American Mcgee's Alice games, or find the the demo and gameplay footage appealing. I recommend giving this a go. It's a very weird, sometimes creepy, but also memorable and beautiful experiance.

This was an amazing experience, one that will stay with me for a long time.
Gameplay-wise, it mostly follows the basic conventions of a point-and-click adventure with an interesting mechanic which makes two versions of nearly every scene that you often have to switch back and forth between to work out the next step. Interspersed here and there are puzzles and little mini-games that are more action-oriented. (Some of those mini-games are interesting takes on other classic games, for instance Frogger.) Those can present some moderate difficulty for the most part, though in a few places I was making them harder than they should have been because some rule wasn't obvious - for instance, not realizing in an early maze mini-game that I could approach enemies from certain directions more closely than other directions until I'd already restarted the sequences a number of times. That's a good warning going in: try not to overcomplicate some of the puzzles and games when the solution is much simpler. Of the puzzles, there was really only one that I found a little ridiculous (it's shown in one of the screenshots on the store page). In all, it remained fun to play without being boringly easy or stupidly difficult.
It was the elements of the story itself, however, that made it so memorable to me. This isn't the first time I've seen very dark subject matter presented in a manner similar to a children's book, but I'm not sure I've seen it done so well. The character of Fran Bow herself is a big factor in this; her stubborn childish innocence throughout everything that was going on was not only endearing, it helped to lend weight to the darker parts of the story. At no point did I feel like this character was acting in a way inconsistent with how she was first presented. She's a ten year old girl and she seems like a ten year old girl. All of the fantastic settings she finds herself in are well worth the visit and I enjoyed her childish reactions to them. In fact, it's odd how in such a dark game I found myself genuinely smiling at certain points. The plot itself is rich, even if the ending, which I'm still working out how I feel about, goes off in a strange (and possibly not completely satisfying) direction.
In any case, if you enjoy a good adventure game and a good horror story, you'll be doing yourself a disservice if you give this game a skip. Get it. Frankly, I feel I could have paid more for it and gotten my money's worth.

You and some friend(s) vs thousands of zombies. They're gonna need more zombies!
Grab a pistol or two, and a shotgun or automatic weapon. Kill zombies. That's it. Pick up some health or ammo along the way as you make it from safehouse to safehouse to, hopefully, rescue. There's next to no plot, and if you play on "easy" and don't care for achievements, people can drop in and have a fun romp without any prior knowledge of the game or thought of strategy. Can be played in a variety of co-op modes with 1-4 players (the remaining characters will be led by AI), or Versus modes with 2 teams of 4. The survivors while distinct characters in dress and recorded lines all have the same skillset, while the zombies (who are the opposing team in Versus) are specialists.
Pros: Good voice acting; great number of recorded lines. Fun brainless (haha, brains) shooter. Levels tend to be linear, gear limited, and operation straight forward. Go-to game for playing with people who don't play much, or who you don't have many games in common with (as it's often cheap, and there isn't much to learn, you can just get going -- you may wish to get L4D2 instead though). Can in theory be played alone (to survey the "lay of the land" before playing online) -- the AI is competent enough for that.
Cons: If you're in the above situation, fine. Otherwise, the game can feel a bit basic (especially compared to other zombie-related titles). Many achievements are extremely hard to gain in single player as the AI players will mess it up by not being in on your private plan, or just generally being too slow. Being swarmed by hordes can get a bit old, especially by fast zombies (says Zoey in the game, "I'm calling zombie ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on that!") that are in fact so fast that they can overtake you and block your path -- as if it weren't enough that them hitting you while you're running away from them also stops you.
Much as I enjoyed the game in its day, I've moved on to more recent titles, except in the "drop-in game to play with people who can't or won't put in a lot of time to gain expertise first" case. Before writing this review, I've revisited the game after a very long pause to gain some achievements I wanted, and after a few days I feel seriously L4D'd out. I might leave L4D2 on disk in case of an impromptu casual romp with some friends, but don't expect to come back otherwise. Greener pastures.
Recommendation: Review your use case carefully; don't buy for single player experience or story. Compare carefully against Left 4 Dead 2. Wait for sale, or pick it up on the rare days when it's free.
