Like (what I'm guessing is) most people, I bought this game, because I had played the original AvP when it first came out.  The original was a phenomenal game.  The graphics engine was super-advanced for its time although it would look primitive now.  If only it ran in Windows 7, I'd still play it because the game design was so incredibly brilliant that one seldom even notices the dated graphics.
This game, on the other hand, is no where near as good.  It is not bad; it has some relatively fun moments (like when the player finally gets his/her hands on the autotargetting heavy machinegun...  Those moments of fun are few and are marred by the game's major flaws.  Firstly, the game designers apparently forgot that this is a horror game and made most everything really bright.  Likewise, the gameplay is also "arcade-style".  There is never a moment of fear, but often moments of frustration.  The designers also spent way too much time on the graphics engine (which only looks sliiiiiightly better in DX11) and not enough time on the soundtrack which is much more important for a game like this.  Even the original game had 3D positional audio that worked.  It helped one tell where the aliens were hiding, but here the audio does not work as a gameplay element at all.  Moreover, there is way too much dialog and it is all super-campy.
In short, don't waste money on this mediocre-at-best game or the equally mediocre one that came after it.  Perhaps if noone buys their crappy games, the company will be forced to do a better job.

It's a good game, however it has a lot of problems with it, and those problems can get kind of annoying sometimes.
It's basically everything you would expect from and RTS: You get resources (2 of them), you can make factories, and those factories can make units.
There are 5 different types of units you can make: Sea, underwater, land, air, and orbital. Every unit can attack only certain types of units, so if you want to invade an enemy planet, you can scout it, find out what kinds of units they have, and make units their units can't attack.
The most interesting part of the game comes into play when enemy planets are so well defended, your armies can't defeat them no matter how hard you try. You can completely obliterate, sorry, *Annihilate*, enemy planets.
There are 3 ways to do that.
- Build a 'Halley Engine' on a planet, allowing you to fire the planet at another planet, destroying both planets involved.
- Build 5 'Catalysts' on a Metal planet (the ones that are covered with electronic-looking stuff) and literally turn it into a Death Star, so you can fire a laser that destroys planets.
- With the TITANS expansion, you can make a 'Ragnarok' Titan on a planet, which destroys the planet it was built on a minute after completion.
Also, the explosions are awesome.
However, the interface is really confusing, and the tutorial doesn't really clear things up. The AI is really bad if not set on the maximum difficulty setting, on 'Normal' it literally sits there and makes about 20 units, which are instantly destroyed by your army of (probably) over 500 units. Or maybe that was the Easy AI.
I still recommend it as a fun RTS to play when you have about an hour that you can spare.

TLDR; great game, large scale, has nukes,  can blow up planets, but can be fustratingly slow in the late game. The gane is totally worth your money if it costs less than 5 dollars.
Ignoring the questionable decisions that the developers have made about the game, in terms of funness (you can say whatever you want, but the word is real to me), PA: Titans is one of the best RTS games that I have played. Unlike many other RTS games, the game runs on a flow economy, so rather than paying upfront the complete cost of a unit, your resources slowly drain as your unit becomes built, which leads to interesting tactics, like destroying most of the power generators of your opponent if you spot them building game enders, effectively pausing their production.
Obviously, the game allows combat over many different planets / gas planets / asteroids at the same time, so managing your bases and armies at over 7+ planets at the same time can become interesting. Although the gameplay can start to feel repetative after playing for a long time, there are many mods made by the community (such as the legion expansion) that completely changes how the game feels, and adds a twist to the game.
With the addition of titans and other units in this expansion, it allows for new ways to defeat your enemies instead of relying on nukes / halleys / unit spam. For a example, if you can't seem to control a planet, using nukes/units, and you don't want to spend time landing on another asteroid and building a halley, and waiting for the halley to hit the planet, you can instead invade a small part of the planet, defend it with everything you got, and blow the planet up using a Ragnorak Titan.
The main issue of the game for me is that everything becomes extremely slow after playing a long game because the servers  can't handle the lag. It can be very fustrating to launch a "suprise" attack onto your opponents with bombers, and having them take 10 minutes to travel across half the planet due to lag, and then watching your opponent blow them up because the lag allowed him enough time to think and react to your attack. Overall, for a game that I purchased for 4 dollars from a sale, the game is a absolute steal for that price. However if you are paying the full price of this game, watch people play the game and see if the sheer scale, nukes, death lasers, exploding asteroids and planets is what you would enjoy in a solid RTS.

Edit: After playing this game for over a year, it seems like the developers have stopped creating content for the game, and are only fixing bugs, performing rebalances, and adding commanders which just have new looks (the community has already made mods for the latter two points, the devs essentialy just integrated them into the game). If you are expecting a game that will evolve with new official gamemodes, etc. then don't get your hopes up (although there are many amazing community mods like the legion expansion mod which adds a entire new faction, and custom maps where you race scout vehicles).

text:
Viking themed RTS. Its unique in the sense that its more about territory management than most RTS's. So you can only build so much in one before you have to move on to another (you have to use food to "colonize" other territories and scouts to see it) while balancing food, wood, happiness, etc. Basically during the warm months, you just have to prepare for winter (food gathering slows and you consume more wood) and hope you don't die during it while working towards a win condition. If you just want to build a bunch of warriors and attack stuff, this isn't the game for you. You have to slowly build towards that goal by, as I said, balancing your economy and territory.
I purchased early access when it first came out. Please read more recent updates and the dev log to see if some comments are still applicable. Also please note, only single player was available at the time of this review.
PROS:
- Really sweet art. You really get the feel of building a viking village. Everything from the buildings, the people, the terrain, really well done.
- The animations are unique to the job you give the villager. Kind of reminds of warcraft. After you tell a villager to do something, they give you the voice line and then march off to do it type thing. "Something need doing?"
- Its easy to learn. Fairly straightforward from the gameplay to the tech.
- When it first came out, it was ridiculously buggy and I read about alot of failed launches and crashes. However, they've done an admirable job patching and updating. Really sets a good tone for the rest of the early access.
- It can be really engrossing. Even though the game seems passive, the inclusion of winter slows down your growth so you can't really "rush" down your opponent. A game can take as long as an hour to win in the worst conditions. At some points, it may feel like you're just sitting there doing nothing but you have to carefully monitor your situation as random world events will occur which you need to be on top of. IE: One time, I thought I could just get a drink of water and missed a "blizzard incoming prompt" (its like a more brutal winter). I failed to stock enough wood and half my population got sick and died. Cost me about 10-15 mins of in game time to catch up.
- Different clans. Each clan has their own unique shtick. Wolf is better at conquering, goat at resources, etc. They plan to come out with more as well which could make for some interesting gameplay.
CONS:
- Of course, there are bugs. And you can read the forums on what they are, but as I mentioned, the first week they patched the game almost daily so I don't think this will become an issue.
- Low replayability SO FAR. It can also be called, awful AI. I've played 12 hours, and I've already beaten the game a multiple of different ways on the hardest AI and all possible combination of AI opponents. As I said, only single plyr is available and I'm sure multiplayer will be alot better. But I'm not sure how much better. My recommendation would be to wait until this feature is included as I've already gotten tired of thrashing the "hard" AI.
- Balance is a bit off. As I mentioned in the beginning, its all about territory management. So some territories are naturally better than others. Most imporant are the territories directly adjacent to your starting terrtiroy as you can't colonize territory that isnt bordering your own. For instance, some let you build 2 buildings and some 3. Some give increased food or wood production and some do nothing like a swamp. Some terrain is more advantageous to start in. Like some starts because of cliffs, give you one choke and other 3 to guard. And the speed of success in this game can largely depend on your proximity to these territories and especially resources. Stone for instance is super important to upgrade buildings in this game and iron can be the difference in winning and losing as it lets you upgrade your villagers/warriors. Of course everyone starts off by a starting amount but it gets mined out very quickly. The "big patches" of resources isnt exactly in the middle of everyone. Sometimes it can quite close to you and sometimes quite far.
- World isn't customizable. I have not read that they plan to address this but I imagine they will. Its basically a randomly generated world. You have no say as to what win conditions, size of the world, resource level, etc. Your only options so far are: # of AI opponents, difficulty, name, color, clan.
CONCLUSION:
If there was a "Maybe" button for recommending this game. I would choose that. I have no huge complaints about it as for the 12 hours I played, it was fun so I clicked "YES". As I said, I would wait a bit to purchase it though. Maybe until multiplayer gets released. I was very excited to purchase the game but have already gotten tired of it in a way. I may play it a bit more to get my RTS fix in but will do so knowing there's no way I could ever lose to the AI. At $20 though, its not an awful purchase. Just keep in mind what my critques are, and if you can live with them go ahead and buy it.

People say the game is mediocre, and perhaps that is justified. However, I feel the game is at least in the higher end of mediocre games, and can produce a lot of fun. At least for fans of the different creatures the game tried (and in my opinion, succeeded) to bring alive.
I am not in a position to review the multiplayer so consider this to be mainly a single player review.
People are usually concerned with the duration of gameplay, and what many have said is true, it's short, with the marine campaign being the longest, Predator in the middle and the alien the shortest. It's a shame, as I found that the alien was the most fun, then the predator, and lastly the marine. Though this is not to say that it isn't fun to play the marine, it's just the weakest of the species. All three species campaigns adding up to perhaps 12h, though I might be slow - spending a lot of time in the shadows as an alien, watching how the marines patrol, and cloaked as a predator, deciding which marine to pick off first.
What this game has that the earlier AVP games didn't have, was a more polished experience as the different species:
Aliens feel like more than just a floating camera with floating arms and a tail that shows up every so often. Now you move as your body moves, you can feel with every turn of the camera as your playable xenomorph changes position and sometimes the tail shows up when you turn around fast enough. The way you can leap, look, attack, all are improvements to a first-person-shooter experience of sneaking or leaping and attacking in close quarters, always in the same brutal sense you pick up from the films.
Predators too feel like they move, behave and look like a predator from the movies. There's nothing like re-enacting a scene so reminiscent from the films: Leap up a tree cloaked, observe the marines below, say you want the smart gunner first, you distract the marine with some distorted human cry, wait for them to get closer, then leap (focus+attack1) on them and pick a trophy.
And that brings me to the full-body awareness. It's a small feature, but I still value it when developers pick up on the little things which can mean a lot to make an experience feel just right. the trophy kills and stealth kills seem to have been the baby of the project to hammer out a smooth way to behave with the character, with little distracting buggy animations, if any at all, just going up to a human and impaling them with your tail, literally, or just stabbing an alien with your wristblades, lifting them up in the air, seeing the dangling xeno giving its last painful shriek, then becoming motionless, and you, the predator, just casting it aside.
The story isn't anything new or particularly gripping, but it's okay, and what you could expect, though the AVP2 game had a better story, this game has a better story than the avp movies, so there's that.
If only they'd extended the Predator and Alien campaigns, I think the game would have gained more popularity. Also, since the games are trying to be close to the movies, I think it's time to make the "marine" human character female, if you want to copy some of the defining features of the films. Which isn't bad, just saying.
Graphics do justice to the details of the predators and their swinging dreadlocks, and the shining, slimey aliens, coupled with great animations, which you can admire both while hunting the different species and while playing them, made it a fun experience.
Personally the game didn't suffer from issues (and I have a mediocre laptop, win7, intel dual core 2ghz, 4gRAM, graphics card shares its memory with ram, only 64mb dedicated), only a flickering mouse in the mainmenu. I'm mentioning this because I've seen so many games suffer from multiple bugs, though often repairable, this didn't really have any issues for me.
Lack of survivor maps as a predator or alien felt like the greatest sorrows of missed opportunities for this game (which I think could have been very feasible additions, as I write in a post on the forums of the game here on steam).
Sure, by my playtime you can tell I kinda like this game. Buy it and ignore the creation club fail (reason for most neg reviews).

I only just bought Starbound for a few days, but I'll try to write a review to summarise what I can see, and tell you if you should buy this game. Keep in mind, that this is an Early Access review, and the content after 1.0 may change
First, the story. The story, in it's current form, is incomplete. They said that the next update is the "Story Update" which will make Starbound's story expand more, and the story will be laid out for everyone. As of current though, there's not much to be discovered in the story (not instantly, at least).
Secondly, the exploration. Games like these are all about exploration. So how does Starbound hold up in this aspect? Well, not too great. The mining is mostly boring, there are not many buildings/ruins to be found, and you only occasionally see an NPC house under/above ground, and it's not even that exciting, either.
Thirdly, the combat. Even after the so-called combat update, the combat system still falls short compared to games of it's kind (eg. Terraria). I just hate the fact that a monster can just appear out of nowhere and takes away 10 health or something. The spawn rate of monsters is very high, too, so that doesn't help it. Also, some attacks are pretty much one hit KOs, because the invincibility frames are pretty much useless. If you are caught in the first boss's lazers, you are pretty much guaranteed to have at least half your health bar taken away, unless you have a shield (which protects you for like, 1 seconds anyways). They will be changing it in 1.0, but as of now, the combat is horrible.
Finally, the performance. I swear the developers really need to optimize the frame rate issues. My laptop, which isn't great, but at least it can run games like CS:GO at a decent framerate, completely falls apart before this game. It runs at 5~ FPS in the Outpost, which makes it less of a game, and more like an interactive slideshow. This, combined with the combat issues, make it very frustrating to play. I have tried every method of optimising possible, yet the only place I can get constant good FPS from, is the spaceship, which literally has nothing on it, bar the few crafting stations and the bed. This issue alone takes away the experience of Starbound by quite a lot.
I have to give credits where it's due though. It is exactly what it's supposed to be, Terraria in space (although it falls short on some features mentioned above). The community is great, and the game supports the creation of mods for the game.  I think the modding community is what gets the game it's reputation. The mods are what keeps the game alive for the community, since Chucklefish so rarely update their games. Without mods, you're better off playing something like Terraria instead.
Overall, if you have a sick gaming PC that can run CS:GO at 400 FPS or something, you can probably pick the game up now and start playing. But if you're anything like me and don't have a $2000 gaming PC, you can wait for the 1.0 update, which promises optimisation and fixes to some of the issues I have with the game currently. There's always Terraria.
P.S: Sorry I mentioned Terraria so much in the review :P

Doom 3 BFG Edition won't be just another re-release with bonus content.
In a recent interview with VG247, id Software's Tim Willits said that Doom 3 BFG Edition isn't merely a re-release of something old with added content:
It's a complete overhaul of the 2004 slow-paced survival horror shooter. Willits said the studio has returned to its roots with this release, cranking up the action so it's not such a gloomy crawl-fest.
Of course, there's more to the BFG Edition than cranking up the action. Levels have been re-designed to match the pace, and the team has thrown in new textures to bring the game up to speed on current consoles. Other goodies include new lighting mechanics, the new eight-mission chapter called "Lost Mission," and bits of Rage tech thrown into the mix.
"It’s not just Doom 3 – that’s what we’re keen to make sure everybody knows," Willits said. "We’re doing more with Doom 3 BFG than just re-releasing the original.  We’ve actually put a heck of a lot of Rage tech into the Doom 3 engine to kind of modernize the game."
As an example, the team tossed in the Rage input control and checkpoints. They also updated the lighting so it's brighter throughout the game, changed the annoying flashlight, tweaked the ammo, and even implemented the Rage network layer to make it run faster at low latency. There's also 3D support, and multi-display support for the PC platform.
"We went through every single level of the original and things that were really frustrating or not fun, we made them more enjoyable. So it is really kind of cool for us – especially as we all love the Doom franchise – to go back and rework the game in such a way," he added.
Doom 3 BFG Edition has enough small changes to essentially re-introduce the franchise to old and new fans alike. "Everyone’s heard of Doom, but you’d be surprised at just how many people haven’t actually played it," he said.
As for the specs needed to run the PC version, they'll obviously need to be higher than what was required in 2004. Willits said the biggest change with the PC version is that it now runs at 120 Hz. The team also revamped the HUD elements, the PD elements, and made map modifications. Overall the biggest glaring change will be for console junkies who purchased Doom 3 for the original Xbox eight years ago.
That said, the interview went on to talk about tweaking the map designs. He pointed out one section in the Alpha Labs that simply had to go because it was incredibly... not fun. "There was this part where you walk up these stairs, and the stairs fall apart behind you and Imps spawn in front of you," he said. "When we were playing through that earlier this year we were like, 'this is not fun right here…this was a bad idea.'"
"We grabbed our young designers and said, 'young designer, this is a bad design right here. How do you think we can fix it?’ and so we fixed it," he added. "You know it’s kind of funny, because most of the guys who worked on Doom 3 originally, they still work there."
"One of the guys wanted to go back and up-rez and make the characters look better, and a texture artist said, ‘you know, I never liked those textures, can I go back and fix them?’ and we said ‘sure, go ahead, knock yourself out and fix them up,'" he said.
Sounds like Doom 3 BFG Edition will be an entirely new experience when it launches on October 16.
(There is more to this interview online, but this was the edited version)

While the community is not as lively as it could or should be, and prior entries to the season (such as Armageddon) are going strong to this day; as a whole, Worms Clan Wars may be the best 2D Worms title yet. Expanding on Revolution's physics-based combat, especially dynamic water, this is a game that requires a change in strategy from say, Worms Reloaded. For example, in Worms Clan Wars, when a grenade is thrown anywhere that is not completely flat land, it rolls. Typically in an older Worms title, grenades would not be nearly as affected by gravity. This makes combat either much easier, or much harder, depending on how you are at the game. Either way, it requires a bit of getting used to.
Clan Wars' strength lies in its customization. While Mac users are out of luck currently regarding the Steam Workshop, everyone has open access to the in-game level editor, which is excellent and very easy to use thanks to a selection of brush and line tools which make precise editing simple.
Unfortunately this is a game, and an entire series that shines with its multiplayer; but the community is lacking, as of now. So, unless you have friends to play with, you may want to get Armageddon instead.
If that's not an issue, by all means buy this. Especially on its current $6 sale.

Firstly, I understand why this game has to exist.  Having a series of Lego games and not having one based on the Lego movie would seem ridiculous.  That being said.... I wish I could give it a "meh".  It was disappointing, although not entirely surprisingly that it was.  But who can resist seeing Abe Lincoln and Shakespeare having a chat?
There are only 5 "minikits" to discover on each level, when many of the other games have 10.  Also, I think this may be the smallest number of characters I have seen in a Lego game.  Each level also contains a pair of pants, which I completely understand is a running joke in the game, but these pants seemingly have no purpose.  And someone correct me if I'm wrong, but it appears that the DLC is only a couple of pairs of pants.  I have played this almost to completion and have never had to wear a pair of the magical pants.  If you want to include the pants, they should matter to the storyline somehow.  Like in Batman, when he and Robin had many outfits, but each served a need.  Overall it took me a fraction of the time to get through this game compared to other Lego games, and I also have no desire to replay it, as I do many of the others.
I also found the overall layout of the game clunky.  There is no minimap or world map with which to navigate the levels.  You are required to travel to the appropriate "land" and find the magic spot at which to start each level.  Unfortunately if you're only missing one kit and don't remember where it was, as far as I know you have to go to each spot and check.
Lastly, (and I completely realize that I'm being petty here)...the main character can't build Legos.  I understand why because of the plot of the movie, but still.  It's so oxymoronic that it bothers the crap out of me.  If you go into this game with no expectations and the game is on a good sale, go for it.  But if you are interested in a better symbol of the Lego series, go with a different one.

Kid finds the Bastion on Steam sale...
It welcomes him with a familiar, yet fresh style. Its landscapes like an oil painting, its soundtrack envelopes the world beautifully and animations are elegantly sleek. Certainly a strong argument that games can themselves be a work of art
Hack n slash... kid's seen it before. But not like this. Elegant combat mechanics and a hearty arsenal that continues to grow throughout the game - each with their own distinct niche and style. Hard to comment on balance... kid seemed to believe that some were stronger than others, but friends found otherwise. Certainly reassuring to see each weapon come with its own learning curve of sorts. But kid can only pick two... that and the shield on his back. Game's not that cruel though... kid can change loadouts, and even change the upgrades themselves for free - allowing the full enjoyment of exploring different combinations to suit their style without punishing the decisions. Certainly more forgiving... than the calamity...
About that... this story ain't anything new. It doesn't twist and turn, but is elegantly spun with nothing more than the guiding sound of a rustic narrator to weave the story together as the world itself continually weaves beneath the kid's feet. Every now and then the plot will be augmented with a single, simple, yet beautiful drawing
Black potions also help the kid to... swing things in his favour in a pinch. A single special ability. Balance is definitely more questionable here. Use the Calamity Cannon multi-shot ability and come tell me the other ones match it. Passive bonuses from the distillery (and my... special stash) futher enrich the level of customisability and allow the kid to really carve the game in his style
Sure the kid's seen games like this before. But what it does, it does to near perfection. It burrowed into the kid's library and found a special place in its heart
I guess you could say it found the Bastion

Bastion is a 2D RPG game with a few "platformer" elements. You basically start each mission from a "home-place" called "Bastion" (of course) and move across the many lands through a hub. It tells the story of a world in ruin after a cataclysm that scattered the whole civilization - not to mention the fauna populating the world - leaving a very few survivors the task to "re-build" the world itself. I'm not going into any details as I would spoil the story but the hero (The Kid) will meet some characters with whom he may have some kind of interaction; the story is told with a mix of short in-game sequences and a narrator, which is kinda a mentor, guide to The Kid.
The game itself is well crafted, with each shard having its unique environment and enemies; the platforming aspects which I mentioned before are of a minimal impact (and that's a good thing, IMO) and they would have you jumping from a platform to another to reach a new area or to obtain some items. As I've already written the game is 2D and you move your character direct-controlling it (WASD) and using the mouse to attack; a primary and secondary attack and a special move are available, the latter requiring some usables.
The Bastion, as a fortress which it is, indeed, can and must be upgraded to obtain new weapons and modify them; to build new structures which can provide you bonus and malus (soon explained); acquire materials to enhance weapons and gain passives. The RPG elements are quite unique and give you a very good amount of customization. For each new level gained you can choose a new passive to use and aid you through the many encounters. Every time a new weapon is found, an area will become accessible to train with that weapon and get more items/resources/xp. Shortly before I introduced a structure that can give you bonuses.. well, how that works? Its concept, and rather surprisingly, its realization, kicks some asses as it not an arcade feat. where you just become more powerful. Nope. This building let you divine a god (amongst 10) with each one of them giving you a % of +xp and +resources.. but each shrine will eventually kick-in a malus, like stronger enemies, mobs regenerating health.. so it's rather game-changing. I want to point out that each and every passive/shrine/some other elements can be swappable throughout the game just by visiting the bastion.
The are no real dialogs neither cinematics (just a bunch of very short sequences); over the journey the player has given the choice only two times.. which I won't be explaining as they'd be major spoils. Original music, nice sound FXs, very good arts and polished graphic.
Overall:
Graphic: 7
Art: 9
Sound: 7
Music: 8
Gameplay: 8
Replay value: 8
Uniqueness: 9
Partial: 8

Based on all the reviews up here so far I was expecting something a little more impressive.
From the getgo I was put off by the fact that this felt very much like a phone port to me. I know this isn't currently available on any phones but the interface seemed to be designed for a touch screen and the visual quality is extremely lacking in a way where it appears to have been blown up to fit the resolution of a larger screen (which is disappointing because the illustrations are very lovely). I checked if there were any graphics options, but there weren't. You shouldn't have to play something in windowed mode to make it look nice.
Some of the design choices also turned me off a bit. The text font and cursor seem to be an afterthought when compared to how lovely the drawing is. I know this is a nitpicky complaint but it cheapened the experience for me.
Since I only played through the first chapter I can't speak to the full quality of the puzzles as the developers may have thrown in some complications, but for me the swallowing pills to swap back and forth between normal/nightmare mode got dull pretty quick. It was fun to see all the insane imagery but it would have been nice if this function offered something a little more in depth than giving clues to solutions that are really pretty simple to figure out. There was no real gameplay motivation to take the pills other than two points where the two perspectives served to directly influence one another and they were a little obvious to be totally satisfying. But as I said, I only played an hour of the game. The puzzles may get much more complicated but the connect the dots logic in chapter 1 was giving me some nasty flashbacks to Broken Age.
In terms of what I got from the premise of this game: clever in concept but could be handled with more finesse (not talking about the full narrative arc here, just nuances I picked up). The dialogue was definitely so-so. Sometimes I got into the mindset of this being a 10-year-old and sometimes it felt very clunky. Yes these characters aren't mentally all there in a lot of cases, but some of this awkward dialogue can be attributed to the hospital's staff. This iffyness is something I felt in some of the game's imagery as well. Some of it worked super well and some of it stuck out  like reading a weak metaphor in an otherwise thoughtful poem
All of this aside, if this game truly seemed to be optimized for pc I would feel a little better about recommending it. As it is now I would say it's possibly worth checking out at a discounted price. NOT SAYING TO AVOID THIS COMPLETELY. I definitely appreciate the effort put into this by such a small team and I would have never written this much about a game I though was flat out bad. It's something way wild to look at and It may just be your thing. Unfortunately in this case there were enough things that irked me to take me out of the experience and felt someone needed to be devil's advocate so they don't feel swindled by the overwhelming positivity (which is what happened to me, I know I'm an idiot)
Try the demo out before you click purchase.

Isaac is a FUN, incredibly sturdy, and immensely replayable addition to the emerging action Roguelite genre.
Gameplay 10/10
With a simple, polished, and intuitive gameplay format, Isaac really shows what the action genre is capable of. The controls are extremely tight, and there are very few occasions where it feels like you are not in control of how your run goes. It's also marked by a near-infinite level of replayability, as the game is tough as nails if you can't break the initial barrier but becomes extremely satisfying and enjoyable if you manage to surpass it with a combination of your skill and game dynamics.
The main thing about Isaac that really stands out is that it takes the concept of breaking a game and builds an entire system of meta-gameplay around this, with secret bosses that practically require you to break your run in fun and empowering ways and unlocks that require hundreds of instances of experimentation and recombination of gameplay elements. The game has hundreds of hours of unlocks that really test your mettle and determination, and maybe thousands of hours more of pure unadulterated fun in replayability.
Presentation 8/10
Stylish and fluid, the graphics are pretty stunning and not oversold by-the-numbers pixel-ification. There are subtle homages to pretty much the entire history of videogames, but despite being obvious to seasoned players they are presented in a very original and uncompromising way. The soundtrack and soud design is phenomenal and while not perfect really suits the game world and tone just as well as the visual feel.
Accessibility 6/10
This, I think, is Isaac's greatest downfall, and i strongly believe it comes from the format of the game. Its random nature extends the gameplay in a way that means you will often have polarisingly difficult runs, from times when you can immediately tell you will win without much hassle to endless streaks of runs where you will be made to feel like a helpless fish out of water. It is the only element of the game that feels out of the player's control, especially when you're first starting out and don't completely know the ropes. I cannot say for sure what could remedy this, because it is sure to deter some players from continuing the experience, but it is certainly not such a sordid detail that it ruins the entire gameplay experience.
Overall 8/10
I cannot emphasise this enough: It is FUN. It can be a ♥♥♥♥♥ sometimes, but if you can allow yourself not to take the experience too seriously you are guaranteed to become totally submerged in all of its quirks and subtleties that create the immensely replayable experience of Isaac.

There was nothing challenging about the final chapter, and especially not in the final scenes. I loved this game so much (the graphics are straight up ART and the story is so unique) and I wish the ending was more satisfying. Still, it's different from any game I've ever played. It's almost like an adult, horrifying Pajama Sam (if anyone remembers that from their 90s/00s childhood), except more challenging and grown up, of course. If puzzling games are what you like, this will stump you for sure. Just don't expect all of your efforts to amount to something amazing in the end.

Developed at Rebellion by the team responsible for the original 1999 PC classic, the all-new Aliens vs. Predator allows players to take the role of three infamous species: Colonial Marines, Predators and Aliens. The game features a unique three-way online multiplayer experience, allowing gamers to battle for survival and the right to be crowned the deadliest species in the galaxy. Each race also has its own distinct action-packed single-player campaign mode, with a storyline that cleverly interweaves with the other two species’ paths. Set on planet BG-386; a human colonist mining group discovers an ancient pyramid containing a dark and horrible secret. Across the galaxy, a race of warriors is alerted to the discovery of their pyramid and a hunting party is dispatched to ensure that it remains sealed at all costs. Deep inside the ruined pyramid meanwhile, nature's deadliest species awakes from centuries of hibernation intent on finding new prey. The Colonial Marine's story is an incredible fight against all odds from horrors lurking in the dark. Surrounded on all sides yet armed to the teeth, the Colonial Marine represents humanity's last stand with the firepower to fight back. As the Alien, players discover what it's like to be the scariest, most murderous creature in the universe, with the ability to traverse any surface at lightning speed in order to get close enough to unleash its deadly claws, tail and teeth. A master of the hunt, the Predator grants the player an arsenal of exotic weaponry with which to stalk from the shadows. Earn the greatest honor by ambushing prey up-close, before butchering them for a gory trophy kill.

I hope that many years from now
is remembered as the quintessential retro game of the downloadable era. Too many game developers have settled to plagiarizing outdated game mechanics, putting the end product through a pixelated filter and justify a frustrating experience by calling it "Nintendo hard" to gain that somehow glorified honor of being called "retro". Well I'm old enough to have lived throughout that period and wise enough not to glorify it through rose-tinted glasses. I also remember the sense of discovery that came from trying out new weapons and destroying everything, so I'm glad to say
has well understood that concept while making
!
The setting behind the story could best be described as "Frontier Fantasy" with your analogs to pioneers, marshals, mines full of mystic crystal cores and dispossessed natives undercutting your mission to rebuild the Bastion, aka humanity's last refuge. You'll read a lot about this game's very own narrator whose grizzled voice is there to give your actions a certain gravitas. It works, but having him be the
source of exposition makes it near impossible to connect with anything else! You barely interact with anyone and if you do talk to other characters,
tells you what they say! A whole universe experienced through the pinhole of one old man's words, that's what
is!
The world itself could best be described as an isometric sky platform badly in need of handrails. Forget pixels, this is all hand-drawn art with individual sprites and the result is a full and vibrant environment with a diverse menagerie of monsters, each with their own characteristics, some even with their own backstory! In an age of heavily processed animations, still having
graphics is the most retro thing there is!
The actual fun in the gameplay comes from trying to find the right combination of two weapons with which to face the dangers ahead. You build quite the arsenal throughout your journey and each weapon has its own skill tree in which thankfully, you can change your decisions if you're unhappy or just feeling experimental. This is important because you'll soon come across a variety of binary needs, most of which aren't readily evident. I mean, you can understand quick & short-ranged vs slow & long-ranged but soon comes factors such as spread damage, weapon stun, poison vs direct damage, the issue of armor penetration and so forth. Needless to say, every weapon is unique and it's the combination thereof that makes the gameplay so engaging.
Much appreciated are the training camps for each and every weapon along with the dream sequences which just has the Kid fight wave after wave of enemies. They're supplemental, optional and a great way to acclimate yourself with the new toy you just discovered in that one stage. I also liked the timed shield reflect mechanic which might be overpowered since it also reverses melee attacks. You also have access to about thirty Secret Skills, super moves for all of your weapons; however since they are all activated by collectable Black Tonics these all turn into so many different ways to press an emergency "SAVE ME" button.
There's A LOT of exposition dump concentrated early on but I'd say that the game really picks up after finding your third or fourth Bastion shard and opening the Forge which allows you to start customizing weapons. There's a self-awareness in that the game realizes all that it wants to accomplish but still attempts to be as accessible as possible; heck, even the difficulty system works on an individual monster upgrade system, though one that is non-essential towards the story.
is this most ambitious of undertakings but still provides gameplay relatable to a child. A rare gem that should truly be enjoyed by all.

Very disappointing. The game looks good enough, especially with ENB, but that's about all it has going for it. Criterion purport the idea of race events on a free roam map as something new, "unlike any other driving experience", even though Need for Speed Underground 2 and Test Drive Unlimited had both done similar things prior to its release. All events are extremely easy, and with no difficulty option (at least not one I could find in the ill-conceived labyrinthine menu system), the game soon becomes very dull.
In-game advertisements are a spit in the face from the developers. Perhaps it would be understandable if the game were free to play, or if it were trying to emulate a "real world", but it's not. These were clearly only put in for profit, not an attempt at realism, since the game is set in a fictional city and none of the cars are licensed. I paid for the game I don't want to see Burger King and EVGA advertisements while playing it.
Various elements of the game are at cross-purposes with each other. Events are put at every intersection, supposedly to cut down on monotony and so there's never an event too far away, but the races aren't gated and the route isn't highlighted on the map as with other arcade racers, which means you have to open your map at the beginning of each race and spend time planning your route. You can't jump to events either, which, in the case of Burning Route events, often means you have to drive halfway across the map just to begin a race.
On the topic of Burning Route events; the game boasts a range of 75 cars, when in actuality, in terms of unique vehicles there is about half that, with the other half being practically carbon-copies with different paint jobs which are rewarded after completing time trials. By the end of the game, you'll only be using about 3 of the cars anyway (the best in each category; stunt, aggression and speed), since the others are relatively useless.
The soundtrack is awful. For reasons unknown to anyone but the developers, there are 3 different styles of music in this game; pop/rock songs, instrumental songs from the three previous Burnout games, and classical compositions. The loudness levels are not normalized either, which means that some songs are barely audible while others are quite loud. The "CrashFM" DJ is obnoxious and detestable.

I should preface my review with the fact that this is my first Lego-based game, and I've never actually watched any of the Lego movies.
For what it's worth, I really enjoyed playing this game. I wasn't looking for a mindblowing experience going into this; I wanted something laidback and fun to play without requiring too much thought or skills. Each level is unique yet not hard enough to make you throw your controller down in frustration, and each character has their own quirks and special abilities. I enjoyed the humour, especially considering I didn't watch the original movie.
I liked that there is never any rush to move on to the next level; you can explore each level as much (or as little) as you want, you can practically destroy everything to earn extra points if you like, and you have the choice to revisit levels later on if you're a perfectionist (like me) to complete random missions. The levels can get a little tedious at times, especially since you're only able to save at certain checkpoints so you have to play until you reach those points or you'd be forced to replay the entire level.
Overall, it's not the best game of the century or anything, but when you're looking to relax after a long day of work, playing a level or two of this definitely hits the spot.

Bastion is an interesting and entirely unique game. Firstly, it posites its artistic style as a centre-point of the game. It's not a shallow decision, but it works with the story and, in building and reinforcing the setting/story. The combat is not repitive, it's rather fun, with role-playing elements to be had in the form of passive buffs, whose slots expand with levelling, different weapon selections (You carry two plus a separate special ability) and more you discover upon purchase of the game. It all works to build the world and its story. Ah, speaking of which, the story is the high-point. It makes you feel. It makes you feel the awe of what has happened. It also evokes feelings of sadness. Feelings in general are helped along by the amazing soundtrack, which also matches certain settings to make you feel a bit more 'in the scene'. Unlike things like the walking dead, or even those moments in mass effect 3 (Dubious), Bastion puts you in your characters shoes and nails you in there. The Kid is who you want him to be.
GTA + Rush Hour + CSI with a spice of crazy = Sleeping Dogs.  If that doesn't tell you this game is fun you won't like it.

*My review is based on the first time I started playing this game.
Ahhh, CABAL, my favorite MMORPG ever. (I have played a lot of MMORPG's) Where to begin, I started playing in 2009, with my first character being a Force Blader called ironman11. That character has been my main character to this date, it's level 166 now (also own all other classes, all around level 100-140). I have played the game a 1000+ hours, and know a lot about the game.
What I like:
- The skill system is a favorite of mine. You don't unlock skills as you level up as in most other games, you have to get Skill EXP to level your skill level up. Back in 2009 you could only get Skill EXP by 'skilling', that meant attacking a dummy for a hell of a long time while being AFK, and then coming back to see that your skill level has increased. One of the best feelings ever. After all those hours skilling, you could finally buy your fresh new skill of buff!
Skilling is not required anymore since an update a while ago, you'll get Skill EXP with the quests.
- Leveling. Yes, I liked it. Because you'd unlock new maps every 15 levels! Every time I unlocked a new map I was hyped! Back in the day leveling went EXTREMELY slow though, now you can quest/grind your way up to level 120 in about four days (I managed to do it, so I know it's possible.)
- Graphics. Back in 2009, I thought the game looked awesome, for now the graphics are outdated and such, but they give me a nostalgic feel.
- The soundtrack! The music in CABAL is beautiful in my opinion, for example, the beautiful theme of Bloody Ice, where you'd hang out to skillgrind or craft. I even listen to the OST outside of the game sometimes, again, to give me that nostalgic feel. :D
- Dungeons. Everytime I entered a new dungeon for the first time, I watched a video before entering so that I knew the quest. Because all the dungeons have an objective, and to progress further into the dungeons need to kill mobs for items or click objects in a certain order etc.
What I don't like:
- Grind for Alz. Alz is the currency in CABAL Online, to get it you need to complete quests, but after level ~120 you don't get Alz anymore. The total amount you get for completing ALL the quests in the game is about 100kk (100 million). That's not enough to buy you some decent gear. I'm currently trying to get a complete set of 'Palladium of Outrageous' gear, the highest gear in the game with an enchantment on it that amplifies your damage output, one piece of the 4 is 100kk (1 slot) to 1kkk (2 slots), depending on the seller.
To grind that amount of money is almost impossible, you'd have to get very good drops to get that amount of Alz. Mot people don't ever bother with that grind and buy Alz instead.
- Upgrading, the fastest way to lose your Alz! It can be extremely frustrating to buy an inventory full of Upgrade Core (Highest) (1kk each) and upgrading your +4 item with high hopes, and ending up with a +4 item after you used all cores. It's like this: 4 - 5 - 6 - 7 - 5 - 6 - 7 - 8 - 6 - 7 - 8 - 6 - 5 - 4... bye 50kk!
- IGNcode. It's the worst gameguard EVER. My game crashes every 30 mins because of this freaking buggy error. Horrible. (Won't happen to everybody, mostly Windows 8/8.1/10 users.)
Although there are those things I don't like, I'll still recommend this game, just play it. It's awesome. :)
That's all the pros and cons I can think of right now, if you have any questions about CABAL, or just want to hear some of my stories in the game, feel free to add me! :D

This has to be one of the best point and click games in the past few years. Sure, Daedalic pulled out quite a few good ones, but not as invigorating and enticing as this one.
The description of this game is as far as spoilers should go when you're interested in this game. If you're not convinced, go play the demo.
The atmosphere, asthetic, music and characteristics of this game are absolutely gorgeous. Yes, there's some cheesy dialogue that made me roll my eyes, but when taking it from the perspective that this game is going for, it's certainly well in place. The protagonist isn't a 'know it all badass' or 'hopelessly confused person' like in most games. Instead, it's just an innocent girl that kind of stays innocent throughout the game.
There are many, many 'oh my, what the hell' moments throughout the game, excluding the very disturbing images after taking the pills. Even without those, it's still gritty and disturbing.
The journey is filled with (unpleasant) surprises, which hadn't taken an impact on me since playing Darkseed or Tormented. Some of the story is vague, but there are many clues to figure it out.
The downside is that 'some' of the puzzles are just plain annoying or don't make sense at all. For me, personally, there was a math 'puzzle' that didn't make sense. Or I had to interact an item in my inventory with a character, which could have easilly solved by just interacting with that character, like the rest of the game functioned before this particular 'puzzle'.
The UI is a bit clunky as well and doesn't respond as something like monkey island or the rather clunky Machinarium, which is strange, considering that the latter is a flash game. The UI in this game just doesn't respond at times.
Despite these slight flaws, I want to thank the developers for this amazing game and hope that they can make more of these masterpieces.
Bottom line: If you're a point 'n click adventurer... Go get this game. like some horror and aren't too afraid of the dark? Then this game is worth every cent.

Video playthrough:
This game is absolutely phenominal! A horrific tale presented from the perspective of such a young heroine. The game is a test of courage mixed with a plea to retain innocence.
The artstyle, reminiscent of the 90s TV show Angela Anaconda (yet cleaner, smoother and, of course, gorier) fits in so well with the plot and the point-and-click style. Flashbacks are presented in a noir style, but maintain a modern presentation and flow that holds your attention until you retain control again. Everything works great with tight controls and easily distinguishable objects and backgrounds.
The music and sound effects only serve to enhance the cartoony, yet horrific, images you will have to encounter on your journey. It will serve to sway and move you as you interact with characters springing to life with their own personalities. Although you need to read dialogue, you will easily be able to find each character's voice and relate to them in your own way within a few words.
The gameplay itself, which involves collecting and combining items and solving puzzles, is nothing new, but is absolutely intuitive to the design of this game. You will get stumped at times, but not to the point where you will feel like something is impossible.
Overall, I had a very pleasant experience with this game. The full release truly showcases the real horrific beauty of Fran's tale.

Fran Bow is one of those games that changes your opinion of life after you play it. Very few games have achieved making me feel this way about them. The gameplay is very gory, but contains a concept that was completely new to me and facinating in the way it is executed. Playing as a 11 year old girl struggling within her own mind. Being told everything through direct thoughts made it much more immersive. I never really knew who to trust. Every object had several sentences of dialogue. I triple clicked on every object, read everything there was to read to see all of her reactions. I'm also planning on re-playing this again to catch what I might have missed which I rarely do. That's how magnificent of a game this is. Playing as Fran really made me enjoy every minute of it too. What I didn't expect is you will play as other characters as you go along when Fran isn't available. Her opinion on simple objects made this game so much more interesting for me. There is plenty of symbolism that tell side stories of the children you're first introduced to. I am so happy Killmonday took the time to include them within the story. It really gave a great deal of emotion and helped influence the mood. The mystery is what really kept me playing. Answers are weaved within the story instead of only at the end. New mysterys are made when old ones are answered. Small hints are everywhere but usually vague, you'll understand them eventually. I really enjoyed making those connections. The puzzles can be difficult but to me makes them much more satisfying to solve. Some unexpected mini games appeared which made playing very entertaining. If you're into mysterious and gory point and click adventures you seriously NEED to get this game, it is outstanding!

This game is a nice spin on the FPS format. Brings something different to the table BUT it does have its share of problems. The single player side is way too limited on what you can do. Three short campaigns and a survival mode (where you can only be a marine) and that is it. There is no way to play your favorite race (Predator in my case) after the campaign other than Multi-player and THAT is where the fun ends. MP definitely needs tweaking. The biggest problem I have found is the "E-Kill." People run around spamming their "E" button in the chance that if they get close enough to GRAB someone ... the "E-Kill" does the rest. It is an instant death command for which there is no defense. That needs to go right off the top. Second, they make the Predator run around the map to collect his weapons before he can use them. So when he dies , he loses everything and has to go collect them again. Lame. People merely camp the weapon spawns and you die horribly trying to get something to fight with. A typical adventure on a MP game goes something like this .... Spawn ... E-killed ..... spawn take two steps ... E-killed ..... spawn ... actually make it to a weapon spawn and try to pick one up ... E-Killed ..... spawn ... take 5 steps ... E-Killed ..... and this is no exaggeration ... I was killed literally 10 times before I ever took 10 steps by E-Kills ..... does that sound fun to anyone?? So, IF you want to brave the MP side of things I would reccommend finding games with 4 to 8 players as oppossed to the maps with 14-18 ... the more players on the map the more likely you will be E-Killed back to back to back everytime you show your face on the map. So overall .. I liked the gameplay as far as what each race can do ... single player is okay ... but the MP side of the game needs ALOT of work to make it remotely fun.

Very disappointing. The game looks good enough, especially with ENB, but that's about all it has going for it. Criterion purport the idea of race events on a free roam map as something new, "unlike any other driving experience", even though Need for Speed Underground 2 and Test Drive Unlimited had both done similar things prior to its release. All events are extremely easy, and with no difficulty option (at least not one I could find in the ill-conceived labyrinthine menu system), the game soon becomes very dull.
In-game advertisements are a spit in the face from the developers. Perhaps it would be understandable if the game were free to play, or if it were trying to emulate a "real world", but it's not. These were clearly only put in for profit, not an attempt at realism, since the game is set in a fictional city and none of the cars are licensed. I paid for the game I don't want to see Burger King and EVGA advertisements while playing it.
Various elements of the game are at cross-purposes with each other. Events are put at every intersection, supposedly to cut down on monotony and so there's never an event too far away, but the races aren't gated and the route isn't highlighted on the map as with other arcade racers, which means you have to open your map at the beginning of each race and spend time planning your route. You can't jump to events either, which, in the case of Burning Route events, often means you have to drive halfway across the map just to begin a race.
On the topic of Burning Route events; the game boasts a range of 75 cars, when in actuality, in terms of unique vehicles there is about half that, with the other half being practically carbon-copies with different paint jobs which are rewarded after completing time trials. By the end of the game, you'll only be using about 3 of the cars anyway (the best in each category; stunt, aggression and speed), since the others are relatively useless.
The soundtrack is awful. For reasons unknown to anyone but the developers, there are 3 different styles of music in this game; pop/rock songs, instrumental songs from the three previous Burnout games, and classical compositions. The loudness levels are not normalized either, which means that some songs are barely audible while others are quite loud. The "CrashFM" DJ is obnoxious and detestable.

Incredibly boring gameplay compared to the other lego games. Most lego games are pretty entertaining for all ages but I wouldn't even think kids would enjoy this chore of a game. The graphics in this game are oddly terrible, Lego Star Wars: The Complete Saga came out 7 years BEFORE this game and its graphics are far superior and its gameplay is millions of times more enjoyable.
The gold page collectibles are very boring to collect and the challenges to collect them are monotonous and unimaginative. Challenges such as "Break 5 of these objects for a page" are cloned in almost every level. The Red Brick that shows you where these pages are is incredibly misleading and completely unacceptable to even 2007 lego game standards. Furthermore if you miss a golden page due to the incompetence of the red brick you have to sit through the whole bloody level again to find that the reason you missed the page is because there was a Horton hears a Who sized door you didn’t notice that led to a secret room.
There is also one pair of pants you can collect in each level that you can then wear on a character for bonuses. But, after you complete a level with these pants they will disappear from the character you applied them to. The bonuses they give is not worth the effort of having to go to a pants machine every time you want to put on a pair and having to suffer through “HONEY WHERE ARE MY PAAAAAANTS” over and over again.
There are many characters to unlock but 90% of them are completely useless filler to make you think there are a lot of characters but they all are completely mundane pieces of garbage with only the ability to punch and kick and nothing else.
Mute the music as soon as possible as it is just a 10 second loop over and over again that will drive you mad. Admittedly, I missed the Bastion hype train when it came chugging past in 2011 and had only ever heard of a brief description of it being 'good' from people around me. How I missed that goodness knows but after playing Bastion I can only say that it completely lives up to the hype around it.
In an action RPG hack and slasher, you play as a character simply called The Kid. What unfolds is a story where there is no 'good' or 'bad' but instead a morally grey area for a majority of the characters which leads to some interesting perspectives. The story is told by the narrator who comments and narrates almost everything you do as The Kid. Perhaps people can see this as being a gimmick for the game but I personally found it delightfully charming and enjoyed listening to the commentary as I played. It helps to try the story forward and serves as encouragement if you should get stuck to keep going. The only gripe I have about the story is that I would've liked to have a bit more of it, plus one of the decisions that you're forced to choose at the end doesn't seem to have much of an effect on the end story.
Graphically the game is stunning, even living up to the standards of 2014. Seeing the ground rise up around my character as I walked was stunning and helped to keep the pace of the game. Every area has been designed carefully so there's a lot to see and do in a story that is around 5 hours long. The foes you come up against have all had thought put into them and both move and look as I'd imagined.
Gameplay-wise the game is clever as it has an almost 'choose your own difficulty' with the shrine settings. By activating more idols  you gain bigger rewards but this in turn makes the game much more difficult. The use of the distillery also allows the player themselves to choose what bonuses they gain from levelling up making it so The Kid is completely customised to the player. The same goes with weapons; a range of melee and ranged weapons drop throughout the game which once again allows the player to play at their preferred style. This isn't something I'm used to seeing in games and it added to my enjoyment.
As for the soundtrack... it's honestly one of my favourite soundtracks and I'm someone who doesn't download soundtracks too much. It fits the mood of the game perfectly and  helps to immerse you straight into the world of Bastion. There's not much else I can say but I can guarantee that at the very least you should be able to fall in love with the soundtrack even if the game isn't for yourself.
The replay factor varies. I'm not the sort of person who'd play a game more than once yet I found myself playing Bastion for the second time through with the new gamemode I'd unlocked. As it allows you to carry over your stats and weapons from your previous save it makes the game a lot easier which some people may dislike but I enjoyed immensely. The game isn't so long that replaying it feels tedious either!
Ultimately I ended up being surprised that this game was made by an indie developer as it's so polished and such a beautiful, engaging game. There's not much I can fault other than one slight disgruntlement with the storyline to be honest. This comes highly recommended if there's anyone else who hasn't played it, even when it's not on sale. If it's on sale... well, there's no excuse to not buy Bastion.

So far, this is the first LEGO game that i'll be giving a 'not recommended' review for.
It's greatest problem, I feel, is that the usual LEGO charm is almost completely absent. Usually, a large part of the fun is seeing how they inject humour into what are normally serious franchises. As the LEGO movie is a humourous movie in itself, the humour you see in the game has already all been seen before (if you've seen the movie of course), and therefore loses a lot of it's impact.
A small amount of new humour is added (mostly by Vitruvius), but it's not enough to carry it.
The game features several flying characters that can't actually fly much at all, due to the flying 'space' being far too small. This results in it feeling restricitve, which ultimately means there isn't much point to the flying characters throughout a lot of the game.
On top of that, are the widely documented technical issues. These are a serious problem. Now, i've played enough lego games to know that some bugs, or even crashes are common in LEGO games - these are usually tolerable, but in this game they have reached all new levels.
Bugs such as the "Everything is awesome" dance scene on the construction site simply not working, meaning you can't progress the level, or one of the jack in the boxes in cloud cuckoo land floating in the air making it impossible to collect one of the red bricks. In addition to this, i have a pretty powerful PC, and this is the first LEGO game i've ever had stuttering frame rates on.
Finally, some of the gold instruction manuals (this games version of minikits) are in scenes where you have little control of your character, falling, rolling down a hill, or chase scenes. Now, this sort of thing is common for LEGO games, but you'll usually get what you need on the second or third try. On this game, they are infuriatingly hard to get, and if you miss one, it means starting the whole level again.
This could be the first LEGO game that I don't 100%, as i'm not sure I have the patience for it.
EDIT: I did manage to 100% the game in the end, but otherwise this review remains unchanged.

Pros: Gets just about everything right for zombie survival. Among the best co-op, always providing something important for all four players to do(cover an angle, use a throwable while the others hold zombies off, etc.) and making them depend on each other(Special Infected tend to immobilize one of the four, and one of the other three will need to help them). There is no "beating the zombies", there is only holding them off until you reach the next Safehouse; and yet levels don't feel linear, and the drive to get to safety propels players forward. The "Director" AI controls the mood, with each match being unpredictable and partly randomized(and still, it never overwhelms) - basically, at any point, you could be attacked by a Horde(which is exactly what it sounds like) and/or Special Infected. Immersive and atmosphere-laden co-op/multiplayer. Limited carry capacity makes you use items and guns carefully. Challenging, and with four difficulty settings *and* off-line, AI-aided campaign mode, this is open to players of different levels of skill.
Cons: Once you've played for a few hours, tried the different guns, levels and modes, there isn't anything "new" there - guns  and items can't be upgraded. While the four characters speaking can help the atmosphere, they do eventually get repetitive,  and they can't be turned off. For zombie survival purists like myself, infinite ammo pistols, plenty of ammo refills, and, yes, running zombies, feel out of place.
My recommendation: For those into zombie survival and/or FPS, this is money well spent.

Graphics maybe looks little outdated but skill and special effects - nah, those are still impresing. CABAL feels more like Multi Massive Online RPG game than 90% of games from this genre made nowadays, which is really sad thing. With all those possibilities, with amazing graphics you could made, Devs are aiming to make another World of Warcraft clone game or some ACTION ONLINE game. Really sad thing happened to this genre over years.
CABAL Online is free to play, so the best you can do is download it and try it yourself. For now, I don't really have high level or didn't spend much time playing but when I feel like I want to play something good from this genre, I just log-in to CABAL and enjoy it.

Well it was game 3 on easy, and I finally got a victory! I'm really enjoying this. The pace is comfortable, it's not an RTS, nor is it turn based, but feels just right to me. The scale is low, which is a breath of fresh air, no more 8 level deep tech trees, or end game units that cost 80,000 resources. The economy is quite good, you might need to think about leaving buildings unmanned for a bit, or torching and moving to another spot, you can't just spam buildings and spike your production at will. I love the random maps, that's what originally got me hooked into buying this title. The devs recently added the ability to turn on and off victory conditions, but what about *randomly* switching them? You'd have to pick a clan without knowing exactly what strategies are available for victory. I love replayability like that. Anyway this is a fun, well paced, city builder.
Oh boy I forgot to mention anything about the ui and gfx. They're A-title grade. The art style reminds me of Dishonored which is nice. I find everything to be very easy to understand and find. Everything I need to know, it tells me. The way the mini-map starts off zoomed in and slowly, as you discover more territory, expands outward, is a nice touch.
Bugs wise, I've seen a few. I once sent my whole army into a territory, just to watch them all spontaneously die as soon as they cross the border. And I've seen peasants who seemed to be stuck on buildings, running in place. But I just rebooted the recent auto-save and it seemed to work itself out. All in all I haven't seen any major problems at all.

Right at the end of the game they became my friends, Blain joined my crew, and let me tell you, we stomped the ever loving horned helmets out of those rascal wolf clan interlopers! And then we made a small mint and I won. So yeah, two thumbs up, would befriend ancient norse mythological giants again.

Fran Bow is a very unique game. What starts as surreal and terrifying only escaltes. It took me aback several times with how creative and strange it could be. Beautiful music, art, and writing all come together to make a game unlike any I've played before. It's not for the faint of heart, with geninely upsetting themes like suicide, abortion, medical abuse, sexual abuse etc, so be wary of that.
The puzzles stumped me several times but, never to the point where I gave up. There's always just enough information (except for one or two parts) to keep you going, to keep searching.
A cross between charming and bizzare, between horror and fantasy, this is a lovely game.

This game is about as bloody, depressing and disgusting as it gets, and I love it.
I'm not much for point and click adventure games (in fact, I'd say it's easily one of, if not my least favorite genre), and while nothing had me particularly grossed out or 'scared' (like some ominous corridors and hallways in oldschool resident evil games often did with the limited saves and potential for lost progress), it's a fascinating storyline and I can only imagine what twists will come next (As of this review I'm up to chapter 3, and all I can say is LOLWAT). As far as I can tell there's no way to 'lose' (the maze minigame being a good example, which just resets you to the start if you touch the bad things) so that does hurt the mood slightly. With a few exceptions (the door code for instance), most puzzles can be solved by simply interacting with or combining everything you possibly can, but most of them make sense and are fairly obvious so you shouldn't have to do this.
A couple of parts in chapter 2 unintentionally (though I have a sneaking suspicion it was deliberate) worked as minor jump scares for me, though I've certainly seen bigger/worse, safe to say this game is not cheap stream bait like so many other budget horror titles. Not that I don't expect people to do videos/streams of it or anything.
Also, avoid spoilers whenever you can. It's worth playing through on your own at least once.

I loved Terraria, so I bought this game. What a mistake.
This game is more of a mess than Jeb Bush. It will never be finished, because Chuckle♥♥♥♥s have already made Stardew Valley. Presumably, this game is only a tech demo. I wish I could get my money back, but I bought this game long before Steam refunds were implemented.

Now, I was waiting for this game to hit release and bought it as soon as it came out. And even though my feelings for it are generally positive there are a few negatives to address, from my point of view.
The game is beautiful to look at, the concept and characters are simply astonishing and the atmosphere is to die for. The game mechanics works just fine and the level of the puzzles do a good job in respecting the players intelligence.
Over all Fran Bow is a great game but I do have some issues when it comes to the plot. I'll try and go through them without spoiling anything. While the first part of the game flows at a satisfying speed and with an interesting twisted environment it feels like it comes to a screeching halt in the middle. This section both amused me and annoyed me. While I found myself intrigued by the surrounding and the new game mechanism it felt like this part of the story was completely detached from the previous part that, despite having weird moments, felt like it belonged in the same story. The middle segment came completely out of left field for me.
After this halt the game sort of came back to the same flow but for me it was hard to get invested into the surroundings that more blended into the first part of the game. None the less it was good and I was starting to hype myself up for the conclusion.
And I have to say that I was sadly disappointed. I won't tell what happens but when I reached the ending I just felt like it was too anti-climatic. It felt rushed in comparison to the rest of the story and it felt more like I just needed to get the ending spelled out to me and then it was over. My rule of thumb with games is that when I reach the ending, I don't want to think “Wait? That's it?” and too bad that's how I felt with Fran Bow.
Now over all this game is worth your money, without a doubt. I got a solid 7 hours out of this game and over all the experience was good. The only let down was the middle segment and the, to me, weak ending. If you like horror and surreal things, go ahead and enjoy this gem.

Sanctum 2 suffers from two glaring flaws.  It can't seem to decide what it wants to be, and it can't stop holding the player on a leash.
Unlike the original Sanctum which was very clearly a tower defense game as well as a shooter, Sanctum 2 focuses almost entirely on the shooting.  The game gimps your ability to build proper mazes or place any significant number of towers, and oftentimes, your towers just can't do enough damage to matter and you find yourself relying more on your own gun. Furthermore, at certain intervals, the game forgoes the standard strategic preparation phase and gives you an abysmally short countdown.  Not only is this countdown unable to be paused if you need to go use the bathroom in between waves, but it hardly gives you enough time to walk across the map, let alone build any towers.  It's like the game itself is telling you "No time for strategy!  Go shoot things! Go go go!"
This wouldn't be that bad if the shooting element weren't so generic and constrained.  The game limits you to a loadout of two weapons, and locks you into your first weapon depending on your character, so your only customization is a single weapon.  Furthermore, unlike the previous game, weapons aren't even upgradeable.  It's like the game wants you to focus on shooting aspect, but at the same time doesn't actually let you focus on the shooting aspect.
Overall, Sanctum 2 feels like a game that doesn't know what it wants to be and, worst, doesn't want you doing too much.  It was not a fun experience and my trust in the developers has been grievously violated.

I have mixed feelings about this game. I still recommend you buy it, especially if you played the first game, but let's go over a few new details. In Sanctum 1, it was all about the towers and a lovely first person tower defense game...however, in Sanctum 2 there are tons of changes from the first game that make it more of a challenge and overall different feel compared to the first game. You get a limit on how many towers can place, they cost more, they are harder to upgrade, and it relies on you to kill most of the enemies with the towers as support instead of vice versa from the original game. To me, I had to rethink and form almost completely new strategies for this game. That being said, it is still a fantastic, albeit difficult, game. The maps are all new with beautiful design to them, and many of which can allow you to go back and play them again by creating a new path they may be better than your original to lead the Lumes (enemies) through. The towers in this game are familiar with the first one with a couple of new editions. Also there are 4 characters you can play as and customize with various perks, weapons, and towers for endless possibilities strategically. Some maps are more difficult than others and will frustrate you as they did me. Sometimes I'm led to believe this game was meant to be played with others through co-op in order to beat the levels, but then I find a new plan that works and even though it may be hard, you can solo this game should you wish. Overall, I give this game a solid 8 out of 10 if I had to, and I recommend it to those of you who love real time strategy, FPS, and/or tower defense games. This game just has it all wrapped into one. Also, I strongly recommend it to those of you who are in need of a game outside of TF2 and looking for another great multiplayer game you can play together and have some fun. The single-player side is great--don't misunderstand--, but that feeling of success when shared with friends after beating a level makes it oh-so-much-more satisfying.
