Admittedly, I missed the Bastion hype train when it came chugging past in 2011 and had only ever heard of a brief description of it being 'good' from people around me. How I missed that goodness knows but after playing Bastion I can only say that it completely lives up to the hype around it.
In an action RPG hack and slasher, you play as a character simply called The Kid. What unfolds is a story where there is no 'good' or 'bad' but instead a morally grey area for a majority of the characters which leads to some interesting perspectives. The story is told by the narrator who comments and narrates almost everything you do as The Kid. Perhaps people can see this as being a gimmick for the game but I personally found it delightfully charming and enjoyed listening to the commentary as I played. It helps to try the story forward and serves as encouragement if you should get stuck to keep going. The only gripe I have about the story is that I would've liked to have a bit more of it, plus one of the decisions that you're forced to choose at the end doesn't seem to have much of an effect on the end story.
Graphically the game is stunning, even living up to the standards of 2014. Seeing the ground rise up around my character as I walked was stunning and helped to keep the pace of the game. Every area has been designed carefully so there's a lot to see and do in a story that is around 5 hours long. The foes you come up against have all had thought put into them and both move and look as I'd imagined.
Gameplay-wise the game is clever as it has an almost 'choose your own difficulty' with the shrine settings. By activating more idols  you gain bigger rewards but this in turn makes the game much more difficult. The use of the distillery also allows the player themselves to choose what bonuses they gain from levelling up making it so The Kid is completely customised to the player. The same goes with weapons; a range of melee and ranged weapons drop throughout the game which once again allows the player to play at their preferred style. This isn't something I'm used to seeing in games and it added to my enjoyment.
As for the soundtrack... it's honestly one of my favourite soundtracks and I'm someone who doesn't download soundtracks too much. It fits the mood of the game perfectly and  helps to immerse you straight into the world of Bastion. There's not much else I can say but I can guarantee that at the very least you should be able to fall in love with the soundtrack even if the game isn't for yourself.
The replay factor varies. I'm not the sort of person who'd play a game more than once yet I found myself playing Bastion for the second time through with the new gamemode I'd unlocked. As it allows you to carry over your stats and weapons from your previous save it makes the game a lot easier which some people may dislike but I enjoyed immensely. The game isn't so long that replaying it feels tedious either!
Ultimately I ended up being surprised that this game was made by an indie developer as it's so polished and such a beautiful, engaging game. There's not much I can fault other than one slight disgruntlement with the storyline to be honest. This comes highly recommended if there's anyone else who hasn't played it, even when it's not on sale. If it's on sale... well, there's no excuse to not buy Bastion.

This game, and both of the prior Build-a-Lot games, are very fast-paced real-estate games about buying, upgrading, and selling homes in order to improve neighborhoods.
By this third installation, the core mechanic is mature, and still holds up fairly well. A couple of new additions, such as homes that start in a run-down state, police, fire, and medical emergencies help to keep the concept from going stale just yet. Premier lots, a feature from the first game that was missing in the second, make their return.
Perhaps the biggest cosmetic change to the game is in the level selection screens.  Instead of the traditional menu-of-levels that are the staple of games like this, Build-a-Lot 2 has you criss-crossing a political map of western Europe. Instead of just playing all of the levels from one setting consecutively, you will often play 1-3 levels in one locale before sprinting off to another, often returning to early locales for bigger projects.
This game to me seemed quite a bit easier than Build-a-Lot 2.  I was able to super-clear 26 of the first 28 levels on the first try.  In Build-a-Lot 2, it was only 16 of the first 18.
Overall, if you are a fan of the first two Build-a-Lot games, you shouldn't be disappointed in this one.

It looks nice and is pleasantly simple. However, I dont find the RTS elements that enticing nor that interesting. Don't get me wrong the game is challenging enough, I've played 5-6 full games and only won the one. But, the resource situation, upgrading, and mangement of your peons is ... overly simple. It is only difficult in the aspect that managing the growth curve is relative to the amoutn of peons versus all other types of employment you have. The feedback of the system to manage this is not great, but that should not be the game mechanic, but rather it should be great, and then you should have a trade-off situation with other resources and upgrade routes.
However, I find that to be too little and it stays in this line throughout. In the course of 6 play throughs I only encountered very few new surprises, and replayability is rather limited.
A shame really, because the game has charm, and new takes on game mechanics such as weather season and earthquakes, but this does not detract from the decision to make a game that is NOT a traditional RTS. And if they'd added more resource challenges, upgrade routes, troop and defense mechanics it would bring the overall complexity to a point where the maps you played on, and the opponents could be more varied.
As is, it is too simple - and I feel that is a game mechanic choice.

It is not an easy game: AI will try to conquer your sectors, winter will slash your stockpile of food and wood and natural disasters will occur on regular bases. There are quite some victory condition to achieve, so gameplay can vary depending on game settings.
All in all it has fleshed our core game mechanics and I am looking forward to be able to play with my friends when multiplayer has been introduced.

I have had my mind blown away for good by this game: I was fascinated by Minecraft, and I was absolutely astounded by Terraria. But now, there is nothing about either of those that truly captivates me like my experiences so far in Starbound.
First of all, ignore the reviews people seem to keep posting about how the developers are breaking the game or ruining it, or any of that stuff. What the devs are doing with this game is absolutely perfect. Besides, the game IS still early access, and considering the size of the game, I'm not surprised that they're still working on adding stuff.
Speaking of the size of the game, you are in an actual UNIVERSE. It's not just some lame scripted chunk of planets thrown together to look big; I'm talking about clusters of planets in orbit around different types of stars (i.e. Gentle, Fiery, Eccentric, and more...), which form a galaxy. And by the looks of it from my ship's nav system, there seem to be hundreds of galaxies, MAYBE thousands: not sure yet, but really considering it. You want non-stop exploration? You want to keep getting the thrill of discovering what lies on a planet's surface? Re-fuel your starship and ENGAGE FTL TRAVEL! You really don't know what you're about to find...
There's plenty of different things that generate on each planet, and the best part is that is all SAVED. Doesn't what you do, or where you go. When you return to that planet, everything will be where it was (although time still elapses for plant growth). I've found secret bases, black-site prisons, alien villages, and tombs of deceased ancient races (which I looted for fun). I'm pretty sure there is still way more to be seen yet, but I haven't gotten there.
The awesome part is that this game uses advanced technology for crafting. I'm not using a wooden workbench, I'm not using an iron anvil, I'm not using a stone furnace. I'm using a robotic-arm assembly table, an atomic furnace, and some kind of super-metalwork rig. Dude, I don't know what how much better it gets.
Oh yeah, you automatically start the game on your ship with a pet. I play using a human character, so I have a cat who loves carrot-bread and NOTHING ELSE (stupid grumpy cat).
Want to understand to road to success so far? I'll tell you in the guide I will try compiling soon. If you're not sure about the game, trust me, it is actually VERY well constructed, and offers plenty for you to do. You won't get bored of it as long as you advance far enough in the quests that you get your ship working again. You will obtain some pretty cool weapons (not too ridiculous, mind you), some of them feature special abilities that do help a lot in combat. This game never gets too easy, and should always provides just a little bit of challenge for your amusement.
Sorry for the long as hell writing, but this game deserves every bit of it. Buy it, you will like it. I do, and I am very picky about what I play.

At it's core, starbound is a very fun game. I mean, exploring a huge galaxy populated with all manner of alien races, ruins, and other stuff- how do you go wrong?
Here's how:
-Although starbound would be amazing as a fully open world game, they feel the need to shoehorn in a bunch of bullhonky quests that you have to complete to advance. Most of the quests are fetchquests, one quest was really, genuinely, actually walking twenty feet to the left to buy a chocolate bar and bringing it back.
-Then they have missions, I think there are about 5 or so of these, but they take you to a short dungeon with a boss at the end. I think these are pretty fun, especially since they actually involve fighting, and not buying chocolate or catching bugs. Anyway, upon completing these missions, you get an implant that allows you to explore more hostile planets.
-this shoehorned linearity gives the game much less replay value. Why make another character and go through all that busywork again?
Really, I think the story should work in the opposite way, as you advance in the open world, you should be able to come back and do this stuff if you want to/ for extra money and rewards. the quests shouldn't be imperitive for advancement.
Decent game, but poorly executed in some respects.
Edit: The game is easily modded, so you can easily make the game more entertaining if you want to. I usually don't play without mods anymore.

Fran Bow is the story of the game's titular little girl who, at the start of the game, experiences the death of her parents and is stuffed away into a mental institution. Fran is determined to get out of the loony bin and meet up with her cat, Mr. Midnight, who she is convinced will help guide her and form a new life with her beloved Aunt Grace. However, some form of shadowy demon warns her to stay in the mad house, for if she leaves he will hunt her down, and do worse things than she could ever imagine. The game's got clever writing, interesting characters (with Fran Bow's childish yet twisted thought-process and approach to things stealing the show), mixed with interesting imagery, thoughtful but not entirely too difficult puzzles, a gripping story with themes of psychological horror, satanism, and cult behaviors, the twistedness of children, and real horror ranging from pedophilia to the history of mental care.
Fairly early in the game you get a jar of pills, which lets you switch at anytime between the 'real' world, and a twisted gorey world full of shadow monsters. Sometimes switching between these worlds provides interesting symbolism and visual imagery, but at other moments it can be crucial to progress. As the game goes on, it becomes questionable if this other world is truly just a hallucination, as things done in one world seem to effect the other.
Depending on how much you take to exploring and getting through puzzles, I'd estimate the game at around 7-12 hours long. They switch up locales and some gameplay stuff enough to keep things interesting, between the 5 chapters you visit 7 different 'main' locales, and four of those locations have two different versions of the location to travel between (and the fifth one has four different versions of itself). In-between main locations, there are often some optional mini-games, which you can skip if you wish but I found most to be a joy. Minor spoiler, but my personal favorite of the mini-games being a nicely timed Frogger reference,
Music is worth mentioning, it is very stylistic with some tracks sticking out, with some melodic tones and synth sounds mixed in. There's no voice acting, but the ambiance sounds are good and captivating. Presentation also gets high marks for some nice animation, visual flair, detail, and some stylization in certain scenes (like the storybook maze scene).
High recommendation if you want a twisted point'n'click. The game isn't scare-your-pants-off terrifying, but there were a few scenes that made me jump, a few kind of chilling and disturbing moments, a sort of grotesque fairy tale feel that resonates most of the game. While reflecting I think I might like the first half of the game more than the second half, it's a fairly paced title worth playing through to the end, and can be an absolutely engrossing experience. Lead by interesting characters is a bit less interesting but still engaging story, excellent writing, great presentation style and audio, and capturing the perfect tone of a twisted little girl's mind in a just as, if not more, twisted horrific world. Fran Bow will most certainly become one of the greats in horror point'n'clicks, it's not perfect and without saying too much, while not an abrupt ending it kind of feels like a sequel hook and a bit anti-climatic, and I feel the middle sections of the game was a bit too long and disjointed from the rest of the title that there was a bit of a slump after the segment to get back into the game's main narrative and atmosphere... But it is entirely worth playing and is a macabre little girl's journey that's twist, turns, and cross-world traveling is more than worth experiencing.

Granted, at first when I heard Left 4 Dead would have only 4 campaigns of 1.5-2 hours length each, I was very confused, however they more I played the demo the more I understood what valve was going for. The re playability of Left 4 Dead is phenomenal.
Gameplay- Left 4 Dead's core gameplay is an incredible amount of fun, and if you've ever played zombie mods for other multilayer shooters and wondered what the most awesome ungodly combination of zombie gaming would be, this is it. Basically you and three teammates (AI or human) go through these campaigns together fighting off hordes of zombies and specialized monsters all while being tormented by the mysterious and much vaunted AI director. Well the director is quite talented at mixing it up. Even on your hundredth playthrough of a given campaign, you won't know where the attacks are coming from exactly. The game does get a bit predictable in terms of spawn points, but that's really only limited by the mapper and the overall feeling is one of scared confusion, perfect for a zombie game. I could describe Left 4 Dead's core zombie gameplay for hours but it's really something you just have to play. It's very intuitive and a whole lot of fun. A few complaints are legitimate, however. In total there are 5 guns besides your side arm(s): shotgun, auto-shotgun, assault rifle, smg, and sniper rifle. A bit more variety and customization would have been nice, though these weapons all work just fine. Also, although you wouldn't know it now, valve has been slow on patching this game up to what it should have been at release, doing things like unlocking all campaigns for versus, and adding survival mode. Ultimately, they will continue to support Left 4 Dead, but they get marked down for being slow.
Graphics- It's a late build of the source engine, but it's still the source engine: nice, but not anything special in 2008, let alone 2009. it does the Job and they have spruced up the lighting and dismemberment effects quite a bit.
Sound- The sound in this game is a lot of fun. The aural cues given off by special infected and the musical crescendos that precede major fights are things you only tune into the more you play. The weapons sound and feel satisfying, and some of the special infected noises are just gross, or even disturbing. Very fun.
Value- Left 4 Dead is a game to be played online, preferably with friends. The bots will give you your money's worth, but the true longevity of this game is in both competitive and cooperative online play. Valves updates both past and possible future ones will continue to add content for the players. All in all, a much better value than meets the eye.
Tilt- I love zombie games and movies, so what might have been an 8.7 on the old scale becomes a 9 on the new one.

This game is pretty basic. If you're not interested in PVP there's not much to do beyond run around and kill samey enemies. But I really like the overall aesthetic that it has going. The crystalline "astral weapons" are really cool, and attack animations are crazy over the top!
There are some cute mechanics spread throughout this game. Force Blader's "battle mode" transforms their magic spells into buffs, allowing for cool customization. You can equip the armor of any class even if it isn't meant for your own class, as long as you can meet its requirements. Although (sort of) recent changes have shrunken build diversity.
And the "COMBO" system is really amazing! never seen it in another MMORPG. Once you hit level 30, you get a special power that can lower the casting time on all of your skills as long as you can keep up the tight timing!
Main downsides for this game are the sheer repitition (nothing for PvE-minded players but repetitive grind), small community, and BOTS. But I don't think you can expect much more from a MMORPG of this age. If you do decide to try this, do NOT get the version on steam! Download client from ESTsoft, and play on the Titan server! In short, this game is a brilliant fighting game wrapped in a terrible interface and dragged down by garbage "freemium" tactics you'd expect from something like League of Legends, except in this case, you're buying into it for the full price of a game ahead of time.
Let's talk about what's great, first. The actual fighting portions of the game are like a dream. This is from someone who put a lot of hours into SF4 but couldn't get fully into the whole focus attack mechanic and clunky feeling controls. Crush counters make your hits feel really powerful-- You get a crunchy sound effect, the screen shakes, and your opponent goes flying when you counter their attack with one of your stronger attacks. The new V-System gives each character some extra properties which make them feel unique without feeling overly complex. V-Skills and V-Triggers are just two button combinations which make new players feel like they're doing something cool even when they're just picking up their first fighting game.
The animation feels quite a bit better than SF4, the cloth physics and slight transforming and stretching of the character models add some wind-up and follow-through to the moves which you typically only see in hand-drawn games. Most of the music choices are great and like 3rd Strike's OST, I find myself sometimes putting some tracks from this game on even when I'm not playing it. Since the game has been patched and the server has been optimized a few times, I've been able to find many matches that don't feel much different from local play, with the expected occasional stinker. If your internet's good and you set your settings appropriately, you should be able to find a majority of smooth matches.
Where do I begin with the things that have rubbed me the wrong way? For starters, as of the 09/22/16 Urien update, I actually can't play the game at all, which spurred this review. Many, many PC players seem to be having the same issue as me, and it's come about because of the addition of what I can only refer to as DRM. The game now apparently requires kernel access to your computer to be able to run, with the stated goal being to somewhat delay or annoy cheaters and pirates. Let's ignore that issue though for the time being, it's been less than 24 hours of a bad time so far and hopefully it will get fixed in a timely matter. There's other, more glaring problems designed intentionally into the game itself.
As the game was preparing for release, potential buyers were told that there'd be no Super or Ultra re-release, and that the base game would include reasonable options for players to earn content they'd like for free if they just played the game enough. They released a Season Pass for real life dollars for people like tournament organizers and more casual players to receive content like characters and stages without any ingame work on their end. That's fine and reasonable. Each character, stage, etc. has options to be earned either through in-game currency or real life currency. Then they started releasing content that flies in the face of this agreement with the players-- costumes and stages only obtainable through real money. Both of these are far more exorbitant than the price for similar content seen in other fighting games. I seem to remember packs of a handful of character outfits in SF4 being released for less than the price of one (1) costume in this game. Furthermore, your ability to gain in-game currency is directly tied to your ability to clear the single player Survival Mode, which is a disgusting business practice. You receive a pittance from online competition, instead having to grind 50-100 matches per character to earn fight money, earning nothing at all if you fail the gauntlet. This is undeniably greedy from a company that requires you to buy in with $60 first.
The game has gone from a game that gave players no penalty for cheating and rage quitting (unplugging your connection during the match) to a game which penalizes you from disconnecting at anytime, even in menu screens of single player modes. The server simply can't figure out which player disconnected during a match and if you fight players who disconnect on you over and over, it's YOU who gets the time out in addition to just having a poor game experience in the first place.
The fact is, I ended a long-standing Capcom boycott (look into Street Fighter vs. Tekken's shady DLC practice, or the carrot-and-stick cancelation of Darkstalkers 3) because their press up to the game's release made me believe in them. The part of me that grew up playing the older games was hyped up knowing that I'd be able to play as Karin, Alex, or Urien again. But-- Capcom let me down again, and I'm conveinced that the only game they still can do right is Monster Hunter, and it's just an inevitablity until you have to pay $10 for DLC to unlock the Bow or something. I'm frustrated, because the gameplay is done so well. I've been able to get people into fighting games through playing this with them, but now I can't even play it, and I'm just frustrated with my purchase. I simply cannot recommend this game to anyone until Capcom stops being shady, hires some real tech support and staff, and shows some good will to the players it desperately needs to win back.

Alright so I've been playing this game ever since 1.0.4, building stuff, killing slimes and getting freaked out by the continuous stream of horrifying yet excellent content coming, so it's about time I should actually make a review on this game. I met a lot of people and learned so many things through these friendships and communities and practically gone through what seems like the virtual equivalent to my childhood, so wow does this game have a special place in my heart.
Putting my sentimental values in this game aside, content-wise this game is practically everything a fantasy-loving, retro game, sandbox, adventurous and architectually creative enthusiast could ever ask for (see if you're not a fan of any of those kind of games, then you probably might not enjoy this considering the beginning is rather.. slow). However there is a Guide NPC, so if you do feel lost on what to do, you should speak to said NPC. The controls of this game is pretty basic; WASD to move, space to jump, number keys corresponding to the hotbar, click to attack, etc.
But once you got all of that figured out, boy is this game one heck of a ride, especially if you haven't read any spoilers and you have absolutely no idea what will happen next in this gem of a game. You'll be quite surprised with how many things you can discover, how many things you can create and conquer; I definitely recommend you play this with friends as progression throughout the game would be so much more funner, meaning you'll get to the fun stuff faster (i.e. the events and ridiculous weapons and mounts).

Bastion, along with Transistor, has turned me into a huge fans of Supergiant Games. Boths games have fantastic music, art, storytelling with compelling plot points, gameplay that's interesting and and offers plenty of replayablility, while staying fairly different from each other.
Although both games share the same isometric perspective, Bastion offers a hack-and-slash sort of playstyle with multiple totally unique weapons that you can equip two of at a time. You can upgrade each individual weapon and take a special move with you as you progress through the world. Each move is different as well, but all can be devastating in their own ways.
The world itself is totally unique to anything I've seen before. It consists of floating platforms that appear in front of you as you progress through each different level. No two levels are the same, each offering more enemies, more weapons, collectables, and occasional puzzles. The art style is brilliant in my opinion, with a good attention to detail. The music is fantastic and you can hear that a lot of time and effort was spent on each track. It all fits perfectly with the world too. The narrator has a comforting, warm voice that guides you through the entire game, making sure you never feel alone.
Honestly, the game is great. If you don't already own it, you should. Plays well on both keyboard and controller. So far, Supergiant Games has flawlessly delivered experiences unlike any other in the gaming industry.

If you're looking for Terraria in space, buy it.
If you're looking for a sci-fi game that lets you play however your want, buy it.
If you're looking for a sci-fi game that lets you play as a homocidal flower, buy it.
If you're looking for a game that takes itself seriously, find another game.
It's in Early Access, obviously, but it's certainly playable. After a incident with people thinking that the devs gave up on it, Starbound's progress is completely transparent. Play the nightly to see what they're doing, play unstable to help bug test, or just play the stable version if you don't want your save dying violently every so often. Every week or so they post something on their website just to say "Hey, we're still here." However, Chuckle Fish does change things up a lot as they find out what players do and don't enjoy. If you don't want to be on that rollercoaster, I'd stay away.
I personally haven't found anything I dislike. The tutorial is nice and if the genre is familiar, you might not need it. Progression is simple and you're soon able to run around and do whatever you want. Quests aren't quite implemented yet (unless you're in Nightly), so there's not a lot to do late game. Building is nice, though, and you don't need a special item to make or break background walls, so that's a plus.
The races and lore are nice. Some of it is quite silly, but this is soft sci-fi we're talking. You can tell that the devs had fun making it all and I hope to see more in the future. The towns and dungeons created for each race certainly fit and it's really a lot of fun to wander the planets and see what each had. They may get a bit stale towards late game, but hey, it's early access. They're planning on adding more.
All in all, I'd say it's worth 15 bucks. Between the normal version and unstable, I've played over 100 hours and will definitely be playing more as new content is added.

DOOM 2 probably was my very first game on PC, back when it just came out. I've played the first part a lot too, but the very first scene in Doom 2 is something I always get reminded about, when I hear "Doom". I've spent so many hours playing it back then, although it took longer to figure out where to go back then, although I was replaying the game a lot (mostly because I didn't have my own PC back then and played it whereever I could install it). When Doom 3 came out it was a big thing for me, as a fan of the old parts, but I didn't get into it... Firstly because I wasn't (and still not quite) into horror games and secondly because my PC wasn't good enough for a smooth gameplay back then. But a few weeks ago I've got a nostalgic mood and decided to replay Doom and Doom 2 among with Duke Nukem 3D. So I couldn't resist the BFG Edition (especially because I wanted to give Doom 3 another go).
Some might say that I should play vanilla version of Doom 3, because in BFG you can use the flashlight and your weapon at the same time and because they did something with the brightness levels. I personally find it way too ridiculous to not being able to use the flashlight and the gun at the same time (one of the reasons I stopped playing the game back then). I mean, of all the "unrealistic" things this is probably the most weird one. It's like all these people in movies that go to check the dark corner where they heard some creepy sounds instead of getting a hell out of there - it might provide the better effect for you as a viewer, but it's unlikely that you would do it yourself in such situation. And connecting a flashlight to your gun is quite simple to do in real life. As for the brightness, I'm not quite sure what people mean by that, since you alway can reduce the brightness and the game is dark enough for me (so that I really have to use the flashlight most of the times to even recognize an enemy in the dark). So for me the bundle was a really great deal.
First I was a bit disappointed by some aspects, like disappearing corpses (what I especially liked in classic doom that the levels felt persistent in a way that if you kill something there then it will stay there forever and not just disappear into the air) or, even more, by the fact that headshots almost never kill with one shot (depends on the weapon, of course). But then I just took it as a game design in it's very meaning and...
Who cares that you need multiple headshots (and some of them take plenty) to kill an enemy? It sticks to the classic games, where there were no headshots.
Who cares that you can reload your gun while climbing on a ladder? In the old games you didn't even need to reload!
But back to the other aspects... The sound of the game is just incredible! I like ambient music and here it plays through the entire game. I mean, all these background noises out there in the dark... they all are rythmical. They add to the horror element, but also bring joy to the listener.
Speaking of horror element. Of course the game is quite old now and it won't be that scary (since graphical realism stepped way forward since then), but it still quite scary at times. In my opinion, they actually made a really good balance that still works: sometimes it's quite scary and you are kinda afraid of checking the next courner (and sometimes I even shouted out loud when something jumped on me), but sometimes it's just a lot of fun shooting. I don't know what is the key to make a really good shooter, but DOOM developers seem to know the secret. It's hard to explain why, but it's simply a lot of fun to play it.
Also I'd like to thank them a lot for keeping the old inventory in which you can carry all kind of guns (not that I think that it should be like that in all FPS games, but here it's definitely a must).
Conclusion: a MUST for those who liked the old parts, quite recommendable overall, but probably already too outdated for most gamers.

This is the perfect mashup of classics. Here you see Doom1, 2 and 3 all come together in one copy. The original Doom brings you to Mars where you are "The Marine" or "Doom Guy" as people call him. Things start out instantly bad in this sort of baseline shooter.
This is the classic, the game that set everything in motion for todays shooters and the devs are still making money off of the original game to this day. You can't go wrong with this game at all, challenging gameplay, different difficulties for every type of gamer, and spectacular grapgics (for the time) even if you didn't grow up with the game it is still worth a shot.
Fastworward a bit and lets hit Doom 2, this game was just as good as the first, if not then better. The gameplay stays the same but the level design is pretty amazing. With the addition of new weapons and enemies this game helped pave the way for todays game market, just as the first did. This plus the 3rd game make the whole pack totally worth it, I would definitely pay even $30 for this package (that's 10 bucks per game, not bad if you think about it)
As for the 3rd game, this was another amazing part to the series of games, unfortunately the graphical quality wasn't the best at the time but the gameplay was innovative and fun. Weapons were interesting and enemies had an interesting AI, although some were a  tad clunky. The game has a more immersive story and an interesting set of tales told through audio logs and information found about levels. The original Doom 3 was modable, which fixed alot of the graphical issues and added in more weapons along with new animations and such. Unfortunately with the BFG edition this is not the case, the game has been tightly wrapped and packaged and is unable to be unpackaged. The modding community was a big selling point for a lot of these games, I am still unsure of the modding capabilities of the first two games but if you are counting on modding the 3rd you are better off buying it seperately. Other than that this game is near perfect and worth the money. I have found myself enjoying the game off steam for hours on end and once I have more time, will probably rack up more hours in it on steam, although I may purchase the seperate Doom 3 for modding capabilities.

DOOM 3 is a dark, demonic FPS, a reboot of the original classic DOOM.  The BFG Edition is a collection that includes DOOM 3, the Resurrection of Evil expansion pack, and The Lost Mission.   It also includes The Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II.
The DOOM 3 campaigns are nice horror-themed shooters.   Most of the levels take place in dark Mars bases, and a downside is that there is very little variety in the level themes.  Much of the game is spent in small corridors and rooms, with monsters that often teleport in and jump out from behind walls.  There are a few other locations:  The outside surface of Mars (which is explored for brief amounts of time), underground caverns, and Hell.  The Hell levels are the best parts of the game, as they have a unique design.  Despite the repetitive levels, DOOM 3 is still a good, creepy shooter.
The games in the BFG Edition have of course been updated.  DOOM 3 now has brighter levels, and the flashlight is now armor-mounted meaning it can be used at the same time as carrying a weapon (however, the flashlight now has a limited battery supply which must be recharged by turning the flashlight off).  The difficulty has been lowered, and now the levels have much more ammo and items.  Quite a few aspects of the game and levels have been improved, but there are a few changes that are basically downgrades:  The arcade terminal mini-games in RoE have been removed and replaced with the same Turkey Puncher game from original DOOM 3, and the RoE Hell level is missing the entire green arena section.
A new DOOM 3 campaign is also included:  The Lost Mission.  This new episode contains 8 levels, but they have the same repetitive dark theme as the other DOOM 3 levels, and the episode is quite short.
As an extra bonus, DOOM 3 BFG Edition contains the first two classic DOOM games:  Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II, some of the, if not the, all-time best FPS games.  Unfortunately, the third game in the original DOOM series, Final DOOM, is missing for some reason.  No Rest For The Living, a DOOM II Xbox expansion, is included; this is the first time that expansion has been released on PC.  The DOOM classics still use the original MIDI music, but the music is now played using the BFG Edition's own included Gravis UltraSound MIDI patches, meaning the sound of the music no longer depends on the system's MIDI synth quality.
Sadly, the included versions of the classic DOOM games are actually worse than the original releases.  The DOOM classics have had several issues added in the BFG Edition:  The function key menu shortcuts are disabled, the Nightmare difficulty has been made easier, the health packs have the Red Cross replaced with a pill graphic, some of the sound effects have been distorted and play at the wrong pitch/speed (e.g., the super shotgun reload sound), the view bob is reduced, the intermission backgrounds no longer animate, the DOOM II Wolfenstein secret levels are censored (SS enemies replaced with zombies, Wolfenstein textures removed, Wolfenstein music removed/replaced), and the NRFTL expansion has the wrong music and wrong par times.  Also, the Xbox DOOM II secret level "Betray" isn't even accessible...the secret exit to that level doesn't function, and there's no way to get to that level without using a sourceport.
DOOM 3 BFG Edition is neither a perfect nor complete compilation.  The DOOM 3 campaigns do have improvements, and the new Lost Mission episode is short but not bad.  But as for the classic DOOM games, they're downgraded and poorly edited.  And as Final DOOM isn't included (neither are the Master Levels for DOOM II), the BFG Edition doesn't even have the complete classic DOOM series.  For those who are new to DOOM, the BFG Edition is a somewhat flawed compilation to get; it might be worth getting the original DOOM releases instead.  And for those who already own all the DOOM games:  It may be worth getting cheap if you want the Lost Mission and NRFTL episodes, or if you just want to replay DOOM 3 with a remastered and "updated" experience.
Overall though, I do like DOOM 3 BFG Edition; it's slightly disappointing but still an okay remastered DOOM 3 compilation.

With the success of the Half-Life community mod Counter-Strike, Valve gave us more tools to wig out the military simulator with silly aburdities by releasing Counter-Strike: Source. Amongst zany things like pillow fights, water guns, playing as Goku, C4 explosives that shoot confetti, flatulant sounds when you jump, or in-depth zombie infection mods, Valve always "found [themselves] going back to the idea of one team having automatic weapons and the other team having melee only" and they discovered that "it had a lot of potential." For a few years, they were working secretly in conjunction with Turtle Rock Studios to make a new kind of dynamic A.I. zombie game known in beta as "Terror-Strike". During the console shooter craze, gamers like me needed something a little more. Valve promised a fresh twist on teamwork and A.I. that spawns zombies differently everytime you play the game. It was Valve, they said co-op, and they said zombies. We were sold already!
Plot 7/10
Well....it's a zombie game....what; it's a zombie game. Everyone's a zombie but you, now go kill them and escape! Zombie plots are inherently lame, so I'll be gracious. Most of the L4D's points in the plot department come from the playable characters. Each one is voiced to perfection, and have fun personalities. Hearing them discuss plans or bicker back and forth is always fun to listen to. "Valve quality voice acting" is all you need to know. There's Zoey (the obvious fan favorite, being that her facial model was based off of often-posing-nude super model, Sonja Kinski), a high school chick that's living the horror movies she's always loved, Francis: the rogue, nihilist biker that comically "hates everything", Louis: the everyday business manager who refuses to part with his optimism, and my favorite; Bill: the noble, battle-hardened, Vietnam Veteran that can still show the young people how it's done. The plot can also be confusing to non-existant when every campaign starts with the 4 being stranded, and ends with them fleeing to safety. For a zombie game though, it works well enough.
Sound 10/10
The series has a very clever use of sound and music. Certain piano clips warn the Survivors of certain "special" infected (that are controlled by other players on the enemy team in multiplayer.) Having abnormal mutations due to the infection, these zombies have powerful abilities to make the Survivors journey a living hell, so alerting players to the danger is important. For example, a tune of five, deep notes warns that a Boomer is ready to spawn into the world. Music ties in very closely with the gameplay, so it's difficult to put this part in either/or. Another clever use is how music is non-existant during most gameplay, but ONLY if something potentially dangerous shows up will the Survivors get a music warning as well as fast paced "OMG HORDE OF ZOMBIES" tune during what's called "panic events". Gun sounds are distinct and satisfying to shoot. Good thing too; you'll be shooting a lot. The grunts and growls of the zombies - especially during panic events - is pretty scary. Each special infected also have very distinct voices from the talents of Dee Bradly Baker and others that not only fit them perfectly, but again, inform the Survivors of who's out there. Speaking of voices, the 4 Survivors also are well-voiced and casted. Every voice fits their character like a glove, and performances cover every emotion with outstanding acting. They sell every line they deliver from "Hey, stop shooting me!" to "I....don't think....I'm gonna make it...". Excellent performances from the cast; maybe even legendary. From car alarms and rifle-butts beating out the brains of infected, to the growling of zombies, to the carefully selective music,  and the voices of the Survivors, the sound is superbly immersive; flawless.
Gameplay 7/10
The concept and excecution of the gameplay is awesome. Certain attacks will leave Survivors stunned and taking steady damage. They can do little to nothing for themselves, so it's vital that the team keep an eye on eachother. The game loses points on lack of content. There are very few weapons available and only a handful of maps. L4D has very little depth or content to explore. Combine this with horrid Survivor A.I., and you will stop playing Campaign in about 10 min. Co-op won't please you for long either, so it's up to MP to make it all up. Unlucky for L4D, MP is littered with bugs, glitches and exploits to the point where they are your main weapon; not your firearm. Valve has patched most of them, but the game lost my interest by the time they did. The coup de grace: this is the 2nd worst, most ego-centric, immature, and laughably stupid community I've ever seen, second only to League of Legends. The basic MP run goes like this:
You spawn as Survivors, no one says anything, one guy rushes out the door WAY ahead of the team and gets attacked. He's so far away, you can't save him. As the team rushes to save him before he dies, the rest of the infected kill the 2 running Survivors. They look to the 4th guy - the diasterous team's last hope - who never left spawn; he's been AFK. Zombie team: LOL gg noobs ez. You now switch teams to the zombies: the Survivors BLOW their way out of spawn at blazing speeds spamming the "laugh" and "no" commands, your team attacks one at a time getting reduced to swiss cheese in .1 seconds while they religiously chant "WE NEED TO ATTACK AT THE SAME TIME!" Everytime the opponent kills one of  you, they leave an offensive spray-picture on your corpse of God-knows-what and call you a baddie or say "fail". In 60 seconds, all Survivors have blurred their way into safety without as much as a minor inconvenience. Finally, as the Survivors say "LOL gg noobs ez", everyone on your team quits. You may now 1) stay and fight 4v1 or 2) quit yourself. THAT'S. IT. In one paragraph, you just read all you will see in MP.
The Verdict
L4D boasts excellent and much needed innovations to the ever-crowded zombie genre in music, gameplay, and voice cast, but the shallow pool of content and unbearable community ensure SP, CO-OP, and MP won't last long. Final score 6/10  It's a pretty good game and cheap nowadays; you should get it and give it a whirl. L4D has earned that much, but MP? The vicious cycle repeats - over and over, my friend. 'Til you log out of L4D, and never log in again.

I had made a pretty lengthy review justifying why I did not recommend this game. I am happy to say that thanks to the long overdue patch 1.5.0, I can actually recommend this game now!
Pre-patch, the Town, who are essentially the good guys, were EXTREMELY overpowered. They barely had to try, thanks to some certain mechanics abuse and way too many powerful roles. If you were on the evil side however, your entire team had to play PERFECTLY, and even if you did, hope that RNGesus gave you great favor because there was so many ways for RNG to screw you over.
Now, thanks to three very important changes, this is no longer the case.
First of all, the dreaded "Mayor game", the bane of all evil roles, and the reason for many people to quit the game altogether, has finally been put down for good. Mayors used to be able to reveal day one, and everyone would spam whisper them their role information. As long as the Jailor jailed them, the Mayor would be protected from ALL OF THE EVIL ROLES' ABILITIES IN THE ENTIRE GAME. Even if the Jailor died, the evils still had to get past the Town Protective, and could still get caught by Lookouts watching the Mayor. All the Mayor had to do was point out the duplicate roles whispered, or call out people who were silent. Any game with a Mayor in it might as well have been a free win for the Town. Now, nobody can whisper the Mayor, and the Mayor cannot whisper anyone else. He is still a powerful role, as if the evil roles leave him alone too long, he can lynch anyone he wants all by himself, but he's not a game breaker anymore.
But, as anyone whose played Ranked a decent number of times can tell you, that's not enough. Any role that the Town can confirm early on, such as a Veteran leaving his signature on his kill note, can fill the role as Mayor. Once a town role is confirmed, the braindead "spam the confirmed Town your role" game would begin, albeit with not as much voting power. However, now this carries a huge risk thanks to the Blackmailer buff. Blackmailers can now see all whispers just like the Spy can. So now the Town needs to confirm that the Mafia deceptive role is NOT a Blackmailer before they can go the whisper lame game, buying the Mafia precious days to get their game going.
And lastly, Investigators got nerfed. Investigators were always way stronger than the Sheriff role that could also fill the Town Investigative role. For one, they weren't useless once the very small pool of possible evils they could find were already caught. Second, there were WAY too many "lucky investigations" that Investigators could find on the first day or two that would completely screw the evil side over. Mayor/Godfather? Reveal as Mayor, or die. Werewolf/Witch/Survivor? 100% lynch material, you can't trust Survivors anyway. Arsonist/Transporter? Nobody was transported, you have no defense. Spy/Blackmailer? Do a "Spy test" with whispers since Blackmailer can't see whispers, and lynch if they fail. Jester/Disguiser? Literally 100% evil. Lookout/Bodyguard/Jailor? Literally 100% Town, better spam him whispers!
You get the idea. Now all investigations have been reworked so that there are no surefire ways to know if someone is evil or not based on the investigation result alone. The Sheriff can still do it, but sheriff gains no information from failed investigations to balance that out. Plus, there are a lot of evil roles who tend to try to impersonate a Sheriff, as it is a much safer claim to make than Investigator.
If at any point you liked Town of Salem, but were put off by the staleness of the meta and how poorly balanced the game was, especially on Ranked, you should try it out again. You might be pleasantly surprised. Just make sure you read up on the new Investigator changes, because they're really important!

Capcom...are you trying to become Konami?  There are plenty of other 1v1 fighters out there that deserve your money far more.
I'll start with the positive.
The graphics may not be everyones cup of tea, but they are crisp, colorful and the animations are some of the best I've seen in a 1v1 fighter since 3rd  strike.
Controls are responsive and I have no problem executing normals, special or combos.
One of the smaller positives is the fact that you can't be killed by chip damage!  Its such a nice feature that I hope other 1v1 fighters adopt.
Now the mixed bag:
The fighting itself is not very deep, but what there is still satisfying.  Impacts sound meaty and like they have weight behind them.  However, like I said in the begining the combat is not very deep, you will discover your characters bread and butter moves/combos and find very little reason to deviate from that.
I leave this as a mixed bag because even though it is simple it can be fun, and can be expanded in future updates.
Online is a very mixed bag, some matches are great some are laggy beyond belief.
The Bad:
Capcom.  Its unfortunate that I can't reccomend a game based on the actions of its publisher.  They have had shady practices in the past ...cough...on disc DLC...cough.  That they tried to deny!
This game is no different in fact its a bit worse.  It launched with an anemic amount of content, and let me be clear, I don't mind that it launched with only 8 characters.  They were all very unique and with fewer characters it made it easier to learn matchups.
What I mean is that this game launched with a broken online ranked and casual system, and a single player survival mode....thats it, for full price!  At least KI didn't launch for $60.
They added very short character specific "story" fights, which at the end it unlocked the ABILITY to purchase an extra costume.  Yup, this costume was done when the game was done but your initial $60 was not enough.  Give Capcom more.
Do you want all the colors for your character?  Better get ready to pay up, or be ready to slog through 50! dull fights against the CPU which are mind numbingly boring.  The AI lulls you into a false sense of security, and when you are on the home stretch of these pointless fights the difficulty spikes causing you to have possible watsed a good amount of time for nothing.
I will grant that you can earn "fight money" through ranked matches and buy everything with the in game currency, but the ranked matches give you so little of this in game currency that its clear you are meant to throw down some extra real money.
Now, you'll notice my playtime isn't that high.  There was a overseas deployment and the fact that I was waiting for Urien to be released.
Well if he is out or not I'll never know.  Capcom added DRM.  Sorry Capcom, you can add any fancy title you want but a rose by any other name...
If it weren't bad enough that they added DRM, the DRM now just prevents the game from running at all, and when it does run its unstable and crashes with no error.
I said it at the begining but there are plenty of other 1v1 fighters out there that deserve your money far more.
When and if Capcom decides to start respecting their cutomers I will update this review to be more positive.

This game is ridiculously entertaining. Change out your towers, primary and secondary weapoons (all of which have 2 firing modes), and add up to 3 abilities that influence you style of play. You can choose towers that wear away at enemies while you go in guns blazing and kill everything that moves, letting the towers pick off the stragglers, with perks (it's the best thing to call them) that increase the damage you deal with every enemy. Or, you could reverse roles, choosing towers that will get every enemy (or at least take out a lot of its health), and let you finish it off, with perks that increase tower damage and overall efficieny. Or, you can play for $h!ts and giggles, with whatever towers you want, any 2 weapons, and some ridiculous perks (like Plumber Shoes, that deals 4000 damage to any enemy you land onwhile jumping. Or Tactial Juxtaposition, that makes fast weapons fire slow but do more damage, and slow weapons fire fast but do less damage. Or... you get the picture.)
The part I like best about this game though? That you can toggle if enemies get more difficult with every wave on or off. Unlike most tower defense, the enemies stay the same health for every wave BY DEFAULT. No more losing on the second last wave because you couldn't kill an enemy that took just 5 shots to kill on wave 1. You can turn that option on though for more XP to level up faster, if you wish.
TL;DR: Fun as hell, no matter what your play style. 10/10, would fail over and over with friends again

What Bastion is can be difficult to initially describe or grasp; and as such, escaped my interest for some time. When I finally did cave in and buy, I regret passing it over for so long.
I would best describe it's genre as an Isometric Action Platformer, with some RPG elements. It's quite unique compared to many other games I've played, so its difficult to describe a genere; and screenshots do not do the game justice. However, I can say that this game reminds me much of a game I played many years ago, called "Lemmings Paintball." While, in my opinion, Bastion is defintely vastly superior to it in every way (Which may not be saying much, considering Lemmings Paintball's age), the way you explore and fight in the isometric world does bring back some memories of the time I put into Lemmings Paintball over 15 years ago. However, if had to make a genre comarison to this game, Lemmings Paintball combined with a touch of RPG and a story is my best description.
Story is not driven by writing, by the main character, or by speach from other characters during the game. Instead, the story is described by a badass-sounding, omnicient narrator telling the story piece by piece, based on your actions and progression during the game. The narration is fantastic, perhaps only better if being done by Morgan Freeman himself... But seriously. The narrators tone, inflection, accent/voice, the word choice (Good job writers); everything about the narration, narrator, and narrations integration with the game is spot on, really making for an enaging and unique story telling experience I haven't found outside of games made by this developer (Transistor and Bastion being those such games, at the time I write this review).
In terms of gameplay, the base gameplay consists of you navigating and fighting your way through a twisted world, with isometric navigation. The iconic isometric split of height "level"  and tiles by an obvious grid or area seperation is not very noticable. The ratio of exploration, puzzles, and story to combat is pretty well paced. You rarely feel like that game has gone too long without action, while never feeling exceptionally overwhelmed by a situation where you never have a moment of rest from the combat.
The combat is nothing groundbreaking or first-of-its-kind innovative; what is does have is it's super solid execution, feeling of power without becoming too easy, choice of actions and weapon loadouts, and overall variety in combat sequeneces throughout the level. I didn't findmyself ever getting sick of the combat, and rarely felt frustrated by the combat sytstem itself (I'm always frustrated when I die or lose in any game, as with many others ;D). While it is solid, and the combat holds its own, I won't lie; you wouldn't buy the game for the combat alone.
Overall, Bastion is well designed, and skillfully crafted in nearly every aspect and capacity. Its art style is unique and well executed, the sound and music is spot on, and the gameplay is great. It's use of narration is ingenious, with great execution from narrator who sounds like he's taken lessons for Morgan Freeman himself. I can reccomend this game to nearly everyone at even full price; if it's on sale, there is no reason to not own and at least try this game.

First of all, thanks to the friend who game this to me for Christmas.
What a game. This review will consist of two different reviews.
The first review is for the seasoned point and click/adventure gamer. Only two words are necessary:
Benoit Sokal.
There, go buy it. Now for the rest of you. If you have played Syberia 1 and/or 2 (which was made by Benoit Sokal) and enjoyed them, this is the first game that he made. Benoit Sokal does not create "games" like we know them. He creates worlds, and invites us to explore. It is seldom about beating the game, but the journey. Considering how old this game is, it is a treasure. This game deserves an HD remake, since I believe that this is a port, and it is not possible to change the resolution. But for what is there, it is wonderful. You start in a rather drab looking countryside of France, but it is a beautiful contrast to the lush world of Amerzone. Even though the backgrounds are static, there is life all around, as you can see Sokal's creations come into view and then dart out of view, or actually confront you. I'm getting ahead of myself.
The game plays like a classic Myst game. Your inventory never gets really large, since each area is pretty self contained, which takes away from backtracking. In the early chapters (there are seven small chapters), you will be asked to do a lot of reading. I didn't have a problem with it, but those who have problems with ornate cursive might want to consult walkthroughs as to what is said. I'm talking about one journal in particular. The other documents are type written letters that should not be a problem. The puzzles are not that hard. Due to the Myst-like controls, you might feel like you are getting turned around at times, and that can be more frustrating than the puzzles you face. The few people you meet give details to the story, with pretty good voice acting. The protagonist is the silent type, who doesn't have much motivation to carry out a dying man's wish, unless he knows that he is in for a treat because he is in a Benoit Sokal world.
Now for what I think is one of the best things about this game: The Hydrafloat. Imagine a vehicle that could be a boat, plane, helicopter, submarine, and a grapnel. Thats the hydrafloat - your mode of transportation from France to the Amerzone. Between chapters you witness the versatile travel you go through, and it is magical. Along with the music that accompanies it you feel like you are really on an adventure to a place that very few have ever gone. In a way, it is a step cooler than the train in Syberia, and that train was awesome.
Now this game is short. Even if you get stumped, it will not take you more than 3 or 4 hours to get through it. The price tag accounts for the age and the length. Honestly, at full price or on sale, this game is worth either price. Also, this game shares the same universe as Syberia, so I plan to revisit pretty soon...

I like Doom 3, and this is the definitive version. It's Doom 3, the expansion pack Resurrection of Evil, some previously-unreleased levels called The Lost Mission, and the XBLA ports of Doom and Doom 2, complete with a new Doom 2 episode, No Rest for the Living. All of this, with all of the achievements from the Xbox 360 games. If you're into Doom, this is a great package. Doom 3 isn't the looker that it was on release, but the gameplay is still fun. Despite the monster closets, which are rampant through the main Doom 3 campaign, the action feels great. The original release of Doom 3 required you to choose between holding a weapon and holding a flashlight, which was sometimes inconvenient as there were a lot of dark areas in Doom 3 that were full of monsters. For some people, it was annoying enough to stop playing. BFG edition lets you use the flashlight at any time. Also, No Rest for the Living is a fantastic addition to Doom 2.
Overall, it's a great package for anyone who likes Doom. I'd also recommend it to anyone who likes classic action games.

as someone who values the Doom series, this is kind of a bargin for 3 games in one package...
however... for the main game, Doom 3, some things are for better, and some are for worse. I'l put a few things up here
A common complaint (and the orgin of the "Duct tape" mod for the original Doom 3) was the lack of ability to wield the flashlight and a real weapon at the same time. In a way, it seems ID has tried to complment this by removing the flashlight weapon outright and just mounting it on your armor. In a way, this is great, for now your not blind firing into the darkness hoping your aiming at the imp your trying to shoot... however, it just seems... idk... OP now.... somehow, I feel it would be better if they kept the flashlight from before, but beefed it up a bit, while also implmenting the new mounted flashlight, but nerf it (narrow and lessen the range of the beam, and make it not so bright, ect.) so that both have reason for use : use the normal flashlight for when your not in danger, and the mounted for when you are in combat.
one thing that IS for worse is the HUD (and some of the weapons, particulary those that had a HUD on them) : it doesnt seem very appealing to me, and is more distracting to me then the original one (even though it's smaller, it has a brigher hue to it, is not transparent, and thus is more eye catching... too eye catching) and the HUD is no longer responsive to weapons with ammo counters (like said earlier) : before, when you equiped such a weapon, like the SMG, the ammo counter in your normal HUD disapeared, and you now relyed on the weapon, witch I feel seemed much better then the normal HUD. now, both the standard and the weapon-mounted ammo counters exist at the same time. I feel this shouldive been different : instead of keep the ammo counter on the normal HUD, remove it altogether and modify all the weapons to have ammo counters mounter on them, and use that (would make the HUD a bit cleaner anyway)
On the other hand, ID did a fairly good job on making the game more "HD", for the sounds have improved (before, it sounded like you were firing toy guns with very bad sound simulators. now, well, except for the pistol so far, now sounds like your firing somthing closer to a real gun, even if it still sounds a little fake) and everything looks considerably better, for now more details can be noted about everything, as it makes Ultra Detail from the original doom look like low quality.... though it didnt do any favors for some characters (the main character and Kelly are 2 examples, for now the main character looks a bit messed up, like Kelly looks way too young (looked like he was in his 50's and had white hair in the original, now looks like he is in his 20's and has red hair))
That aside, while this seems to be a downgrade if you have the original Doom 3 (and if you have mods for Doom 3 such as LMS, i recommend you hang onto your original copy if you get this, for most mods will not be compatable with this new version due to the change in the game engine), This is well worth it if you never got Doom 3... or any of the dooms in general.

So i`ll start this with some bad news. I personally had some problems with the game. Sometimes the screen would stay small and windowed, other times the game would freze up and the worst thing that happend was a gamebreaking glitch that made me start from the beginning of the game. The game got stuck in such a way that I could not give items away, no mtter how far I got back in my safe files.
The reason I am telling this now, is becouse this may not be a problem for your game, and therefore it should not be part of my review of the game. Overall I enjoyed the game and it`s story and if your game dose not break like mine, it would make a better experriance for you. Now on to the accual review.
Preentation:
From the beginning of this game, it is clear it is an older one. The graphics are really low qulaty and the animation can be a bit wonky, but you quicly get use to the older graphics and apriciate what is going on with the story.
The game begins with you as a journalist on his way to speak to a profesor, when you enter his lighthouse he tells you that he is dying, and that you must bring back an egg to the Amazone. You then find the egg and the profesores plane and you are on your way.
The presentation and premess is really simple, and that really helps the game, since it is very basic in itself. You can read more story if you want too, but it is not necesary in order to enjoy the game.
Gameplay:
The game is a point and click game, and you have to progress to the next area via the professores plane. The plane is the hightlight of this game, it can transform into many diffrent kind of vericels such as a helicopter and a sub-marine, it also has a grabeling hook whitch helps throughot the game.
The gameplay is really simple, but the exploration in this game is really well done, since you see many interesting locations, and you can roam more or less free and find out how to progress. It is hard to explain more about the diffrent areas whitout spoling the game, since it is very short, but you get to go to the amazone, underwater, an uncerground hangar and other cool locations.
Charecters:
All the charecters are really flat and uninteresting, but really this game is more about exploring and discover the truth about the egg you are carrying. You don`t really know much about your own charecter and as said any other charecter is not really interesting to talk about.
Visuels:
Eventhough the game looks old, the visuels are the stroingest part of this game. All the diffrent locations are buetifully crafted and looks very good. There is also a great veriaty in locations, that helps the game very well.
Music/Voice acting
The main theme of this game, is pretty good, and it is clear that the creator liked it, since it seems to be some of the only music in the game.
The voice acting is pretty decent on some parts, but not that great on othersm it is pretty mixed here.
Story:
So the story is simple; get the egg to the Amazone. There is not a huge plot anywhere to be found here , but really this game did not need it, it survievs on simple exploration, whitch I really enjoyed doing.
Conclution:
The game is a fun point and click game, that is well made and very funny. It can be a bit hard to know what to do at times, but overall it is pretty simple and good. If you game for a story rich gaem, you would have to look elsewhere, but if you want a simple and fun exploration game, you would properly like this.

I had made a pretty lengthy review justifying why I did not recommend this game. I am happy to say that thanks to the long overdue patch 1.5.0, I can actually recommend this game now!
Pre-patch, the Town, who are essentially the good guys, were EXTREMELY overpowered. They barely had to try, thanks to some certain mechanics abuse and way too many powerful roles. If you were on the evil side however, your entire team had to play PERFECTLY, and even if you did, hope that RNGesus gave you great favor because there was so many ways for RNG to screw you over.
Now, thanks to three very important changes, this is no longer the case.
First of all, the dreaded "Mayor game", the bane of all evil roles, and the reason for many people to quit the game altogether, has finally been put down for good. Mayors used to be able to reveal day one, and everyone would spam whisper them their role information. As long as the Jailor jailed them, the Mayor would be protected from ALL OF THE EVIL ROLES' ABILITIES IN THE ENTIRE GAME. Even if the Jailor died, the evils still had to get past the Town Protective, and could still get caught by Lookouts watching the Mayor. All the Mayor had to do was point out the duplicate roles whispered, or call out people who were silent. Any game with a Mayor in it might as well have been a free win for the Town. Now, nobody can whisper the Mayor, and the Mayor cannot whisper anyone else. He is still a powerful role, as if the evil roles leave him alone too long, he can lynch anyone he wants all by himself, but he's not a game breaker anymore.
But, as anyone whose played Ranked a decent number of times can tell you, that's not enough. Any role that the Town can confirm early on, such as a Veteran leaving his signature on his kill note, can fill the role as Mayor. Once a town role is confirmed, the braindead "spam the confirmed Town your role" game would begin, albeit with not as much voting power. However, now this carries a huge risk thanks to the Blackmailer buff. Blackmailers can now see all whispers just like the Spy can. So now the Town needs to confirm that the Mafia deceptive role is NOT a Blackmailer before they can go the whisper lame game, buying the Mafia precious days to get their game going.
And lastly, Investigators got nerfed. Investigators were always way stronger than the Sheriff role that could also fill the Town Investigative role. For one, they weren't useless once the very small pool of possible evils they could find were already caught. Second, there were WAY too many "lucky investigations" that Investigators could find on the first day or two that would completely screw the evil side over. Mayor/Godfather? Reveal as Mayor, or die. Werewolf/Witch/Survivor? 100% lynch material, you can't trust Survivors anyway. Arsonist/Transporter? Nobody was transported, you have no defense. Spy/Blackmailer? Do a "Spy test" with whispers since Blackmailer can't see whispers, and lynch if they fail. Jester/Disguiser? Literally 100% evil. Lookout/Bodyguard/Jailor? Literally 100% Town, better spam him whispers!
You get the idea. Now all investigations have been reworked so that there are no surefire ways to know if someone is evil or not based on the investigation result alone. The Sheriff can still do it, but sheriff gains no information from failed investigations to balance that out. Plus, there are a lot of evil roles who tend to try to impersonate a Sheriff, as it is a much safer claim to make than Investigator.
If at any point you liked Town of Salem, but were put off by the staleness of the meta and how poorly balanced the game was, especially on Ranked, you should try it out again. You might be pleasantly surprised. Just make sure you read up on the new Investigator changes, because they're really important!

1) Righteous and deserving heir to SFIV, my favourite fighting game of all time. Points!

5) Game is still developing at a nice steady pace. Metagame is advancing, a year later. New characters being introduced excites me! Urien looks fun to fight. Points!
6) Netcode is alriiiiightish. I have a good connection, so I don't get issues on that front! However, a lot of people do. No points.
7) Character design and visual design is outstanding! I love the costumes. Points!
8) Much more demanding towards one's computer than its predecessor. MUCH more. No points.

10) Great community, as always in the FGC. Points!
11) Tournaments are hype! Capcom is doing well in supporting the competitive events. Excited for CPT! Points!
Overall, I'm ready to stuff at least another thousand hours into the Street Fighter franchise, all thanks to this game! I'm really pleased with it. However, the cost and some of other people's complaints cause me to lower my rating a little bit.
MY MORE OBJECTIVE RATING: 7.5/10
MY PERSONAL ENJOYMENT: 9.5/10

Lets just say maybe you don't have a clue what "Worms" is. I think this is HIGHLY unlikely, and certainly embarrassing for you if that is true in anyway possible. The Worms of a decade ago is much the same as the Worms of today, with newer titles adding a few spins and twists on the classic formula but generally sticking to what made it work all these years to go
Basically its just all the lovely new features from Worms Revolution have been retained by its wriggling, younger sibling: classes, water, and physics. Combatants are split up into soldiers, scouts, scientists, and heavies, all with different movement speeds, health, and special abilities, like the scientist worm's knack for healing his chums. They've been tweaked and balanced since Revolution, with area of effects for special abilities being added or increased.
What makes Clan Wars above its predecessors is the effort that has been put into multiplayer. There's local multiplayer, then your standard online PvP, but the truly special, properly new addition is the titular clan feature. With the same tools used to make a team of deadly, slimy worm-warriors, you can put together a whole clan, with a distinct appearance along with a shiny emblem and a clan name, and then recruit members to this clan, not that it matters at all since the pvp on this title is most likely dead or with 1-10 players.
Ultimately, its success lies in its ability to maintain a healthy population, which certainly won't happen if Team 17 keep churning out more Worm titles, so one hopes that they will take a breather. If Revolution was the best that Worms had ever been then this definently is a title worth having.

Instead of adding the new stuff introduced in this game to Worms Revolution Team17 decided to make another new Worms game, which is even not as good as Worms Revolution. To be honest, it almost feels like a beta version of Worms Revolution.
Here are just some negative points in this game:
- You can not zoom the camera to the point you want, for me it's either too close or too far, which makes it difficult to play this game. In Worms Revolution it was easy to zoom the camera to the point I enjoyed.
- Fat worms leave a massive explosion behind, feels unbalanced
- Whats the point with the name? Worms is not meant to be a clan-game.
- The environments are not as interesting as in Worms Revolution and they even don't look as good. Sadly they did not include the environment from Worms Revolution in this game.
I like most of the new weapons they have included and I also like Steam Workshop support but that is almost it. There is no reason to play this game because Worms Revolution is much more fun. I think the time they spent creating this should have been used to improve the good concept of Worms Revolution.

If you're looking for Terraria in space, buy it.
If you're looking for a sci-fi game that lets you play however your want, buy it.
If you're looking for a sci-fi game that lets you play as a homocidal flower, buy it.
If you're looking for a game that takes itself seriously, find another game.
It's in Early Access, obviously, but it's certainly playable. After a incident with people thinking that the devs gave up on it, Starbound's progress is completely transparent. Play the nightly to see what they're doing, play unstable to help bug test, or just play the stable version if you don't want your save dying violently every so often. Every week or so they post something on their website just to say "Hey, we're still here." However, Chuckle Fish does change things up a lot as they find out what players do and don't enjoy. If you don't want to be on that rollercoaster, I'd stay away.
I personally haven't found anything I dislike. The tutorial is nice and if the genre is familiar, you might not need it. Progression is simple and you're soon able to run around and do whatever you want. Quests aren't quite implemented yet (unless you're in Nightly), so there's not a lot to do late game. Building is nice, though, and you don't need a special item to make or break background walls, so that's a plus.
The races and lore are nice. Some of it is quite silly, but this is soft sci-fi we're talking. You can tell that the devs had fun making it all and I hope to see more in the future. The towns and dungeons created for each race certainly fit and it's really a lot of fun to wander the planets and see what each had. They may get a bit stale towards late game, but hey, it's early access. They're planning on adding more.
All in all, I'd say it's worth 15 bucks. Between the normal version and unstable, I've played over 100 hours and will definitely be playing more as new content is added.

I'm sorry, but I just can't reccomend this game. Before level 20, the game seems to be fine- you keep getting better gear and feel a sense of progression. But once you reach 20, the game comes to a screeching halt. Do you like grinding for tens of hours just to upgrade one piece of gear? No? Then you're not going to enjoy this game. The entire experience turns into hoping you get lucky with your gear drops and an item called "gems" which are a type of equipment collected once you reach a high enough level. These gems are probably the worst problem with trove at the moment. Once you reach end game, the only things that matter are gems, as they are what increase your "power rank"(the total sum of all of your equipment) the most. How convenient too, seeing as how they're the only gear you're able to pay for with real money. It becomes almost impossible to get the gems you need without dishing out some cash. This wouldn't seem to be a problem until you realize that your power rank determines if you can progress through the game and reach another world, or "portal". Besides that, the servers in this game are horrendous. Have fun trying to get gems when you're always getting teleported backwards every couple of minutes. Overall, go play another MMORPG actually worth your time. This game had potential- before the gem paywall.

This game is not Age of Empires. It’s not Settlers. It’s definitely not Grand Theft Auto.
Northguard borrow heavily from several games but brings it together to make something new, and exciting.
Currently in a very playable alpha, Northguard is still very thin on content. There’s presently only one tier of upgrades and a couple of military units. The campaign and multiplayer mode aren’t ready yet either. It’s likely that some serious balancing adjustments will be made after multiplayer is released and the devs see how real people play against each other.
I will provide a more informed review when the game leaves early access, but I will point out the game’s biggest drawback in its present form. Currently there are long periods where you can’t do anything except wait. Generally, this is early on in the game when your waiting for enough resources to be able to do something else. The scouts are automated so you can’t even kill time exploring. The game needs a mechanism to warrant constant attention.
