Coming from Worms 2, this game has the two features I always wanted... dynamic water and non-destructible terrain. Unfortunately, Team17 is the dumbest game developer out there and simplified this game to death. There's only one kind of water generator and you can only have two on a map, not to mention they are huge and take up a lot of space. They also remove any terrain around them and can waste water particles filling up the space they inhabit. The rope physics might be technically more realistic, but feel terrible and clumsy compared to the W2 rope. The amount of worm customization is very limited. The level editor is clunky and does not allow for precision land design with it's weird 3D look that makes it hard to tell what is actual land and what is decorative land around the actual land. As I stated, the game is terribly simplified in options of customization. You can't make wooden beams fixed, nor make them indestructible. There are no door objects or other nifty things. The water generators are also succeptible to being blown up and cannot be made indestructible. You can't set things to float on water either. You can't set the bounciness of the terrain, or the gravity, or a dozen other options that they could have easily made available. Why? Because it was designed for consoles and ported to PC/MAC. I really really hate this design mentality. Why limit your game by stupid consoles? I love my PS3 but at least make an enhanced version of the game for PC/MAC. Team17 gets 1 star from me, for being a terrible, narrow-minded company. They could have added lots of game modes like real time combat, which would open the door for even more modes, like soccer, capture the flag, american football, etc. There's also no snow or ice, which is another example of their short sightedness. The snow theme was my favorite in Worms2. Basically, this is a decent game if you need your worms fix, but I'd recommend not buying it and teaching Team17 a lesson.

Amazing game, absolutely worth both your time and money, and the only thing I regret is not buying the full DLC pack right away.
I started out with some missions and had some conversations with a pig mask on my head that made me laugh more than it should. Then I discovered the game isn't just for laughs, although it has that in spades - the story is excellent too. I also had the pleasure of experiencing the awesome Batman: Arkham Asylum style combat in the game, including putting a guy through aquarium glass in a night club, breaking legs and arms, and just generally being a wrecking machine of a fighter. Good times, really good times. But there is more.
Because there are times in the game that are not only good, they're almost transcendental.
One evening, I woke up after a hard day/night before. I had some texts waiting on my phone, from both police investigators and thugs, and said to myself it was going to be alright, even though I was playing both sides. I got out of my apartment, picked up a car and started driving to my next mission. And then...
I found myself just keeping on driving around the city.
Time had stopped.
I no longer sensed the room where my sorry gamer butt was actually sitting because I was no longer there.
I'm in Hong Kong - for real. I can't stop driving. It's raining and the reflection from the neon lights in my car, the fan-♥♥♥♥ing-tastic music from the radio, the streets and back alleys, the people, the crowds - I'm completely immersed.
And like throwing game money on pimped up outfits (that actually gives you bonuses sometimes, so they're more worth than just for "show"), and awesome, fun, expensive cars, I'm looking forward to throw a little bit of real money on United Front again - this time to buy the whole DLC pack to continue my stay in Hong Kong. It's been a journey like nothing else and it has been the best digital vacation ever.
Recommended with all my heart - it rivals some of the best games I have ever played in my life.

You can play in which ever order and each one gives you a slightly different experience.
As the Marnie, the game takes the traditional route like any FPS with you typical arsenal of weapons but with a survival horror twist. When playing, you really got to be on your toes and stay alert as the xenomorphs can pop out of nowhere.
As the Alien, the game shifts to a 1st person stealth game as you lurk through vents and pick off the enemy one by one. Stealth is the key and the darkness is your friend. To regain health as the Alien, you must devour your prey. Playing the Alien is my personal favorite.
As the Predator, the game is a mix of stealth and the ability to use your wide varity of gadgets with a touch of brute strenght. The predator is the more powerful of the 3, but however don't get too cocky. Predators can be killed too. To regain health for the Predator, he uses a gadget in his arsenal with also drains power. Just remember, electric weapons such as the blaster and should cannon use power.
The game's story is not as great as the previous two Aliens vs Predator games and at times can be murky but it makes up for it in the gameplay.
If you are a Aliens vs Predator fan, you will not be disappointed as it stays true to the Aliens vs Predator lure. I rate this a 8/10.
If you know know nothing about Aliens vs Predator than this game could look average to the casual FPS gamer and may come on as a 6/10.
It's fun to play minus the game throwers and dickweeds. Overall 7.5/10.

I wish I could reccomend this game after sinking $90 and 6 months into this wreck. Stills feels like an incomplete product. Still lacks game modes and promised features. still feels like a F2P game that you have to pay for. Still doesn't support direct input so no ps4 arcade sticks- where the previous title does. The way capcom is dealing with criticims and simple issues like rage quitting and connectivety problems is disapointing.
This "service" model the game is taking is quite ugly, expensive and ineffective; all it does it make me feel like I've been swindled. It is a higher priority for capcom to ensure that it can charge players for every possible feature from comstume colors to stages; than it to make players feel like their getting a complete package with aditional goodies for unlocking. The rate in which you earn the in game curriency is horrifically slow, and the price of many items in the game store is disgustingly expensive.
For example: One ranked match where you WIN will net you 50 fight money (you get nothign if you lose). You need 5,000 to unlock a fighter profile design. You need 40,000 to unlock an alternate costume, or alternate stage (day time/night time stages). You need 80,000 to unlock a new stage. you need 100,000 to unlock a DLC character. The game comes with 16 characters and you have to unlock 6 additional DLC characters for a cast of 22 total. that means you have to accumulate 600,000 to unlock these guys, and while the game offers a couple of boosts to your income if you go through the scant and mostly dreadful singleplayer gameaplay, be prepared for a LOT of time in online matches to unlock these guys without spending money on something as terrible as a season pass.
Oh, and there's this wonderful little feature where the game cites a "connectivity issue" after an online match and you don't get the rank points or Fight money you earn in that match that happens every so often. Months into the game and after how many updates, this is still happening. I've never encountered similar problems like this in any other game I've player in the past. what's even more curious is the game will record your win (so if you have a win streak, it will keep track of that and add you win to your record) but you still don't get your points.
so how's the game itself? interesting to say the least. Its certainly very unqiue among the franchise. throws are slow (5 FRAMES! even the COMMAND GRABS are 5 frames! what were they thinking?), defense is bad, returning characters have been heavily reworked. Variable system is ok, but ultimatley feels gimicky. every character has a gimick, some good, most meh. If the character is good at rush down and mix up, they are going to be strong in this game. Zoners do terribly and traditional grapplers are awful and cannot defend themselves from rush down outside of a V-reversal (Think "alpha counter". A counter every character can perform to cancel block stun ang get the opponent off you.).
Basically the engine is fun but nothign to write home about. A few things here and there make it substantially different from street fighter IV in big ways but I'm not a big fan of how some of these expirmental features panned out. Seems like there is a big lack of diversity in the gameplay style and that comes from how the engine is cartered to certain play styles. When the game is better balanced to support a greater scope of play styles, maybe I'll change my perspective.
Art, music and animation are all great. Stupid things like clipping and lack of Lip Synching in story mode detract from the visual design though.
Find an altenative fighting game to sink your teeth to. If you absolutley must get it, wait for a substantial sale.

Bunker 58 is an indie horror game that I would not recommend playing. For starters, the goal of the game apart from survival, is clearly nonexistent. I’ve spend much of my time exploring, and killing mobs of zombies – but to no end or progress is being shown. Exploration is also useless, when 50% of the time you are collecting items from the bodies of zombies that you kill. The other half is the frustration of encountering the many bugs and glitches present. The ones I’ve found include:
-Spawning with an empty inventory (losing all items you had originally started with) after your 1st death
-Spawning in the middle of the zombies that were and will be attacking you again
-Finding objective-like items such as keys, cans and other items that can NOT be picked up
-Finding weapons (ie. A shotgun) but being unable to equip them in your current set-up
-Glitched items, notably the plate covering the vents in the hallway with the large fans.
-Scary sound effects being triggered at the wrong time.
To be fair, the only portion that was done at least half-decently were the menu-screen and the environment. There were many turns and narrow paths within the area, which would make any player take extra caution. You just never know what’s around the corner.
The controls were all clearly established, as well, on the top right of the screen in game. But even these were not enough to disregard the many errors present. It’s a shame the developers had also included the note of “state of the game is a complete version and may never change, […]”. Any of the issues mentioned above may never be fixed. Hence, why I do not recommend trying out Bunker 58.

I wrote a review for this game a couple months back not recommending it. Now that I've approached it in a different way, I can recommend it but only to a specific group of people.
ONLY get this game if you can get it cheap (physical copies go for £20-£30, I managed to get it for £25) and/or only get it if your style of play is solely multiplayer. If you got this for single player, you will be extremely disappointed.
I like fighting games but I'm usually pretty bad at them and never try to learn them... ever so I don't tend to go online and always stick to local or single player. Street Fighter V changed that in a way for me as I just wanted to get the most out of the game and the fact that I can't afford the season pass for characters so I depend solely on fight money. Online is fun and it honestly has gotten better. I still get the awful match now and again but that's more down to the connection between both players. The netcode has improved since my last review and I am getting games a lot faster. If you're still getting bad games, you could always use the lobby system. You don't get fight money but you're assured of a good connection. The matchmaking, however, is garbage. I played today at Bronze rank and fought super bronze which is okay but I did so terribly, I went down to Rookie and I still was getting Super Bronze, some with triple my LP. This seriously needs to be fixed. I also wish there was a character select screen for ranked and casual rather than changing your "favourite character" on your profile every time you wanna play someone different but I guess it isn't an issue if you don't have any secondaries.
Other than that, the graphics are fine, the mechanics are solid (Balance is sort of an issue. Expect to see a thousand Nashes and Karins online) and Capcom are listening to their fans... slowly but surely. There's still barely anything regarding single player content (the main story mode they brought out a month or so ago can be beaten in about 3 hours and has a dreadful story) but again, only buy this if it's on the cheap or if you think you will really get into the meta game... or you know, you could buy Street Fighter IV.
TLDR; Only buy if you wanna get into competitive.

Amerzone is an old school adventure game.  Initially released in 1999, it was the first game designed by Benoit Sokal who is better known for his later Syberia adventure games.
Although it runs remarkably well through Steam, it has all the drawbacks you might expect from such an old game.  The graphics are very dated and most scenes are static except for a few cut-scenes.  You can’t run in windowed mode, nor can you minimize/Alt-Tab out of the game.  This can be a big deal if you need to consult a walkthrough for help with one of the many puzzles as you will need to save and quit and then restart the game after getting help.  Thankfully, load times are short and you can save at any point.
Amerzone's story is interesting, but not action-packed.  The puzzles are fair.  Most solutions aren’t instantly obvious, nor ridiculously complex, and they seem to make sense for the most part.  The pixel hunting is kept to a minimum and you won’t have dozens of inventory items to keep track of.  The voice-work, music and sounds are passable.
Amerzone can be completed in less than five hours if you are an experienced adventurer, but it can purchased very cheaply, usually as part of a game bundle.  As long as your expectations are reasonable based on the game’s age, most adventure gamers will enjoy this classic.

A great adventure game that is still enjoyable nowadays. What makes Amerzone stand apart from other adventure games are things that, at first, might seem like negative aspects: it's easy and it's short. This works in its favour, though, because the adventure never gets tedious and you won't have to resort to old-school habits like pixel hunting and combining every possible object in search of an answer. The story and ambience also set it apart, with an old-school, adventure film type vibe, that makes you feel like you're actually exploring uncharted territory (or, to be more precise, following in the footsteps of the only person who had travelled there before).
On a technical side, this version is a mere port with all the inconveniences of running such an old game. There is a set resolution, almost no options and, although it should run flawlessly, you never forget you're playing an old game. What Amerzone truly deserved is a remake, with all those beautiful landscapes rendered in high resolution, but since that probably won't happen, this original version is more than an adequate substitute.

I'll be ingoring the Creation Club in this review, while I loath the business decision to include it and the way it was handled, it should not reflect on the game as a whole.  Also, this review is written with the usage of free mods in mind.  I have a heck of a time playing Fallout games without mods as I love the new content they add.
First off, if you have played previous Fallout games, do not come into this game expecting more of the same.  Much of the game was changed in this iteration.  Especially comparing it to Fallout: New Vegas.  This is not a great Fallout game, however, it is a great game on it's own, if you treat it like a game without the Fallout branding.
Pros:
The world is pretty immersive.  It certainly feels like a post-apocolyptic world.
The gun play is fun and responsive.
Settlement building can steal your life if you even have just a little interest in it.  Especially if you use mods to add to the things you can build.
The weapon and armor modding system is really cool and feels at home in the Fallout world.
There is a lot to explore.
Fair amount of freedom in where you want to go, if you want to ignore the main story, that's possible.
The official story DLC was very well done.  All 3 of which added a good amount of playtime.
Cons:
It's too easy to become overpowered in mid to late game, even on survival difficulty.
Melee in particular is incredibly overpowered in the late game using the Blitz (think that's what it was called) talent, being able to one shot an entire group of high level enemies in a single string of VATS attacks.
Survival difficulty limiting saving to only beds was a bad choice, Bethesda games aren't exactly known for their stability.
Voiced protagonists.  While I enjoyed the lines they did have, it severely hinders immersion when you want to alter any of the vanilla quest content.
Serious lack of choice and consqeunces.
The factions you can allign with in the story do not alter what happens at the end of the game, regardless of who you choose, aside from one faction, of which all the other factions oppose.
Difficulty settings are handled poorly, just like in Skyrim.  Increasing the difficulty just makes you deal less damage, while taking more damage.  Aside from the basic needs added in survival difficulty, increasing difficulty just makes enemies bullet sponges. (I do tend to only play on survival)
The building system could have used a bit more tweaking to get right.  Fine placement can get incredibly frustrating.
Conclusion:
Despite the faults, and even without using mods, one can get hundreds of hours out of this game.  It has a good replayablity factor.  Just don't go into this game expecting it to be more an RPG than FPS like Fallout 3 and New Vegas were.  Skills levels were completely removed.  Play it as it's own game and it's likely you will enjoy it.

I had a lot of fun playing this game, but I just expect more from a strategy game. Northgard is beautiful, with great base mechanics, but it is shallow---terribly, tragically shallow.
Many of the game's best features are rendered pointless due to the rapid snowballing of the mid to late game. When Northgard reaches the point of expansion and development where most strategy games start to really stretch their wings, it is over. This makes the map seem too large, as most of is never used, exploring the whole continent is pointless outside of a domination victory, and the potential for real strategic gameplay based on geography is lost---which is really unfortunate, because the map is gorgeous, and the exploration mechanic is great.
A deeper, better imagined sense of building and kingdom development in conjunction with the gorgeous and well diversified map could have made this a real strategic gem, instead of a dud. If a real layer of long term strategy emerges during EA or before final release, I will happily edit this review.
The other great disappointment of this game is the abrupt and simplisitc victory conditions, which are painfully easy and reached in a few hours of gameplay. This would not be quite as bad if the game had any real strategic depth, but alas, it does not. Some people may take exception to my criticism, because there are tough choices to be made. And those choices matter a great deal, but I would contend that they are more akin to tactical choices rather than stategic choices that require planning and allow for early moves to yield long term fruit. The game is simply too short for any real strategy.
There are many necessities to be met in this game, and aside from military strength, they all come in the form of resources. I found myslef making choices to meet my most pressing need, and then the next, and then the next, and then the game is over. Any plans I had about how to focus and compete against the other clans was irrelevant. From a single late game save, I was able to achieve every victory condition except domination within 4-5 minutes of the save point. I was not aiming for any of the victories, but simply doing my best to build the strongest clan I could.
And that seems like shallow game design to me, or poorly designed victory conditions at the very least. In a well designed strategy game, reaching different victory types should require at least a little bit of variation in what strategy is employed. In that regard, then, Northgard is not a strategy game, but a very complex tactical game where what victory condition you want is more of an RP choice than anything else.
By all of the positive reviews here on Steam, it seems that many people enjoy very short games that begin and end in a few hours. I do not. With only a single improvement level to each building and such rapid gameplay, a new game feels exactly like the game I just finished.
So replay value seems extremely low. With short games, and almost no replay value, this is a game I would refund if I could---despite the fact that I had a great time playing those first 12 hours.
If multiplayer is your thing. Then you should perhaps ignore this review, as I do not enjoy multiplayer strategy games, and was/am not intending to ever even try the multiplayer aspect of this game. I could see Northgard providing hours of great fun for gamers interested in multiplayer, and there are reviews here by folks who like that sort of thing and speak to the game in that capacity in a way that I cannot.
Perhaps with the addition of the campaign, or some desperately needed adjustements to pacing, victory conditions, and mid/late game tech & building costs, I might recommend this game.
After 11 hours, I feel as though I've seen everything this game has to offer. I will try the campaign when it is released, but otherwise, I don't see myself playing this game again. There are too many other games that offer real strategic challenges and gameplay. For these reasons, as a consumer of primarily single-player strategy-games, I cannot recommend Northgard.
If you've got twenty dollars burning a hole in your wallet, or if Northgard is on sale, this game does provide a really fun, good looking 10-20 hours of gameplay. I just can't recommend it, when there are great RTS games that provide hundreds if not thouands of hours of gameplay, and much greater challenges to boot.

Hi reader, I've invested a fair amount of time in this game and thought you might wish to know a little bit about this game before installing it onto your harddrive.
EDIT:  Before you install, spend any time or money, here's a little tid bit I wish I had known before mindlessly clicking accept on the EULA.
"TRION MAY SUSPEND, MODIFY, TERMINATE OR DELETE ANY ACCOUNT AT ANY TIME FOR ANY REASON OR FOR NO REASON, WITH OR WITHOUT NOTICE TO YOU. Accounts terminated by Trion for any type of abuse, including without limitation a violation of these Terms of Use or a Game EULA, will not be reactivated for any reason. For purposes of explanation and not limitation, most account suspensions, terminations and/or deletions are the result of violations of this Terms of Use or any applicable Game EULA."
-Keep in mind the above is for ANY REASON, if they don't like you or just decide to ban you out of the blue one day, they will.
-The gameplay is fun in the beginning, you feel yourself progressing quickly and - with the new craftable classes, you can do even more for the mid-late game.  Collect a bit of gear here and there, but you'll quickly find yourself hitting a wall, the early game is...Well, short.  Around level 20 is where your mid game begins, from there you'll likely be grinding for your first Shadow V's or maybe even your first Radiant pieces and if you've been fortunate, you figured out the chat box can lead you to progressing just an inch further than you'd normally with a group of people your own level.
-After level 20?  It's very, very grindy to get to level 30, which, a lot of people who have stuck around in this game probably really like the grind.  But even when you hit level 30, you'll still be grinding, for more gear, likely to try and get your first Stellars, probably around level 20-21 you'll have gotten your first empowered gem which you may or may not be able to equip depending on your level.  Along your way to 30, you'll be able to equip more gems - most of your power comes from gems, though a full set of Stellar gear gives a considerable amount that cannot be ignored as you gem up.
-When RNG is good, it makes you feel fantastic, as opposed to the heavier side of the coin - the bad RNG, will make you want to rake your fingernails across a sidewalk, or any chalkboard you can find.
-You can skip much of the grind by simply throwing extremely large sums of money into their store, which - if the game did have a price tag of say, 20$ - 40$, you'd make yourself blush by how much you could spend in one sitting, especially on their "value packs".  Some purchases will seem necessary as you reach the late game, especially if you want to have an easier time collecting the PERFECT gems for your slots once you've reached level 30.  You'll likely be very tempted to purchase tomes as well, when they're available as tomes give you a secondary reason to be out in the world grinding, as you grind, their XP bars fill up, once the bar fills out, it poops out whatever it says it'll give, into your inventory.
-I myself was blushing as I spent a fair amount of cash during my own grind to try and get into what is essentially the late game.  Though even with what I'd spent, I found myself still needing to grind excessively, in this game.  You can effectively increase your luck through a stat that is known as "MF" or "Magic Find", the most common way to do this is by crafting sick♥♥♥♥♥dragon mounts that can lob bombs down onto blocks and fly.  Unfortunately for me, somewhere along the road my prepaid card I used for the shortcuts, must of had a hiccup and whatever money I did spent seems to have vaporized into nothing, moreso than just pixels on the screen - with that said, I did give the game a break only to come back seven months later, I was able to log in and play about two times, until finally a few days ago, I found myself banned.  I had no mail concerning the reason for my banning, nor did I have any spam mail.  It took two days for the first reply, bumping my ticket up because the guy who responded couldn't do anything I guess, then another two or so days pass and I get my most current reply, - as you know I mentioned a pre-paid card, seven months ago to now, apparently that card was the reason I got banned.  I hadn't been expecting anything to do with money when the good customer support stated the reason, I myself had thought I got banned because after I linked Steam and Glyph together for easier login, I tried launching the game through the folder it was installed in, instead of through steam, on admin (there was a problem with the auth server, it was likely my firewall blocking trove for whatever reason) and that'd been when the first error of being banned appeared (it only happened then).
-SO...I'm still unsure if my banning had anything to do with money, why hadn't I been banned seven months ago (or the few days I logged in recently?).  I've got a strong suspicion that it had something to do with trying to log in through the folder (technical support said to try and set the Glyphdownloader to run as admin but there was no option for that.)...With that said, it could very well have been a very, very delayed issue with a prepaid debit card.
-Still unsure of what exactly got me banned as they will not tell me, me but I got the end result regardless, perma ban, not a temp ban.  Please keep in mind that I did nothing wrong in game at all during my time of play and whatever financial aspects of a pre-paid card were completely out of my hands.

First, it's important to note that the only reason why this game is getting "mixed" reviews is because the majority of those writing a review here are only playing the game for an hour before doing so. An hour of game play as a completely new player of the game will get you as far as 10-15 levels. The majority of the game caters to those above level 120 and the reason for that is because the game has been running for years now.
Levels 1-100 have a storyline they can follow to quickly gain levels and progress. Everyone else is at "end game" and from there can only keep playing to run dungeons (there are tons of them!), go to war (3-4 wars per day), and improve on their gear. It takes maybe 3 days of full dedication to the game to get to level 100 and you typically do not require assistance from other people to get that far.
You can talk in chat once you hit level 10, I do believe (it's been a LONG time since I started a new character), so until then you are on your own, but the direction given to you is extremely easy to follow. Most of your 1-10 quests are "go to this person and do this to learn the game mechanics."
Yes, you have to share kills. There will be times where you will be asked to kill a specific creature and there may only be ONE of that creature that 10 people are trying to get to. The up side is that respawn times are EXTREMELY fast. It's nothing like WoW or even Cabal 2 where respawning takes a full minute or more. These creatures respawn within seconds of dying. This can pose a problem if you're in a hostile area and are being beat up on, but in general it's fantastic for fast leveling while grinding and getting what you need when there are 10 other people on the same quest as you. As you progress through levels, this becomes even less of an issue, unless you're trying to kill map bosses. The higher level maps each have several bosses that drop epic items for your character. Many players hunt these bosses for those drops, so they're much harder to find and respawn time is much longer. I think most of them are about an hour long, making them that much more important to hunt and kill when you have the chance, if you have the strength to do it.
I won't get into the actual story of the game, but I will point out a few pros and cons of the game, as a player since 2008.
PROS (just to name a few of the many):
--- A step-by-step storyline that is easy to follow.
--- Individual maps instead of open world design that allows for fast and easy traveling (no loading screens.) These also accomodate skill level, so you'll never be caught in an area that is unreasonably too strong for your character to handle.
--- Easy-to-master combat system. It's more automatic than anything, because each move is a 1 button press, but there is some skill involved in how you level each skill you have and what order you use them to deal maximum damage.
--- Skill variety, including everything from DPS, stun locking, PvP mastery, and buffs.
--- Class variety
--- Constant gear updates
--- Constant dungeon updates
--- Tons of friendly guilds and dedicated players, always willing to help those in need
--- Tons of customization options including costumes, face/hair change kits, pets, vehicles, weapon skins, etc.
--- UI customization, from fonts (face and size) to sizes of most of your info/chat bubbles, etc.
--- Massive high level tier player base, which allows for tons of assistance and fun once your story ends
--- Constant developement of game mechanics from the GMs. The game is updated frequently and often gets new content and bug fixes.
--- Security codes for extra protection that can be applied to your warehouse, your gear, and your account in general. EXTREMELY worth it to protect your account, however. If a password, a sub-password, and a sub-password for your gear and warehouse aren't enough to protect your items and your account, then you're doing something wrong. Not the game.
CONS (most of them!):
--- Security codes. They can get annoying.
--- Difficult leveling for higher tiers. Once your storyline ends around level 100-110, you're pretty much on your own until level 140-150 when the better dungeons become available to you. Map grinding is your best bet for leveling, or gathering friends to enter dungeons until you can solo them yourself. MOST of the dungeons CAN be solo'd by the majority of players once reaching a certain point, so don't feel like you will always need friends to complete dungeons.
--- Grinding in general. Sorry, this IS a grinder game for the majority. The higher tiers grind less and dungeon a LOT more, but grinding is still necessary for gaining levels. And the 190-200 grind takes FOREVER. But that's end game, so good luck.
--- Chunky UI for some, depending mostly on your resolution. (Mostly cannot be adjusted at all, so that's why it's a huge con) Mine is about mid-sized. I haven't figured out how to make it any smaller, but it doesn't get in the way of anything for me, so this isn't an issue. Others, I've seen their UI take up most of their screen.
--- ALZ SELLERS! They're annoying, they're everywhere. All you can do is click on them and block them. It takes all of 3 seconds to do, but it's still annoying as hell, because they do spam the chat if you don't get rid of them quickly. Nothing can be done about this, however. They frequently get banned, so you'll never find more than one or two of them in town, but that's an MMO for ya.
IMPORTANT CON:
This game is PAY-TO-WIN. Though you can get by with luck and dungeon runs for epic gear, the really serious players who play this game to BE serious and not just to kill time will PAY for ecoins and BUY tons of stuff to enhance their game play. I've done it as well. It IS possible to farm like mad and make bank alz in game, but the likelihood of you getting as good as the people who play day in and day out and go to Cabal conventions and stuff like that is highly unlikely unless you play like they do.
IMPORTANT PRO:
The GOOD NEWS IS that paying is not required, nor is it necessary to enjoy the game. There are fewer people who go extreme and pay-to-win than there are people who generally just play the game, which means that in most situations, you will NOT be outmatched by random players. You will hear about the greats of the game, like Super and Manbear and yada yada, but (from experience!) these people are nice and it's HIGHLY unlikely that a super serious pay-to-win Cabalster is going to randomly ruin your day. They're more likely to HELP you, not ruin your gameplay experience.

Aliens versus Predator, the 2010 edition. Or so we could have hoped but unfortunately this is not as much a reboot of the extremely well made original as it an entirely new take on the franchise. Some features and concepts familiar to old players make a return but unfortunately the game only plays them lip-service and this new AvP game ends up feeling nothing like the original.
The AvP campaign takes place on a remote colony where Weyland-Yutani, in another instance of completely brain meltdown, finds a captured queen and immediately begins breeding aliens for the glory of scientific discovery, or something. As expected, the aliens get lose and start making a mess of things so the colonial marines get sent in to clear up the mess. Also a bunch of Predators show up because well, that's what they do.
All the campaigns share the same maps like in the original and they are simply approached from different angles. Unfortunately they are far more linear and closed off than in the original. There are very few vents for the alien to use and you only rarely have the option to skip killing someone.
The Marine campaign is obviously the one that has had the most effort put into it with plenty of voice-acting and even some audio diaries to be discovered around the complex that tells the story leading up to all hell breaking loose.
Most of the Marine gameplay is more survival horror than straight up shooter with a few boss fights and "Hold the line!" scenarios to break up the mold every once in a while. Unfortunately both the survival and horror elements dissipate quite quickly, limited regeneration and being able to survive quite a few hits from the aliens make fighting them trivial and the biggest threat to you is killing one of them at close range and getting splashed with their acidic blood. All of the alien encounters are scripted and you are almost never surprised when they show up. Your one fight with Predators is easily forgotten and the only real challenge comes from Weyland's combat androids simply because they can one shot you.
The Alien campaign is somewhat more entertaining, with you stalking your prey and taking them out, one by one. The extremely linear maps and the low number of airducts available means this is nowhere near as well made as in the original however and you'll find that stealth is not quite as rewarding as it should be.
The Predator campaign however is where the game truly fails. Despite ostensibly being the strongest of the 3 species he depends almost 100% on stealth kills for half the game, barely being to survive a burst from a marine or a few stabs by an alien. The famed shoulder mounted energy launcher holds 2 shots before it has to be recharged. About half-way through the game however you will come across your combi-stick and never use another weapon again. It one shots everything and doesn't de-cloak you making the rest of the fighting trivial.
The multi-player is nice but unfortunately nobody plays it anymore and getting a game going requires an enormous amount of patience.
All in all, Aliens Vs. Predator 2010 is a classic example of a game that takes it's roots from a great old game but doesn't understand any of the concepts it's trying to use and in the end it's not much more than a mediocre mess.

And before commenting, please read the full review first.
Before getting this game, I played the first binding of isaac and I had many of issues with the game. One of those issues was the randomization feature of items. While randomizing the room layouts in the game is a very cool touch, I was not okay with how the items were arranged at times.
Beating the game required luck and dodging skill, meaning you would need to get really good items if you wanted to finish one your the many playthroughs. As for me, I am terrible at bullet hell games, but the first binding of isaac wasn't that bad in that department. The whole luck mechanic the game revolves around though is ridiculous.
The worst feeling I get is trying to beat the final boss after countless losses before, only to die and start over again. It took me several tries before actually beating the game the first time, only to find out I have to beat it several more times to unlock more stuff. At the time of making this review, I've beaten this game about 9 times.
Then later, a friend bought me and the afterbirth dlc for this game, encouraging me to give this game a try. I did, and I enjoyed this game for about a month until I just stopped playing it.
There is a lot of things fixed in this game comparing it to the first, but as well as more problems.
One lingering issue is how there are more bullet hell-like bosses in this game at which I have more trouble with than I should be.
Many things that were added to the game were unneeded and put in for the sake of the game's difficulty. And with the luck factor still in play in the game, I was constantly discouraged to play this game after a lot of my losses. And at the moment, I've only beaten this game about 4 times (including 2 challenges).
This is by all means not a bad game, but I feel like too many people come to this games made by Edmund McMillen expecting to have a grand time. That's not what I got. I'm betting Edmund's a cool guy, but I haven't really liked his games all that much because of their absurd difficulty.
If you want to be frustrated and try to beat a really hard game, this game is for you, but if you are think you aren't built for it, wait till you think you're ready.

Aside from the stupid marketing decision of making Titans a separate game, Planetary Annihilation is a fantastic and unique RTS which allows players to create vast armies of land, sea, air, and orbital units.
The Titans add a great twist to the game. My favorite Titan is the Ragnarok which drills a hole to the center of the planet and drops a bomb down there, exploding the entire planet. There are ground combat Titans like the Atlas, which smashes the ground to create seismic mayhem, the Zeus which rains down electricity upon units, and the Ares which is a highly durable super tank with massive range.
There are other Titans like the Ragnarok (mentioned above), the Halley thruster which (if enough are built) can cause an asteroid or moon to smash into a planet and the orbital Titan, the Helios which fires lasers at everything and can teleport units right into the enemy's stronghold.
Aside from the Titans, playing with the default units can be fun. It's always nice to see two massive armies of bots, vehicles, and air units clash with perhaps some support from orbital battleships.
My advice, don't use Tier 1 units. Tier 1 units die too easily and are only useful for very early game. Tier 2 units are where it's at since they have enhanced durability and firepower.
Overall, I rate this game 8.8/10, whatever that means (I literally just came up with a random number I thought sounded good). Whatever you do, DO NOT BUY THE CLASSIC VERSION. They did a really stupid thing by making Titans and Classic two separate things. This game is great and provides hours of planetary annihilation, certainly worth the purchase, especially if it's on sale.

Too many things are gated behind extremely hefty requirements. For example, the first champion you can buy requires 100 quadrillion diamonds. And to level up your king even once you are required to buy said champion. This means countless days of resets. By comparison, Clicker Heroes unlocks Ancients when you get your first hero soul and ascend, which is normally around level 100-130, a good few hours of play.
Pets are as meaningless as life itself. To level up your pet, you need to cook it food. 10 meat requires waiting 12 hours, and that only gives you half a level.
The Clock of Morpheus artifact gives +% profits when you are offline. The Helm of Apollo gives +% profits for 12 hours when you first log in, and this bonus lasts even if you are offline. This is the only clicker game to actively encourage you not to the play the game.
The Glove of Zeus is your in-game autoclicker. Unfortunately, it's expensive and useless. Your first upgrade gives you only a single click a second, with every upgrade after that adding another click per second. Rage mode (active clicking) is garbage compared to Mana mode (idle).
The only upside is that when you spend your diamonds they aren't used up, but rather they are added to the reset pool. Unfortunately, this means that there's no risk/reward with buying upgrades. Just buy what you want, then reset and get all the diamonds you spent back.

I binged this game back when access to Port Lux was an achievement.
There has been MAJOR improvement to this game since then and it honestly ease some pain off for players, both old and new.
One being the removal of leveling SWORD spell and MAGIC spell seperately.Back then, each Sword based spell you cast only gives you sword exp and vice versa. You have to pay a large sum of cash to a particular instructor to temporary learn the ability to convert Sword exp to Magic exp.  The only way to evenly level them is to literally punch enemies for HOURS. Your spells are not restricted to your level like most mmorpg, you can be very VERY low leveled and have punch your way to access the highest spell possible (to those who play WoW, this is Cabal version of a Twink) and absolutely annihilate people in duels.
Pro :
-Flashiest and most unique skills in all MMORPG I've ever played
-Most unique class variant
-Easy to learn rotation to maximize DPS/survivalbility
-Forum is rich with topics to help you learn your class. Knowledge is power.
-The most beautiful design of swords and armor. (For the lads, most steamiest armors for female characters)
Subjective (some people have zero problem with this compared to me) :
-Traveling to dungeons is somewhat off putting due to the distance (unless you have a hoverboard /bike )
-Limited bag space unless premium player (Think Diablo 2 /Path Of Exile level of bag space)
-Your skill =/= your level, you do not gain new spells base on level , but base on proficient . You will definitely be leaving your character AFK-ing at the Training Dummy to gain the SKILL exp to be able to learn the new spell (Think of it as Ragnarok 1 ,where you have a Base Level and Job Level). This really isn’t a problem unless you are concern about your PC/Laptop overheating if you log in to park your character at the training dummy to go out to do something.
-Certain class may seem over/underpowered at certain level bracket but they all simmer down to being "Eh"
-Winning the Nation War does actually matter to an extend. When the faction you choose wins the War, premium players are granted access to warp points shortcuts which lets them transverse to dungeon much quicker and faster.
-One particular class, the Force Shielder, is very versatile. You can be the standard DPSer (add more str), A tank (Add more dex) or a Magic user! (add more Int)
Con :
-When you reach roughly lvl 50 (I think) you are somewhat forced to choose a Faction (Alliance vs Horde, Exile vs Dominion yada yada yada) If you maintain neutral, both factions will be able to attack you. It will almost always be a 3 faction combat. (Your chosen Faction) vs (Enemy faction + Neutral Faction) . When you reach that point in the game, it's all open PVP from here (as far as I know). Certain dungeons are located in said dangerous zone,so be prepared to be ganked from the bushes when you are on your way.
-Pay2SaveTime but not Pay2Win much. The Cash Shop (Microtransaction) lets you buy the materials that you need to upgrade your gears with, nothing you can't get with a little diligence. You and I will get the same identical gear in end game, just that whoever forks out the cash gets it soon, THAT IS ALL. I’M LOOKING AT YOU MAPLESTORY!!
-There is somewhat of a grind after lvl 100 onward, but there are dailies that you can do to rake in a few exp and money from.
-Tutorial is mandatory if you wanna proceed , can be a drag when you want to level an alt.
-A small portion of your money will be used regardless to buy spells, had you been doing quest, this really shouldn’t be an issue.
These are all the pro and con I can think off from my experience.
I know it seems that there is a wall of text for con, but it is solely to justify it, so don't get too offput by it!

Why are there so many negative reviews about this fantastic game? The devs always tell people that some features are not permanent and almost everything is subject to change. This could be tragic in some cases, but mostly changes are awesome! Nonetheless, it is probably one of the most content heavy games in Steam and one with the greatest potential.
There are several races with their own lore and personality. The lore might be slightly shallow right now, but it is enough to give a solid foundation for future characteristics. Plus they have their respective racial weapons, ships, and pets (and soon racial abilities, i.e. Novakids are getting a glow in the next update).
There are a ton of planets to explore with things like pirate airships, abandoned villages, prisons, high tech facilities, etc. Sure some biomes were removed, but the game is not precisely small in terms of planet scale and variety.
Customization is refreshing. You can partially paint your ship, there are a ton of furniture options, you can have homes on different planets and teleport between them, and there is a huge variety of costumes you will come across. (I've come across alien costumes, venice masks, a bunny you can wear on your head, capes, samurai armors, cowboy outfits, etc.)
Combat is fun. There "standard weapons" like racial weapons, boomerangs, gauntlets, checkrams, and some special weapons. Yet, it has random weapon generation and most weapons (including guns) have secondary abilities. I came across a sword that could dash and form a trail of ice behind me, a sniper rifle that could shoot bouncing ammunition, a hammer that could create a fire forcefield, and more.
There is so much more! Vehicles, quests, pets, dungeons, crafting, etc. Plus the modding community is brilliant and they add races, tools, or fuse the universe with mods based on other franchises.
I know that its been a while since this game has been on early access, yet I can't stress how exciting is to read the dev progress and expect exciting changes in the next update. The devs still have a gigantic passion for the game, and they are constantly working to improve it and test new or fixed features. It is not perfect, yet it is not finished. Are there going to be things you do not like? Yes. (I patially do not like the current tech system for example) However, all the good features still make the game great, and as I said it is constantly changing.
Should you buy it? If you are tired of AAA RPG's that have pretty graphics and the vanilla progression and features, buy this game. It will surprise you how fun it is. The artstyle is great, the music is beautiful, the questline is evolving into a mysterious story that is affected by your race. Starbound is probably one of the few game in steam that is original in a lot of ways. It brings new things and has a great potential thanks to its dedicated team of devs and the community. Plus, exploring and fighting is FUN.
P.S. All those features that people complain about are probably going to be fixed or improved eventually. The devs are amazing, and before buying you should be aware that it is an early access game. Feature will and can change, so don't complain about change. The game is NOT done (but its still constantly becoming more amazing).

Normally you would call it a mess in a bad way: lot's of visual error everywhere like teleporting people, weird animations, wrong positioning etc... but in this game it just makes it so funny that you actually might enjoy this :D
There are no NPCs in the world, so it's mostly a pure PVP, but there are also different gamemodes - so far I tried derby with huge vehicles smashed against each other and a race with buses.
Derby needs quite some work to become something that you don't want to quite after 1-2 minutes: there are no damage indicators and cars take so much damage that it feels like it's going to take forever to blow something up (even though it's normally hard not to blow things up in this game). It still brings fun moments when there are enough people participating.
Racing was fun as at it is, although it seems that driving through without damaging others is the key for the victory or maybe it's just me/my bus: I tried to get a guy out of the road, but instead got out of the road myself while he was just driving forward (even though I hit him hard).
Overall it's a good and quite promising bonus for the game and I hope they'll keep working on it, so that it could become something you can spend hours playing. Who knows, maybe this mod will become something to this game that DayZ was to Arma 2?..

AvP 2010 has very haphazard opinions if you google it on the internet. The general consensus of the title is that it's alright, but could have been better had the developers spent more time on it.
The single player portion of the game is where it shines the most. The three campaigns are alright, though their length is a primary concern. All three wont take you very long to complete, and this is particularly jarring since the previous two PC games AvP and AvP2 both had very long campaigns.
The biggest problem with this game is in it's multiplayer. The races are absurdly balanced, to the point where it's not enjoyable for anyone. The Predator is an overpowered demigod, the Marine can knock away Xenomorphs and the Alien is a fragile speedster that is fragile as ♥♥♥♥. This is possibly the biggest sin this game committed since AvP2 had amazingly good balance for it's three races. If you end up finding yourself in a multiplayer game all that ends up occuring is players spam the melee counter button.
Add in the lack of modding support (something that added longevity for AvP2), and lack of dedicated servers (For a series previously renowned for it's multiplayer clans) all you have here is one of the biggest examples of wasted potential. AvP2010 depresses me moreso because of how average the game is, and had they spent more time on it the game could have been the greatest in the series.
Thankfully it still isn't as bad as Colonial Marines.

Trove. A lovely and loveable game. I put MANY hours in it. I really love this game. I am gonna write out ALL +es (and some -s) about it.
General:
+ Very blocky and colorful game.
+ Lots of classes to play with. A respectable 15 types of classes with each of them having their own unique skills trait and game style.
+ The characters look both cute and cool in some way.
+ LOADS of possibilities. You can rush through small and big dungeons for loot and gear styles, You can do a balanced PVP battleground (opinions about the balance vary, from bad to weird, but come think of it, dealing over-the-roof damage to a tank who does not stand a chance? come on! It is scaled down to just your level and character without the gems.) You can build club worlds and your own Cornerstone in the way you like it, You can challenge the fabled Shadow Tower, and finally beat down the Daughter of the Moon herself with your friends, club mates, or even ALONE! (If you have the skill, right build and persistence though...) Also good if you have been building a lot and need a break, you just go back to the world portal where you have been grinding XP and finish building your structure later! :D
+ More and more content like each couple of months, and the game keeps getting better and better!
+ Power up with wearable/equippable gems to get even stronger than you could ever imagine!
+ Nice difficulty system, from the easy Novice to Master difficulty to make you get to know the game and mobs a little more, and getting to know more and more content as you increase level (Level 10). The Uber worlds (From Uber 1 to Uber 9, commonly known as U1-U9) require a higher Power Rank to enter, but you are better off entering the highes Uber portal you can enter when you are ready and geared for it. More gems still require higher levels, up to a maximum of level 30.
+ Do not be shy to help a stranger! You BOTH get the XP and reward benefits!
+ A well balanced community. Sometimes a bit more on the "salty" or "toxic" side on the global chat, as people call it lately, or a bit too nice topics on the global chat (e.g. American politics (Personally I don't mind, but please, do not bother foreigners with it (like me), making it free for everyone to read.), weird stories, etc.), Some people are just mean though... but on overall, if you are nice to other people, and help them out if needed (Shadow Tower, recommend gear stats, or even give out free Shadow-tier gear with the by you recommended stats), you certainly earn their respect. It's easy to make friends with new players, and club mates. When the global chat gets a bit too unconfortable, just keep this command in mind: "/leave 1". That's the command for leaving the Global chat. :) It's true, the saltyness and other stuff are like everywhere, but this game has a good balance in community. It is still up to the player if they like to be mean or friendly, or neither, so I cannot really judge about that.
- One major problem that still has not been fixed: The server is laggy. The bug fixes are a bit crappy too. They remove one bug, another comes in its place, but with the new head developer, that has become irrelevant. Still, the server needs a replacement.
- The gameplay, crafting reagent usage and crafting is a little bit too complicated for new players. This causes them to ask a lot of questions around, and for free stuff like mounts.
- Something is missing on the classes: the kind of damage any class actually deals. For example: Candy Barbarian deals Physical damage, and a Chloromancer deals Magical damage. They should just add that to the classes on the shop HUD or the Chaos Crafter's HUD, when you preview classes before considering to buy/craft them, or in the Class Changing HUD, to you get a reminder on what kind of damage which class does. Since the primary class type of damage is missing on the Chaos Crafter's HUD, the Shop HUD and the Class Changer hud's classes, new players, or players who hadn't been playing Trove in a while (several months or about a year) keep asking others what kind of damage a certain class does.
- Requires a beefy computer for the best results and graphics, but the lags are in the server, and not your computer.
Combat:
+ The combat is nice and easy. Turn around and attack with your mouse, and every now and then use the M2 (right mouse button, or button 2 on your mouse) and two other abilities.
+ You can build your character to be either tanky, making you as good as unkillable, with lots of health, or to go full on damage and critical hits, causing you to deal calamitious damage, but die easily. I personally go for both, enabling me to solo all of Shadow Tower.
+ You are capable of taking roles when playing with friends or club mates. One is the tank and the others deal damage, and such.
- Mostly other people just rush and wipe it before battle tactics are spoken on bosses, or when there is like 1 or 2 more people needed before engaging combat in the Shadow Tower.
- Mostly people prefer high power rank and huge damage over skill, causing a lot of battles to end with a wipe (loss).
Overall:
KEEP THE CRITICS IN MIND, AND KEEP UP THE GOOD WORK, TRIONWORLDS! :DD
In other words: I would HIGHLY recommend everyone else to give this game a try. It's worth every moment.
P.S. Do not make it too complicated for new players, as they are mostly young too, and sometimes have trouble with general game mechanics.

Doom 3 BFG edition nicely wraps up the full DooM game series in a nice little bundle. However, when I first bought it, I really just wanted Doom 3.
The reason for this is in the old Doom 3, you were able to create custom maps and load up mods for the game to spice it up after you get tired of the campaign. I mean, the missions are almost all dark cooridors with enemies that ambush you at every turn. Carmack himself stated he wanted to make the next Doom game scary, and so he sacrificed the gameplay for this. Yeah, the horror game gimmick is there, but it wears off fast. After ten missions of it, you expect having closets full of Zombies open after walking into a room where all of the lights go out because you touched an armor vest lying on a table. The reason why there was a map editor there at all was probably to encourage players to make their own levels if they were dissatisfied with the unchanging gameplay of the missions.
The BFG edition comes with Doom and Doom 2, which have extra missions you can play, but no multiplayer. The only game that comes with multiplayer is Doom 3, and I was a little disappointed with it for the reasons mentioned above. Despite that, the game is easier to play with the flashlight attachment to your weapons instead of needing to take it out to see what you are doing. Shadows in the new version are doen better IMO, and there is a lost mission campaign to go along with the main campaign and the Ressurection of Evil addition.
I recommend this game to players who mostly use Steam, or if you don't know how to map or mod. But if you are like me who would rather make my own custom maps, or have fun with fan made modifications and addons, I would rather just get the original Doom 3 game.

Just to add injury to insult (in that order), Sleeping Dogs (STILL NOT A TITLE WORTH TRADEMARKING!) suffers from the bästard child of console controller schemes, namely multi-function-single-buttons, or one-button-used-for-eight-hundred-different-functions. Whoever thought a PC game needs to have sprint AND jump bound to the same key should be executed. Publically. Braveheart style, with lots of torture before he'll be beheaded.
Then, we have another thing that's "like GTA but not even remotely better in fact it's a shïtload worse": vehicles. In every single GTA game since 3, we've had some pretty decent vehicle controls. Whether it's the rough 'n' heavy handling of GTA 4, or the crazy-stupid gooey and ultra-unrealistic insanity that was San Andreas, it's all been good in some way or another. Sleeping Dogs (STOP TRADEMARKING CRAPPY TITLES ALREADY!) handles vehicles like... I don't even know. This is a 'if you liked the previous ones, want plenty of achievements and get this on sale' recommendation. Otherwise known as 'mixed'.
Zup! 4 returns with another 60 level set of box explosion puzzles. The game does come with hundreds of alphabet style achievements just like the previous ones. (Though these are the most attractive ones, in my personal taste.)
The game mechanics are the same. Click the red box for explosion, get the blue ball on the green platform. The green moving boxes and grey deletable ones return. The new mechanic in Zup! 4 is the orange box which will slowly erode after the blue ball touches it. For me, the orange boxes was a nice addition, but maybe not enough to make this game stand out from the others: this easily could have been just a DLC to the previous ones.
Out of the 4 games in the series, I found this one clearly the easiest. It took me less than 35 minutes to 100% the game. Personally, I think this is too little content even for a $1 game since I'm not interested in the alphabet achievements. The number of achievements, while more moderate than in the previous installment, is still too much in regards to content. Still, there is something oddly satisfying in completing the levels as easy as they might be.
All in all, nothing really new, but nothing wrong with the game either. It takes a certain person to enjoy these kind of puzzles, but they are addictive and very relaxing which is the basis for my 'recommended'.

Let me start off by saying that Bastion won Best Downloadable Game at the 2011 VGX Awards as well as Best Song and Best Original Score and it shows!
From the get-go you are introduced to the most compelling aspect of the game imho: its near-constant narration that's delivered with gravitas and is the primary method through which the story is told. I found myself completely drawn in and absorbed by the excellent voice acting and was made to feel like I was being read a story by a gifted grandfatherly figure. Speaking of the story, while many have criticized it for its lack of originality I loved it as you gradually learn of the shocking cause of the calamity that has befallen the world and how that knowledge affects its few remaining survivors. Not every game story has to have multiple twists and turns, it's totally fine for them to be simple but well-crafted.
Further enhancing the story-book feel of the game are its lush and beautifully-drawn stages that are stunning to behold despite the fact that this is a 2D game.
Next, the combat: another point of contention among some, it's been criticized as being too simple and lauded as having a deceptive depth to it. I myself am of a mind with the latter camp as I found the many combat options to be quite diverse and open to experimentation that allow you to customize your combat according to your playstyle.
Finally, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention its fantastic musical score and song, "Build That Wall" (written and composed by Darren Korb): my head kept bobbing to the excellent tunes and it's so good that I've since added the entire soundtrack (minus a song or 2) to my Spotify playlist and you very likely will to once you play this great game :)

If you're like me, been playing Street Fighter since before controllers had joysticks, let me give you impressions of the game, six months after launch or so.
I avoided this game at launch as we all saw it suffer from lack of content and network support.
I remained on the fence about purchasing it up until this latest steam sale.
If you are living with a Street Fighter sized hole in your life maybe this will halp reassure your angst.
>> Cons >>
I'm still upset with Capcom. If this was the debut title release from Capcom they would have sunk. I'm mad that the game is sixty bucks, but to unlock all the characters they want another thirty. I remember back in the day when you unlocked characters just by playing the game alot. You can purchase the in game characters with in game currency, but after completing the story modes and survival modes you still wouldn't have enough I don't think. It is an option but it is heavily stilted.
The online matches I have played (about a dozen) at least half of them the connection was garbage, my opponent would teleport around and land hits while the game was buffering. I have great internet where I am so rule that out. It may be just that those opponents have crappy internet and not actually the netcode though. I'm not putting the blame solely on Capcom for that, however it did kill the mood a bit!
And still no arcade mode. I know I know survival, or play online. But I'm oldschool. I want to practice my combos on each character for a few rounds in increasing difficulty! You know, like arcade mode!
>> Pro's >>
Ok so if you're still with me first let me say that I am very happy I bought SFV. I would advise you to either wait for another steam sale, or maybe visit one of those shady key sites (only because I'm still mad at capcom) and pay 30 or 40 bucks rather than 60, that way you can buy the extra characters that should have been included in the damn game anyway.
There is something about this latest SF that really grabs me. Maybe its the art, or the character design, but I'm loving it. I love that they remixed alot of characters. Be warned though some charge characters have been converted to quarter circle inputs so that may put you off, but for me I'm happy. I like the new characters, I like the new outfits. I just can't stop playing this. Maybe because I went through a drought of no SF ha ha.
If you have a friend to play with its so much better. When you join a battle lounge (online matchmaking "party") you can't really type to message, you have to select prewritten text, so communication is clunky. Also its hard to display your intentions that way, but if you've got a friend to spar with, grab a voip and its a blast.
The Story mode is in game now and its splendid!
Survival mode is a challenge, though the AI goes from numb to killer in the last few matches so watch out.
Training mode is outfitted with everything you can imagine. If you plan on really drilling combo's or specific actions you can do it. Also you can just turn your opponent into AI mode (which I've been doing and pretending its Arcade mode). The AI can be adjusted for difficulty too, so if you need to practice blocking, reversals etc you can do it here without giving up any League Points.
Finally there are some really good players scouring the ranked matches nightly. I have been beat down a bunch of times which gives me hope! Its not a game if you can never lose and its not a fun game if the challenge is easily overcome.
>> Conclusion >>
I'd say now is the time to jump into SFV if you've been holding out. This was a chance to start over for me, I switched my main character and alt, and have been loving just training with them. It also helps that I have a friend to play online against a few nights a week. Nonetheless, if you love SF as much as I do, its safe to go ahead and jump in now :)

Bastion is a narrational led hack and slash game.  It runs smoothly,
and offers leaderboards for those that enjoy them.  The music is wonderful,
professionally done and really complementary to the combat and actions of
the game, as is the voice acting.
The story is based around surviving an apocalypse, and bringing
the other characters together.  The story reacts to your actions, which
makes the player feel like they are actually making a difference.
The game offers several different options for tailor making the
difficulty of gameplay, which can be changed in game.   Increasing
difficulty will allow the player to level up faster, but the game does
get harder with options such as the relic outpost.
Resources can be accumulated during gameplay, which can be used
towards upgrades, potions, or building.  Again, even the use of resources
depends on the choice of the player, which I can respect.
The combat is fluid, and is tied to the story where who the
player chooses to fight effects later battles and the universe.  I never
felt like my time was being wasted, and every aspect of this game is
integrated and complimentary of each other aspect.  I have no problem
recommending it.

This comes from the perspective of a relatively good player (ie, top ranked Juri in USFIV).
It took me a long time to come to this verdict, but I intensely dislike this game and I recommend you do not play it.
Prepare yourself for feelings like:
"So, uh, what did you want me to do to get out of that, exactly?"
"Ha ha, of *course* that's a frame trap, why wouldn't it be"
"Why is that safe.  Why is that move safe.  Why"
"We all had so much fun fighting SF4 Rolento, they made a whole game about it!  Get hype!!!"
"WELP I MIGHT AS WELL JUST PUT DOWN MY CONTROLLER"
"Combofiend, you filth, you absolute scum"
It feels like every single design decision in this game was made to promote a certain playstyle:
-There are more characters with anti-fireball moves than there are fireballs.
-Most normals are safe and lead to increased pressure.  This makes blocking a bad idea and gives advantage to the aggressive player every time.
-Neutral game is very stale, there's practically no such thing as over-extending.  You have little reason to be cautious.  You're penalized more for blocking than you are for throwing out a random heavy punch.
-Antiairs are the least reliable in series history, making those 40% damage jump-in combos quite common by comparison.
-Wakeup is a hugely disadvantageous situation, worse than any game I can think of.  No options are smart, even doing nothing isn't smart.
-"Get-Off-Me" type moves were removed as thoroughly as they could get away with.  Moves they couldn't realistically remove (shoryu, EX SBK) were given crush on punish, increasing the risk of using them even more than before.
-Every returning character was redesigned more in the direction of mixup/pressure based play.  Even dhalsim, the archetypical zoner going back two decades, is now a mixup character.
-Per character V-Triggers seem interesting at first, but about half of them are essentially the same thing: a "zany" tool for opening the opponent up (as if you need it?).  Nash, Mika, Ken, Vega, Cammy, Rashid, Bison...
This all adds up to a game that is 100% about "in-your-face pressure."  Zoning is unrealistic, neutral game is not really doable, punishes aren't there, grapplers are weak other than the mixup-crazy Mika, etc etc.  If you were hoping for a clash of different strategies and an interesting variety of options and opponents, tough, the game doesn't have that.

Sanctum 2 is the sequel to Sanctum, a phenomenal blend of tower defense strategy and a FPS-game.  Playing the original Sanctum, it was pretty intuitive; construct the path and populate the defensive towers and engage in FPS-action.  Phenomenal.  The beauty of the original Sanctum was its practically unlimited resources (gained after each round per group member) to build as many towers you can fit on the map as well as upgrading each one of them (including your weapons).  The original Sanctum is indeed a great multiplayer game, but it's weakness was the ability to play the game solo - as each added member to your group provided more resources to build more things per round and added another FPS-shooter to help take down those aliens the towers fail to take down due to their inconspicuous weakpoint.
Sanctum 2 seems to be an entirely different concept of the original, more focusing on FPS-action.  It evolved into a more Borderlands look-and-feel; that is, character progression, character perks, and selectable weaponry and tower lineup (as with the original); however, a 15-tower limit is imposed (each tower can be upgraded) however you will still be able to layout additional blocks to create intricate pathways.  Similar towers (from the original concept) but having slightly different functions as well as new ones.  One of my favorite items (in the orignal Sanctum) were the slow pads that can be constructed on the path the aliens traverse; however, Sanctum 2 replaces that with a tower having a fixed-area (upgrading expands the active area a bit larger).
Comparing the two is difficult as Sanctum 2, despite it's clear differences from the first, is in fact another phenomenal game from a different conceptual view.  It features the ability to harden the game by enabling various "Feats of Strength", making the game more challenging.  It's definitely geared toward focusing more on FPS-shooter than relying on Tower Defense aspect.   Its notable strengths are a more viable single-player game, outstanding multiplayer playability, variable difficulty, and character progression & customization.
So for those who love Tower Defense and FPS-games, this will be another diamond-class addition to your gaming arsenal.  For those at Coffee Stain Studios, great work and looking forward to see what else you come out with.

With the recent release of Aliens: Colon Miners I decided to dust off the ol' AvP for a bit of alien vs slightly-different-alien gameplay. I've got to say I quite enjoy this game despite its many shortcomings. Like the length, for one thing. According to Steam it took 7.7 hours to beat all 3 campaigns, and that included pausing it while I ate dinner at least once, as well as time spent in menus. But I digress...
Firstly you've got the Marine campaign with the-- hold on, who invited these guys? Anyway, firstly you've got the Marine in a very generic and somewhat dull FPS campaign. You wander around shooting at anything that moves. You know how every shooter you've played that was made in the last decade has let you hold the right mouse button to use ironsights? This one doesn't have that, right-clicking instead uses your secondary ammo, so until you get used to that you can enjoy grenading yourself to death. That's not really a problem after a the first 2 minutes, I'm not sure why I wrote an entire paragraph about it.
Secondly you've got the Alien--the err... Xenomorph one. This guy is excellent. You're a stealthy little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ running around on walls and ceilings, pouncing on anything tasty-looking and pressing R to screech your♥♥♥♥♥♥off. This is the best bit. If they could expand on this and release it as a full game I'd play the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it.
Last but not least you've got the Predator (least would be the Xeno, with a whopping hour and a half campaign). You jump about ripping human heads off, or enagaging in fisticuffs with the Xenos. You can also be more stealthy and distract baddies and use ranged weapons, but there's really not much point. I don't know what using the cloak is meant to achieve, that thing didn't actually help hide me once, the piece of crap.
There's not much I can actually write because Steam recommendations are woefully short, but there's a very basic look at the game. I recommend it if it's on sale for a few bucks, but definitely don't buy it full price.

I really want to be able to recommend this game.  It's enjoyable, has lots of layers ontop of a fairly linear system, and by all accounts is a quality idler/clicker.  Not the best but solid.
Unfortunately, I can't recommend it due to 3 main factors:
1) Gambling.  The bulk of the things you need to progress are easiest to obtain via gambling in the 'events'.  They're expensive, predatory, and it's the only realistic way to progress.  You can get some for free but the amounts needed are absurd and the only way is to spend real money to gamble away.
2) Past about ~e75 gold it grinds to a halt.  The only way to progress is to use massive amounts of raid loots... by e85 gold I was using ~50 of each between temple resets.
3) Most of the layers aren't available until too late in the game.  The majority of people will likely walk away before they get to half of what's in the game.  By e78 diamonds you'll have the bulk of the game unlocked but that's so far into the exponential climb as to be unobtainable for your average player.  Only the truly dedicated/rich will get anywhere.
You can easily spend $10,000 and still not complete the game (this is based on testing not suposition)
One of the problems is the Raid system.  The timers are too long and the rewards too small to provide what's needed to progress.  Same goes for the pet arena - just in terms of food required you'll need at least 600 days of logging in once every 12 hours to reach the Void Dragon (best pet) let alone the potions needed to beat the Diamond tier (up to 6 days of potion making for a single 10 second battle)
