Problems such as multi-player de-synchs, audio effects cutting off mid-game, usually after the first round, and framerate drops are plaguing it. There are very few additions in terms of weapons and their area of effect seems rather limited.  They feel completely unsatisfying. Also don't be fooled by the contraptions you see in the snapshots. They're not available in multiplayer.
I won't talk about the clans because neither I nor my friends are interested in building some sort of reputation amonst unknown players. But if you're after this sort of entertainment, you won't find any people to play against.
In the end, all I've got to say about this title is that if you're after shiny graphics buy Worms Revolution instead, otherwise stick with the classic titles in this series, most notable Worms Armageddon and Worms World Party, where you get a pletora of satisfying weapons to decimate your friends with.
The trend nowadays seems to be: throw to the bin a good game, apply a fresh layer of paint on top of a shaky new engine, ignore some good ideas from the successful releases in the franchise, and sell it in whatever shape it is. The good old reputation won't keep this franchise afloat for too long, Team17.

I'm very disapointed with Starbound and Chucklefish.  I believe that their ultra successfull crowd funding project, plus the very large amount of cash they have gotten here at Steam have changed the devs. Back when the game was first proposed the devs had excitement and passion....they had a great vision for Starbound.  A few million dollars later: no so much.  The project has been worked on now for many years. Sometimes the patches would improve the game, but mostly the content has been fluff. There is no "backbone" to this game. I can tell that the devs have lost their passion for Starbound, they just want to release it to start working on something else. Starbound is a perfect example of what happens when a indi dev team is flooded with more money than they know what to do with.  They have taken their eyes off of the prize, as the sales of Starbound no longer matter to them, they don't need the money.
Alright, so the game has finally been released. In my previous review I gave the game a down-vote due to the fact that despite millions of dollars and nearly 5 years of work,the game was still not finished.  Everything I have written about CF and how they have handled all of the money that was shoved at them remains true.
However, now that the game has been released, and to be fair, it IS a proper release, not rushed out the door because the team is running out of money. I feel as though I should now review the game based on the final product. I understand that I will never be able to be 100% unbiased, but I will do my best to give a thumbs up or down based on the final gameplay.
SO far, I am really enjoying some of the changes they have made in the 1.0 patch, I am going to be changing my recommendation at this point based on how much fun I've had in the game since it released...I will conintue to make updates as I play more.

This game has been in development so long that Stardew Valley came out fully finished - with 1 person working on it - while this game is still in "Early Access" , and that game has likely more content.
There is a lack of content in this game that leaves it feeling dull after a little while.
MOD MAKERS add more content to this game than the developers.
This Game is an absolute must read for how NOT to develop a game - When it was released this was the next best thing to Terraria and likely could have blown up even bigger due to its concepts, however , the games developers consistently released tiny updates that invalidated many mods - and of them there were MANY fantastic ones. This was done over and over again so that many modders , nearly all of them, quit the game.
The vanilla game is not upto snuff after being out this long and I understand modders should not normally be considered with making updates to the core game - but when they are producing literally 400-900% more content in SINGLE mods than exist in the entire vanilla game , then yeah , they should have been considered. Me and my friends only played this for the mods. That says ALOT , infact , it says it all.
This and many other decisions led to a complete die-down of the momentum this game had at the start so that eventually it became just a mediocre title - but they got their vanilla changes in! and after ALLLLL of this time? Thats not saying very much at all since the game itself isnt too far off from where it started originally , 90% of the features in vanilla were fleshed out , thought out and released by modders early on. Only to have the mods rendered incompatible for the umpteenth time for some additional run animation , or jump animation , or a quest overhaul etc.
This game was an enormous disapointment to alot of people , myself included.

The void, The Dread...there is nothing left to game, after completing SUDOKU. with DLCs. Ruined all games for me, as I try to find the replacement, to play something so astonishingly brilliant, intelligent and deep. This game is near perfect and it annoys me that I might have to wait till 2018/19/20 till Cyberpunk, which I hope will be another masterpiece.
There is a sense of completeness after beating this, and a hole big enough that I do not think will be filled by any other game for a very long time.
SUDOKU. follows the story of Geralt of Rivia, in search for his lost love Yennefer of Vengerberg. As the story progresses, He is looking for Cirilla Fiona Elen Riannon, sort of eh... Daughter. Anyway, This takes us to swampy and haunted Valen, Rich and “Civilized” Oxenfurt & Novigrad, and islands of Skellige.
The world is huge, detailed, beautiful and lively. NPCs are doing their daily tasks and while they are limited, and slight feels slight repetitive after awhile, it feels much alive. Monsters will attack you and well, fighting them is fun. Sometimes you have a choice to not kill them and outcome changes drastically along with reward.
Let’s talk about quests, because that is the real meat of this. There are lots of (Side)Quests, meaningful ones I tell you and not just - go there, fetch this, and done. Side quests, Treasure Hunts and Contracts. While many may feels same, there are almost always multiple ways to complete the quest. In some of the quests, just how you start the quest may change the outcome drastically, and then there are some quest which may not have direct hint in the log towards that different path, but exploring will find alternative endings and it’s so much fun.
The main quest is good, except the Villain is not really scary. Apart from that, quests are good, diverse, rich with detailed dialogues. There are couple of quests where you travel, using thing that Geralt hates most, with a certain Elf and bloody hell, it was good. There is a deep sub story in that quest, which you can find using notes scattered around. It’s a sad and chilling story of how that particular event happened. Then there is Baron storyline, with multiple endings depending on choices, which you must find using notes and talking with people. I think this is the biggest plus point of this game. The stories are so good that we are lost in it with an urge to complete it.
Another good thing is, there is lots of (optional) reading. Character entries, Detailed Bestiary, Books and Notes found throughout the world which tells the Micro stories which will help understand why a certain NPC is behaving like♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or is too nice with you.
Then there is Gwent. Oh man, a game within a Game. it’s a card game like Hearthstone, but with SUDOKU. characters and different rules. It’s fun and there are multiple quests which I enjoyed much. It’s nice to take a break from adventuring, having banter and playing Gwent.
Finally, The Music. Oh my God, beautiful, deep, melodious tunes. I use this music when I’m working, want to relax or want to look at my life and mistakes I made (heh) and it fits amazingly well in each situation. I don’t know how, but no videogame has ever done this to me, as I feel empty sometimes while listening to the soundtrack, as what to do now after beating this.
Now, some cons. The game is extremely easy, even on the death march difficulty. This was the same problem with Kingdom of Amalur, which may be a con for some. The starting is challenging, but damn after level 10, I was breezing through path without much struggle.
Just make sure to kill that Wraith at the well without taking damage, and you’ll know what I’m talking about.
Economy is flawed and at mid-game, if you are doing all side activities like me, then you will so many crowns that you don’t know what to do. Visit a brothel or two may be.
Third act is rushed job. I mean, this was the case with Witcher 2 as well, so IDK if it was intended or not, but was slightly annoying for me.
Still, for the content it provides, and gameplay, I’d give 9.9/10 for this. Just Amazing and well worth at full price.

Serious racing simulator enthusiasts can stop reading, because this isn't the game for you.
On the other hand, if you're the kind of person who loves: watching stuff slam into other stuff at 100 miles an hour, vans doing barrel rolls through the air, and the concept of "getting extra points for driving on the wrong side of the road", then this is DEFINATELY the game for you.
In Burnout Paradise, you start off with one car. It's okay, a little slow, and just generally "yep, that's a car". You can unlock more cars by encountering them in the large, open-world map, and then RAMMING THEM INTO♥♥♥♥♥♥ Then, go get your new car, and go nuts. There are many kinds of activities to loudly persue while breaking all known rules of the road. Races, "Marked Man" challenges, Stunt Runs, and Burning Routes (which unlock an upgraded version of the vehicle they're associated with).
Now, zipping around in singleplayer is fun, and lets you get acclimated with the gorgeous (even this long after release) world of Burnout Paradise. It also lets you get new rides, and so on and so forth.
But then you log into Multiplayer, and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥
Massive, sprawling, high-speed BRAWLS of ten, twenty, however many cars just roaring along, causing destruction and mayhem wherever they go. Custom challenges, grudge-match crashing, and just general shenanigans are the norm. Think it was hard to nail the landing on a super-jump in singleplayer? Try doing it in multiplayer while four players in large, angry-looking SUVs try to ram you out of the air.
In summary: Good for fun, not so good for realism. Great multiplayer potential, but solid Singleplayer. Good price, good graphics, small size on Hard Drive. GREAT soundtrack, excellent open-world map, extreme replayability.

If you have never played Doom, this collection is a great way to introduce you to the franchise. With the seminal Ultimate Doom, Doom 2, and an idTech 5 port of Doom 3 to start with, this package also contains a couple of expansion packs that have never been released before. Namely, No Rest for the Living for Doom 2 and The Lost Mission for Doom 3. In the months following its release, ZDoom and its derived ports have been adapted to be compatible with this version of the Doom and Doom 2 data files, so if you're into modding, you should no longer have an issue running ZDoom mods with this package's version of Doom 1 & 2.
If there is one thing that really disappointed me about this edition of the game, it's that it does not include other commercial iWADs that were included in previous classic Doom collections and compilations. Namely, there's no Plutonia, TNT, Master Levels for Doom or even D!Zone levels included. It would also have been nice if this was finally the legitimate way to acquire Hell 2 Pay or Perdition's Gate.
Considering who this is marketed to though, I can't really blame them too much for it. If you've never heard of Doom, I would recommend it. However, die-hard doom fans can very much afford to skip on this, or failing that, wait for a sale if they HAVE to get No Rest for the Living or The Lost Mission.

After feeling the old times again, I thought i help the interested people with this review, a bit out.
Alright let's begin with the basic informations about this game.
American Conquest: Fight Back is the standalone add-on for the "American Conquest" the RTS succesor in year 2002. (Fight Back was published one year later [2003]). The Ukrain developer "GSC Game World" (Who also developed the famous Cossacks games) set a great step towards the massive fights in RTS games, we currently play. With a limit of around 16.000 Units on the map, a big step was made.
To cut it short. American Conquest (in addition: "Fight Back and Divided Nation") has made it's place up to one of the greatest RTS games ever made so far.
Moving on to the Pros and Cons section:
- 2D Graphics (But don't let yourself get shrekt by that, for a 2003 game, the graphics do look smooth and pretty)
- No running problems on 2003 compared systems (Currently used: Windows 7 Home)
- I only experienced 2 crashes so far after a long play time.
- RTS game.
- Tutorials are existent
- A huge variety of campaigns (Europe site and Native American site)
- A huge variety of civilizations (Europe site and Native American site)
- The units for example the fusilier does never look the same, each civilization has it's unique units
- The AI is challenging even on "Easy" Mode
- Balanced play
(Europe units are mostly based on gunpowder but cost more and take longer to built, while the natives mostly rely on arrows and a minimum of gunpowder, but are cheaper and faster to built)
- Morale and defenses are pretty well built in the game
- Mechanic of people dying when there is no food left is within the game
- Mechanic of archers not shooting arrows when there is no wood left is within the game
- Same goes for units with the use of iron and coal for gunpowder (KEEP YOUR RESOURCES UP!)
- The price of 4.99€ is worth every cent
The neutral section here is a section where i simply can not tell whether it would be good for you people or not.
- The music, does fit, but it can get annoying i guess
- You need to be fast to built up your defenses (depends on the peacetime you set in the menu)
- The AI how easy they might be, can always find a way around your guarding troops. So be careful and guard well.
- I do experience lag at somepoint in the game if a number of units is produced, but this can be because my computer has to run multiple things in the background
-  The game sure can be frustrating if you look more for the economic state of the game (Example: Research everything before you actually produce units/an army) and the AI smashes your efforts with one offensive strike
- Sometimes (atleast if the enemy is the civilization: "Pueblos" (which i assume are the mexicans) it can happen that the enemy is not attacking at all, but patrolling their city. (To fix this you simply need to attack them)
I played this game around 2005 or so and i loved it. Since steam brought it back into the store, I do play it often.
I can only say that every player who likes good old RTS gaming experience, should buy this game. I did not tryout the multiplayer matches, since i do feel like i'm not that good but that's an other story.
Still though. Buy it if you feel like it, or feel like you should try out the RTS gaming.
I do hope that i helped with this review, if anyone still feels unsure, feel free to contact me, I'll try to sort things out and answer your questions you might have, as good as possible.
At last a pro tip: DO NEVER EVER MAKE ALL YOUR ENEMIES AND YOURSELF DELAWARES!

Have you ever wanted to play a strategy game? If yes then this is perfect game for you. American Conquest series are one of the classic RTS games. I am huge fan of this series and I can recommend this game to anyone.
Technical stuff:
Well you can say that this is one old game. It is 2D, but do not be fooled. Graphics in this game are quite good and it is timeless. Due to its requirements it is quite easy load game and thanks to steam you can play it on newer systems with no glitches. There can be thousands of units on the battleground and you will not experience any lags. Engine is based on cossacks series with little improvements, and that engine I have to say is quite good. Sounds are nice too and will not affect you in anyway. When you first time run the game, you should adjust the game speed since on newer computers game will run on insane speed.
Gameplay:
It is classic RTS game but unique. There are different civilizations with their unique gameplay. Common ground is: every building which has units placed inside it will fire something (bullets, arrows, cannonballs). To produce soldiers you have to put some peasants into production building and turn them into soldiers. Workers can be captured if there are no units guarding them (you can't steal civilization like in cossacks), although some nations are exception (indian mostly). You can storm buildings (send your units into enemies building, and if you overpower garrisoned ones you overtake the building and it becomes yours. Mines can be captured same as workers. There is morale mechanics where soldiers can become frightened when too many die, from gunshots, cavalry, etc. Units have basic stats: slash/pierce attack, base armor, HP, morale. storm force. If they are armored they will have resistance to gunshot, arrow, scatter shot, pierce/slash attacks etc. There are various unit upgrades and economic upgrades. There is famine mechanics where workers and soldiers will die if there is no food. Food is farmed using Mills which automatically plant squares of wheat or corn. There are 2 gatherable resources: food and wood, while stone, gold, iron and coal are mined in mines. Buildings when dmg for example with fire arrows will start burning and if not repaired with workers will easily be destroyed. Also when shooting arrows or bullets into garrisoned building, the ones inside will die.
You can categorize nations into 2 factions: European nations and Indians. Europeans start with peasants building a fort. Fort is like 1st tier barracks which produces 3 types of units: Heavy armor pikemen, harquebusier  (heavy armor rifleman), musketeer and 3 officers types: drummer, flagbearer and officer for making formations. Once you build 3 officers and enough single type soldiers (15,36,72,120,196) you can make formation which provides base armor and dmg (one flaw would be that while in formations soldiers get dumb and won't move as you command them, they will stop at certain points). Workers are built using houses T1 and T2, and main upgrades are placed in town center. There is church to build priests who act as healers only. Shipyard builds epic ships and gunboats as ferries as transports. After than using mines mine stone and gold and build fortress which is stronger barracks. It can train musketeers too. officers, and fusiliers from infantry. Fortress is also place where you upgrade it with stables to produce cavalry and artillery depot to produce single type cannons. Regarding firepower Fortress is impregnable and is hard point to capture/destroy with indian nations. Cannons are game finishers produces slow and expensive, move slow (kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ movement) but they pack quite a punch and can have range even half the map. True epitome of artillery.
Indian vary much, from mayans, delawares, iroquois, sioux each with unique gameplay. Indians rely on quantity and arrows, build buildings much faster since most require only wood. Some indians do not use mines (sioux). Indian can also build formations using chief and shaman which are produced ridiculously slow. Some indians have fortresses (like aztec, maya, incas), while others use barracks to make soldiers. Indians soldiers are pikemen, archers and single type cavalry and each indian nations is quite unique but in raw firepower and armor none can reach european nations. Shipyard plays better role for indians since it can produce fishing ships and war canoes which are good siege artillery unit.
So gameplay starts with nothing but few buildings, ends up with big town which produces massive armies whom you use to peel your enemy off (hit mines, hit mills, hit storehouses, basically pick off his economy). There is campaign, single players maps which are autogenerated, battle simulations. Maximum number of players on one map is 7. Map sizes go from small to epic (and epic is quite the distance). I have not played multiplayer since I find AI quite strong and challenging and when you finally overpower him it takes ages to finish him. And he can recover fast.
All in all game is fun and relaxing and if you enjoy playing RTS games, you should buy this game. I will continue updating this review with more details as time goes.

It's very rare that I can be bothered to write reviews but this game is just worthy of one.
It's early access however, so take everything I say with a grain of salt.
Northgard finds itself being classed as a Real-Time Strategy game but only has minimal elements of other games in this genre. If you want to be controlling the ultimate minute details of everything then this game is not going to scratch that itch. It takes a slower paced, almost board-game esque approach to the real-time strategy genre. Your workers automatically get to work on producing resources when possible, and if they can't they will let you know. Your 'military' is not especially varied or has any depth to it, but it suffices to be interesting as combat isn't the focus - there are multiple avenues of victory in Northgard, akin to Civilization, and as such domination is not necessarily the best option for your playstyle. Not only that, but with so many neutral enemies to contend with, I have had several games where I never fought my neighbours at all, instead dealing with wolves, draugar and evil valkyries. There is enough depth in these mechanics to stay interesting, but not too much that would overwhelm all but the staunch veteran of the RTS genre.
Graphically, the hand-painted art style is gorgeous and always a treasure to see. There are stutters when the game changes seasons but this seems like a hardware issue that patches could solve. Frame rate was never an issue. I am very happy to play this game even with it's simplistic art style. Less is more, in this regard.
On the sound design, it's beautiful. The background music is fitting enough for the theme and quite calming. The voices of the (all male, currently) vikings at your command aren't too repetitive enough to get annoying. Overall, it seems a lot of attention was paid to sound, which is good to hear.
Here are my concerns, however: there are not many features present, enough to keep you interested for around 9 games or more possibly, with each round being roughly an hour (or more depending on difficulty). The AI does not seem terribly bright and is easy to manipulate. The victory conditions leave a lot to be desired, as they are not terribly exciting. Multiplayer might take a while to be implemented based on balance. The clans have only a few behind the scenes aspects distinguishing them.
These concerns could well be all addressed over the course of development. I'm hopeful they are.
All in all, if you want a slower-paced RTS and/or enjoy the viking theme, this is well worth picking up.

I'm sure some will like this aspect of the game, because it makes it overly easy. It breaks my heart Sudoku, but I am giving you thumbs down.

This is probably my biggest concern with the game right now, as there are likely many people who want to play this multiplayer but don't know how to port-forward. Luckily, there are some alternatives to this, and one could easily find a tutorial online. I have to say that it is very much worth it to have the multiplayer working, as this game only gets better with friends.
Keep in mind as well that this game is in early access. The current build, which is amazing on its own, doesn't fully represent how much better this game could become in the future. When you get this game, it comes with an unstable build that you can use to play around with features no built into the Stable version yet, which is also pretty cool.
Final Verdict: Get the game and play it with some friends

I played CABAL Online for about 3 months nonstop a couple of years ago. The only reason I stopped was I got back into WoW hardcore for a while. I kind of forgot about the game, so I'm excited to see it pop up on Steam.
CABAL is not a new game, and you can definitely tell that right off the bat. But it doesn't play badly like some older MMOs do. You just have to deal with some kind of ugly outdated quest texts/fonts and some iffy (yet readable) translations. You can click to move if you want, or use WASD (or reassign keys to whatever you want). I don't care for the camera very much, honestly.
The combat is pretty fun and low stress. The classes are about what you'd expect, your general MMO variety. They do play quite differently from eachother though- very unique. It's essentially a themepark with some neat mechanics. PVP is fun, but very DPS-focused (tanks and healers don't really play much of a role). Music is really weird for the genre, but it's pretty good. (It's like weird hard rock)
There is a cash shop and premium and whatnot, but I wouldn't necessarily say it's p2w. It's DEFINITELY pay-to-advance-way-faster, though. but I think you can have a good time with CABAL for free.

The game itself : If you like suspenceful roleplay where everybody is suspicous this is your kinda game.
Has a bunch of fun roles, that seem pretty evenly balanced from a Jester who just tries to get the townsfolk to hang him, to a Spy who can listen in on whispers and hear mafia chat at night.
No useless roles. Everyone has some kind of ability and goal.
There is an executioner who is assigned a random target and must get him to die no matter what but the executioner cannot do it himself. Jester want's the town folk to hang him so he can return as a vengful spirit and kill someone who called him guilty. Mafia has a framer who can make a someone else come up as mafia positive to a sherif/investigator inspecting them. There's also a few more roles in the game's "Chaos" mode that throws in more roles like Witch who can control people, A werewolf , a body gaurd ect.
One problem I can see so far though is that the medium role is going to be useless 90% of the time because the dead are either going to quit the game when they die (thus they can't talk) or the only dead people are mafia who you shouldn't be listening to.
It's exciting when you're on the town side and you forge an alliance with someone you trust and you try to find other town members.....or you get back stabbed by telling the wrong person your role.
I was a jailor and once had a great partnership with an escort and we managed to find the last GodFather among all the remaining players.
Summary : Buy/play this if you like detective (or being a lieing sneaky mafia) roleplay.
Also please don't cheat and party up with friends and chat outside game..it ruins the whole point.

Definitely worth a buy. Originally did not like this game, but grew to love it due to the environments. I think I like BFG Edition even more. I've read all the complaints. Some of them are valid (or were valid before fixes were implemented) but a lot of them weren't... such as brightness levels (looks better now), ammo count (it's true that the whole PDA thing is optional now most of the time because you're never short on ammo, but it means the game is more action-packed and faster-paced), reworked menus (they look and control better now, in my opinion -- also like the new Doom 3 logo much better). Etc..
It also controls better. Seems much more responsive and faster due to the increased framerate and probably other improvements they made. Motion blurring is a nice addition, too.
Classic Dooms are ported well and appear high resolution (can see sprites clearly at a distance). Also controls well with everything set up for modern WASD controls. The "No Rest for the Living" episode by Nerve is quite good (already available on Xbox 360). Overall this port is a lot better than some of the detractors said it was. Even the music in Doom Classic seems pretty good-- I notice it has Gravis sound files in the Steam folders.

So I bought USFIV during the summer sale and needless to say I quickly fell in love with that game. So a few weeks later I picked up SFV with high expectations. I read lots of reviews and watched lots of videos on SFV and most of them said this game was not complete. But after my good experience with USFIV, SFV couldn't be that bad of a game...or so I thought. The first thing I noticed when I played SFV was that YOU CANNOT CHANGE YOUR KEYBINDS. Well, you can, but you have to choose from crappy preset keybindings. WTF??? I don't know in what world that would be okay for a PC game. I had to use external software to configure the keybindings to my liking. Then the next problem I encountered was that there's no arcade mode. In USFIV, I played arcade mode a lot, and I had lots of fun doing so. But in SFV the only thing you can do single player based are non-challenging, boring, and easy story modes. Seriously, you can just button mash your way through each and every story and beat all of them in around an hour. Although there is training mode, but it's not the same as arcade mode. The only thing I liked about SFV was the fighting. It was a lot smoother than USFIV and combos were a lot easier to perform. I had to run this game at the lowest possible settings because this game probably requires a beefy computer to run, so I couldn't experience the beautiful graphics I had seen on YouTube. But the bad outweighs the good and SFV is a terrible game. And to top it all off, YOU HAVE TO PAY 60 ♥♥♥♥ING DOLLARS FOR THIS GAME! Until Crapcom does something about these problems (especially keybindings) this game will forever be a horrible mess. I'm glad I refunded it.

The core gameplay is amazing, lots of improvements over Street Fighter IV and the battle mechanics are a lot better as well. The BGM is brilliant and Unreal Engine 4 gets the job done on the visual side of things, except for clipping, which is awful to look at in some instances.
On PC, there are no keyboard or language settings which were present in Street Fighter IV from day 1. These should've been there from the beginning!
The absence of Steam Cloud support means that some settings and single-player progress are not preserved when you install the game from scratch.
The online infrastructure and netcode have been problematic since release which is unacceptable for a AAA* fighting game. Sometimes one player gets all the rollbacks, one player has a flawless match while the other sees nothing but lag which results in an overall terrible experience.
The game lacks standard single-player game modes, such as the arcade mode, that are present in other fighting games. Certain game modes (survival mode especially) are awfully designed and playing them is agony rather than fun.
Capcom has terrible communication with its player base, it is never known what they are planning to come up with and we don't know what issues are being worked on or what issues they are aware or not aware of.
All gameplay related content is either free or purchasable with in-game currency which can be earned by playing but you don't get enough money from game modes so you have to spend real money if you want to get all the characters. And I haven't even mentioned the stages, the costumes, etc...
The game was promised to come for SteamOS. There have been no news since the original announcement in February 2016, not even a "it's cancelled, sorry guys".
Overall Street Fighter V is a great game but its flaws leave me dissatisfied, especially if I think about what the game was like on release nearly a year ago. And it's still not good enough...
*Don't tell me it's not AAA, it costs 60 EUR.

A classic game that I used to play for hours on my childhood.
Nevertheless I will try to be as objective as possible.
Pro`s:
- New Factions
- New Missions and campaigns
- Huge variety of countries, tribes, units and building types.
- Realistic economy (food is consumed constantly, coal and iron are needed for firing guns, gold is necessary for paying mercenaries, wood and stone for building and repairing
wood and stone for buildings. Subsequently that means that:
1. No food: Your soldiers and ppl will starve to death
2. No coal and iron: European ships and units that use pistols and muskets can not fire!!!!
3. No gold: certain unit types (mostly mercenaries) will rebell attack any faction
4. No wood and stone: obviously you can`t build.
Cutting of the enemies supply of these materials can be a vital key to success.
- several historical campaigns
- 7 player skirmish or multiplayer matches (It is possible to get a population between 2000-3000 persons per faction: 14.000 units in one match!!!1)
- Naval and land combat.
- extensive training and tech trees per faction.
- Buildings cannot be destroyed by simply hammering on it with a sword like in some other real time strategie games
They must be destroyed with cannons or fire-arrows
- Innovative city combat: it is possible to put units in any building. they will shoot (bullets or arrows) out of these buildings. Sending units into enemy buildings will get them fighting inside to take over the building.
- damaged/burning buildings will slowly lose HP.
- Moral system: Units are susceptible to fear. Especially if they get attacked from the rear or the flanlk. They will start running back to the base.
- Formations increase moral, power etc.
- there are independent indian tribes which can be persuaded to join your side and deliver scouts and troops or trade with you.
Con's:
-City warfare: Innovative but does not work as good as it should. AI and other players use the del button to explode the buildings they are about to lose. Meaning that your soldiers inside die!!! Furthermore for every building you take the Ai builds another on the other side of the city. This can create an terrible drag and prolongs the fight unnecessary. On top of that in order to take over buildings the formations get dissolved automatically, causing the soldiers to flee quicker.
- As the point above (City Warfare) is the final stage of every match, which can become very annoying, it dimishes the overall game experience.
- Population cap: It's cool to be able to have so many units. However the result is that it is nearly impossible to have a good overview of what is going on. Fleeing and fighting units run between each other turning the battlefield into chaos.
A further problem is that it makes it possible to run over the enemy using numbers alone (except in the city), strategy is hardly needed or, considering the numbers, impossible to execute.
Conclusion:
American Conquest is a game that is worth experiencing for Strategy gamers that like the more traditional RTS games like AoE and EmEa. Despite the Con's it is an innovative, fun game.

Well, I bought this game about a year ago or so, and I thought that by now this game would be up to the level they promised it would be a year ago. The game only came out with 12 characters and barely any modes. Turns out all they did was make the rest of the stuff that SHOULD'VE been in the game at release behind a paywall. So, if you want more than 12 characters and like six stages in your fighting game that you paid $60 for in 2017, then you'll have to go somewhere else. Sure, you CAN unlock the characters via in-game currency, but as of now the system is grindy as hell. Pretty much all characters are 100,000 "fight points", the currency which you can earn via fighting online and playing story mode. Story mode gives a good amount of fight points, but not enough for a character, and if I remember correctly you can only earn fight points from it once. Winning an online match gives you 50 fight points, so if you wanted to unlock a SINGLE character via playing online, you'd have to WIN 2,000 matches. There are a few other modes in the game, like character stories, tutorials and survival mode, but the former two are like the main story where you can only earn money once, and survival mode sports a similar grind to online, but without the fun of actually fighting another person. Currently to get all of the fighters, you're looking at an extra $50 on top of the base price of $60. If you're a human being who values money, then I suggest you spend it elsewhere. Tekken 7 and Killer Instinct both seem to be excellent fighters according to their ratings.

As a fan of the comic book, I have to say that I'm biased toward the "original" walking dead premise (even though the story there dragged on and on and on) and that in my eyes the TV show really, really sucks. Why, you might ask? Well, there are two main reasons: stupid, utterly stupid characters I wouldn't want to get caught with in an elevator for more than 30 seconds and massive, utterly massive plot holes with a healthy mix of broken plot devices. To be honest, I managed only to watch the first season (looking back, a magnificent achievement in its own right) through and reasons for that are aplenty.
Why, what could one do in a walking dead apocalypse, on a regular basis? Taking a strawl through a walker infested forest during the night, for one. Or maybe find yourself jammed with a bunch of walkers, usually several hundreds of them taking you by complete and utter surprise. It's not like they stink, are quite noisy and tend to bump into stuff all the time. One moment there's nobody there and the next you're swarmed by slow, loud, stinking, rotting dead people. Great. Further compounds with the fact you like entering new places without checking every nook and cranny before letting your guard down. Nah, better just to assume everything is hunky dory right off the bat.
Why waste so much time on a TV show review in a game reviews section? Because most of the stupid stuff has made it to the game and my forehead got a sprain injury due to the constant warp speed facepalms. Why do the characters in this game like to shout that much and have petty fights during the most inappropriate moments? Because a) they are stupid b) they are badly written c) writers are stupid d) all of the above. Also, what's up with all the interpersonal drama? Dead are getting up from the floor, trying to eat you and you ♥♥♥♥♥ about how someone said something that hurt your feelings. That's one part of the TV show that didn't manage to find its way from the TV show to the game in the full capacity, but it's still very much present.
As far as game plot holes go: to the best of my recollection, none of the characters had anything to eat nor drink for more than two chapters now. That would be the train ride thing and the whole Savannah thing. Granted, not much time has passed, just a few days, but oddly the "we need food to survive" topic (while we do have a whole bunch of bullets, luckily) has been dropped completely as soon as the team left the hotel. Food scarcity was, and rightly so, the main plot device up to that point, as soon as walkers became a bit more than a nuisance. Afterwards that got completely dropped.
Another thing that boggles the mind: lets push through everything and get to that boat. We don't know if there are any boats available, we don't know what to do with one when we get there, we don't know how the hell shall we survive on one even if we do get on it and cast away... lets just get to the freaking boat. We don't have food nor fresh water... lets just get to the boat. We don't have fuel... lets just get to the boat. There are probably too many of us to fit on a boat... lets just get to a boat. Maybe all of this resolves magnificently in the final chapter, I don't know.
As as game mechanics go, there isn't much to tell. Ridiculous "puzzles," fixed camera angles, minimum exploration options, some quick time events and that's about it. The game boasts all of them choices and whatnot, however I'll abstain from forming any opinions on how such a shabbily written game could weave several story strands together to make playthroughs remarkably different. I had some plans to play once again, but I doubt that's going to happen.
I'll now issue some rewards:
Most loud character, should have been dead a lot sooner: Kenny.
Must lame character in any game ever, should have dropped his sorry butt: Ben.
Characters which didn't manage to make me heave, kudos to them: Molly and Clementine.

Realm of the Mad God is a bullet-hell roguelike MMO, with a high diffuculty and large replayibility. The dungeons are challenging, it's easy to get into, and it's free, if you don't mind the current pay2win.
However, the reason for both the writing of this review and my return to the game is this: a few years ago, RotMG was bought from Wildshadow(the original devs) by Kabam, a company who exists pretty much entirely to makecrappy pay2win games. Over this time, the game almost completely stagnated, with very few changes to the game besides pets(with the only efficient way to grind the up being real-money pet food) and the addition high-tier items to the game's real-money shop. I, along with many others, quit around this time, and this caused Kabam to care even less, and so on.
However, a week or so ago, a company called Deca Games finished their buyout of RotMG. They've formed pretty much entirely to buy RotMG, and while we don't know anything about them yet, it's unlikely that they'll be worse than Kabam.
You will likely enjoy this game if you can handle dying fairly often at the beginning. The difficulty curve isn't awful, but it takes a bit to get used to. Additionally, drops can be a bit hard to get, and grinding up can take some time - time in which you can lose your character, having to start over. However, the combat in the game requires attention and care, even with a get-out-of-jail-free button, and I find it a fun challenge. I'd highly recommend it, and I hope you try it out.

Everything about this game is well executed; the gameplay, the visuals, the soundtrack, and to top it off, the narrative. THAT NARRATIVE! From the get-go, the game sucks you right in with its rich and very well narrated story of how the world got to how it is. In a post-apocalyptic world, a young boy sets out in search of any survivors. He then finally reaches the Bastion, which is a sort of flying vessel (more like a flying small island which later in the game you can pimp out with some stores and armories, and a... distillery?! xD). Upon arriving on the Bastion, he meets Rucks; an old man who guides the protagonist, and also plays as the narrator of the story (gg Rucks). Finding various weapons to help you in the search for survivors across the many visually fantastic and memorable places; Bastion is simply a masterpiece. Definitely a must-have if you like action rpg with good pacing, captivating story, and a soundtrack you'll be sure to be glued onto some of the tracks.

This game often recieves a lot of flak and negative attention, and, after playing it, I cannot figure out why.
Aliens vs Predator is not the best stealth game, the best brawler, or the best first person shooter I have played. However, it does a lot of those things adequately, and I had a very enjoyable experience in each of the three campaigns, as well as the cooperative multiplayer.

Nonetheless, the game did so many things RIGHT that it's hard to hate it for its shortcomings.

If you are considering getting this game and have been a fan of the Fallout series then get it. It is seriously a solid game when you look past the typical Bethesda faults.
Pros:
There is a lot of content. As far as I can tell I'm only about halfway through the main questline for one of the factions and whilst conducting various sidequests, settlement builds, and exploratory trips I have currently invested 152 hours whilst still feeling that I have barely scratched the surface of this game.
I'm not one to care much for graphics or visual fidelity but even on low / medium graphics this game looks amazing. The models are detailed, the colours are vibrant, and the textures are decent.
That's another thing, colour! This game has so much colour! No more orange Mojave or green Capital Wasteland.
Less levelled areas. This means that the game no longer panders to the user. If you go somewhere dangerous at a low level you will die and this makes it all the more rewarding to come back later on with some power armour and a modded up minigun.
Weapon mods, armor mods and all the mods. I love crafting in games and so that entire aspect is really enjoyable to me. I love the settlement building. I love the scavenging. I love the process of creating what feels like a weapon truly personal to you.
Infinite levelling. This pleases me.
Modability is neato.
Game mechanics are much more streamlined now. The way radiation directly ties into health is one example of how Bethesda has clearly taken time and effort to reconsider systems that were standard in the previous games and try to make improvements to it.
The environment is really good. That short description doesn't do it justice but hopefully it's simplicity conveys the correct meaning succinctly. The fog, rad storms, underwater, dungeons, city, wilds all feel tangible in this game. They also feel amazing.
Sprinting. Finally, at long last ther is no more need for a sprint mod. We are free!
Legendaries are cool in my opinion. Some people don't like the system but I do. I feel like having a legendary in the end of dungeon chest as well would have been nice as sometimes it's a bit disapointing to see a muffled leather leg and some random 10mm pistol and nothing else after clearing a dungeon full of enemies.
Movement is really nice in this game. The added verticality is amazing and with the adiition of jetpacks things get even more exciting.
Gunplay is smooth and feels rewarding. The sounds and animations of the guns is so much better in this game than in previous iterations. No longer do your shots feel like they are doing nothing against a target.
The crosshair is cool. Seriously I spent a good while just looking at how the crosshair moves around when you switch between weapons.
Some good lore for my lore addiction.
Cons:
Some things such as optimisation are an issue. I got a new computer to specifically play this game and I couldn't get get things to run without FPS drops in certain areas.
Less in-depth systems in many places make me feel kind of sad. The removal of skills in favour of a solely S.P.E.C.I.A.L. based system is kind of a shame. However this does come with the bonus of removing some of the unnecessary skills in previous games.
Some things are clunky. Trying to shop with a vendor requires a fair bit of hassle of going through menus to do so. It wasn't any quicker before but it's still a shame that Bethesda didn't manage to adress this specific issue.
I had to do a fair bit of config fiddling to get the game running optimally. I would have hoped that this wouldn't have had to be an issue but it was. Some things were a bit broken and needed fixing.
Lack of quality of life things that should have been obvious in playtesting. Fortunately there are mods to fix this but it would have been nice to have those features built into the base game.
You can't get achievemnts whilst you have mods installed. This is mildly infuriating as some of the mods are there to fix the issues with the game and so being robbed of your achievements whilst having a normal running game is disappointing. However there is amod which fixes not getting achievements whilst you have mods so thigns turned out all right in the end.
If you made it to the end of this review then well done. If you are still consdiering whether or not you should get this game. Then stop considering. Get it.

Good game but has many flaws/bugs;

2. You'll give your men orders to move across the map, they only move 1/16 of the way and stop, and you have to keep massing them orders and pay attention to them.
3. AI rushes you constantly, even before you have stable defenses (the game doesn't give you enough time to set up like other RTS games do).
If you want a good Cossacks game, stick to the original Cossacks: Back to War, it lets you build true defenses, less buggier and a little less micromanagement.

This RTS really shines in 1v1 competitive multiplayer mode. The replay function makes learning easy as you can watch the top players duel and improve your game accordingly.
Vehicles, bots, air, naval, orbital units, nukes and titans.  There are so many strategies for winning, so many options. You can snipe your opponent's commander with bombers, or you can wipe out their base with tanks/bots and make them surrender. Or you can target their resources, surround and eventually overwhelm them. If there is water on the map, you can surprise your opponent with an early tier 2 naval factory, which can produce ships as well as a powerful hover craft. You can nuke them. You can build titans, which cost a lot but can wipe out your opponent's whole army. You can blow up the planet that they are on and evacuate your commander, or you can make an asteroid collide with that planet. Or you can just expand, build, upgrade and annihilate. Best players expand very aggressively.
Every unit has a counter, as does every strategy. For example, if you go for an early tier 2 factory then you are foregoing on expansion and quantity of tier 1 units, which can be risky if done too early. Having a lot of air units can be decisive, as it gives you good map control, but if your opponent makes tanks and AA units, they may be able to punch a hole through your defenses before you have expanded and built up.  Bots are weaker than tanks and have weak AA, but are faster and give better map control, so you can strike quicker and gather your forces quicker for defense but you need to protect them with your air units.
And most units in the game are useful. There are very few units in the game that are not used in competitive play. Which speaks volumes with regards to the game balance. For example, the tier 1 naval factory produces fabricators, which build and repair your structures. It also makes an AA ship, which has moderate anti-surface capability but is defenseless against submarines. There's a powerful but expensive ship with good anti-surface capability and it can also do okay against submarines, but has no AA capability.  There's a fast and cheap attack boat which has no AA and no means to attack submarines either but it's a good unit to use as skirmishers early on. The submarines are the most cost-efficient unit against other ships but are somewhat weak against torpedo launchers (stationary defenses), especially the ones placed on land and they need protection from enemy bombers. And there are also engineering ships which heal your units as well as lay and detect mines.  A well-placed minefield can be a game-changer in some situations.
What other strategy games allow you to battle it out on a spherical map/planet? This is such an awesome simulation! And you learn a lot from your defeats, adjusting and refinining your strategies as you advance up the ranks. It may take a while for you to figure out the optimal build that balances your energy and metal production with your factory output, but once you start getting it right, it feels very rewarding.
If you're not into competitive 1v1s, then you can play casual multiplayer games in FFAs, 2v2s, 3v3s etc... There is also a single player campaign, which is a little primitive, but can still be a good test of your understanding of the game.
There is a picture in picture (PIP) feature which allows you to keep a constant watch on the important areas of the map. Plus you can also bind hotkeys to those places and cycle through them at the push of a button.
The multiple build order/waypoints feature, along with hotbuild and continuous build mods really minimize your micro efforts and makes your strategy thinking/macro understanding much more important. And you don't need to be a super gamer with a crazy APM because this game is really forgiving when it comes to that. If you get the strategy down right, you can beat players with twice your APM.

This is your average clicker game, a little dry and basic with a few glaring faults. The ones easily seen in the fist day of play are:
- Limited buildings/income sources
You'll hit a very hard, exponentially increasing cost wall that forces frequent 'soft' resets for the next issue.
- Diamond progression bogs and active or background play feels insignificant overall
You need diamonds to increase income, use them for unlocking upgrades, and unlocking content via heroes. Spending them on any upgrade sets you down that amount so getting back to even a lowly 1e5 diamonds feels miserably slow
- Many small features, little payoff
Pets take lots of time, no feeling of immediate gain within the first day or more of play. Similarly, raids, artifacts (doubled by the diamond costs), and the blue gem upgrade system (think golden cookies except they're a special currency) are insurmountably slow. Couple this with 1-3 research per critical (at start, progression is slow regardless) and the growth hitting 1e4 and up withing 1-2 upgrades and you're looking at incredibly slow, time consuming processes that give you inefficient gains for the time it takes to get to them
Overall the game is an average clicker or idler if you don't mind having the game run 24/7 and check on it once a week or so. If you want something a little bit more progression rewarding even if it's more random then try other clicker games on Steam and skip this one.

I'm someone who defends Doom 3 still today. It's not a perfect game, and it's not exactly like the original two, but it's a solid horror shooter with great style, mood and combat. Unfortunately the "BFG Edition" is a step back in most ways, worse than the original game on PC.
First off the lighting changes are for the worse. Everything is brighter, but Doom 3 is meant to be dark. The textures look worse under harsh lighting and the mood of each level is thrown off considerably. Even on a gameplay level this matters, since many ammo clips and armor packs were previously hidden in darkness, but now stand right out. The flashlight, long a thing people have complained about needing to switch to, can now be on permanently, but this ruins a lot of the level design and mood of the game. To be blunt: this game and these levels were not meant to be seen under bright lights, and the gameplay is thrown off by the changes as well as the visuals.
Other changes annoy. Quicksaves now pause the action and pop up a menu prompt, which throws off the pace and takes you out of the game. The in game touch screens seem less fluid for some reason, and the PDA is now designed more for a gamepad than a mouse. On top of this the game takes a lot more HDD space, a lot more GPU power and has less ability for tweaking, which will annoy if you want to play it on an older machine or laptop.
The only reason to get this on PC is for the "lost levels," eight additional levels exclusive to this release. The problem here is that Doom 3 and its original expansion are already so long and packed with content you don't really need any more, and these added levels look identical to the main game and play worse, since they aren't as well designed. Just not worth the effort, let alone the money.
I knew the BFG edition wasn't perfect, but I didn't expect it to be worse than playing the original. That makes it worse than a pointless release, it makes it a damaging release.

Realm of the Mad God is a bullet-hell roguelike MMO, with a high diffuculty and large replayibility. The dungeons are challenging, it's easy to get into, and it's free, if you don't mind the current pay2win.
However, the reason for both the writing of this review and my return to the game is this: a few years ago, RotMG was bought from Wildshadow(the original devs) by Kabam, a company who exists pretty much entirely to makecrappy pay2win games. Over this time, the game almost completely stagnated, with very few changes to the game besides pets(with the only efficient way to grind the up being real-money pet food) and the addition high-tier items to the game's real-money shop. I, along with many others, quit around this time, and this caused Kabam to care even less, and so on.
However, a week or so ago, a company called Deca Games finished their buyout of RotMG. They've formed pretty much entirely to buy RotMG, and while we don't know anything about them yet, it's unlikely that they'll be worse than Kabam.
You will likely enjoy this game if you can handle dying fairly often at the beginning. The difficulty curve isn't awful, but it takes a bit to get used to. Additionally, drops can be a bit hard to get, and grinding up can take some time - time in which you can lose your character, having to start over. However, the combat in the game requires attention and care, even with a get-out-of-jail-free button, and I find it a fun challenge. I'd highly recommend it, and I hope you try it out.

A beautiful arcade game with hand painted graphics supported by an interesting and original story and an even more original storytelling. The world you are evoling in is building itself while you are moving, and nearly every of your step is accompagnied by a deep and grizzly narator voice.

You on the other hand have a big choice of weapons and perks allowing you to always be best prepared for the next world you enter. Weapons are upgradable with "fragments' of the world you collect during your adventures, and you can also gain fragments while completing challenges related to your weapons or to the story.
Expect 20 hours of gaming at least on your first run, and 10 to 15 more if you want to complete the "New Game Plus" mode and/or all Steam achievements.
I highgly recommend it for anyone wanting to play a "different" arcade game.
One last thing: there is no way you could not enjoy the beautifully crafted soundtrack.

Review from a new player:
I'm a total beginner at fighting games but after watching EVO this year I decided it was time to give them a shot. I decided on Street Fighter over other fighting games simply because it was the main event at EVO and seemed the most popular. I was a little skeptical after all the negative reviews but I'm glad I still decided to purchase the game. At the time of this review I've logged around 20 hours, purchased a used fight stick, and plan to continue playing which is more then most $60 games keep my attention for.
Pros-
-Nice demonstrations explaining how the game works and terms new players might not be familiar with.
-Character guides that help describe how you should use each character. Its nice for those not familiar with the Street Fighter franchise.
-Story mode was enjoyable. Sometimes the screenplays were a little long but overall I enjoyed it. It started off super easy and became more difficult towards the end. I still haven’t been able to beat it on hard mode but provides a nice challenge and something to work towards. I also liked how it allowed you to play DLC characters to see how you liked them before purchasing.
-Trials are fun and challenging. They provide more content to do for the person who is a completionist like myself.
-Online replays are easy to find and watch. I enjoy watching the top tier players go at it.
-Training mode is easy to use.
-You earn a lot of fight money right away for completing single player features in the game. It is nice to be able to get a DLC character or two that you liked from the story mode for free.
-Both my fight stick and xbox 360 controller worked with no problems. Reconfiguring buttons was very easy.
Natural-
-Character story fell a little short. I like their attempt to further explain each characters story but each one is only 3-4 matches and way to easy, even for a complete beginner like myself.
-Survival mode is redundant. I still find it fun but I just feel like its missing something.
Bad-
-No VS. CPU mode or arcade mode. You can technically do this in training mode but being a fighting game you just expect this to be in the game. My guess is it'll be patched in eventually.
-After the initial wave of fight money you get from single player, the fight money progression is extremely slow. I understand that Capcom needs to make money somewhere but its almost insulting at how little FM you earn after the initial wave. Personally, I'm at a point in my life where I can spend a little extra money on a character I want, but not everyone can do this (especially for a $60 title).
Thoughts on online play-
-I've only logged about 30 or so matches but I find the match making to be pretty good. I realize I am going to be beat a lot online but I do feel like it matches me with people who I can feel like I at least have a shot against. It is pretty simple, you earn points if you win and lose points if you lose. It tries to pair you with someone that has similar amount of points as you. It would be pretty heart breaking if it just paired me against “pros” all the time so I'm glad the game does not do that. Out of my matches, I have only had 1 match that was so laggy it was unplayable and maybe 1 that had periods of slight lag. One compliant is the amount of time it takes to search for an opponent. Sometimes I feel like I am waiting forever. I do think the fact that it auto uses your favorite character pretty annoying. For someone new like me that doesn’t have a main character, it forces me to log out of battle network to switch my favorite character every time I want to play someone new.
Overall I really enjoy the game and think it is a great fighter for someone looking to get into the genre. I would rate it a 9/10. All it is missing is VS CPU mode and arcade mode and I would think of the game as perfect.

A fun mixture of fps, with a tower defense. This sequel has expanded the story quite a bit in the campaign with comic book style storytelling. They have streamlined and expanded the tower building system along with giving a leveling system which lets you unlock new towers and perks to use in missions which you can choose a number of turrets before each map to bring to support your team with something they need, or to take a couple similar ones so you can help them upgrade without giving them any of your credits. Each enemy has a special ability other than the most basic walker and require different strategies or towers to take them out easily. There are 4 different characters with their own weapon sets that let you choose the style of play from a rocket launcher to a shotgun for starters. The campaign is definitely difficult as I had to restart several maps before because of the difficulty, but that is what makes this game enjoyable with the struggles. Though the number of enemy types you have in this game are limited, a handfull you could could on your hands, some enemies are never easy no matter how often you fight. Overall a great combination of FPS with tower defense that I could see more taking after it.

Similar to the styles of Grand Theft Auto and the Saints Row series, this game is a visual impact of what gang life would be like on the streets if there was an exaggeration on the realism. Allegedly being trained in a kung-fu training school at your home town of Old Prosperity in Hong Kong, you’re equipped with martial arts and the ability to smoothly defeat any enemy you come across with ease. As much as this fighting style is fun and easily playable, it does leave little challenge and it would be better if enemies were faster or even if more bunched on you at the same time – similar to that of the Batman: Arkham series. The whole customization scheme is great for your player, buying clothes and the DLC packs that allow more custom outfits. However, I would love it if Square Enix put emphasis on the customization on the character himself (Wei Shen) and allow you to maybe change his looks a little bit e.g. his hairstyle. In addition, a positive feature would to allow vehicle customization, not to the extent of Saints Row where it almost seems tacky, but maybe the addition of NOS or bulletproof windows etc (seeing as you are an undercover cop). The map is easily explorable but can feel a bit repetitive or leave you with the feeling that more could be added.
I actually love the graphics on this game, even though some improvement could be made. The graphics do seem quite decent in my opinion; although the problem I seem to find with them is that everything seems to be a little too reflective or edgy. Although this seems really picky, these factors are highly noticeable and can become a little bit of a nuisance – especially to those struck with OCD! I think for a sequel the graphics should definitely be improved to the quality of more recent games to make it seem like a more scrutinised game: if that’s even the correct term for it.
As previously mentioned, the combat style is really playable with this game with the only problem being that the techniques – although look rather good  - are really simple to complete; this leaves the game drought of challenge at times. Staying positive however, this game’s combat is definitely more advanced than games such as Grand Theft Auto, Saints Row and the most similar game style is the Batman: Arkham series however that has a little more complexity: with combos at a more developed stage. If the next Sleeping Dogs (or True Crime) took a shining to this then they could make the game a percentage better than it already is. The main fixture they should improve though is the gun system, as much as I love the slow-motion action scheme sometimes, I would like it if you could store guns and/or aim with a bit more ease.
The storyline to this game is actually very, very good. I find that it’s more intellectual than most games these days and has had a lot of thought built into it. The game makes your character experience a series of feelings and emotions and different thoughts such as revenge or anger. Although you’re an undercover cop cooped into the life of a gang called the Sun-on-Yee, you actually become sucked into their life more than your police life; you’d consider yourself as one of them before calling yourself a cop. You rise through the ranks and earn your place through hard work and unthinkable tasks to have your mind played and traumatic experiences – for the character, not us. With side stories and missions you are able to take a break from all the action and lay low as a racer or simply as a civilian hanging out with some girls *cough* the girlfriend experience needs improving *cough*.

The storyline fell flat for me, riddled as it is with cliche on top of action hero cliche and the same trashy style as GTAs but with Chinese flavour this time. I soon felt I was wasting my time once the most cringeworthy romantic scenes started fulfilling my character's bad-boy fantasies.  And the world was bland and non-immersive, not tempting me to explore it at all.
All in all, the gameplay did not have enough depth to grip me in spite of the uninspired narrative. Like I said, low-brow culture is definitely not my thing so if you can stomach something like GTA or Saints Row you might find value in the genuinely fun combat. It's definitely a better game than the aforementioned titles. Or if you really have to kill some time, grab it for a low-low price and expect to see all there is to it in a very few hours. But for me, it's a thumbs-down.

Having a free city to roll around in has been quite the staple in the Need for Speed series. Now it's Burnout's turn. Does causing automobile mayhem in a free roaming genre work well?
The graphics in the game can be pretty impressive if you have the computer setup that's powerful enough to run, say, any Crysis game. You'll start to wonder if it's even possible to walk the streets of Paradise City without freaking out over the passing traffic and catch a glimpse of the rowdy, wreckless cars smashing each other up. Beautiful scratches and traded paints between every crash and takedown marked on each car!
The library of music for the game is a mix of top past rock, metal and remix hits for shredding through the streets, along with some orchestral classics for when you need to wind down and soak in the view of the city. However, if you had to classify them separately, then there's not a lot for the soundtrack. And depending on how many times you wanted to re-launch the game, you'll start to wonder if Guns N' Roses' "Paradise City" is worth having in your head for ages to come.
The controls leave a little to be desired, while some features in variety, such as the way boosts are used in different classes of vehicles (bringing back the classic or using it if desired for stunt-specific purposes), others can get a more Need for Speed feel with the controls. At the very least, you can still get some air and maintain a drift well enough to keep up with the competition. And of course, there's no limits to how rowdy you can get with other opponents.
Because the game now goes free-roam, you'll have to navigate yourself to each point in the city. There are no invisible walls or navigational lines on your radar to aid you to the finish line, apart from your vehicle signaling and the street signs blinking on the screen telling you where to turn next.
When playing online, the system requirements stretch beyond further than what is recommended because of multiple players racing everywhere across the city. So your computer will need a boost in hardware or reduction in graphics settings in that area.
To all the Crash enthusiasts, you'll find no such tradition in this free-roaming pot-stirrer. Instead, all realism and logic gets thrown out the window and you can now throw your vehicle around everywhere, wrecking the poor victims driving across the streets of Paradise City in Showtime Mode.
If you need a more real-time competitive edge by mixing together Need for Speed and Burnout, you've definitely found your game here. But abandoning the roots that the franchise has once made itself famous for can be a big, risky trade-off not only for its stapled name, but also for its player-base.

Fallout 4 was a hit, naturally, but it isn't a particularly good game. At first glance and for a first play through, yes, it seem and feel pretty damn good. However, unless you're a Fallout fan-boy (like me) there barely is any replay value and the added so called DLC’s are not up to par, with the exception of Far Harbor and Nuka World.
There were a lot of things they could have done better, too many things to list, in fact. Still, even with it’s flaws and arguably poor gameplay, Fallout 4 does offer around 20–30h of fun, if not more. Depending on how you play it.
Fallout 4 is not gone and not forgotten and with it’s VR release closing in, having to pay for that too after you’ve already purchased the game once, is just money grabbing madness. But if we disregard how poorly designed the upcoming VR version seem to be with no added functionality from the basic gamplay (and ignore the paid mods madness that's already available) along with what I've said above, Fallout 4 is a game I DO recommend.
Why?
Simply because you can easily squeeze out 100+ hour of gameplay from it if you explore everything and do every quest you can find. Main story wise it's a poor choice of game as the story leaves a lot to be desired, but if you play sidequests or just explore the Wasteland you will find yourself with an immersive world that will bring you back for more.
Having finished the game three times on Playstation 4, yes I know, and having just purchased the game for PC I can honestly say that it plays smooth and it looks great. I don't have the best setup in the world, but I can still run it on UItra at a solid 60FPS. However, avoid the Texture pack add-on you can install if you can run the game on UItra as you do NOT need it. Besides, downloading and installing that will take up an additional 70GB of space on your harddrive and will eat your GPU and RAM like a Super Mutant eats humans in the Fallout universe.
Overall, despite it's ups and downs and somewhat frequent crashes, Fallout 4 is a game that I enjoy very much thanks to everything there is to do in it and everything that there is to explore. If you find yourself revisiting the game, as I do, you will undoubtably find something you have previously overlooked or missed. The world is huge and highly detailed, locations are much more fleshed out compared to Fallout 3 and New Vegas and there's a lot more lore to them.
Lastly, should you pick this game up at full price and possibly get the DLC's or Season Pass?
No. Rather pick up the GOTY edition either on sale here on Steam or on an external website such as♥♥♥♥♥or similar. I got my GOTY edition for €25 on a site similar to♥♥♥♥♥ so you can definitely find it cheaper than here on Steam.

This one was actually pretty hard to decide whether I should recommend or not. The game has both many improvements and many drawbacks from previous titles. For the sake of time and clarity I will be sorting these into pro's and cons. I could also list the stuff that is kind of inbetween, but that would take much more time.
Pros.
1: Enemy AI is much better than in previous games. The enemy actually using cover when in firefights and making regular use of grenades/molotovs to try and flush you out or do more damage. Some enemies have abilities that they did not have in previous games, but that make fighting them more interesting. Like Mole rats and Radscorpions which can now tunnel through the ground and appear somewhere else.
2: Dungeons have greater variety, decoration and attention to detail. An example being if a Subway station is a raider base they will have lots of cages, dead bodies, trash, and chems laying around. A different subway station infested with Ghouls may instead be relatively untouched aside from some dead people the ghouls presumably killed. Two examples you can actually find in game are rather small but nice touches. In a certain tunnel inhabited partially by ghouls and partially by raiders. The raiders have set up a little minefield and a barricade with a turret on top to keep the ghouls away. Another small detail is in  USAF station Olivia where a teddy can be found apparently dressed up by the raiders. Wearing a army helmet and with a cigar.
3: Survival mode is much more challenging and fun then it was in new vegas. It is much, much harder in fights, you can get sick, and you need food, water, and sleep to survive. Also only autosaving on leaving buildings or sleeping makes it possible to potentially lose quite a bit of work. Adding a large risk factor into it and making you play more carefully.
CONS:
1: Settlements. Don't get me wrong they are fun when/if you want to actually play around with them and they can technically be avoided. Notice how I say technically... Do you want to do the minuteman main quest? Welp, you have to build some settlements! Which have an annoying habit of coming under attack at the worst times and needing you to help defend them. Even well defended settlements often fail to defend themselves. Those ten turrets you built only do so much good apparently.
2: The companion friendship system is horrible. disagree with something major in a quest and make Codsworth unhappy? don't worry, you can just upgrade a weapon or piece of armor and he will forget all about it. Want to get someone's unique follower quest? Do you have to visit a certain set of places and talk with them about some personal stuff before they relent and tell you? Nope, all you have to do is pick a bunch of locks and suddenly Piper will tell you her life story!
3: The game and enemies at first seem to have a wide variety of weapons. You quickly realize however that the different weapons are just the same base weapon with minor differences. EG. There are three types of pipe weapon. Lever action, revolver, and normal. The sniper rifles, rifles, pistols, etc, are just variants with a different addon. Such as barrel, stock, and in the sniper rifles case, scope.
4: It is nearly impossible to roleplay as someone other than the character the game gives you. Want to pretend to be some cruel raider? A druggy down on his luck? A farmer pulled into a conflict bigger than he thinks he can handle? Well too bad, as the game will constantly refer to you as coming from a vault and constantly talk about your missing child who was taken by the institute. Both by Npcs terminal entries, and radio. You can't escape it.
5: The dialogue wheel is extremely vague and limited. Often to the point of a single word. Not as the actual reply mind you, just the description. For example: the actual reply given may be anywhere from a couple words to two sentences and may be playfully joking or outright insulting. What does the game describe this option as? Sarcastic. Just that one word, no context of what he will say. Another issue is that you often can't choose to disagree or not take a quest. The Dialogue often equating to "Yes, Sarcastic yes, angry yes, and maybe later."
I want to like the game, and I actually do. I would not have as much time in it as I do if it was not a good game. That's just it though... It's good, not great, not bad, it is okay as far as a game goes. Good level design, pretty intelligent AI, and base building. From the perspective of a game in the fallout series however? It is bad. There is little freedom in actual quests and stories, little to no consequences for your actions, and you will be given a entire set of power armor and a mini gun literally on the first quest chain when you leave the vault. You may say it is limited in use by fuel, but it really isn't. The power cores are easy to find in military bases or just buy from vendors. It is for these reasons I can't recommend the game.

Town of Salem is one of my new favorite games. If you ever played the game Mafia as a child (I did and I was obsessed), then you will definetly enjoy this game as it has the best aspects of that game. TOS is a bit more complex, but after a few games you will get the hang of it! Now onto the pros and cons
Pros:
-Super fun and easy to play and use
-All roles have the potential to make a difference in the game play
-Great for bringing back those childhood memories
-Plenty of people will play the game seriously (You just need to find the time that works best for you, mid-day is typically the worst time during summer and I would assume that during the school year the worst time would be directly following release from school)
-Many interesting roles and a somewhat fair trial system (Just gotta have people who don't random lynch)
-If you made an account and you want to link it with your steam account, it's easy to do that
-The steam version saves your password (if the account is linked to your steam account) so you don't have to type it in every time
