This game is basically a standalone expansion to Revolution.  It's a much better game overall, and the workshop support is very cool, but you can't help but feel like a lot of this should have been in Revolution to begin with.
The problem with the game though, is that even though it's better than both Revolution and Reloaded, it's still a shadow of a game compared to Armageddon.  Sure, it has the same number of weapons and even lets you use the Armageddon HUD for your weapons, but that's really the only areas where it matches that old classic, and even then it replaces fun weapons from that game (such as the bow) with newer weapons that, honestly, just aren't as fun.
The graphics are decent, but you will have stutter and FPS drops even on decent rigs when you play games with a lot of onscreen objects/worms.  They've said for some time now they have been working on the FPS issues, but the fact I have not heard anything in a while combined with the fact that one update actually made my performance *worse*, doesn't exactly fill me with confidence.  Also, the game does not have an FPS cap on background objects, but the foreground objects are all animated at 30FPS.  It's incredibly awkward looking and makes it blatantly obvious the game was made using an engine designed for consoles, not exactly the grand "PC exclusive" we were promised.
Even looking past that, it's just painfully obvious that you cannot have a game like this in 2.5D if you play for even just a decent amount.  You can't always tell just what it is you can actually stand on, not to mention if a chunk of landscape is small enough, you can't even see it at all (I even have proof of this in my screenshots for this game).  We do not gain a single thing going to 3D graphics, we only lose precision and performance.  Team 17, please stop trying to make Worms in 3D graphics.  If you want to do that, make another 3D Worms (and make a decent 3D camera while you're at it), because it's not like 2D graphics is some kind of forbidden thing to have in a video game these days.
Admittedly, all the new weapons and tools do serve their purpose and can be useful at times (to be honest, this is the first time in a Worms game I actually *like* using the mortar), but they range from fun to boring.  And frankly, one weapon isn't even new, the Bovine Blitz was already in Ultimate Mayhem, yet they act as if it is new (maybe to 2D Worms, but they should specify that instead of just saying it's new).  And everyone who cried that the rope is overpowered in Armageddon?  The water jetpack is far, far more unbalanced than the rope ever was (and the rope wasn't OP to begin with...but the aqua pack sure is).  To be fair though, the winged monkey is a very useful tool for stopping darksiders, and it's amusing to block someone between two physics objects and then go blast them out ("Oh, are you stuck?  Here, let me help you...heh heh heh").
As for the teleport gun being the compromise to the rope no longer allowing Armageddon levels of speed?  It's not a compromise at all, it's incredibly easy to use and has no real skill ceiling to it.  It's like whoever was in charge had no idea what it was about the rope that made it so fun to use.  Had it been developed with the mindset that you need to do a lot of practice to master it, it could have been something really cool, but it's a big disappointment if you're an old roper.  Team 17 needs to stop being so pigheaded about the rope and just revert it to the way it was before, because I just don't see how anyone could think the new rope or the teleport gun are more fun, even after having spent hours using both.
But let's say you can ignore all that, and are willing to play anyways.  What's that you say?  You want to play Hysteria?  Not possible because you can't fine tune the turn timer in this.  Bow and Arrow?  Haha, sorry, there is no bow in this.  Shopper?  You'll get bored when you realize the limitations of the rope.  Heck, you can't even really get crazy with something original, because...and this alone is *THE BIGGEST PROBLEM* with the game, and the series since Reloaded in my opinion...Team 17 keeps removing gameplay options with which to customize schemes.  We don't exactly gain anything worthwhile in their place either.  Frankly, the only reason this is better than Reloaded is because Reloaded's physics were just that bad, Reloaded has far more options than Clan Wars, and that game is only a few years old.
I don't recommend any of the newer Worms games at all.  Not because I'm a die hard Armageddon fan (I actually preferred Hedgewars, back when it was more active), but because these games are cash grabs that have obvious signs of Team 17 just flat out being lazy, all while promising they are listening to the community and that this game will be "the best Worms yet".
Heck, they barely acknowledge the old Armageddon fans, and make it pretty obvious they are not listening to their input on these games.  So...they want to build a game with an active community, yet all but shun the oldest fans unless they are willing to lavish praise on their half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥sequels?  And yet they wonder why the series has been losing fans.  They also tend to delete negative topics on their forums (even banning users for telling people how to get refunds on the Revolution board...myself included), and I wouldn't be surprised if this review gets flagged by them.
So why did I buy this?  Because I'm still a fan of Worms.  And it was cheap with a discount and trading card money.  But Team 17's rotten attitude and laziness make it extremely hard to like the new games.  I seriously doubt I'd ever buy any of their future games, Worms or not.  Not until they stop being all talk and actually make a game designed for people who don't just play casually (as casuals are less likely to notice a lack of depth or laziness on the developer's part).
TL;DR version: Another half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Worms game from Team 17.  One I wanted to like but I just can't.  Avoid unless you have to have every single Worms game ever, and even then, get it for at least 75% off, as $25 is nothing short of overpriced for this game, especially considering Armageddon is $15 on steam and will last you far longer.

I've played RTS games quite a bit and probably my most notable acheivement might be Diamond in SC2, which is nothing crazy, but gives you the idea that I have spent some extended time learning and theorycrafting an RTS game. I listed some of the things that I think would make this game way more succesful and some things that this game desperetaly needs in order to not be one month wonder.
First thing's first:
Basic commands that pretty much any RTS has. Right click should (imho) always be a force move command, when attack move should work like right click works right now; Aggressive move which makes untis attack hostile units that are within certain range from them or when there is combat nearby, they run into it. Stop command just for stopping units from doing whatever they do and reset them to their normal idle state, while hold position forces does the same but instead of idling they are forced to stay put.
I'm not sure if it's a known bug or the developers don't care about it as much since I remember reading the future patches would give improvements on combat *'if people felt they are needed'*, but if you spam right click an unit in combat, enemies wont follow it. There are some wonky stuff like that in the game which makes combat forced to be pretty non-micromanagable right now. Unit collision is a must in order to keep some kind of competetiviness in micromanaging combat units.
Also what thing that I feel I can't stress enough is that the game should have
. Just a simple leaderboard, chat channels, automatic matchmaking system would be fine at start, but if it's just a player versus player with no rewards or no long term statistics, it's gonna dry out really quickly. People won't keep playing long term just for the sake of playing, there should be some recognition for good players and players who have played a lot. Maybe some sort of avatars/profile pictures when you hit certain milestones, such as "10 wins, 50 wins, 100 wins" or "10 fame victories, 50 fame victories--" or "10 victories as the Stag Clan" and so on. I feel like I can't stress it enough that just a matchmaking system won't be enough but you need to have statistics or some kind of over simplified rating system in place at least once it launches.
Some sort of rating system, even though it's overly simplified or just win-loss ratio that you can track your multiplayer games helps a lot in keeping players playing the game, but won't keep them interested in the long run. Some sort of rewards or achievements are really important for people. Maybe in-game profile icons for certain amount of victories with certain clan or victory condition and stuff like that. Something to work towards so it's not just playing for the sake of playing.

Very well done gold clicking game.
WARNING: It also last for a veeeeery long time, so don't expect to finish it in a month or 2 or 6! Even if you do spend a lot of cash in it.
Here are the features:
- You start by simply clicking on the big rock to generate gold. The faster you click the more gold. Eventually, you research and develop auto-clicking so you don't have to do it as much anymore or at all (with mana mode).
- There are a bunch of heroes, each different in teh way they generate gold (Rage, mana, energy). And each new hero is much better than the last one generally speaking, but i did use an older hero for getting more Spells points for improving buildings golds generation.
- You have a bunch of buildings that you can spend gold to improve their levels. They generates gold by seconds (GPS) and every other gold generation spells/technique depends on this holy number. So the higher your buildings levels, the better gold generation you get.
- You got the concept of spells points, which are used for research that improves buildings GPS and also mana mode and click gold generation.
- You also have the concept of holy diamonds that you get while generating gold. You need them for 5 other special research: Critical chance, Critical bonus, diamond bonus, Spell points bonus and All buildings gold bonus. The diamonds also improve your gold generation depending on how much you have (The more the better). Another nifty things about diamonds is that you never really lose them. You spend them and they are removed from your 'active' diamonds (which means you generate less gold) but they go into a reserve and when you reset your buildings, you get them back as active!
- You have the option of reseting your buildings level to zero. This is mainly used to get the 'inactive' diamonds back into your active pool. You keep everything but your buildings level, which must be re-leveled. This is not a long process to do even if it took you a lot of time to raise them the first time.
- Lots of heroes. I count 12 at the moment. You can see the next 2-3 heroes that you can get, so at first when you start with only 2 heroes, you don't even know that there are a lot to unlock. Don't know why they did it like this. A fun surprise maybe?
- They introduced pets that you can improve and battle in arena. As you improve you arena rank, you get better GPS. It's very new and at the moment, not well fleshed out. It's also the most boring part of the game for now.
- And there is a lot more to unlock...
As soon as you finish a goal (For example, all the first artifacts), then another goal open for you. Even another city! And war eventually (after a very long time!)
I recommend it.

Just putting my opinion in because i don't feel like this deserves a Mixed review average. It deserves Slightly Positive or whatever the level above Mixed is.
It's overpriced, lacking features, has way too much downtime and not enough social features or esports integration.
The story mode has tons of plot holes and inconsistencies.
But it's one of my favourite games of the year.
The ranking system and matchmaking are fantastically solid, almost always giving me fun matches. The fighting system with V-skills V-triggers, a lack of true combos, tons of ways to get around spam based gameplay, and a mindgame focused core means that I feel like I don't need to know the secret tricks and flowcharts of street fighter to still be competent and still have fun.
The character designs are utterly impecable. The only one I think looks weird is Guile with his too tight shirt. They're either excellent advancements on an existing design (particularly Balrog, and in my opinion, Ken), reflecting both their personality and their fighting style well, or they're stunning new designs that bring a fresh flavour (Raaashiidooo).
The story mode certainly has its problems but most fighting games and capcom games do. For what it is, this story is a hell of a lot of fun with insane anime moments, a bunch of likable characters (except birdie) and a real flair for the dramatic. Rashid's moments in particular are glorious.
If you can buy it cheaper on other websites, I sincerely suggest that you do. I got mine from cdkeys for £25 and it was totally worth it.

I do enjoy this game, and highly recommend it to any fans of the LEGO video-game franchise. There's lots of similarities to some of the newest LEGO games as well as the older ones, such as high-jumping female characters, character selection wheels, and of course, buildable portions of levels
However, there are some major issues I have with the LEGO Movies' video-game partner:
Firstly, the graphics. It seriously seems like LEGO thinks that the graphics for LEGO Worlds is the greatest thing in the whole world. In reality, it makes it look plain awful for a company well-known for making their games look and feel like you're actually in the world that the game is set in. It looks like the older LSW (LEGO Star Wars) games. It looks incredibly childish and doesn't do the LEGO video-game franchise anything.
Second, a pre-determined story that is incredibly predictable when you've seen the movie itself. I get that LEGO wanted to incorporate the movie into the game, but a different storyline would have given it more "oomph", as they say.
Third, I found the levels to be rather long. There's a certain length that the first LEGO Batman: The Video-game had for it's levels, and the last chapter in each of the three campaigns was always the longest and most action-packed parts, Plus about every level had a boss fight, with the exception of a few where the would-be boss had already been captured and taken back to Arkham Asylum during the villains' side of the story.
I'm not saying that it's all-around bad,'but there's a lot to be desired with it. I highly encourage you to play this game yourself and decide whether it's worth it or not.

It's great!  I love it! Whether you're a tower defence nut, or a FPS nut, you should definitely give this game ago. Personally, I cannnot really compare to the first Sanctum game as I bought this first, but I bought it after playing this so it's next on the list.
I'm writing this review at 55 hours in and I'm still playing. I've played the whole thing through (including DLC) with a friend and now we're going through again with all Feats of Strength (your usual upgrades to make the game more challenging) enabled. I think it's safe to say we've both enjoyed the experience.
While I believe this game is mostly about the gameplay, it does manage to fit a story in there. You play as one of four Core Gaurdians sworn to protect - you guessed it - cores from an alien race known as Lumes. The importance of cores as well as the story behind them becomes apparent while playing, seen in comic book-like screens used while a map is loading. Sanctum 2 also features a fair amount of easter eggs including codes the player might enter online to discover for about the universe too.
The game eases you in gently with a nice tutorial and builds up the difficulty and you level up in a well designed system in which you unlock new perks and weapons. The DLC also raises the level cap from 20 to 40 (assuming you have all the DLC) as well as featuring a whole load more weapons and perks. As the game goes on you do come across fair large difficulty spikes; levels that are extremely challenging (especially in the DLC). I have to be honest, we found ourselves looking up a way of doing one or two levels after failing at least 10 times. But you shouldn't have a problem if you're good at that kinda thing.
The art style of Sanctum 2 also takes more of a comic-like approach too, straying from its predecessor who attempted a more realistic art style (from what I've seen) but didn't quite pull it off (from what I've heard). Art style shouldn't be a reason not to buy a game though, if it is to you, stop reading this and go get some common sense. Or go outside if you some realistic graphics so much.
Some inexperienced players may have a problem with that in co-op play, a proportion of health is added to each enemy for each other player, making them harder to kill. While this isn't always an issue, it sometimes become a problem when the health of a enemy becomes unbalanced with the amount of damange that it is possible deal as the ammount of towers you're allowed to build is always capped at 15, no matter how much health they have. While this can make things very, very challenging using Feats of Strength, everything is still perfectly possible when you know what you're doing.
Coffee Stain Studios has quickly become one of my favourite game developers and Sanctum 2 is probably the best game they've created in my opinion. A subtle sense of humour, tens of gameplay hours and a brillaint, worked on concept. I loved playing this game and I still love playing this game. Although it would be nice to include some sort of 'prestige' system to allow veteran players to still have some sense of accomplishment after reaching their level cap, that would be the only really thing I can personall complain about. This is definitely a game you should buy if it falls anywhere near your field of interest. 9/10

I'm giving this game a hesitant recommendation.  The game did a lot of things that made the best of a short campaign, however unless this is a game type you really like or really like the challenge of hard mode there isn't much left that really makes you want to come back.
The story is pretty short and to the point, there isn't any major twists or turns but was overall enjoyable.  The art style/graphics of the game also compliment the story.
There is 4 difficulty modes to choose from, I played the campaign once through on Normal difficulty.  I don't know how the harder two difficulties hold up, but the normal difficulty would be slightly challenging up until you captured enough territories to be in the positive for food production, at that point there was little challenge left and it became more a game of managing the additional spawns while conquering a few new territories while waiting for more spawns.
The battle system is interesting.  When you go into battle it adds up the collective strength of you team and attacks the opposing team, the opposing team will then attack you, even if you KO'd them, they will still get off their attack.  You choose who can take that attack and for the most part you'll always be able to absorb those hits and heal up with ease.  You can also capture crafting facilities on some of the maps that will give you weapons and armour that will help you deal more damage as well as absorb stronger hits.  The only challenging part of battles was dealing with taunt enemies, they can only be dealt one at a time, so if there are multiple small taunts hiding the large enemies, a few of your team could be killed before you get to the real threat.  However if you also craft explosives (Molotov cocktails/grenades) from the same place you get weapons/armour from, those taunts become a lot easier to deal with, since you can use an item before the attacking phase.  As well another strategy is just filling your team with junk expendable recruits you can hire from a tavern, in the easier difficulties there isn't much of a penalty for having them get killed so letting them take a few hits won't hurt to much.
The one real big downfall to this game for me was the maps.  Almost every map seemed to be this giant interconnected web with multiple paths from every piece of land you can capture.  There was hardly any real choke points and I had to constantly move my army back and forth across the map dealing with attacks from all sorts of angles.  This would seem like a challenge at first, but it just felt like busy work.  Your army can move to any point on the map during your turn, there is no restriction on number of spaces they can move so it's not that hard to deal with those attacking armies, you can group all your characters for the attack and then move them back wherever immediately after.  The only worry you would run into is if you didn't have enough food/healing to top up your group before the next spawn.
I think there is a bunch to like here, especially for the price.  However if you are not a fan of the genre I don't think I would recommend it.

Easy mode is too easy, hard mode is too hard.  The game doesn't save level progress either, yet the later levels require bringing the right unit types to start with.  That means if you didn't finish the previous level with the correct purchasable units leveled up, you'll either struggle or won't complete the next level.  Yea, you can restart the current level and pick different units among those you finished with, but you can still only progress with the units you finished with.  Redoing a previous level to finish with different units and gear altogether isn't available.
Combat is really boring too.  Your unit strengths add up, and trample the opposition unless it had a shield unit which means you attack them one at a time until all shields are destroyed.  The enemy counterattacks while you select which of your units take all the damage.  Basically, it's lopsided in your favor... until you realize you can't spread out damage among your units nor assign specific targets to units.  This is especially problematic since you have to keep a family of hero units alive.  Yea, you can tell stronger units to absorb damage to begin with and weaker units to absorb damage in future rounds, but the problem is sometimes, the first round itself deals enough damage to kill your strongest unit.
Strategy feels like a race where you're trying to run around the map faster than the enemy can recapture where you've been.  The enemy is everywhere by default, and you're just drilling through it.  There's no neutral territory to compete over.
Ultimately, this is a game that has a lot of potential, but flops.  It looks great, the interface is smooth, and the unit abilities and conquest locations all make sense.  It's just not assembled well together, and the lack of multiplayer is disappointing since it could easily make for an enjoyable experience.

I liked this. The game mechanics are different/refreshing - it looks like a strategy/RPG game but is very board-game-ish. You get limited units, some of whom mustn't die. When you fight a stack of enemies all of their damage has to go onto one character, so some fights are virtually guaranteed to involve sacrifices. Health and damage-dealing are the same stat and damage is dice-based RNG. So it's more to do with managing damage than either levelling up and upgrading equipment, or army-building. Enemies' spawn rate gradually increases, while your spawn rate is limited by the map resources - an interesting way of creating urgency. There isn't really any AI, the enemy stacks move and attack according to strict rules - which feels like some wasted potential. A possible exploit of this is to take a hex, retreat, then take the hex again from the stack that moves into it after you leave. The computer then treats the hex that stack moved from (which is now empty) as friendly territory, so you can move units that were (probably rightly) holding a position round to the offensive. Artwork, story and music are really polished it is nice when people put effort into these things and don't rely on pixel art and irony. I think they should have ignored the RPG elements for the ordinary units - crafting axes for them individually is a bit much, and there aren't enough portraits for them not to repeat. Minor quibbles though, it's a nice game and one that doesn't outstay its welcome.
Highly recommended to install if you like madness!

This is my first Blitzkrieg game I've ever played, and I just finished my first missions. Upon initial review, I am having a blast with this so far. Visuals all look really great, effects are awesome, I love the size of the maps. The variety of vehicles and infantry are great so far. One of the best things so far I am really enjoying is the ability to dig unlimited trenches, even though it is a small feature, it is the most memorable for me. The globe map is an awesome feature to view missions and tasks.
Cons:
Transport trucks: Maybe I haven't figured it out yet, but It would be awesome to be able to use empty transport trucks to actually transport your troops on the battlefield. So far, there are transport trucks, but you are not able to climb on and put troops inside them, wasted opportunity. Perhaps they can be used to transport troops onto the battlefield when calling reserves as a feature as well or even call them as a vehicle?
- It would be really useful to be able to transport troops in any vehicle as well if there are enough spots available for them to be transported in. (I.E Half track can maybe take 1-2 troops as transports if there is an extra space available for them and be able to also defend and shoot from cover)
Spotting range: The spotting range for medium tanks could use an upgrade, the spotting range for the light tanks are alright.
Health pools: The health pools for tanks can use an upgrade, for instance medium tanks I think take a little bit more damage from grenades, perhaps be able to turn a little quicker. (If being able to upgrade tanks in such a way as a perk that is currently available, disregard my comment)
Trenches: When selecting an area to trench, if you don't choose quickly, it deselects itself. Having it so it doesn't deselects itself after a few seconds of inactivity would be better. Even if you change the inactivity to a few minutes rather than seconds wold be preferable. Sometimes when selecting and trying to connect trenches together, you are not able to because whatever reason.
-When entrenching tanks, could we be able to combine them into the trenching system as well?
Unused fixed weapons: Sometimes you come across unused fixed heavy machine guns, flak cannons or anti tank cannons. Could we actually have the ability to take them with us please?
Description and reward panel prior to missions: There is "first victory" and then "mysterious" victory reward for missions, could there be an explanation as to what that secondary mystery reward is or how to unlock it? thanks.

After reading several reviews towards the HD remastering of this Horror Masterpiece, I must say that DOOM 3: BFG Edition is not getting the reception it deserves in my opinion.  And, here's why.
DOOM 3 was one of the best Horror FPS/Action games ever made due to the immersive setting, the very scary atmosphere, great story telling, and it's ability to drag a player into their world where Hell tries to rule your world with you standing in their way.
D3:BFG Edition deserves more appreciation, since this Doom game looks far better than it's older version and the sound is upgraded slightly to make it sound heavier, unique, and distinct.  The addition of the other Doom games really fits the bill, especially if you are a huge Doom fan.  If you gave a negative review just because the older Dooms were censored, then there is something wrong with you.  If you play Doom only for the blood and gore, then you need to get yourself checked.  Doom is about being entertained, not just the blood and gore.  Doom is about blasting zombies' heads off with a shotgun while cutting down Pinky Demons with a chainsaw and your fist.  Same with Doom 3.  Even if it's slower paced, the game still feels like Doom.
Doom 3 is still a lot of fun to play today as it was back then.  It's frightening, immersive, and action-packed at some points.  You will feel the fear flow through your veins and you will not sleep at night properly after playing the game alone in the dark with TurtleBeach headphones.  For those Amnesia players out there, give Doom 3 a try.  Doom 3's atmosphere is like Amnesia's darkness.  It's unsettling, un-nerving and frightning and does a good job of keeping you on your toes.  I guess you could say without Doom 3's clever use of its atmosphere and horrific environment, Amnesia wouldn't have used its level of darkness and fear as effective as it did.
Overall, Doom 3 is great, especially the BFG Edition if you want to book a flight back to Mars City.  Grab a copy, have fun, and remember to change your pants every session.  Each playthrough is scarrier than the previous and Doom 3 proves that Dead Space is a big Doom 3 wanna-be.

An idle clicker game that incorporates a bit of strategy with increasingly difficult side quests to further the game.
At the core, Midas Gold Plus is an idle clicker game.  There are times you will have a lot to do and other times where you jsut have to wait and farm before moving on.  The game will get slower as you continue, but will also offer more to do than just the base game.
Throughout the game you will have buildings to level, upgrades to purchase, and a Champion to help you on your way.  As you progress more of the game will open up to you.  Unlike some clickers where you constantly need to tend to newer developments, you can actually finish off these stages and have that feeling of accomplishment in the game.  While the base game is still there, buildings leveled and reset for more power, you have all these new challenges to work for and then work within to give you more bonuses to help further your game including events that are short lived but give rewards that aid in the game.
The game is still being worked on.  Recently they added a new component to the game that gives bonuses, but it also in the same vein of building up slowly to get the higher rewards.
The only real drawback to the game that I have found is that if you play it and don't look up strategies and read the forums or wikia on advice you might not realize what is coming next and you won't know to adequately prepare for it.   Since the game is a bit intuitive to those who place idle clickers you might not realize that you should only upgrade to a point and then hold off or you might spend too many of your boosting raided loots not realizing how many you will need later on for building purchases.  This will not make for a failed game, but will lead you to a point where the game will come to a grinding halt for a long time as you work to get the resources stockpiled again to proceed.
I have a lot of fun with the game and found because it offers these different stages as well as an ever change auto clicking mode for each new Champion the game has yet to bore me.  I've done a few of the longer waits while concentrating on the next challenge and found it fun to finish and be able to continue on with new power.  It's a nice game to have in the background and check on it once an hour or so to see if there's stuff you can do.

Sleeping Dogs
+ Good graphics. The city lights of Hong Kong, shadows and rain effects are truly well done.
+ Awesome Kung Fu melee combat, with a plethora of different moves.
+ Interesting storyline and some of the best missions I've played in this sort of game genre.
+ Open World exploration and cool activities (DLC packs add more).
+ Triad and Cop skill tree where you gain new abilities or Kung Fu moves when you level up. Additional martial arts training for collecting rare jade statues.
+ Really cool shooting and firefights towards the end of the game.
- Bad controls for PC. You can't bind arrow keys for movement at all. I don't use the wasd keys and I know many others don't either. There's so many keys to press in combat it can take quite some time to become fluent at the game. The complexity of the combat, sprinting and cover system is a double-edged sword. While it results in great chase scenes, acrobatics and sweet Kung Fu action, it requires the use of many keys, and often it doesn't quite work as intended. The controls could have been implemented better.
- Mouse sensitivity cannot be adjusted in options..
- No difficulty setting. Why? This is basic game design.
- Minor problem with car handling when driving, although nothing major.
- Camera for reversing in vehicles is terrible and doesn't work conventionally like a game such as GTA IV.
Overall Score: 8/10
Sleeping Dogs is a great game. Even with all the negatives, I absolutely loved the storyline and epic missions towards the end. It could have been 9/10, but the controls pull it down slightly. The fact the developers weren't dedicated or interested enough to port it to PC properly from consoles means the game deserves a lower score than what it could have had.
There is brutal Kung Fu fights, with amazing missions, nice cutscenes and lovely, detailed environments.

I guess it's because I don't keep up so much anymore, but for me this game came out of nowhere (thanks, Garam!) and surprised me very pleasantly. How to describe it? Think... a good portion of something like Settlers, a dash of Age of Empires, and a seasoning of Company of Heroes/Dawn of War, and there you are. Wonderful and effective blend of different RTS design elements wrapped in a highly attractive and tasteful art style. The UI is clean, crisp, modern, the mechanics are intuitive and clean without being remotely shallow or "mobile," and there is not a sour note to be found anywhere.
The controls do take a little getting accustomed to, but they leave little to be desired once you do a little digging. For instance, I was initially frustrated by the inability to assign action groups. But the designer(s) of this game were way ahead of me there! I was drag selecting like a dope, and sending my villagers off to fight alongside my warriors until I stumbled on the tooltip telling me "hey, you can assign warriors to group up with your leaders," and the leaders themselves, and the groups that are assigned to them, are the control groups. Just a wonderful little piece of quality-of-life design from Dawn of War that I've almost never seen anywhere else, and one that made me feel all fuzzy inside.
Yep, this game not only works but delights, and I regret that I don't say that nearly often enough.

Insane grindiness and repetitive content aside, it's extremely hard to recommend this game based on the lag alone.  Even after years it seems nothing has been done to address the fact that having 200-500ms ping is a regular occurence, and it can make playing very frustrating.  Playing EU servers on Trove feels the same as playing Australian servers (From EU) on any other game.
The progression system is kinda unsatisfying, max level is 30 but gear equip requirements stop at level 10 and the only drops that matter are around the 7-10th tiers of rarity where you can use resources to continuously upgrade them until they are end-game tier.  Once you hit level 20 progression slows down massively and it turns into a huge grind to get to level 30.
The world system basically has you connect to a lobby when you start the game, with a bunch of portals that equate to different difficulties which you can only enter when your gear score reaches a certain number.   These worlds are mostly the same aside from a few slightly different themed ones or certain portals starting you in certain biomes or worlds with majority one biome, you run around doing dungeons that litter the land. The dungeons mainly consist of running through a preset building/tunnels (Sometimes with a degree of randomness) and killing a few boss creatures to get loot and a portal out.
After a few hours and a bit of time in each biome you have seen most of the dungeon presets and the only real change higher portals make are that monster health, damage and XP gained, and droprates increase.

When I first played Sanctum, I thought it was a really cool idea. I love tower defense and the thoughts of being able to be part of that instead of just watching was amazing to me. I bought it and it was just exactly that. I liked it.
Then here is Sanctum 2, the sequel. How does it fare?
I enjoy the fact that the AI for monsters are a bit more responsive (as in they attack you) rather than just running through the maze. It gives you the feeling that you are actually a person who is in the game rather than a random entity shooting at monsters who don't even realize you're there.
There are new guns, new weapons. A leveling up system and perks. I find that as you level to the max, the game becomes a bit easier because you have some pretty amazing towers. But I find that countered by the "strengths" where you can make the enemy a lot stronger.
The problem I have with this game is that they focused more on the shooter aspect rather than tower defense. Sure, you can still build mazes but the reason why I liked the first was that you basically have unlimited tower blocks until you ran out of resources. Splitting up blocks and resources and giving me limited blocks each turn kind of turns me off a bit. I mean, it's not exactly tower defense if the game gives you only three blocks on the first match. The whole point of TD is so that I can build mazes.
And then a limit of towers? Seriously? What I enjoyed about Sanctum was that I did not participate in the match if I wanted to. I could've just allowed the towers to do all the work for me. Note that when I say this, I mean when I play in singpleplayer. You can't really do this with other people. In this game, it forces me to be a part of it.
This leads up to the next thing that bothers me. Bosses. They destroy your mazes. So... what's the point of building mazes if they're just going to wreck it?
All in all, I thought this was a good game. It does attract me a lot more than Sanctum did (as it got boring over time), but I felt that they lost a bit of the TD aspect.

Really good game. I picked this up in Summer 2013 and was pleasantly surprised. First combination of FPS/Tower Defense that I've ever seen, and Sanctum pulls it off very well.
Pros:
- EXCEPTIONALLY WELL-BALANCED! Here's what I mean:
- - Towers are well-balanced with each other. None are OP or wimpy, and each fills a specific, essenital role. The variety is great, but not too many as to be cumbersome.
- - Towers are well-balanced with player weapons. Both are about equally essential to completing any given mission.
- - There is enough customization to give you control over your strategy and tactics, but not so much that it's hard to decide what to do. There is the possibility of failure in choosing the right towers/perks/weapons, but it's not overbearing.
- - The variety in enemies is great. Each enemy has tactics they are weak to and tactics they are strong against. Few enemies are impossibly overpowered or completely worthless.
- - No mission is too easy or too hard. No specific strategy works for every map, but each map works better with some than with others.
- Graphics are GORGEOUS! Artwork and design are really exceptional, and really well-implemented.
- The game is very well-polished. I've never experienced a single bug or glitch of any kind, which is pretty impressive, given the kind of game this is.
- 4-player co-op is well-done. You can strategize with your teammates, and each pick different towers to fill the different roles. Sharing resources is easy, and everyone has some semblance of what to do. Voice chat support!
- It has that "x-factor" that makes it fun as hell.
Cons:
- The story is basically non-existent. It takes place in two or three comic panels before each mission.
- There's voice acting for each character. That would be fine for most games, but in this one, it's completely useless, and the dozen or so lines get old, real fast.
- Some people have no idea how to play TD games. They ♥♥♥♥ up your strategy and lose the match for you.
- There aren't many people online. Often I'll host an online game and finish without anyone ever joining.
-Sound design could use some work. The music's not great.
Overall, 8/10 would DEFINITELY recommend. I know I haven't played much, but I'll update this as I play more.

If you're looking for a casual strategy game with simple, straightforward mechanics, this is your game; if you're looking for deep strategic gameplay, look elsewhere. Overall, the game was a joy to play and a great value at its current price ($5).
PROS:
* Well-balanced strategy game that’s easy to learn
* Gorgeous art style
* Great value
CONS:
* After the first three chapters, all the game mechanics have been presented, so chapters 4-7 vary only by map and can start to feel a little repetitive.
* The UI feels a little fiddly at times. Movement is drag & drop but doesn't always happen cleanly when scrolling across screens, so moving units over long distances can be a nuisance. Units perform one action each turn, but can only equip one "skill" item at a time; so to make proper use of items you'll be equipping and unequipping items depending on the unit’s action each turn.
* Randomness can have an outsize influence on combat. As the game progresses, both you and your enemies deal higher maximum damage, but the minimum damage remains relatively unchanged. With smart tactics, you can generally withstand unlucky rolls, but sometimes the only thing standing between decisive victory and crushing defeat is a die roll.
* Little replay value, since the progression is linear.

Highlands is a well-presented and moderately-challenging strategy/tactics game with RPG elements.
There are 7 chapters + a prologue (tutorial), each played on a risk-like game board of interconnected tiles. The player's units fight for control of these tiles with the aim of each chapter (usually) being to occupy a certain tile. Combat, like in risk, is a game of numbers - total strength of player's units vs that of enemy units and a dice roll for damage dealt. There are abilities to use and items to equip, units gain levels and stats and additional units can be recruited periodically.
Good for a few hours on the lower difficulty levels if you're only after the story, plenty more challenge on the higher difficulties for many more hours of gameplay. Unfortunately, beyond the difficulty settings there is no replayability as the story is linear.

Highlands is a turn based strategy game of resource management.  Each turn you allocate your forces around a node-based map, setting them to various tasks and utilizing various special abilities.  When you're satisfied, you execute, time rolls forward, and you see the results of your actions.  These results are often very predictable, if you're doing things right.  Your enemy isn't chance, its your own planning skills.  If you fail its probably no one's fault but your own.
At standard difficulty I've found it challenging enough that, were I to make an actual, serious mistake, I would probably lose.  But the game is comprehensible enough that I've been able to reason my way through logically.  This isn't XCOM where no matter what you do, sometimes you fail a 99% chance.  This is more like a logic puzzle, where, if you fail, its on the merits.
If I had to criticize, I suppose I would note that there is a bit of a mismatch in art direction.  The characters in game are very happy and cartoonish- plucky lady engineers, gentle and wise academics, can-do soldiers with a positive attitude- but the story and between level artwork is often grim.  I won't spoil any of the story, but it really can be a jolting difference if you're reading along.
That said, I didn't find that it ruined the experience in any way, and at $5 this is really worth it if you've got any sort of interest in strict but fair strategy games.

An RTS that definately deserves a look from any fan of the genre.  Anyone who remembers the game Total Annihilation will be right at home here.  Each battle starts you with your commander unit dropped into a solar system with one objective - be the last commander standing!  How you achieve this is up to you.
You build mines and power generators, solar satelites, and gas-giant harvesters to feed your ambition with mass and energy.  To defend these resources, you rely on a wide array of land, sea, air, and space units, as well as defensive buildings.  A skilled economist might overwhelm his opponent by spamming tier one units from a hundred factories, but "teching up" is usually your best bet.  Eventually you will be building Titans - fortress sized units, which may be an asset or a burden (they are a huge resource-sink and also can get stuck if you don't watch them.)
If you control multiple planets (or if you are just mad/insane,) you can take advantage of the game's most unique feature - destroy the planet!  There are a few ways to do it, and it is definately a satisfying way to win or force a draw.  You can rush the end-game techs fairly quickly and get the ball rolling - most 1v1 games are over in 20 minutes.
Overall I have had a blast with it.  If you like playing the AI, be sure to download the community AI patch, I use "Queller," as its behavior is more inline with the game's mechanics.  Even it's "Bronze" level AI can get out of hand if you let it, and it definately breathed new life into the game for me.  There are many other popular mods as well, and a great community.  The client has integrated replay playback so you can watch others' games and learn new strategies.  It also has twitch integration, though there are usually only one or two streaming.
Honorable mention also goes to its soundtrack, which really took me by surprise.  The tracks played during your battles have a very cinematic feel to them - it sounds like a duel between two cartoon supervillains and sets the mood very nicely.
My only criticism is the campaign at this point.  It has too many battles that feel the same (I had "1 metal planet" skirmishes like three times in a row) and the AI used in the campaign tends to idle around in base.  If these problems were fixed by dev or mod, I'd be playing the campaign again.  Since skirmishes are where its at anyway though, this is a minor concern.

It's been a long wait, but well worth it. Massive props to the devs for all their hard work on making sure most of the kinks have been worked out before final release. Now it's just a matter of seeing what server owners can come up with!

The Doom 3 BFG Edition is the ultimate collection of Doom games. This edition contains Doom 3, the expansion pack Resurrection of Evil, a new expansion called The Lost Mission, Ultimate Doom, Doom 2, and the Doom 2 expansion No Rest For the Living. All of these games have full Steam integration which includes achievements, leaderboards, and multiplayer support (which is dead by now because Doom 3 multiplayer always sucked♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Doom 3 and its expansions are remastered in new HD graphics (I personally don’t see much of a difference).  In fact I’ve noticed that the environments are a lot brighter in Doom 3 which really kills the atmosphere that originally made the game so scary. The textures are noticeably enhanced, but not enough to really warrant paying the retail price.
The Lost Mission is short and uneventful. Essentially just a few more recycled corridors from Doom 3 with nothing new or special. I was expecting a significant expansion like Resurrection of Evil, but it was far from it. I’m happy to be playing the original Doom games though. They run perfect on Windows 7 with great controls and even have achievements. For the first time ever, I’m actually going to finish Doom 1 and 2. It’s fun to play games that defined a genre and the Doom 3 BFG Edition allows just that.
On the whole, it’s a nice edition, but the drawbacks from Doom 3 and the disappointing Lost Mission expansion really let me down. Although they aren’t terrible, they’re still enough to put off fans of the series.

TL:DR: Avoid this game at all costs. For now.
So, I really liked Starbound. I love the CONCEPT of Starbound. The idea that you can look around countless worlds and find new and weird randomly generated stuff is such a great concept to me. The races are appealing too from a character design standpoint, and the worlds (at one point at least) were fun and interesting. It was the makings of a perfect game, at least for me.
So, why am I not recommending it?
In short, the problem is that the developer, Chucklefish, has seriously mismanaged the project. Let me be clear, it's only the developers that are holding this back. The concept and world they've built is strong. They just seem to enjoy pulling anything unique out and making the game bland and generic. I would strongly recommend this game when Chucklefish either goes bankrupt and sells the assets or if a new development team comes in. Let's go through a list of changes.
1. Monsters are no longer all randomly generated. They added "hand-crafted" monsters to most worlds. If the ridiculous hipster name didn't turn you off, the mundane attacks will. They add nothing to the game, but they were heralded as a great feature.
2. Damage on contact. This was in the game when I first started and it was annoying. They removed it in favor of combat using tells from the monsters and dodging attacks. They then added this back in for no reason. This is the biggest reason I have for abandoning the game. The game is not built for damage on contact. You have to move the (barely visible) cursor to one side or the other of your character, otherwise moving backwards makes you crawl like a snail. When the combat was all about dodging, this was great because it meant you could jump out of the way of an attack and use that time to get yourself back under control. Now, that's impossible because, if you jump, you then have to spend all your attention trying to NOT land on the stupid thing. Keep in mind that almost all monsters are faster than you and will run to your position making this a futile endevour. FUN!
3. They're taking the exploration out of the game. What used to be a fun trek to see what you could find on a planet's surface has devolved into exploring a world to see what micro-"dungeons" (loot rooms) have spawned there. Given that there are only a handful of potential microdungeon themes, you're done pretty quickly. As a minor side note, they went over random weapons and turned them from cute rusted weapons that made sense... into a series of pallate swaps. "Oh boy, I found a random axe! Unlike my current random axe, this one has a blue spiky head instead of a red swooshy head."
4. They've taken out interesting summoned bosses and have given us bland, fairly easy boss "quests". Don't get me wrong, the summoned bosses were terrible. Mostly because you could cheese them really easily. But they needed tweaking, not removal.
5. Content removal. There used to be tentacle planets. There used to be a lot of things in this game. But it's just gotten blander and more generic every update. The races are even getting blander. They SHOULD have had racial traits that made each one interesting to play. They don't. In fact, in the next update, you're losing racial themed weapons. So, you're losing anything identifiable about the race outside of the sprite, and even that's covered up by armor most of the time.
Verdict: Get this on sale for >80% off.

Fallout 4 is a sprawling, open-ended game about exploration, combat and lore - and what it does, it does acceptably well.
Recent furore about the "paid mods" Creation Club aside, Bethesda has created a game which provides a great deal of opportunity for players to enjoy themselves and a rich world of lore to immerse themselves in. The easy availability of a great deal of mods for the game through Nexus is also a boon, providing even more for the player to experiment with and experience.
Is the game perfect? Far from it - Bethesda is notorious for their games being glitchy and uneven and Fallout 4 is no different. Fallout 4 does, however, achieve something that many other games fail to achieve - it's /fun/ to play and the player can get a sense of achievement out of completing the many, many, many quests on offer.
7.5/10.

If you are looking for a thrill, not so much.  But it is free, runs well, looks good, has a lot of variables for a clicker/idler and seems to be well loved by active devs.  That is more than enough to make it worth trying, and if you've the patience for it (I refuse to use cheats or auto clickers, so yes, I mean patience) it has enough depth to make it worth keeping.
Would recommend.

I'm not sure how to structure this review, so I'll just list all the things wrong with this game. I preordered the game, and as an avid fan of fighting games, I really wanted to love it.
1. NO XINPUT SUPPORT. I need to use joy2key to play with my controller, by mapping my stick to the keyboard controls. The keyboard controls which I cannot change. This means that I cannot play with my friend, who typically play on keyboard, or have PS4 controllers, which also do not work natively. (Reminder, Skullgirls, a fighting game which you can get on sale for $1, instantly recognized my stick, as well as any other controller we threw at it.)
2. NO PUNISHING RAGE QUITTING. People can and will disconnect from you all the time, to avoid a loss. This is because Capcom has no way to tell who actually disonnected, due to their horrible netcode.
3. DLC IS A SCAM. We were very excited when this game was announced, as Capcom said they would be implementing a store in which you can buy DLC characters with in game currency, instead of forking over $20-$40 for a new edition. However, basically the only way to get enough of this in game currency to buy anything is by completing their extremely broken and boring "survival mode" which takes the place of a proper arcade mode. Fortunately, PC users can cheat to complete survival, something which Capcom is helpless to prevent. Anyway, most of the DLC is only available for purchase with real money, so its almost a moot point.
Maybe check back in a year to see if Capcom has figured their game out, but this is an incredible waste of money, even on sale to be honest.

After months of waiting for Capcom to fix their online connection problems (glitchy roll back, false connection readings, unexplained slowdowns between rounds), we have far less in terms of a functional game than what we paid for. Asking 60$+ for a game as incomplete, non-functional, and just down right ugly as Street Fighter 5 is a scam. There are far more complete fighting games than this one for a much lower cost.
It doesn't matter what the pros say about the game like "Turn a blind eye to the 8 frames of delay," or "Wait on future updates," because they are not the vast majority. It seems to me that them and Capcom would rather push an unpolished pile of rubish and make money off that than try and create a fun, PLAYABLE online experience for the rest of us that can't afford to make it out to big events.

The Good: Amazing creature campaigns, excellent visuals and audio, fun multi player
The Bad: Terrible Marine campaign, boring weapons, stupid story, everything is so short
The Aliens vs. Predator license has struggled for the past decade, and this recent entry tries to revive the brutality and haunting ambiance of it’s predecessor (Aliens vs. Predator 2 from 2001), but falls flat on that main aspect. The original game was a bit slower paced and slowly wrung the fright out of you with jumpy dark corridors, and haunting atmosphere, but this game just falls flat, and I’m talking about the Marine campaign. The weapons don’t really pack a punch, and there are only a handful of weapons, and you only kill Xenomorphs (Aliens) and only once due you encounter a Predator. The original game really made you dread wanting to fight a Predator, and when you finally did you were scared out of your pants by it. This game just throws one at you and that’s it.
While the Marine campaign was the strong point in the last game it’s the worst in this one. However, the Predator and Alien campaigns really shine and make you feel like those creatures. The Predator allows you to stalk humans with thermal vision, turn invisible, using your shoulder blaster and proximity mines, and witness brutal kills that will make you cringe. Watching the Predator rip off a head with it’s spine attached and pet the spine in admiration is gut churning, but it’s awesome and never gets old. Jumping around trees and high cliffs is a great way to stalk prey, and the distraction ability is great for isolating a Marine from a large group. Being a Predator is just so awesome and it’s a shame the campaign is so short.
Playing as an Alien is just as cool with fast movement, and the Xenomorphs deadly fatalities that will also make you cringe. Stabbing someone in the eye with your tail or eating their brain with your tiny mouth is nasty, but satisfying. You can crawl on walls and ceilings with the touch of a button and jumping towards enemies from afar and lashing out is awesome all the time. While these two campaigns pack a serious punch I just wish it were more cinematic instead of just kill, kill, kill. Also the environments all look the same in every campaign and this is a shame.
The story really takes a back seat as well with you trying to stop Weyland from unleashing some powerful artifact or something…it’s never really clear, but the story is seriously lacking despite the decent voice acting. In the Predator campaign you’re just trying to recover the fallen Young Bloods’ technology completely disregarding what’s going on between the humans and Xenomorphs. In the Alien campaign you’re freeing yourself as well as your siblings and the Matriarch.
Despite the huge disappointment of the Marine campaign the game looks amazing with DirectX11 and all the features that go along with it. If you have the powerful rig to run it you will be treated with astounding visuals that really make the game pop and the creatures come to life that was only seen in the movies. The multi player is decent, but won’t last too long, and I just wish the Marine campaign wasn’t so boring! The previous game’s campaign was just so amazing and spooky it really makes the game fall quite a bit. The game is worth a purchase just for the creature campaigns and the visual aesthetics, but in the long run the game could have been so much more.
--Score: 7.5/10

Really good game. I picked this up in Summer 2013 and was pleasantly surprised. First combination of FPS/Tower Defense that I've ever seen, and Sanctum pulls it off very well.
Pros:
- EXCEPTIONALLY WELL-BALANCED! Here's what I mean:
- - Towers are well-balanced with each other. None are OP or wimpy, and each fills a specific, essenital role. The variety is great, but not too many as to be cumbersome.
- - Towers are well-balanced with player weapons. Both are about equally essential to completing any given mission.
- - There is enough customization to give you control over your strategy and tactics, but not so much that it's hard to decide what to do. There is the possibility of failure in choosing the right towers/perks/weapons, but it's not overbearing.
- - The variety in enemies is great. Each enemy has tactics they are weak to and tactics they are strong against. Few enemies are impossibly overpowered or completely worthless.
- - No mission is too easy or too hard. No specific strategy works for every map, but each map works better with some than with others.
- Graphics are GORGEOUS! Artwork and design are really exceptional, and really well-implemented.
- The game is very well-polished. I've never experienced a single bug or glitch of any kind, which is pretty impressive, given the kind of game this is.
- 4-player co-op is well-done. You can strategize with your teammates, and each pick different towers to fill the different roles. Sharing resources is easy, and everyone has some semblance of what to do. Voice chat support!
- It has that "x-factor" that makes it fun as hell.
Cons:
- The story is basically non-existent. It takes place in two or three comic panels before each mission.
- There's voice acting for each character. That would be fine for most games, but in this one, it's completely useless, and the dozen or so lines get old, real fast.
- Some people have no idea how to play TD games. They ♥♥♥♥ up your strategy and lose the match for you.
- There aren't many people online. Often I'll host an online game and finish without anyone ever joining.
-Sound design could use some work. The music's not great.
Overall, 8/10 would DEFINITELY recommend. I know I haven't played much, but I'll update this as I play more.

I don't write many reviews, but this game is unique, and to me was a gem that I found amongst the steam sales.
To put it quite simply, this game is a fast paced RTS, with no unit cap, that utilizes units that exist on land, sea, undersea, air, and in orbit. If those grounds don't prove enough, that's okay, expand to the nearest moon and strip it of it's resources too. Still not enough, take over the next planet, just make sure that your oppenents know you're not in any mood to share with them.
And if your opponent doesn't want to share/is turtling too hard on a moon or planet, being the big baby that you are, you might consider building giant Halley engines on that asteroid from the asteroid belt, or that other useless moon that nobody's touched (Or better yet, your enemy has touched it and you manage to sneak on to the other side of it.) to SMASH INTO YOUR OPPONENT'S PLANETS AND DELETE THEM. Yeah, and if that's too boring and not cool enough, no problem, just find a Metal Planet and take control of the GIANT DEATH STAR LASER BEAM, and destroy planets with pretty lights.
There are no physical "Bases" That you need to destroy in order to win, all you have to do is destroy the enemy commanders. I find this adds a greater sense of simplicity to a win objective as opposed to destroying every single building that exists in order to win. You can be super behind, but if you can find a way to flank out, or deal enough damage to the enemy commander to kill it, you win. Of course, you can just always send a nuke from the other side of the planet or just blow it up, and win. Hopefully you knew if they were there or not.
This game is 40 bucks, and I don't think it's worth 40. There isn't a story. There is a single player mode, and its good to help you get the hang of the game, but that got boring really fast. There also isn't a very big community for this game. Get this game when it's on sale.
Also, I never played this game before the TITANS add on, but what it basically does is adds gigantic super units called Titans to the game, and these range from Giant Tanks, to Giant Orbital beam satelites, to Seismic inducing stomper things. Oh and there's also one that drills a hole into the planet it's on and detonates a nuke in the core.
Here's a scenario
I'm learning to play against the AI, and upgraded to hard difficulty, everythings going well, all the pressure is on, I'm destroying the AI's metal extractors, and his economy is failing, it isn't able to operate at 100% efficiency, because now his units are craving energy, and he doesn't have the metal to build (Resources can only be stockpiled so much, so it is important to produce at the same rate you are getting your resources.). As I get ready for the last push onto his commander which I've seen multiple times towards the center of his main base of operations, and got some damage onto, I get a warning that a nuke is inbound , and sure enough, flying towards the very heart of my base from across the south pole, was a nuke. Just like that, the tide of the battle turned, because my economy was running very innefficiently, and all building was basically at a hault because I didn't have the metal or energy income to support the large scale that I was working at.
Moral of the story, I needed anti-nukes
But that's just a small scale example of how the tide of war and battle can be changed in an instant if you're not on your toes and scouting to see what your enemy is up to, whether it be building a naval base at the south pole, constructing nukes, or getting ready to drive a moon into your home planet.
But for now, I think I'll stick to trying to learn how to control a single planet before driving others into others.

I got this game on sale for about $2 during the winter sale. That being said, I definitely think that it’s worth even its full price of $10. The in game art is fantastic—Disney meets steampunk— with cutscenes that are reminiscent of Endless Legend. The soundtrack is excellent as well, similar to Contre-Jour but it can get repetitive. Which brings me to my first gripe of the game: while the UI is clean and intuitive, the lack of assignable control groups makes micro-managing later on a chore. However, the worst thing about the game isn’t the UI, it’s the writing; I understand what the writer/s were going for, and I think the concept of the story is fine. But the way it’s written is just painful to read; though I attribute this more to being lost in translation than bad writing, seeing as the developers are French speakers.
Overall, the art in the cutscenes is strong enough to carry and convey the story without words, and because of that, I would recommend this game. More than anything I finished Highlands wanting more. At times the game feels a bit barebones—my playthrough was about 6 hours, but when you take into consideration that this is the first game of small studio, it’s completely understandable. If you're a fan of turn-based strategy please give Highlands a try! The creators bring forth an exciting and beautiful world at war on the streets of a hand-drawn flying city.
Like many TBS games, it's easy to grow attached to your squad of characters and devastating when you lose one. Something I found fresh about the mechanic in Highlands though was that you're forced to discard some characters at the end of each level thereby opening up your squad to new area-specific characters in the subsequent level.
The story treatment was rather light, and set in stone. I would have enjoyed not only more story, but also a means by which the story could be impacted by player actions. There are definitely more polished TBS games out there, but the unique choices made by Highlands and its unqiue fantasy setting makes it worth at least one playthrough.

Too often these days, RTS games are a competition of micromanaging units, actions per minute, and following a rigid build order. At this price point, it's a must-buy if you are a fan of slower-paced, strategic RTS games.

TL:DR: Avoid this game at all costs. For now.
So, I really liked Starbound. I love the CONCEPT of Starbound. The idea that you can look around countless worlds and find new and weird randomly generated stuff is such a great concept to me. The races are appealing too from a character design standpoint, and the worlds (at one point at least) were fun and interesting. It was the makings of a perfect game, at least for me.
So, why am I not recommending it?
In short, the problem is that the developer, Chucklefish, has seriously mismanaged the project. Let me be clear, it's only the developers that are holding this back. The concept and world they've built is strong. They just seem to enjoy pulling anything unique out and making the game bland and generic. I would strongly recommend this game when Chucklefish either goes bankrupt and sells the assets or if a new development team comes in. Let's go through a list of changes.
1. Monsters are no longer all randomly generated. They added "hand-crafted" monsters to most worlds. If the ridiculous hipster name didn't turn you off, the mundane attacks will. They add nothing to the game, but they were heralded as a great feature.
2. Damage on contact. This was in the game when I first started and it was annoying. They removed it in favor of combat using tells from the monsters and dodging attacks. They then added this back in for no reason. This is the biggest reason I have for abandoning the game. The game is not built for damage on contact. You have to move the (barely visible) cursor to one side or the other of your character, otherwise moving backwards makes you crawl like a snail. When the combat was all about dodging, this was great because it meant you could jump out of the way of an attack and use that time to get yourself back under control. Now, that's impossible because, if you jump, you then have to spend all your attention trying to NOT land on the stupid thing. Keep in mind that almost all monsters are faster than you and will run to your position making this a futile endevour. FUN!
3. They're taking the exploration out of the game. What used to be a fun trek to see what you could find on a planet's surface has devolved into exploring a world to see what micro-"dungeons" (loot rooms) have spawned there. Given that there are only a handful of potential microdungeon themes, you're done pretty quickly. As a minor side note, they went over random weapons and turned them from cute rusted weapons that made sense... into a series of pallate swaps. "Oh boy, I found a random axe! Unlike my current random axe, this one has a blue spiky head instead of a red swooshy head."
4. They've taken out interesting summoned bosses and have given us bland, fairly easy boss "quests". Don't get me wrong, the summoned bosses were terrible. Mostly because you could cheese them really easily. But they needed tweaking, not removal.
5. Content removal. There used to be tentacle planets. There used to be a lot of things in this game. But it's just gotten blander and more generic every update. The races are even getting blander. They SHOULD have had racial traits that made each one interesting to play. They don't. In fact, in the next update, you're losing racial themed weapons. So, you're losing anything identifiable about the race outside of the sprite, and even that's covered up by armor most of the time.
Verdict: Get this on sale for >80% off.

4.7/5 Absolutely Recommended.
: There are many graphics settings which is good for those without super good computers.
: The sound quality is fine, voice acting is good.

: The game is set in Hong Kong, a unique setting unlike most cliche open-world games.
You are an undercover cop and you get the best of both worlds being a triad member you work your way up the hierarchy of the triad gang and get better skills for both sides.
: Versatile and extremely enjoyable. You can do kung fu moves, smash people's heads in, grab them and throw them off of a building roof, and many more things.
: Pretty average for your open-world action game.
: The game is a bit short. It took me about 25 hours to beat it. It will take you about 20-30 hours to beat the game depending on how many events you do and how often you do the main story missions.
: The events in this game are quite different from any other games. You can fight in a fight club, do races around the city, bet in cockfights, bust drug deals around the city, do various favors for characters around the city to increase your Face level, and more. Not to mention the lockboxes and health shrines placed all around the city. Lockboxes are pretty much chests filled with money and sometimes rare clothing. Health shrines increase your maximum health after you find a certain amount in each city.
: The game is extremely immersive. The developers did a very good job of capturing the essence of Hong Kong, or at least our perception of it with the sounds of lots of yelling, street vendors, night markets, and generally the Cantonese language. The radio plays good songs that you would expect to hear in a car.

What a wonderful game Bastion is, it takes you to a very unique world (visually gorgeous and weird) with all it's ways, be it the amaizing music, the constant narration, the RPG elements or the story, that evolves like you were un-sheatheing it.
It does have some level of challenge, your skills do matter in this game, but you can perfectly develop them by playing the game, and you can adjust the level of difficulty between missions. The gameplay was good, aim with the mouse and move with WASD, and it was pleasing, you had to know how to defeat certain enemies and how to maximize the power of certain weapons. Good variety of weapons and skills.
The visuals are sharp and well defined, which is good, because it isn't a very demanding game and looks better than other games that need a high end GPU... The style, you can see in pictures or videos, is caracteristic and adds spice to the game, in no way crippling the experience. The only complaint I have, si that this games haves bugs when running at more than 60fps, so you should adjust your screen refresh rate if needed, to play this game properly.
The OST, I already commented, is outsanding. High quality sounds, fitting style for the game, and even some sang pieces. Musically speaking, I found it very pleasing, inventive and therefore, not mainstream, which is a common downside you find can in AAA titles. The sounds are very good also, though not remarkable. The voice acting, mainly the narrating character, Ruck, was very cool and gave an atmosphere to every part of the game.
The lasting appeal may not be that much, as the story is not so long and this is not a very open-world title, but you can revisit places to see if you missed something. But heck, I do want to play it again, it was something I would repeat, and the game does offer new stuff when you complete it. Besides, you do have different endings...
All in all, I recommend this game to anyone bored of the same stuff, but willing to play a hardcore title. I'd give it a 8.5/10

To make a long story short: this game is fun. I can only recommend it!
Graphics: I like the style and the animations are smooth. The only down side is, that in a few places the ground seems to be passable, but isn't. It didn't get me killed though, so it's more a cosmetic thing.
Sound: Was there sound in this? No, really, the music is not bad, but it quickly turns to plain background music. The really good music are the singsong and the ending theme.
Gameplay: You have everything you need in an action game: different weapons, special abilities, dodge and guard.
All in all it is a very nice action game, but there are a few minor setbacks:
- The different weapons are nice, but there is this one killer combination that's only needed. And since you cannot switch weapons at will, there is no real tactical element. So later on I sticked to one weapon setup.
- The narrator is definitely a very good idea and has a comfortable voice, but it gets old really fast. Somewhere during my second playthrough (NG+) I sometimes wished I could turn him off.
- Score attack mode: Why start with no weapons and at level 1? This mode isn't about leveling, it's about getting high scores in the levels, so you level up, tune your equipment and return to get higher scores. It would have been better to start with everything you have like in NG+. This way it felt like they tried to artificially make the game longer. That said, I still played it to get the achievement. :)
But the main reason that I recommend this game is that it simply gave me goosebumps on more than one occasion. I won't spoil it, but that choice you can make shortly before the end... I still get them when I think about it.

Is it worth ~$40.00 -- no. But on a decent sale, Planetary Annihilation: Titans represents good value and above average replayability for an RTS.
