When I bought "Highlands" over a year ago, the beautiful art style had me sold on the idea, but I only started playing it this week for the first time. The description made me expect a roguelike style game with the prospect of a gruesome campaign with corpses behind me to save a country. Many corpses...
It wasn't that bad, but on the highest difficulty it was damn well trying, forcing me to consider the meat grind more than once during the build up of an initial base or to survive the resource gauntlet in mission 5. All points considered I am guilty of killing 3 allies on brutal, including the Hero unit Sophia of Bridgetown in the gauntlet of mission 5 to win against the final doomstack. No one died on normal and all achievements were earned in the first run to get familiar with the mechanics.
The game is only hard if you want it to and then it wants to eat you alive. For those wanting to experience the story, you can do so with all 'challenges' on easy - the current normal - or with some problems on challenging - the old normal. The story isn't anything to write home about though. It is an acceptable story for the scenario, but suffers from several instances of bad-writing. You will quickly notice them when they appear and break character or overshadow the actual scenario with illogical considerations. The many minor events during sector captures will also quickly reappear, falling short of telling a self-made war story. Your decisions also only have an immediate effect, none for the long run. This painfully shows a huge lack of diversity. There is no 'two runs, five versions' system in here, it is the same group of events and items in different sectors all over again. The game therefore has little replayability story-wise.
Where the game shines ultimately is foremost the challenge of brutal difficulty, but be prepared, the difficulty isn't joking! It will turn from a light-hearted strategy game to a complex puzzle with RNGesus as your worst enemy and best friend. But no matter what RNGesus does, knowledge of the mechanics and the right priorities of resources at the right time will carry you through brutal if you so dare. This games mechanics are able to counter RNGesus, most of the time.
(Tips: Militia is the one most broken ability in the game. Use it for area control + DMG. Pulling enemies in to secure the surroundigs of a sector to properly defend it is important. Never open too many new frontlines on higher difficulty! Stalling a mission at the end to equip for the next is also important.)
But aside of its beautiful soundtrack and visual style, as well as challenging gameplay if one should chose - with those being well balanced by the available mechanics - this wouldn't be a review without mentioning the bad sides of the game. And aside of the lackluster events and story which are okay for an indie title - but would get punished in a AA or AAA title -, this mostly concerns the performance, UI and controls.
So what did Burrito Studios mess up most of the three? The controls! A mouse has at least three buttons and that goes double even for over ten year old mouses. Yet, the game wants you to click and drag the left mouse button until it is dead. And for older mice like mine, the button is already weary. So colour me intrigued that they didn't allow the player to right click the target tile to move the selected heroes to the chosen field. You have to drag and drop them at all cost. If your mouse isn't weary before, this game wants to kill it. It is the click, hold and drag simulator. This costed me dozens and dozens of minutes each mission, especially in micro-management situations in brutal. Sure I can blame my old mouse, but dragging troops over the entire battlefield instead of right-clicking the target is not my short-coming. It is the game and the developers oversight to incorporate proper controls.
The second major problem of the game is the performance. Highlands isn't a graphic ♥♥♥♥♥ of the modern age and no number cruncher for mass scripts like Paradox games. Nonetheless it manages to need medium load times and tremendous times to calculate the previously mentioned drag and drop movements for each character. The time it takes the game to move your troops to the next tile if you move more than three at a time would be more than double the time it took to pick them... if it wasn't for the terrible controls. Most things in the game are quick and optimized, but the one thing you will do on higher difficulties often - moving your own doomstacks to counter the enemies - takes ages. The Q&A process clearly failed here. Be prepared to get unnerved by it if you accept the challenge of brutal.
The last major concern is the UI. As beautiful as the graphics are, even on the highest resolution, an army stack will quickly overcrowd your lower UI and can even go as far as to hide the end turn button. Leaving the selected characters out of the UI would have been the easiest solution to this problem. A player should always know who is selected. Afterall we have to drag and drop them by bad controls so we see them all the time. The round will also not end on a mistake, you can always take actions back. There was no need for it. Another mistake of the graphics department are the story pictures between missions. Just one word: Contrast. They fail to make the text readable against the background. They could have chosen the upper or lower black area to write or use a picture appropiate color. They did neither. So expect to do some close-up reading to decipher them. Further some of the speech text in the game dialogue scenes are shifted to the lower right border of the character and are misaligned. I am also pretty sure there were two or three sentences at the game start which lacked one or two words at the end altogether due to bad cut offs.
To be honest, the last part sounds more drastic than it is. The clunky UI, shifted text and bad contrast are disappointing, even for an indie game. The performance shows the code for troop movement could use some optimization and the controls just need a proper right mousebutton support. All of it could be easily fixed, but it will most likely never see a fix in this final release. Nonetheless the game itself is definetly worth the 10 bucks it demands and any sale is a just cause to buy and support Burrito Studios.
I can fully support this game in the name of all puzzle fans and armchair generals for a brutal battle of attrition with a relentless enemy on the highest difficulty. Or propose it for those loving a good music theme with some art to enjoy during a casual ride on normal difficulty (previously easy).
Six out of ten indie points for Burrito Studios for this kickstarter result. It would have been at least a seven without its problems and proper controls and for a better story and more event diversity maybe an eight. But as it stands it still is one of the good indie project examples in the sea of mishaps currently flooding the market... one I enjoyed.

While it's not a game for everyone, if you enjoyed tower defence but got bored with the monotony, get this game and hail the triumphant return of Tower Defence.
It was several years ago, and I'd had enough of the tower defence genre. With countless flash and mobile games that felt almost like carbon copies of each other, it had pretty much stagnated in my eyes. It looked as if the games I had once loved was dead.
And then I discovered Sanctum.
Sure, the internet connection I had at the time made it impossible for me to play co-op online, but with what little FPS skill I could muster I made due, and I absolutely loved it.
Flash-forward to late October 2013, when I found Sanctum 2 on sale. I immediately snapped it up and started playing, and I was far from dissapointed. Coffee Stain had used the 2 years between Sanctum and this game to truly make it worthy of being "the sequel to the world’s first Tower Defense/FPS hybrid game."
For those of you that played the original, the biggest difference by far is the new resource system, which now has seperate units for constructing the tower bases that outline the maze and the towers that shoot the creeps ("Lumes"). New characters open up brand new strategies for demolishing the relentless horde. Gone now are the teleporter towers, now made pretty much unnesesary by smaller, more focused maps. Recycling towers also gives you all the credits put into them now, with the option to revert to only getting half your resources back avaliable in the "Hardcore Mode" Feat of Strength, which also includes no respawn. There are other fairly large differences (was there a 15 tower limit in the original?), but I found that they, like the ones mentioned above, actually added to the fun of the game so much I didn't actually care.
For those of you who haven't played the original, this game is possibly the most rewarding co-op game I have ever played, effortlessly combining high-brow Tower Defence strategy with fast-paced, cooperative First Person Shooter action. So for those of you who, like me, became tired of simply observing your towers attempt to beat back the horde, come join us. LOEK III can always use a few more Guardians.

id is my favorite video game company in existance. I consider Doom to be one of the most influencial video games of all time. I was really excited to get this when it came out. I launched the game and was greated by two unskipable cutscenes that must be watched every time the game is started. I thought to myself "Hey, I could skip cutscenes in the original Doom 3; why can't I skip them now?" Let's think of this as a forshadowing for the rest of the game. Right off the bat though, I noticed it does have Steam Play achievements. Those weren't in the original game. That's an improvement,  right? It is also in full HD now, so I can properly run it in widescreen. That's awesome, except for the fact that Doom 3 already looked pretty good.
Doom 3 did and does not need an HD remake. Nothing was really added to improve this game at all. The only real improvements are that it is properly fit for higher resolutions and has Steamplay. This game would have been really good if it came with an official cooperative mode and a playable multiplayer system. Unfortunately, the game feels like it is running on a Playstation 3 emulator. There are next to no graphics options, a console that can only be enabled by cheating, a matchmaking system instead of a server browser, no dedicated servers, and a user interface that wasn't designed for a mouse, amongst other things. Coming from id, the company that defined what pc gaming is today and how games on the pc should be made (if you need an example, play Quake), this is pathetic. You know which games need HD remakes? The classic Dooms.
None of the games feel optimized at all. It feels like all of the games were just taken from their original releases, thrown into one packaging, and shipped off. They changed how the flashlight works in Doom 3 but didn't make changes to the level design to compensate. It's understandable why they wouldn't add features such as jumping and mouse look to the classic Dooms, but they didn't optimize them for new systems at all. They still run in 320x200 in 4:3 and don't even allow for things like autorun, which was available in Vanilla Doom by editing the config. After Doom's release, id has put autorun in their other games so they've clearly learned that it is more convienent. Why did they not put it in this one? Because that would have taken effort.
There is no way to play multiplayer on the classic Dooms at all, but if the multiplayer is anything like Doom 3's multiplayer support, you probably wouldn't want to. Even in a LAN connection, it isn't playable. I've posted a video demonstrating this:
The classic Dooms have absolutely no way to play custom WAD files, which was one of the biggest things keeping the originals alive. Not to mention that for a "complete collection", it doesn't include Final Doom. Also, if we're considering it an "HD Collection", I guess that's fair because the only thing they did was allow it to run in higher resolutions. The problem is they only did this to Doom 3. Doom 3 came out in 2004 and looked outstanding for its time. It's ten years later and it still looks pretty good in my opinion. It's been 21 years since the original Doom released and it still has no HD collection. It would have been nice to see that one instead, with official multiplayer support on Steam so I could easily connect with my friends and not have to worry about which source port to use.
In a nutshell, just stay away from this. It's not worth it, and just tarnishes id's name. The only people who are going to buy this are hardcore Doom fans and the few people who have never played Doom before. Hardcore Doom fans probably already own all of these games, and people who have never played are going to get a terrible impression. For a more 'in depth' review, check out this video of mine:

Game at its core isn't really that bad. Skirmishes can be fun, while I do enjoy base building and creating defenses lack of those options don't really take away much from the game. Fast paced combat does reflect the idea of Blitzkrieg but all the other things take away a lot from the experience.
Aside from the authentication problems, game is always online. Even if you don't want to play online, you have to be connectced to Internet in order to play. Global war theatre while a good way to select missions and keep up on the events, combined with player bases, it reminds me of those grindy tablet games way too much. You build a base, spread your troops around to defend it and then enemy comes knocking trying to take it down. Essentially, it boils down to graphically glorified tablet game for the online part and because of this, you can't play it offline. Not to mention if  you lose your troops, you have to grind for them again from repeatable battles. Battle wins sometimes do not register and you are sent back to main menu like nothing has happened in the last 30 minutes of your life. This game is showing great promise in its early Alpha stages. I've never written a review before but here goes:
I've been an avid strategy gamer all my life, it is my favourite genre, but it is hard to get right. A good strategy game has to allow the player to, well, strategise. Some are just inevitable grinds where it is about who can do the same thing the best. This game allows a lot of scope for multiple paths to victory, which is crucial, as well as severely punishing or rewarding the player for incorrect or correct tactical decisions. Multiplayer in this game will be exceptional.
Pros:
- Decisions have major consequences, for better or worse. For me this is the great thing about this game. If you decide on an early raid of another player, or region, you may lose all your soldiers and be doomed, or you might secure vital resources and territory that will go on to win you the game. Resource managemant decisions can also either win or lose you the game, at every decision. The Winter and Blizzard handicaps, as well as the random events really punish you for incorrect tactical decisions.
- Many different victory conditions. If you are to win you need to conceptualise a effective strategy to achieve that condition.
- The mechanics of the game are very simple, but it takes skill to master them. I think multiplayer will highlight this.
- Art style. I think the art style really captures the mythic Norse feel of the game.
Suggestions:
At this stage in its Alpha development it would be unfair to address these as cons. I'm sure most of these will likely be added, or have been considered.
- Add the ability to modify victory conditions.
- Add more clan specific buildings.
- Add more variety of military units.
- AI needs to improve. It is a steep learning curve, but the bar isn't very high. I lost my first game, but i've played 6 after that and won them all on hard, using different clans.
- Victories need to feel more climactic. Add a cut scene for each victory, or spawn demons from hellheim that try and prevent you from achieving the map specific victories like Odin's sword etc.
- More lore! Norse mythology is in my view one of the most interesting and what really draws me into the game. Play even more on the Norse roots of the game.
Overall this game is in a fine state for Alpha, and I deeply hope the devs aim to make this into the great game it has the potential to be.

A friend got me this game saying it was rather decent. The sale was on and well i decided to say yes, from what i had seen, the game didn't look to bad, looked fun but also looked a little boring, which left me a little unwanting to play it. The steam sale was on when my friend got it me, so i had all of the DLC along with the game, which being honest, is a lot, from two extra DLC missions which add on, to ones which add to your triad and police level, to cars and clothes. There's plenty given from this to help gain your interest within the game.
So, from that being said, lets start from the beginning. From my own slight worries and fears for the game, the opening looked promising, controls are standard and decent but felt a little clunky at first, i played more and got past the opening. The story showed it's inital idea and the concept was rather interesting but was... slow to really push this idea until much later on in the game.
Once the story had been laid out and i had done the starting missions i found myself sitting there for 15 minuets as it showed me all of the DLC, what it had given me, and all the bonuses.. Which is great and all.. But it meant that my Triad and police levels shot to level 8, same with face meter, meaning by a quater way in i was max leveled on triad and police. It meant i could do more fun earlier on, but made the game a little "to" easy as it clearly laid out missions with mind off you gradually gaining upgrades, but, it was still fun to be kicking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of enemies from the start and feeling like a Kung Fu master.
After a few hours into the game the story had been slow. Wasn't gaining my interest and the side missions were fun up to a certain amount of time, even with all the extra content given out to me. So, i ended up leaving this on the side, in my libary for a time.
I eventually came back after a few weeks and decided to have another go, i had an issue with the game crashing, easily fixed by validating the files but still was a pain. I opened my save and didn't remember anything, nothing suck in or stuck with me for the weeks, but, determined from reviews and some walkthroughs i started another new game and worked my way up to the place i was. But this time, i found myself more involved into the story when i started to understand the situation the player is in, what you're doing, and why the story is so evidently slow from the go.
I managed to start to work my way through and found myself becoming more and more engrossed into the storyline, but not just that, i found myself starting to have conflict between being a traid and being an undercover police officer, something, that isn't easy to do, question a player: Are you a traid? Or are you still an officer? Especially when you can just run down people without stress, kill police officers, break speeding limits and more. Depending on this it kinda made me think well where do i go. I moved into the police cases aspect to the game then.
The cases are a welcome additon, technically, a side mission spanning through the game the police cases are truly interesting and allow for you to keep to your roots as an officer while being drawn more and more into the crazy, murdering world of the traids. The missions slowly unlock as you play through the main missions, all cases being diverse into what you look into and some even being rather shocking from the final result. But in the end, you still feel like you've made an achievement into solving them and trying to stick to being a cop. Especially when you go from missions stealing/Killing and all this, to doing something for the better.
From being more into the game now i took a look at the aspects of gameplay. Fighting was solid, guns felt powerful and fun to use and even driving on a keyboard and mouse was very enjoyable and responsive. Fighting is similar to that of Batman: Arkham series where you hit people with combos and then counter attacks as they start to come in landing on you. Despite feeling like a kung-fu god, going more and more in lead me to being killed and defeated easily by larger eneimes and more in groups. So i explored, found health shrines to take more hits, and went and found the statues to learn more moves as well, it made it interesting but, the statues are all generally in the way in missions, making searching for them kinda irrelivent, it's almost like they put them in the way in missions so you pick them up anyway and learn the moves, not like you have to go looking to truly gain an upper hand, just a way of slowly keeping your fighting up to par with the rest. Despite that, it was still very, very fun and the fighting never really got repetative when you're breaking someones leg and then flying kicking someone else in the head.
So i had gotten later in. SPOILER
And i found myself being more and more drawn in, especially to the traid side, beggining more to forget about my police side and loose myself in order to gain more into the traids. It was around here i found that sleeping dogs wasn't afraid to deal with much more horrid situations. The game had been very tame, not a lot of blood, some decent fighting but nothing counting as shocking.
Until...
Boy, did the game soon show me is was taking it more seriously, and was not afraid to show much more graphical violence, showing me the world of which i was trying to get into. It showed the horror of what can happen inside of this world and the danger i was in.
It showed me it was prepared to shock me and show me more of the horrors of the world, making it show, sleeping dogs was able to remain serious and deal with these situations in a decent way.
Past that the game toned down a little but the story, REALLY, picked up for me. It moved up more and more, making it even more interesting and getting me even more into it, so much so, i found myself playing it late at night as the battle between being with the triads and being a police officer forever was nagging there, and was clearly showing for Wei as well.
Much later in and near the end a lot happened, a lot had to be taken in, the game had built up this tension that just.... fell short. The ending felt like all this tension and hard work into getting me to think of either being a triad or police just wasn't brought to a full conclusion. For those who have finished.
. For those who haven't, the ending only makes you feel like you've done it for one side or the other... and nothing else than that, which was a damn shame to all that hard work going into it. Regardless, it was still fun and enjoyable.
Before the ending there is also another bloody scene, which i warn, those who cannot stand blood or worse, look away when it happens, and trust me, you know when it will.
Overall sleeping dogs truly got me into it, got me to battle how i felt with being an undercover cop and got me to see the grousome side of everything which happened and could happen in such a game. I look forward to the DLC and would recommend this to anyone. It is slow to get into, but damn fun and interesting once you do get into it. I would say buy with all the DLC as well, as it's more worth it that way, but either way, sleeping dogs is a damn good game and i would rate it 9/10 from everything i've played. Just make sure that during some scenes you're prepared, as much as the game seems a little goofy, it handles some truly horrifying moments seriously and well.

As veteran player from the first game the first jolt is the horrendous character designs that make you think some coder thought it would be funny to leave Big Head mode on by default.
The user interface can be used after enough reading of the tool tips and playing the tutorial (what passes as one) a few times, but it takes a level of patience that gets hard to justify after the first 15 min of gameplay.
Planes or the lack there of are a particular sore spot with me as I was a massive fan of the HiTech AKA design your own plane feature from the original game. You can change out parts but its sometimes hard to tell if that super expensive new wing design is worth the price tag as you don't see much in the way of radical stat changes. Passenger capacity can be changed but even in the largest plane you'll feel like there should be more seats.
All of this is topped off by the fact that the planes are not surprisingly hyper cartoony with closer relations to the Stay Puff marshmellow man of Ghostbusters fame, the Michelin man, or a Airbus Beluga. You stop caring early on about paint jobs and logos because of this.
Another major gameplay issue is hiring staff feels like a massive chore rather then a quick formality as you have to assign  manually all your staff and if you want a fully staffed plane its at least a 2 day ordeal because only a handful of staff ever apply at one time.
Moving around the airport is at least simular to the old game to a point but you'll be using the hot keys to skip all the walking in short order, as the layout of the airport can be hard to follow because for example the used plane dealer (junkyard in this case) is simply a tiny door in the back of the new plane retailers shop.
The sole good things that I have found in this game are in making routes you can set aside time for maintenance and I found some of the characters at least somewhat entertaining namely the tutorial guy with some of this references and the Airport Manager who is literally the Godfather.
Even with a steep Steam sale 80-90% off this game just isn't worth the time, money, or hard drive space especially when you can get the original game on Steam as well likely for less to boot.

Here is a game much maligned but it's not that bad. It has a faster, more efficient engine and comes with Doom 3 expansions Resurrection of Evil and the Lost Mission, and the first two games in the series. Lost Mission certainly does recycle art from the main campaign, but it's reasonable because the mission takes place in the same locations, concurrently to main campaign. However, all is not acceptable for this BFG edition. For example, mods for the original version of the game are unfortunately incompatible. The developer has released the tools to develop mods for this version, but as of this time, there is no easy way to upgrade the shocking textures of the vanilla game.
As for the older games, there have been slight edits to remove Red Cross trademarked material, but other than that, there are no obvious improvements. In the end, the controversy around this game is a shame, because this is a solid and enjoyable experience that is superior to the original release in many ways. Unfortunately, the game is buggy, such as when it thinks the console has been used when it hasn't; this deactivates achievements and wastes your time. It seems that the best Bethesda can offer is 'reinstall the game', and it's up to us to 'deal' with it. That is a shame.

Do you like Minecraft or Terraria? Do you ever wish you could travel to distant planets fighting aliens with high-tech laser shotguns and exploring abandoned research facilities? Starbound is the game for you.
The game starts off on a bit of a low point- you're stuck on a basic planet and the only way to get off is to dig to the centre of the Earth, which is veeeeeery boring. But stick with it, because once you fix your broken spaceship, you'll be able to visit planets ranging from monster-infested deserts to dense forest worlds teeming with life.
There is also lots of emphasis on raiding- from simple, helpless villages to well-guarded fortresses filled with treasures and weapons. There's also quests so that you don't get bored exploring the huge galaxy.
And then there's the outpost, a hub world that you can beam to from your ship. The Outpost is filled with NPCs who chat, trade and give you missions. Visiting the outpost and completing the missions there was great for me.
Pros:
-Open-world exploration
-Quests
-The Outpost
-Raiding
-Character customisation
Cons
-Being stuck on the first planet

I just spent damn near an hour writing a lengthy review about why I do not recommend this game, and Steam opted to not save it when I clicked "post review." So, unfortunately you will be reading an incredibly shortened version. Sorry.
Positives -
+Characters look good
+Audio is nice
+Gameplay is solid; combat system works well, no issues with controls
+Endless Battle mode is always a welcomed addition to the multiplayer
+The IDEA that Capcom wanted to emulate MK's successful story mode is great. The actual result... well, see below in the Negatives section.
Negatives -
-Clipping is prominent. Ken's hair clips through his neck/shoulder line; Birdie's necklace clips through body, etc.,.
-Limited single player options
-Story mode underwhelming and full of confusing scene cuts, limited character development and overpromotion of characters who offer little in terms of moving the story forward, or are mishandeled and end up being useless to the story (Charlie, Necalli, etc).
-Overpriced DLC - $3.99 for a single promo costume? GTFO.
-Multiplayer matchmaking is wonky (from my experience). Oftentimes get paired up with a guy 3 ranks higher than me, resulting in limbo where I can never move up because I don't play people in equal skill. Hinders multiplayer.
Overall, it's just a really rushed game by a developer who should know better. Single player was ignored prominantly in the early stages, and a lousy story mode was dumped in to placate. Multiplayer is what it is - a screwy matchmaking system and people rage quitting to avoid losing points. There's some fun to be had in it with endless battle. It's a shame, because the core gameplay is great. I love the battle system, the controls are fluid and fully functioning, but there's not enough here, and what IS here is full of half-hearted work. There's no reason the ugly clipping in the game should exist, especially with a major game developer like Capcom. Shoddy work. In a world with MANY options for fighting games, don't waste your time with this when older installments or other series altogether are better.

Sleeping Dogs’ blurred lines come to the fore as soon as you’re introduced to the game’s unique leveling system, which allots Shen experience points in three specific areas: Cop, Triad and Face. The experience points are, in turn, used to unlock new, unique abilities. Cop and Triad points often intermingle with one another as you complete the game’s primary missions, rewarding you for how careful you are with innocents and personal and private property (Cop) while simultaneously challenging you to brutalize your enemies with as much reckless abandon and gore as you can muster (Triad).
Face, on the other hand, has everything to do with how the citizenry of Hong Kong feel about you, making it not only the most abstract of the experience meters, but perhaps the most interesting as well. Doing all kinds of favors for the anonymous masses net you Face experience, so whether you’re assisting a merchant, chasing down some drunks or otherwise generally helping out the working class folk (and the occasional two-bit criminal) of Hong Kong, expect your Face meter to rise steadily.
A unique, multi-faceted experience system like this makes Sleeping Dogs a more deliberate affair than its contemporaries. On most main story missions, for instance, you will be docked police points for ramming into street lights with your car, accidentally striking a civilian or letting stray bullets seep into a storefront. But this is balanced by your brutality with Triad members. Using the game’s array of exceptionally gory kills is a great way to build that Triad meter to its maximum level as quickly as humanly possible. The experience system’s dynamics will keep you on your toes, and because you can replay missions once they’re completed, you could always go back to try things a little differently if you’re unsatisfied with the outcome as it currently stands.

I wanted to hold off on reviewing Street Fighter V until more content was released, since Capcom themselves admitted that the game was incomplete at launch.  Nonetheless, I immediately bought the game as soon as it came out because I wanted to jump straight into the online multiplayer mode.  Since then, I have been regularly playing it every now and then, and it still hasn't gotten old yet to this day.  Furthermore, there are still plans to release additional content in the future.  Now that the story mode has been released, I feel like I can give the game a fair review at this point.
The biggest attraction of Street Fighter V remains the online multiplayer mode.  The battle system has more depth to it than any previous iteration of Street Fighter, and there are plenty of opportunities to make a comeback against an opponent who is overwhelming you.  Your character's V-gauge will fill up as you take damage, allowing you to perform special techniques that could potentially reverse the direction the match is heading in.  At the same time, your character's special gauge will also be filling up both as you give and receive damage, so it is still rewarding to go on the offensive.  The developers also did a great job at ensuring that the characters in this game are all balanced (well, maybe except for Zangief), and that the play style for each character is a unique challenge to tackle and become accustomed to.  Personally, I was satisfied by this game's multiplayer mode alone, but I understand that this might not be the case for everyone else.
Thankfully, Capcom has added enough single player content to keep many players satisfied by this point.  Sure, they still haven't added Arcade Mode yet, but the amount of single-player content currently available was enough to satiate my needs of fighting against the game's AIs.  This is just my personal taste, but I found that I didn't need Arcade Mode considering everything else the game had to offer.  Survival Mode helped test any foolproof strategies I'd thought up against hordes of AI opponents, and Challenge Mode helped me practice vital combos for the characters I wanted to become familiar with.  The long-anticipated Story Mode was well worth the wait (in my opinion) and definitely has the most fully fleshed-out plot in any Street Fighter game to date.  It also pays homage to many of the earlier Street Fighter games in ways that might surprise some people.
The only real complaint I have about this game is that there still aren't too many characters  on the roster just yet, although I am aware that this will change in future updates.  Plus, the amount of variance between the playstyles of the different characters is enough to keep me entertained for now.  Despite a difficult launch, I still have very high hopes for Street Fighter V, and I believe the amount of depth the game possesses is enough to keep most hardcore players hooked - therefore, I would certainly recommend it to fans of the series.

I have to say, it's been a long time since I played a proper isometric RPG/explorery game.    I've tried to play Baldur's Gate again, but it's just too sprawley and big to fit in the little time slots I have right now.   So it was with some curiosity that I tried this much-lauded game.
First-off, I was impressed by the music.  Right from the start, there's a deep, mellow quality to it which instantly put me into the right mood.  I felt like liquid chocolate had been poured over my head, and I was being invited to relax and listen by Barry White.
The next thing which I really enjoyed was the narrative style.  The music and the narration just slipped, hand-in-hand, sat either side of you, and told you a tale.   Without any prompting, the whole scene was set...  Even some of the curious things which only get answered later are delivered in such a way that you think "Hmm.. I should know that, but it would be rude to ask.. I'll let him just tell his story, and pick it up as I go along".
The story is.. well.. different..  The same lines as usual.. World gone to heck, boy.. girl.. antagonist.. good guys.. bad guys... plot twist.. narrator..  All the usual elements are there.     The usual gameplay elements are there too...  Weapons (Melee, pistols, shotgun, repeater, ranged, over-powered).. No really exotic weapons, although there are a few duplicates in those slots..
The game starts off telling you very little.  A lot is completely unexplained at the end of the story, and it doesn't really matter.   The way the game is presented, and the semi-linear flow helps to guide you along.  The nice little narration points as you travel along also kind of help as well.  It's not "The Stanley Parable", where the fourth-wall is broken, but it's just nice to have a little colour added to the story as you walk along.. People's names, places described in a relaxed sort of way.  Very nice.
I played the game all the way to the end with only two or perhaps three  irritated moments. Usually these were quickly dispelled by a change of weapon/tactic, and starting over.   And when I say starting over, the levels are mostly pleasingly short, so this isn't a major disaster.
The end of the story is nice.  You have the usual choice, although unlike most games, the two aren't "Good" or "Evil".  I'd say that the writers chose a very Star-wars approach where "Good" is mapped to "Altruistic", and "Evil" is mapped to "Selfish"...
If there's one downside, I'd just say that the game DOES require you to grind a few of the levels.   Some of the 'challenges' can be a little tough, and there's no real indication when you've levelled up enough to make it through the level without extreme difficulty.  Usually when you CAN make it through the challenge, the reward isn't really the "gee-Wiz!" that it would have been, if the challenge were a teensy bit easier.  But I'm only talking about two or perhaps three of them, and they're not crucial to the game anyway.
The side-plots, optional training missions, and other bits and bobs add to the game feeling 'fuller'.  If it was just the main campaign, it would feel too short.
All in all, I'd say that Bastion was one of the best little games I've played in a while.  I utterly love the music, and will be buying it.  I started the "Play-though Plus", but realised I was just doing it to grind for Achievements, and I have a room full of other games to finish before I shuffle off this mortal coil.  If I had the time, though, I'd play this through again.

Picked it up during the sale and was only expecting it to be decent at best. Boy was I wrong; this game turned out to be amazing! It is pretty simple yet incredibly deep,
Other reviews complained about the difficulty but hailed its gorgeous scapes. The latter remark is became very evident as the sky-city steampunkish world came to life, an aesthetic that sort of reminds me of Bioshock Infinite. However, the complaints about the difficulty I have to strongly disagree (I should note that the developers did already address those complaints before I picked up a copy as they shifted the "normal" difficulty to "challenging" and have now created an easier "normal"). But after I beat it on the new normal I decided to give challenging a shot and that is where I discovered how the strategy of this game really starts to come out. Honestly, this game reminds me of the old Advanced Wars games for the GBA in the way that it is pretty straight forward and easy to follow yet requires a ton of strategy and maneuvering of forces.
I'm now going through the game for my third time on the "brutal" difficulty and I have to say that I'm still loving it! Only thing I can knitpick is that their is no skirmish mode or challenge missions outside of the story mode. But as is this game is well worth the money, so lacking those other things only gives me hope that the developers are still working!

There are very few human characters and the path of stages fill in as you move, giving a cool sense of isolation, discovery, and mystery throughout. I feel like this is a very visual and audial satisfying game. The combat feels very stilted and unbalanced in ways, some weapons seem near impossible to use without a tradeoff from your enemy, and you always have such a large supply of health potions that it often feels you can get away with any and all tradeoffs. Recommended to gamers looking for a simple but uniquely delivered story, maybe not for those entirely uninterested in storytelling in their video games.

I cannot recommend the game in its current state, and maybe not at all in this first year. There's a lot of anti-consumer practices in the game, there's no proper punishes for online rage quitting, there's a lack of features for casual players and it's just lacking as a package. No amount of, admittredly good, DLC characters can change the overlying flaws in this game.
While the game plays relatively well when compared to other fighters on STEAM, there's many other options on other platforms that offer more for less of a cost. The game also gouges the user for so little DLC at such a high price, that the people who were against the old update system from Street Fighter 4 are getting what they wanted, but by cutting their nose to spite their face.
Here's a list of the cons I have with the base product:
-The biggest con; NO RAGE QUIT PUNISHMENT
-8 frames of input delay
-Training mode doesn't save settings or have frame data
-Survival mode is a blatant attempt at hair-ripping difficulty just to get people to spend money on colors
-No way to check stats, win percentage
-No messaging between PS4 and PC users even though we have to make proprietary Capcom Fighting Network (CFN) Accounts
-No support for DInput controllers/fight sticks
-PC players can gain an advantage over PS4 players just by alt-tabbing
Now, here's a list of the pros of the game:
+The gameplay promotes commitment and strong decision making
That's it.
Now, we also have a pricing issue with the DLC. You can buy individual costumes for $3.99. In USF4, we were able to get costumers for 5 characters for the same price. You can either play through an intentionally hellish Survival Mode for alternate colors, or buy them with real money. And don't worry, you have to buy or play for the colors multiple times because you don't get them for all costumes the first time through. THEN there's a new CPT DLC that has exclusive content on the PS4, screwing out the PC user base.
If you're looking into a fighting game, I recommend Killer Instinct or Guilty Gear: Xrd. On Playstation consoles, there's Guilty Gear: Revelator.

I have to say, it's been a long time since I played a proper isometric RPG/explorery game.    I've tried to play Baldur's Gate again, but it's just too sprawley and big to fit in the little time slots I have right now.   So it was with some curiosity that I tried this much-lauded game.
First-off, I was impressed by the music.  Right from the start, there's a deep, mellow quality to it which instantly put me into the right mood.  I felt like liquid chocolate had been poured over my head, and I was being invited to relax and listen by Barry White.
The next thing which I really enjoyed was the narrative style.  The music and the narration just slipped, hand-in-hand, sat either side of you, and told you a tale.   Without any prompting, the whole scene was set...  Even some of the curious things which only get answered later are delivered in such a way that you think "Hmm.. I should know that, but it would be rude to ask.. I'll let him just tell his story, and pick it up as I go along".
The story is.. well.. different..  The same lines as usual.. World gone to heck, boy.. girl.. antagonist.. good guys.. bad guys... plot twist.. narrator..  All the usual elements are there.     The usual gameplay elements are there too...  Weapons (Melee, pistols, shotgun, repeater, ranged, over-powered).. No really exotic weapons, although there are a few duplicates in those slots..
The game starts off telling you very little.  A lot is completely unexplained at the end of the story, and it doesn't really matter.   The way the game is presented, and the semi-linear flow helps to guide you along.  The nice little narration points as you travel along also kind of help as well.  It's not "The Stanley Parable", where the fourth-wall is broken, but it's just nice to have a little colour added to the story as you walk along.. People's names, places described in a relaxed sort of way.  Very nice.
I played the game all the way to the end with only two or perhaps three  irritated moments. Usually these were quickly dispelled by a change of weapon/tactic, and starting over.   And when I say starting over, the levels are mostly pleasingly short, so this isn't a major disaster.
The end of the story is nice.  You have the usual choice, although unlike most games, the two aren't "Good" or "Evil".  I'd say that the writers chose a very Star-wars approach where "Good" is mapped to "Altruistic", and "Evil" is mapped to "Selfish"...
If there's one downside, I'd just say that the game DOES require you to grind a few of the levels.   Some of the 'challenges' can be a little tough, and there's no real indication when you've levelled up enough to make it through the level without extreme difficulty.  Usually when you CAN make it through the challenge, the reward isn't really the "gee-Wiz!" that it would have been, if the challenge were a teensy bit easier.  But I'm only talking about two or perhaps three of them, and they're not crucial to the game anyway.
The side-plots, optional training missions, and other bits and bobs add to the game feeling 'fuller'.  If it was just the main campaign, it would feel too short.
All in all, I'd say that Bastion was one of the best little games I've played in a while.  I utterly love the music, and will be buying it.  I started the "Play-though Plus", but realised I was just doing it to grind for Achievements, and I have a room full of other games to finish before I shuffle off this mortal coil.  If I had the time, though, I'd play this through again.

The LEGO games follow a strict formula: Take a franchise/movie, recreate it in the most amazingly silly way possible, and make the audience replay memorable scenes in beautifully designed set-pieces. Star Wars, Middle Earth, Batman, you name it- in each LEGO game you get what could best be described as an affectionate parody, with MiniFigs and an awful lot of brick.-smashing. And The LEGO Movie Videogame is just the same, with all the good and the bad this brings.
The LMV follows the basic plot of the movie: Normal everyday construction worker Emmet is pulled into an ancient prophecy that claims him to be the only one to save the world from a doomsday weapon called "The Kragle". Despite being utterly unqualified for the job he does his best, and hilarity ensues.
If you know the movie (and you should) you'll find it hard not to smile a few minutes into the game. The complete cast is there, the setpieces are amazing and occasionally outshine the movie, the voice acting is pitch perfect and the undiluted charme of giant scenery build out of LEGO is as ever-present as ever. The game looks amazing and pulls a lot of awesome scenes together to form a narrative that is pretty close to the movie.
As per usual, you control a growing cast of characters, each with their own ability set. Emmet can build sturdy objects with the proper instructions, and can smash through special bricks with his drill. Wyldstyle has some extra agility and can jump and climb on certain ledges, Batman gets his ever-useful Batarangs and grappling ropes, and so on. Using and combining these abilities make the bulk of the level's challenge, and the game does a good job of adding layers to the formula as the cast expands.
Controls, also as usual, are nice and tight enough. The keyboard is a bit inferior to a good gamepad, but both work in a pinch. Switching characters and pulling off their moves is easily learned, and the game goes the extra mile to pop up tooltips if you keep missing a hint. Despite the cheerful toy aesthetic children will probably be overwhelmed by the action. There is always somethign going on, there is always something to do, and while death is cheap (you only lose a couple of studs, which are the in-game currency for everything) there is a certain difficulty here, a tad bit too easy for older, experienced players and a tad bit too hard for someone who's just learning the ropes.
With a ton of unlockable characters, mission and freeplay game modes, and downright over-the-top-awesomeness, the LMV should be easy to recommend: It is an awesome game and filled to the brim with charme and action.
Still, I need to stress that this game makes not exactly much sense if you do not know the movie. And even IF you know the movie, you'll have a hard time following events, so much that the levels stop being a string of related missions and instead become little self-contained bits connected with (occasionally edited) movie footage.
And this is odd, because the game clearly knows what it is doing. The movie has a bike chase, which is awesome. The game stretches this chase over a whole level, and adds to it, and makes it just twice as awesome because this time, it's you playing that scene. I would have loved to see the team make their own plot, with in-game rendered cutscenes, and maybe explore the LEGO world a bit more.
Still, this is nitpicking. The fun is there, and chasing down all achievements and unlockables will take a while- and this is a game where you abseil into a LEGO chicken, get encased in a rainbow eggshell, have a unicorn-cat smash that eggshell and build a toy-mouse car out of the bricks, which you can then ride, as Batman, all the while grumbling how rainbows are soo corny.
Need I say more?

This game is a blast, I bought it while it was on sale with all DLC for around $5 bought a copy of it for my friend and my other friend bought his own copy. The base game features 4 playable "classes" each sporting a signature weapon that go with the characters strengths for instance there is a Shotgun wielder and because a shotgun requires you to be upclose and personal the character gets a higher health than the other characters. In the DLC they add a new "class" who sports a crossbow, last bolt in the clip does extra damage, hard concept to wrap your head around but it works. The game itself is....well the best way i can describe it is if you mixed a tower defence game with a FPS, multiple towers to unlock, multiple weapons to unlock including ones from the other classes, you level up in this game unlocking new stuff as you go. Perks, Towers, and weapons are the 3 categories you can unlock from Perks as with any other perk in a FPS increases a stat or gives you a bonus thats active all the time, for instance in one unlock you get a perk that if you jump on an enemy's head you deal extra damage to them, theres also ones to increase movement speed, make your jumps higher, resistances higher, and even a perk to make you deal damage to enemies who are close to you. the Towers range from damage towers like Lightning, Slow towers and theres even some Mine towers that you must set up yourself. There are a wide array of enemies that come through during the waves each enemy has a weak spot that makes you deal more damage when you shoot it, some are easy to find and some take some searching to find, but it is highly recommended you do so from the get go. Levels too easy? add Feats of Strength to your mobs for added difficulty there are 5 Feats ranging from reduced damage to having them heal per second. Want just 1 perk cool want all 5 go for it or any in between. The game does start to feel repetitive after awhile and some of the Waves seem almost impossible even with 3 players but the fun you get while playing makes this game a must buy for any library. I would however wait for the next sale before buying.

After playing nearly every one to date, I can safely say that this is by far my favourite LEGO game.
Pros:
-The writing is perfect and the humour exactly like the movie
-The gameplay is simple yet engaging, constantly changing the pace and mechanics to prevent boredom
-Each characters voice actor make a return from the movies in this game, adding to the true charm of it all
-Animations and style is much more true to real LEGO than any other game, with stiff movement emphasising the fact that they are just toys
-Levels that directly follow the movie, adding more to it while still feeling relatable and not just "filler"
-Appropriate length; not too short yet not too long that it becomes stale in any way.
-Very high replay value
-That bonus level; A true guilty-pleasure to me!
Cons:
-For some reason all cutscene and game music is different from that from the movie, even the lovable "Everything Is Awesome" is altered negatively.
- .... That's it really...
From start to finish I enjoyed every moment, captivating me like no other LEGO game could do, and forcing me to play just one more level even though I told myself I'd get off 3 levels ago.
If you're in any way a fan of LEGO games, the LEGO movie, or just LEGO in general; I can't recommend this game enough.

Midas Gold Plus is one of the best idle/clicker games to be released in a while.
The game is very fair to anyone who doesn't, or can't, pay money to advance. You can buy red gems that allow you to speed up the progress of various things, but these are awarded free of charge for simply logging in every day. In addition you can gain blue gems simply by playing the game, which you can use to increase your gains in the game. In this way you can make steady progress in game without spending a cent, which is terrific.
It does function like a normal idle/clicker game, in this case you click a stone repeatedly to turn it into gold (being King Midas and all, you can turn anything to gold really) and then spend the gold on various upgrades. Among these upgrades, you have,  have nine buildings which produce money, and all of which can be upgraded, along with upgrades for all the buildings that increase their speed and their gains; you gain a resource called knowledge from critical clicks on the stone which allow you to research special upgrades at your university; lastly you can send out armies to raid cities for special item boosts.
The typical 'reset everything' mechanic comes in the form of you making an offering to the gods at a temple, and gaining diamonds in exchange. Every diamond gives you a boost to your profits from the buildings, and can be spent on special diamond specific research options at the university, or can be spent on artifiacts that do everything from giving you idle bonuses to making the raids finish faster.
You also have two special champions right off the get-go, one specializing in idling and the other specializing in clicking. There are at least six other champions to unlock when you get enough diamonds, which unlock other features and upgrades. When you get far enough there is apparently options to build and level a city, and level up your character in various ways, but I haven't gotten that far yet.
All in all, there's a lot more to this game then your average idle/clicker game, and for the fact that it's free, you really can't go wrong. So, you have a 'golden' opportunity to try this game out and have a great time. Go and take it.

This version of Doom 3 actually comes with all the original Doom games. So I'll summarize what I felt about all 3 of them.
Doom 1: One of the first shooters ever made. It's actually a lot of fun. The first thing I noticed is that you can't jump or aim vertically. You basically strafe and shoot at enemies and use the shotgun as much as possible. You get a minigun, a rocket launcher, a plasma gun, and of course, the BFG to kill progressively more difficult swarms of enemies. There's not much of a story and the levels are very arcade like in structure. The music fits the era it was made: 8-bit rock music.
Doom 2: Nearly identical to the first Doom but with what seems like more difficult levels. There is a new shotgun which has a higher spread and damage which is great for taking out lots of guys fast, but reloads slower. There are a lot of new enemies that are much harder. You'll face some of the bosses from the first game in almost every level. Doom 2 is like the challenge mode of Doom 1.  There's also more of that 8-bit rock music in every level.
Doom 3: It's making me crazy dizzy. I just set the FPS lower because the 120fps made me so sick. The gameplay is pretty narrow compared to the last two. You're stuck in very narrow corridors similar to Dead Space. I've noticed some similar enemies from the original two games, just now they've been given a more modern look with better graphics and physics. Unfortunetly, even this game is starting to show its age. The textures are basically absent from this game. There's also a more obvious atempt at having a story to this game. I haven't finished the game so I can't say whether or not the story is any good, but it's more interesting now than it was in the past two games. The 8-bit rock music is finally gone. Almost seems like a shame as now the game feels like a typical horror game. It feels like Doom had a baby with James Camerons "Alien."

Time to update an old review! Oh boy here we go, a 2010 title and yet here I am 6 years later loving it to death. To put it quite simply, this is an amazing game for its time. Id say that for an attempt to make not only the alien and predator come together, but add in marines to the mix for an amazing 3 way bloody orgy? They did an amazing job. Once more, this is my review on the game and with my love for the Alien and Predator series, this review may seem bias. However I will do my best to give an honest review. So ready to kick this off? Lets do it!
Today were gonna do something different, were gonna start with the cons of the game. Why? Why not, and no Im not starting with cons because they outweigh the pros. I just want to go ahead and spill the beans on what may potentally ruin this game from being well...one of the greatest.
Cons: The multiplayer is DEAD. Thats the biggest con I can think of truth be told. The game is 6 years old, yes, but the multiplayer was dead within the first year of the game coming out. Sadly that might have been the death of this game all together. There are plenty of modes to play from, such as hunted and infestation. TDM and even flat out DM, which would pit alien on alien, predator on predator, and marine on marine. Of course like I said before, it was a massive bloody orgy so all 3 would still fight eachother. If this game was still alive, the multiplayer would certainly be worth playing.
Some weaponry. I say some because Im talking specifically about the flame thrower and smart gun. The smart gun was literally just an aimbot in the hands of a marine. Cloaked predator? They can see you. Alien hiding in the dark? They can see you. Now the flamethrowers only problem is the after burn, as an alien I have little to no clue to get rid of it other than sprinting fast down a corridor and hoping the fire stops. As a predator you have the ability to heal so Im sure that may negate the whole burning thing.
As far as cons go, thats about it. Now for the good stuff, right?
Pros. The story, well, the story as far as campaign goes, is something that I loved to play over and over. All three stories overlap yet none of the 'main characters' never really meet up. The alien story follows an alien who has been in captivity since birth and escaped when Weyland opened up the predator temple underground, he then aims to free his queen and make a hive. I wont speak any endings so no spoiler alerts. The predator story consists of a predator going onto the planet to find out what happened to a team of young bloods, and honor his code. Lastly the marine story is to contain the xenomorph outbreak in the colony.
The multiplayer (While it was alive I mean). Back when the game came out me and my good buddy played a ton of multiplayer and honestly? It was one of the funnest things to do. Mostly TDM since it was two teams that could consist of any combination of marines, aliens, and predators.
I think I gave the rough and short of it, truthfully its a great game single player wise and if the multiplayer wasnt dead (Boy Im just running that into the ground, arent I?) that would be another great thing from the game. Even for a 6 year old game, Id still go give it a try if you even enjoy the AvP series.

First, I'd like to attach a warning label that says: PLAY WITH CONTROLLER OR NOT AT ALL.
Okay, now that that's out of the way, Bastion is fantastic. The narrator is smooth but his voice is rough and cowboy-ish, commenting on what the main protagonist (known as The Kid) does as you play as The Kid. The narrator effortlessly tells you the tale of a broken civilization, and everything you find, from collectibles to weapons to new levels, gives you just one more small glimpse into what the world used to be, even as the narrator laments it's destruction.
The combat system is fun and every weapon will have you oooing and ahhing at the novelty and simple to use, easy to master design. Unless you're a huge fan of ARPG's and are blessed with a quick reaction time, I would reccomend No-Sweat (read:Unlimited Lives) mode, as I found it challenging as a person who isn't particularly fast in terms of reflexes and still didn't quite get how to combat certain enemies by the end of the game. The latter complaint is mostly my own fault.
The soundtrack is pretty sweet to boot, and I only wish I had bought it during the Steam Sale, as the fighting doesn't give enough time to fully appreciate the music with the exception of the ones by

The Marine campaign is a blast. It's like "Doom 3" had it figured out a way to use its abundance of atmosphere to create real tension. However, the game really shows its console roots in the subpar Alien and Predator campaigns. Whereas "Alien vs Predator 2" from 2001 had elegant control schemes for each species which were easy to learn but difficult to master, the 2010 iteration reduces too many actions to button bushing quicktime sequences. It can be annoying when, as the predator, you realize that you can only jump to specific designated areas or that as the alien in order to crawl through a vent you have to push a specific action button rather than just..you know..crawl through the bloody vent.
Multiplayer suffers as a consequence. Whereas the 2001 version rewarded skill and the effort it took to master the various species controls (especially the alien who could go from weak to powerful in the right hands), the 2010 version is nothing but running around and spamming quick kills.
Just play Magicka.

A satisfying sequel to four. As a long time Street Fighter fan, as well as player (since the days of ST) I can say without a doubt that this is a welcome addition to the series. In it's current state I believe that Capcom has more then madeup for the awful launch of the game. Also this game really welcomes new players to the series by making the learning curve not as steep, while still having enough depth and complexity to it that veterans can still feel fufillment in playing and discovering as well as performing with their sick tech. The removal of one frame links, and the implication of simpler anti-airs really help new players grasp the neutral game better, while also solidifying their playstyle as a whole. I also believe the roster has a character for just about any kind of player. If you like rushdown try Rashid, Necalli, or Ken. If you like to turtle try out Ryu, Guile, or Dhalsim. I can say there are many steps forward from four. Removal of Red Focus and FADC, Not as many annoying characters: Rolento, Hakan, etc. While the netcode is still a tiny bit shaky (pairing you up with bad connections regardless of the connectivity limits you put on matchmaking) I believe that the online is not nearly as bad as some make it out to be. The pros definitely outweigh the cons when it comes to this game. I also can say I have legitimate grounds to make this review as I have 200+ hours on pc as well as around 100+ hours on consoles I have used for offline as well as local tournaments. I cannot state enough that you should try out this game if you are interested in becoming part of the FGC or are still contemplating the purchase as a fan.

PROS:

So do i recommend this game?
Yes. Absolutely
But i recommend getting it on sale
and having a beefy computer when playing.

I've never been too big on racing games (short of Mario Kart because...well, it's Mario Kart) but the Burnout series has always held a special place in my heart. Lets face it, how many other games out there
you to smash the living daylights out of your competitors and still be considered a racer?
Where to begin? The graphics are unbelievable, honestly some of the best I've seen. The car variety is also fantastic, each one with its own personality and querks making every race unique. And there isn't just racing; stunts, smashing other cars or just driving around the city exploring give you plenty to do. The open-world racing concept is a big plus as well. Half the fun of the game is finding new routes and shortcuts to give yourself an edge over the competition. Or there's also just doing crazy stuff like launching a stock car off a cliff while spinning and landing on the highway completely intact (Yeah, that happened!). There's even hidden...nevermind, don't want to spoil it.
While there is a motorcycle mode, it's actually pretty boring. You only get a grand total of 4 bikes to chose from, 2 sport and 2 cruisers, and there's very little difference between them. Once you complete that mode, you probably won't be touching it again. Another issue is that the crash physics can glitch up at times, showing that your car "crashed" into something when really you just grazed another car/obstacle or avoided it altogether. But, the system does catch this fact (letting you drive off after a few awkward and confusing seconds of slow motion photography) often enough to make it a minor nuisance. And, as other reviews have stated, the "DLC included" doesn't seem to work. And while this does kind of suck, I personally don't care. There's enough to the game to keep me satisfied...at least until Criterion or whoever fixes that part.
One of the events in the game is called "Marked Man." The goal is pretty straight forward; drive from point A to point B while avoiding the other cars out to wreck you. I've come to loathe this event due to one glaring issue: the mechanics of the game seem to go out the window in this event. Even at the start of the game, when the difficulty is at its lowest, the "enemy" cars are unrealisticly nimble. Somehow they're able to make hairpin turns without drifiting at insane speeds. If you manage to lose your pursuers by making a sharp turn down a cross-street and
them fly by, they're back on your tail within moments regardless of the amount of distance you covered. And somehow even the most burly vehicles seem to be made of glass. The 4x4, for example, can only be wrecked by a full speed, head-on collision with a stationary object or about 8-10 low speed collisions. But in Marked Man, you could get tapped by a pursuer and get "taken down." My "favorite" is how the other cars can T-bone you out of nowhere, like on a bridge which
And let's not forget to mention how the E-brake on your car tends to fail during the mayhem. Yes, I'm ranting. But for a game that is great at being a "realistic racer," this is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Burnout Paradise is certainly an awesome game despite it's flaws, but if the DLC bit is an issue, I recommend waiting until this one is on sale.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Blackbay Asylum is a game developed by TAD Productions AB and published by KISS Ltd.

This game is showing great promise in its early Alpha stages. I've never written a review before but here goes:
I've been an avid strategy gamer all my life, it is my favourite genre, but it is hard to get right. A good strategy game has to allow the player to, well, strategise. Some are just inevitable grinds where it is about who can do the same thing the best. This game allows a lot of scope for multiple paths to victory, which is crucial, as well as severely punishing or rewarding the player for incorrect or correct tactical decisions. Multiplayer in this game will be exceptional.
Pros:
- Decisions have major consequences, for better or worse. For me this is the great thing about this game. If you decide on an early raid of another player, or region, you may lose all your soldiers and be doomed, or you might secure vital resources and territory that will go on to win you the game. Resource managemant decisions can also either win or lose you the game, at every decision. The Winter and Blizzard handicaps, as well as the random events really punish you for incorrect tactical decisions.
- Many different victory conditions. If you are to win you need to conceptualise a effective strategy to achieve that condition.
- The mechanics of the game are very simple, but it takes skill to master them. I think multiplayer will highlight this.
- Art style. I think the art style really captures the mythic Norse feel of the game.
Suggestions:
At this stage in its Alpha development it would be unfair to address these as cons. I'm sure most of these will likely be added, or have been considered.
- Add the ability to modify victory conditions.
- Add more clan specific buildings.
- Add more variety of military units.
- AI needs to improve. It is a steep learning curve, but the bar isn't very high. I lost my first game, but i've played 6 after that and won them all on hard, using different clans.
- Victories need to feel more climactic. Add a cut scene for each victory, or spawn demons from hellheim that try and prevent you from achieving the map specific victories like Odin's sword etc.
- More lore! Norse mythology is in my view one of the most interesting and what really draws me into the game. Play even more on the Norse roots of the game.
Overall this game is in a fine state for Alpha, and I deeply hope the devs aim to make this into the great game it has the potential to be.

This game is basically the original Doom 3 and its expansions on the IDTECH5 engine, AKA the engine RAGE uses. There are no new art assets, but there are a few changes. Besides having the option to run at a max 60FPS or max 120FPS, it also features a shoulder-mounted flashlight (although you can turn it off if you wish), Oculus Rift support, and some other graphical options. I have also heard that iD tweaked ammo and health placement, although I can't say what's different since it's been such a long time since I played the original Doom 3.
At the time of writing, I do not know any mods for Doom 3 BFG edition. Since this uses a different engine than the original Doom 3, this version is NOT COMPATABLE WITH MODS FOR THE ORIGINAL DOOM 3! However, iD recently released their source code for BFG edition, so perhaps mods could be made/ported to this game in due time.
Although multiplayer includes deathmatch, CTF, and other modes, it's dead as of time of this writing. It uses peer-to-peer, so it's difficult to see who is playing, assuming anyone is. Perhaps the holiday sales will change that, but I am doubtful.
If you never owned Doom 1 +2, Doom 3 or any of its expansions, I still have a hard time recommending this. You could probably get all of those games for cheaper than what BFG edition costs, and be able to use the plethora of mods for each.

The artwork in this game reminds me of Banner Saga, but the underlying gameplay is much shallower. The setting and characters were good, and the story (though mostly told in prose between chapters) was decent. I especially liked the character designs. The gameplay was interesting to start with but got tedious by the end of the game.
Primarily this is a game about map control and gathering resources, rather than direct combat. This leads to a fast-paced start as you try to defend against enemies on multiple fronts while improving your income. Once you've stabilised though, it's a slow mindless grind through large groups of enemies that have no real chance of breaking through your lines. To make matters worse, the combat consists of random dice rolls with a huge variance. You can see damage ranges of 1-90 odd, which means the enemy could do nothing or one-shot your character. You can mitigate this with character ablities, but they cost resources which means that grinding out the last areas of the enemy is a repetitive cycle. Namely: hit end turn to gather resources, activate skills to capture a location, drop back to heal and gather resources, repeat. Higher difficulties make the early game more frantic, but don't help with this gameplay cycle.
The game is fun enough to last most of its short length, though I recommend avoiding the higher difficulties because the fun of putting out fires at the start of levels is quickly extinguished by how tedious it is to finish off a level.

Mediterranean Chicken and Pasta
Makes: 4 servingsPrep: 5 mins Cook: 15 mins Carb Grams Per Serving: 38
Ingredients
1 6 - ounce jar marinated artichoke hearts
1 tablespoon olive oil
12 ounces skinless, boneless chicken breast, cut into bite-size pieces
3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1/4 cup chicken broth
1/4 dry white wine
1 teaspoon dried oregano, crushed
1 7 - ounce jar roasted red peppers, drained and cut into strips
1/4 cup pitted kalamata olives
3 cups hot cooked campanelle or penne pasta
1/4 cup crumbled feta cheese (optional)
Directions
Drain artichoke hearts, reserving marinade, and chop them.
In a large skillet, heat oil over medium-high heat; add chicken and garlic. Cook and stir until chicken is brown.
Add the reserved artichoke marinade, broth, wine and dried oregano.
Bring to a boil; reduce heat. Simmer, covered, 10 minutes.
Stir in chopped artichokes, roasted peppers and olives.
To serve, spoon chicken mixture over pasta. If desired, sprinkle with feta cheese.
