A little background first:
The first fighting game I ever played was Tekken 2. That game kinda made me dislike fighting games in general for giving me the impression that fighting games in general are just chaotic button-masher games. Anyway, long after that I somehow ended up playing Street Fighter Alpha 3, which I immediately fell in love with for I was convinced that random button mashing was not a valid strategy in all fighting games and everything else was solid. After that completely outside the fighting game genre I got an interest in competitive multiplayer games, though I was slightly disgruntled that most of them were team-based and most one-on-one competitive games (like most RTS games) are just mind blowingly over-complicated for me. That's when my attention shifted back to fighting games.
Coincidentally me already being a Street Fighter fan I already had Street Fighter IV on steam, although I hadn't touched the online multiplayer yet in fear of me getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to myself. Eventually I got bored of the singleplayer experience and logged online and getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked was exactly what happened. Of course I knew I just had to get better in the game, but nonetheless over time I started to dislike certain properties of the game. Most noticeable ones being that the gameplay was way too fast-paced for my taste, grapple being somewhat overpowered and focus attack in general. In addition the difficulty curve was almost a straight wall and there was no skill-based matchmaking. Basically it was nearly impossible for new players to get into.
Then Street Fighter V came out...
I had a chance to play it over at a friend's house. Initial reaction was: "It's like Street Fighter IV... but with none of the bad things. IT'S THE PERFECT FIGHTING GAME!"
There is simply very few things NOT worth praising. The gameplay is tight, mechanics are easy to learn, there's cross-platform compatibility IN ADDITION to skill-based matchmaking... and there's so much more.
Seriously, in case you're not that particularly interested in fighting games even if you are into competitive games this is a great game. It's straightforward, it has impeccable balance, it has no RNG and every mistake you make is ALWAYS your fault. Leaving this game without recommendation would simply be outrageous.
As a small heads up though, I did experience some performance difficulties with this game which essentially made it unplayable when I first started this game, although thankfully I got it fixed. Just make sure your graphics and ethernet drivers are up to date and you have a decent PC. I've heard talk you may run into issues nonetheless, but I won't speak for or against it on that matter.
TL;DR: Street Fighter V is the best fighting game and the best competitive game I've ever played.

So I Played Street Fighter V.
I always had a huge likeness for fighting games, starting way back when with Mortal Kombat 4 for ps1. As years went by I finally managed to get a Xbox360 for christmas, and with it came a copy of Street Fighter 4. I played the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of that game, 100% completing the single player stuff. I was a stupid little kid back then, so of course I mained Dan Hibki, but I still had a blast playing it. I was very excited for when they annouced Street Fighter V, as I had a history with the series. And hey, maybe now that I am older and stuff, maybe I'll be better at the game. Was I satisfied? I would definetely say so...but there is a lot of problems that I need to address. In order to say what I truly feel about this game, I will talk about every aspect of it, so thats a lot of reading, sorry about that. ALSO SPOLIERS FOR THE PLOT OF SSV BECAUSE I DONT WANT PEOPLE TO GET TRIGGERED.
The Gameplay
---------------
I think the gameplay is freaking awesome. I never played a fighting game that felt so tight with it's controls. When I lost a fight, I didn't blame lag or faulty inputs, cause I couldn't. The game controls very smoothly, with that classic Street Fighter gameplay that we all are used to. I still can't get the hang of charge characters, but that's more a problem with me sucking then the game. There is a play style for everybody, the average shoto, the tanky grappler, the agile annoyence, and charge characters-for people who like to hold the stick back and start wagglin like you were playing Resident Evil 4 while hopped up on cocaine. No characters feel under or overpowered, with each having their own unique fighting styles and weaknesses. Learning every character is vital to getting good at the game, but the game provides great tools for learning. Everything from a tutorial mode, command lists for every character avalible on the fly, and even a combo trial mode. The game mostly focuses on the multiplayer competitive aspect, and thus it gives you the proper tools to do so. I say the gameplay is spot on, and I can't find problems with it.
Online
-------
I honestly didn't play much of the online mode. I was too busy learning to play the characters, and doing the story bits. From what I have played, I do like it. People do complain about the bad netcode, but I didn't have that many problems with lag or desync. Granted, I didn't play many matches, so that could be the reason why. I do like the counters telling you how every person plays. It helps you devolp strategies and make for more competitive games. It also means you can't always use the same tatics, as it will show on your grid. From what I played, eh, it's alright.
Character Stories
------------------
As what was orginally the only story the game had, it was pretty lame. Every character only got like, 2-3 fights, and their stories were really bland. Oh, R.Mika is obsessed with Zangeif, cool. Oh, Ryu is trying to surpress that Satsui No Hado still, cool. Oh, Ken has a family, cool. Oh, Alex is dumb, cool. Oh, Sakura is here, coo....WAIT WHAT. Yea, this game has a huge fetish for rubbing characters you don't get to play as in your face. Karin fights Sakura as her ending, except you don't get to play that fight, cause Sakura isn't in the game. Alex fights holographs of E.Honda and that Oil guy from Super Street Fighter 4, except you don't get to play that fight. AND DECAPRE, DON'T EVEN GET ME STARTED ON DECAPRE! Yet at least. The game was released with these as the only story bits, which sucked, but as a way to try out every character, well, they could have done it a hell of a lot worse.

I've never been too big on racing games (short of Mario Kart because...well, it's Mario Kart) but the Burnout series has always held a special place in my heart. Lets face it, how many other games out there
you to smash the living daylights out of your competitors and still be considered a racer?
Where to begin? The graphics are unbelievable, honestly some of the best I've seen. The car variety is also fantastic, each one with its own personality and querks making every race unique. And there isn't just racing; stunts, smashing other cars or just driving around the city exploring give you plenty to do. The open-world racing concept is a big plus as well. Half the fun of the game is finding new routes and shortcuts to give yourself an edge over the competition. Or there's also just doing crazy stuff like launching a stock car off a cliff while spinning and landing on the highway completely intact (Yeah, that happened!). There's even hidden...nevermind, don't want to spoil it.
While there is a motorcycle mode, it's actually pretty boring. You only get a grand total of 4 bikes to chose from, 2 sport and 2 cruisers, and there's very little difference between them. Once you complete that mode, you probably won't be touching it again. Another issue is that the crash physics can glitch up at times, showing that your car "crashed" into something when really you just grazed another car/obstacle or avoided it altogether. But, the system does catch this fact (letting you drive off after a few awkward and confusing seconds of slow motion photography) often enough to make it a minor nuisance. And, as other reviews have stated, the "DLC included" doesn't seem to work. And while this does kind of suck, I personally don't care. There's enough to the game to keep me satisfied...at least until Criterion or whoever fixes that part.
One of the events in the game is called "Marked Man." The goal is pretty straight forward; drive from point A to point B while avoiding the other cars out to wreck you. I've come to loathe this event due to one glaring issue: the mechanics of the game seem to go out the window in this event. Even at the start of the game, when the difficulty is at its lowest, the "enemy" cars are unrealisticly nimble. Somehow they're able to make hairpin turns without drifiting at insane speeds. If you manage to lose your pursuers by making a sharp turn down a cross-street and
them fly by, they're back on your tail within moments regardless of the amount of distance you covered. And somehow even the most burly vehicles seem to be made of glass. The 4x4, for example, can only be wrecked by a full speed, head-on collision with a stationary object or about 8-10 low speed collisions. But in Marked Man, you could get tapped by a pursuer and get "taken down." My "favorite" is how the other cars can T-bone you out of nowhere, like on a bridge which
And let's not forget to mention how the E-brake on your car tends to fail during the mayhem. Yes, I'm ranting. But for a game that is great at being a "realistic racer," this is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Burnout Paradise is certainly an awesome game despite it's flaws, but if the DLC bit is an issue, I recommend waiting until this one is on sale.

Well, well, well, Realm of the Mad God, it's been many long hours of maxing, dying, and coming back to do it all again. With about as many hours to match on flashplayer this game has kept me coming back for years. I quit and find myself back in a month or two along with the same friends who "quit" as well. For any new players coming in this game is very addicting, but  is a very long grind that will most likely not end for most. I've really only in the last year of play come to a stable play of having multiple 6/8 or even 8/8 characters at once. If you plan on spending money on this game I suggest getting Character slots and vault chests. These will help you get multiple strong characters so you can do multiple different dungeons. Knight is OP and can steam roll anything with a 70/70 pet. Now... on to pets, pets are a blessing to this game, but also a curse. Pets have allowed this games pace to speed up and aid players who have the trouble of dodging most bullets. While they help these players, they also hurt these players pets can be a money pit that is hard to resist the urge of investing a few or a thousand dollars into. You can get by on a 70/70 Heal Magic Heal pet fine even less if you are a rather good player. All-in-All Realm has been one of the greatest games I have ever played and will hold a special place for me because so many of my friends on steam I met through this game. I look forward to the new ownership of Realm after being saved of the Kabam clutches. Thank You DECA and I look forward to the future plans of Realm!

To start, I haven't read any other reviews on this game. I have played it and tried hard to like it. I just can't. I wanted to enjoy playing Airline Tycoon 2 so much, but it was a swing and a miss. The Freemode is lackluster which is what you play after beating the rest a few times over. Free mode should offer a challenge that varies game by game based on the AI... The game is pretty much a rinse and repeat of 1 of 2 strategy choices.
1) Buy a brand new, reliable plane, keep chugging along and slowly take over your enemies knowing you have your reliable horse to carry you along as you buy more of the same one. Slowly climbing the same ladder with no risk.
2) Buy from the junk yard. Find incredible deals and eliminate everyone insta-fast with no real difficulty or risks.
The game doesn't play out any differently. I wish there would be more to routes and business decisions. Being able to have a ton of departures from one airport in the exact same moment as well.... c'mon, really?
Didn't they have that RIGHT in the first game with finite gate space?
Imagine your airline starting at a very small FBO with small operations and as your airline grows, invest your revenue into your airport as well, slowly growing it up and butting up against more more competition, with decision making AI. That's what you'd hope for in the modern sequal to such a great game. Again, swing and total miss. It's the re-hash of the first game with elements removed.
Cargo is a purchased add-on which does little more than offer a way for you to make money even faster.
If you're looking for a fun, tycoon game that challenges you even a little bit to try new things, this isn't it. I'm hoping there is a 3, and I'm hoping they try, instead of beating a dead horse that by luck, spat up some money.

I have nearly 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews.
One Hour Reviews - Game 5
Airline Tycoon 2
Purchase Date: 9/11/2014
Like a number of games in my Steam library, I came across Airline Tycoon 2 as part of a Humble Bundle.  I really like Humble Bundle because not only do I get to donate to a good cause, but sometimes in that bundle I'll come across a really good game that I never would have bought otherwise.
Sadly, Airline Tycoon 2 is not one of those games.
Right off the bat the game scored a negative when I realized I'd have to login to play this game.  Given that this is a completely single player game with no internet component whatsoever, I really don't see the point in forcing me to login.  The only thing that kept this from being more annoying is apparently I've played some other game from Kalypso, so it remembered my login from that.  So at least I didn't have to make another account.
Airline Tycoon 2 tries to inject some humor by presenting you with various cariactures of people like Albert Einstein, who is exactly the person that comes to mind when I need an airline mechanic.  You know, cause he's smart.  This is the kind of humor you get to look forward to in Airline Tycoon 2.
I played through the tutorial, which does a decent enough job of introducing you to the game concepts.  It sent me around the airport to talk to various people, so I could meet all of the goofy characters the game has to offer.  It doesn't sound so bad when I say it, but eventually you get tired of running around the airport to visit the mechanic or go to the personnel office to hire a pilot, or hightail it back to your office to plan an airline route.
Imagine playing a city builder except every time you wanted to build a new building, you had to run over to the mayors office and talk to a caricature of the Godfather so you could tell him you want to zone a new block of houses.
So once I talk to Albert Einstein to get my plane decked out, and talk to someone else to get my pilot and crew hired, and someone else to actually tell my crew which plane they are working on, after all that then I can find the manager, so I can rent a route to fly my plane on.  They should have put out a version of this game for the Wii that is compatible with the Wii Fit balance board.
After all that, I can head back to my office to plan my flights for the week.   It's a bit like setting up meetings in outlook where each route takes up a chunk of time for the day, so the idea is you slot in as many round trips as you can, with some occasional maintenance inbetween flights.  You can also set the ticket price on your flights.  As the day progresses you can check on your flights and get statistics on things like how satisfied your passengers were and how much money your flight made.
The tutorial did fine at showing me around and introducing me to people I'd rather not talk to, but it doesn't really explain much about the actual strategy in the game.  For instance, there are a ton of different planes you can buy, and lots of ways to tailor how the plane looks, both exterior and interior.  But I have no idea if it's purely cosmetic or if these choices somehow impact customer satisfaction.
That's really where I ended up at the end of my first hour, wondering how and if my choices affected anything.  In the end, I realized that there's really only one choice that matters, and that is the choice not to play this anymore.
Overall Recommendation:  Pass

The best comparison to "Northgard" is the boardgame "Settlers of Catan",

and you have to build up your clan.
Gathering resources, fighting animals and undeads, managing your economy

The game takes place on a map that is seperated in different segments,
each segment has its own attributes, for example animals to hunt or farmland.
The building space on the segments is limited,
furthermore segments will remain hidden until you explored them with a scout,
so you never know what the conditions around you are.
After a few hours of play time and trying out different winning conditions

It's a fun game. Beautiful art style, good story, relaxing music. The mechanics ae simple, the stats are clear and don't require an advanced algebra degree to understand. The combat is diced-based with permadeath, and while it  can feel a little repetitive sometimes, it has moments of intensity that keep it from being to dull. If you main characters die in battle, it's game over, so you're often forced to sacrifice of your other units in order to save the main ones, which is difficult because they are usually just as, or more, powerful as/than your main charcters.
The map is beautifully drawn, but there isn't a huge variety of tiles, so every map kind of looks the same. Each tile can be fortified by your units, and some come with resources that you need to hire units, build armor and weapons, or heal, so you have to take into account risk/reward when choosing which tiles to conquer. Also some menus can't be closed by "esc", you actually have to hit the button for that menu again to close it.
There's a decent variety of missions, though they all essentially boil down to "get from point a-to-b", it's what's in between that changes, some missions have you fighting on two fronts, some missions have you fighting without access to any reources (which forces you to get though the mission before you run out of food for healing), Luckily, any weapons or armor you made in previous missions carry over, so at the very least you won't be forced to fight with your barehands after a few missions). You also get to keep all the surviving units you've recruited, though there is a limit on how many you can start each mission with.
The biggest drawback I think is that the game feels like a mobile port (it's not, to my knowledge) but the UI feels like it was designed for a touch screen, which makes moving around with a mouse a bit cumbersome since you have to drag and drop your units to get around the maps, and you can't reallly zoom out that far to make it a bit easier.
All in all, it's a fun, little game. Not too difficult to learn, but definitely not easy to beat (though there is a casual mode). And I'd say it's definitely worth the full asking price. Even though I got it on sale.

If you like idle and auto clicker endless games. Which I have a love/hate relationship with. Then I think it's worth checking this one out as well. I like that in order to progress, that the champions require different play styles. You have active and idle play champions. But then you also have a hybrid champion type as well called Energy Mode. While you can switch back and forth with different champions, each one has higher and higher stats as you unlock them. So I haven't seen a valid reason to go backwards.
There is also a rewards tree to apply points to. I don't know enough to make this a strategy guide. And it's an early game in development.
A few items that I hope they resolve/change.
- Leveling up. Like everyone else, you can pick increments like 1x, 25x, 100x, MAX. But it's an "up to" button and not an "exactly" button. So if you have level 10 of something and you have 25x for the level up button and you only have enough to buy up to level 22, you end up with 22. But luckily if you have enough to buy up to level 30 it stops at Level 25 (as the bonuses are every 25) But really this
- Mini game Mythical Invasion. As you collect tokens (or buy them) you can hire mercenaries to fight missions shown as islands. They are expended at each island , 1 island per fight. 10 warriors per fight. And you always win the battle. Nice. BUT, the problem is that right now the items contained in each chest is not predetermined before you click. But AFTER. It's NOT already determined before you click. There is nothing chosen until you click. So what chest you pick means nothing. It happens after you click a chest. If it was like a scratch card and determined for each chest before clicking, then if there was a crystal in a chest, you would have a 1 in 8 chance of picking it. But since they chose what you win AFTER clicking, they can make up whatever odds they want. And it's way lower odds than 1 in 8.
Will be nice to have more achievements for this game as well.
To the developers, perhaps look at Clicker Heroes and Tap Tycoon for some progression ideas. I also like the events idea which isn't quite implemented yet, but could be good in this game.
My love/hate with these types of games is the lack of a real ending. A sense of accomplishment. So I will play them in spurts. Daily bonuses help drag me back to check on the game. As a fan of turn-based strategy games and board games like Risk, Highlands was a very picturesque combination of the two. Make no mistake about, the art style is very attractive, and the setting was one of the reasons I ended up getting the title. So, how does the game function overall?
First, allow me to say that I ultimately enjoyed playing Highlands. The gameplay mechanics work, and function without too much issue. I will say that if you've experienced playing strategy games beforehand, the game will be noticeably easier as you might recognize the patterns/quirks of the gameplay. I should mention that earlier on, the game was apparently MUCH more difficult, as what is now the Challenging difficulty used to be the Normal mode. After finishing the game once and now starting over, I can say without hesitation that you will see a difference in how much you struggle--I finished normal mode without losing any units or resetting, but now I've lost at least 2-3 people in Chapter 2 alone.
So ultimately, Highlands has good versatility in its challenge (pending one's ability with strategy games), and for those that really want to test themselves, the harder modes will certainly grant that request.
Highlands functions very simplisticly--like Risk, you control regions of terrain on the map and send units to attack adjacent regions. Having a higher total number equals higher potential attack and a greater advantage against the enemy. When attacking, you choose a unit to block the incoming strike from the enemy. If the strength of the attack depletes their Combat points (which functions both as health and attack power), that unit dies.
Highlands strictly functions as a campaign of several maps, so the goal will usually be either clear the map of foes or reach/capture certain destinations. You are given a variety of "hero" characters, but you can also create generic units of your own from Taverns. There are four classes available: Combatant (soldier), Mechanic (defense-builder/crafter), Leader (region capturer), and Academic (medic).
I felt this system was effective and straightforward, but lacking in versatility. There's no real limitation on equipment for the different classes, so I found myself equipping shotguns and two-handed swords to my Academics in an effort to boost their "health", which seemed...strange. I feel having more items to craft and limiting them to certain classes would diversify the gameworld more. Otherwise, crafting devolves to "make the most powerful weapon for every single character, regardless of stats or class".
Similarly, I wouldn't have minded more situations to deal with in combat. You'll quickly become familiar with most of the enemy "types" there are, and apart from some additionally being "blockers" or "medics", fighting is mostly the same pattern. If the system was to be revisited/expanded on, perhaps units that did damage to more than one of your units (such as a flamethrower-type weapon) would open more options for combat, troop organization, etc.
Of the classes, I enjoyed the Mechanic the most. They serve a multitude of purposes, from item crafting to
, and were quite fun to get around the map.
Highlands is very beautiful--what could have been a much more generic combat "map" looks more vibrant and alive, with billowing clouds and moving flags and sails. Personally, I would have liked more character artwork, as the pallet of potential units seemed to get exhausted pretty quickly. Some classes clearly had more emphasis--like the Combatant--while others such as the Leader only had a handful of designs.
There's also some issue with reading text in certain aspect ratios. Granted, this happened mostly with unit names in the combat screen, so this was usually not too critical an issue. In large battles, however, the Combat points of the units come become distorted, which could be dangerous if you chose a lower-level soldier as your defender by mistake.
I'd also occasionally see vertical tears between certain tiles of terrain on the map or points icon, but these were minor issues. The rest of the world looks great--I give it a pass.
Being a musician myself, I always love a decent soundtrack in a game. Simon Tardif has given us a great, albeit limited, soundtrack to the world of Arislaan. The music gives an excellent, floating ambience that fits quite well with the design of the Highlands. My only complaint again is the quantity--all maps use the same tracks, and given they all take a while to complete, you can expect to hear all of them a few times each chapter. They blend very nicely, though, so unless you're consciously paying attention to the soundtrack all the time, this isn't too repetitive or intrusive. For what was available for the team, Tardif's music works well.
This is by far the biggest love/hate relationship of mine for Highlands. The world is beautiful. There's plenty of characters. Yet despite all of this, I struggled to really get into the story of the game. The story is relatively familiar, especially if you've played games from the Fire Emblem series: A peaceful, proud country (Arislaan) suddenly finds itself under attack by invading forces, threatening the royal family. Despite this downfall, they rally their people and fight to reclaim their country from the antagonizing force. It's a standard plot, but it has been shown to work well in numerous games, movies, and books.
The problem is that, even with all of the characters--Cecaelia, Leoric, Micah, Eldrich, and so on--I never felt a really strong emotional or personal connection to their struggles and achievements. It suffers a similar issue as Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon. Once introduced to a character, very little in terms of personality follows; it's just another (more powerful) unit. I really want to know more about Arislaan-- Who are these people? What are their likes and dislikes? How did they begin their service to the Duke, or what was their life like before coming? And where will they go or what will they do after the invasion is over?
As I said, I enjoyed playing Highlands--don't get distracted by my gripes. While its gameplay is simplistic, it was quite easy for me to get into. And allow me to say to Burrito Studio: I would certainly be interested in seeing another game to continue or expand this world. For those that aren't aware, Highlands was a Kickstarter game. Simply making the game was no doubt a challenge for them (they had just over $23,000 to work with, which quickly disappears in game development costs). Some of the limitations can be attributed to this, as a much larger budget would have given more room for expanding game mechanics and aesthetics. Hopefully, with Highlands' release, we might see more works from them in the future.
$15.00 might be a little steep for the amount of gameplay given (I completed the game in about 12 hours, with only a few achievements left), but for those that enjoy strategy games (especially Risk) with a mild steampunk-ish design, I'd say take a look at the very least. Finding the game for half price was more than satisfactory for me.

Doom reloaded - if you loved any of the Doom games, this is a MUST HAVE!
The Doom 3 BFG Edition as the ultimate Doom collection contains all four Doom episodes ("The Ultimate Doom"), of which most gamers only played the first one from the original shareware version, not knowing that there's something more awesome - but harder to play - after being Knee-Deep in the Dead.
Furthermore, Doom II including its add-on "No Rest for the Living" is also part of the package. The add-on was primarily developed for Xbox only but found its way into this ultimate collection for all platforms. Again, most of the Doom II players are not familiar with this absolutely great expansion, for sure.
The Doom 3 BFG Edition would be nothing without Doom³ and id Software's official expansion "Resurrection Of Evil" ... BUT: The Lost Mission will kill you! From my opinion, this is the best single player part of all three Doom³-based contents.
As some technical information, it's needed to be said that the game was originally released based on the id Tech 4 engine, but with the BFG Edition, some id Tech 5 engine's improvements found its way into Doom³ and its expansions. Also, Steam functions have been added, so you'll get achievements for PC like for all other platforms as well.
Furthermore - if you played the original Doom³ release - the player is now allowed to carry the flashlight AND a weapon. Remember the moments when you were to choose to use flashlight OR weapon?
The Doom 3 BFG Edition comes UNCUT for Germany and the rest of the world, so you won't buy a Piñata with this collection. In addition, if you manage to buy this edition in Germany's game shops, you'll get a valid RAGE copy in addition - for the same price.

Street fighter has always been one of the best fighting games in the industry, it was the flagship of fighting games for a long time, with street fighter Iv it renew the once great name of the game.
With street fighter V, it didnt reinvent the formula, but it polished it a little bit more, this is talking about pure game play only, as a fighting game, the actual fighting is great, it is one of the best in the present, basically, it just feels right, it just feels good, from the normal atacks, the atacks animations, the small but significant and relatively easy to pull combos, to the looks and animtions of some of the reworked special atacks and supers, the array of characters (even if they arent that many, even with dlc's) it is just good, if not great.....
Now with all that said, we will talk about the bad stuff: first of all, graphics in the pc version are not performing as it should in low to mid grade pc's.
My rig an asus rog gaming laptop with a Nvidia GTX 670MX graphic card, which it may not be top of the line now a days, but it certainly is not on the low end of the spectrum either, and im really sad to say, the graphics engine sometimes it perform really bad, even with autoadjust graphic tools like GeForce expeirience (which get it right with most of the other games i play on my pc), it never get its quite right. It should look at the very least, as good as a console (PS4 or Xbox one), but honestly it should always look better, all the other games ive play in both a pc and ps4, the pc version always, i mean ALWAYS, looked better. In this game, some times it look better, if you adjust for a lower setting, it looks blurred, if you set higher, some times it lags (videolag). The most jaring thing, are the shadows, they show it freaking big pixels that  belong in the era of the NES, they are just too distracting and make things look plain bad, espcially in characters like Zangief, Chun-li, Karin, to name some. In other words, it suffers from the same problems MKX suffered at lauch, which cost them really bad reviews for a long time,  they were fixed in the end, and the game looks and permors godly, with the side effects that warner no longer supports pc versions of the game... : / .... sigh, but that is another story.
The other big proble is lack of single player mods.... No practice mode, challenges, survival are not enough to engage people, specially casual audience, and they are the bigger population on contrary of poppular belief.
Mainly the lack of arcade mode it diminish the gametime value of SFV, and it hurts the game very much, hell, arcade modes were where all started, were you enjoyed playing and replaying ours and ours, were you try new stuff in a safe enviroment, it is missing from this game, and it still is after the lackluster story mode in the new patch. The game will keep suffering bad reviews until this essential play mode its added.
About the dlc story mode.
First: WHY THE HELL IS SO CUMBERSOME TO EVEN DOWNLOAD THE DAMN THING IF ITS FREE ??????  and WHY ITS A DLC IN THE FIRST PLACE?????, and that is only for starters, i had to research several posts, websites and people before i found out that you had to go to the library, then to game properteis, check a box there for the dlc to start downloading, to find out that in top of the 8-9 gigs i just downladed i had to download another 7.4 gigs more.... bad, simply bad.
Then i started playing, i hoped it was like story modes in other streetfighting games, where you select a character and you play through a series of fights to get to the boss, with cutscenes in between (A.K.A. arcade mode with story elements), its not, its  a single fight, in the lowest setting of  dificulty, with some game characers and some generic soldiers ..... :/ .... and then the cutscenes, most were made in game graphics, with really bad dialogue, and really bad english dubbed performance, it wouldnt feel so bad if they were few and farther between, but they 3-5 mins long, before and after a less then a min very easy fight.... and story itself.... well ... an arcade mode with no story at all would have been a way better way to spend resources and not waste our time.
Lastly, it seems the game was made with only fighting focus, sadly, i have play 1 game only, and not for the lack of trying,  the match system doesnt ever let me play, ever, ive try, many many times, because outside of realy money, it is the only way to get ingame currency to be able to get new colors, characters, stages, costumes, etc.... so basically, im being force to pay more to get some of the normal, regular stuff i use to get by playing the game, but since i can only play practice and survival mode (cause story is a big pile of BS), there is no way else to get them.
It is sad, cause the fighting is good, but all they other issues are too big to ignore. I was dissapointed, it was a really big let down from capcom, i always had better opinion about the company
Until they fix all those issues, i will not recomend the game. 5-6/10 (only because the fighting is good when you have friends to play with, but honestly most of the time it scores even lower than that)

Easily one of the best single player games I've played in years.
Great atmosphere, it feels like the game is actually alive. This applies to the menus and the game design itself. Driving my car at night during rain (especially with the high definition texture pack dlc), listening to Chinese music from the radio, people shouting at me for bumping their car.. Great work on this one.
It is really nice how the game designers could make a balance between armed and unarmed combat. Most games fail to do this, they go with the "brawling at the first few missions and guns for the rest of the game". The fighting system was complex enough and the gun battles were great too.
Another thing that captured me was the voice acting. Very few people realize how important this is, bad voice acting can really ruin the game. Here the voice actors did a great job, the characters felt like they were alive and not just a bunch of code, script, 3D model and voice files.
I've read from the other reviews that some people had issues with the controls. For me they were flawless, once I got used to the unusual keyboard layout (run with space, walk with shift, aim with shift) there were no problems at all.
The only strange thing is the story. It is very deep and you can lose yourself in it completely. It is unlike most of the videogame stories, more like a good movie. The ending however feels like it was cut short and there could have been more to it.
Almost every game of this type wants so bad to be GTA that it fails badly. In my opinion this was not the case with Sleeping Dogs.
All in all, it is a 9.5/10 game for me, I recommend it to anyone who likes open world games.

I used to have an old review of Street Fighter V, written a few weeks after it's relase, with the final conclusion of NOT RECOMMENDED at that time. This new review is written roughly a half year later.
For those who are not familiar with Street Fighter as a franchise and compare it to other similar games, thinking mainly Mortal Kombat here, you should know some key differences regarding gameplay. Street Fighter isn't for those, who are looking for an easy entertainment. It isn't famous and loved for the same thing MK is loved for. Mortal Kombat on the surface may be the more popular among casuals, but because it is flashy - it's all about violence, blood and gore, execution / fatality animations that go beyond ridicolous with their level of violence, HOWEVER it lacks the depth as a fighting game taken seriously, because Netherrealm is always aiming for the potential mass sales instead of trying to appeal for the diehard fighting game fans. Street Fighter has always been the latter, but that slightly changes with SFV.
With Street Fighter V, CAPCOM tried to open up the fighter genre to more people, while keeping everything that makes Street Fighter so much better as a serious fighting game than MK or anything else. The complexity, depth, strategy, meter mangment and mindgames are still there, several layers more than MK9/MKX/Injustice. You still have to time your moves after each other, learn what canceling a move to another is, linking a move to another is, and so on and so on that MK never had because of it's automatic combo system where you just "type in" what you want and the game plays it for you regardless of your timing, is still here, and it's still an exellent fighting system, HOWEVER it is made much more friendly to new players by loosening the strict 1-2 frame timings to a much wider window, so those who spend time with training, learning, playing WILL be able to master the game without absolute perfection required. Plus, the game has absolutely EXCELLENT training sessions now that explain and teach you all the battle systems you have to be familiar with from the basics of blocking and attacking to the more advanced techniques, everything, knowledge that applies to all characters so you can improve, and Street Fighter IV really missed this and it's propably why the playground of the advanced-dedicated players. SFV however, is for everyone.
SFV had it's problems on launch. The servers were unstable as hell for a very long time on PC while CAPCOM claimed to have "fixed" it a few days after launch. Keyboard controls are simply outragous, you have GHJK/BNM[,] and WASD plus Enter/Escape for menus, and the game didn't recognize ANY other button from your keyboard. The starting set of 12 characters was a very low number compared to the starting ~16-18(?) roster of SFIV back in it's time, not to mention the later expansions raising this number almost up to 40. The game suffered from unstable framerate issues that outright kills a game like this for the hardcore scene, and without the hardcore scene to promote the game and TONS of missing singleplayer content, casuals aren't really coming to play it.
Now, some things have changed, some didn't.
POSTIVE CHANGES:
The server issues are gone, the framerate issues are gone, several characters has been added to the game (earnable ingame or through 4-5 euros per character OR season pass... people didn't understand how new editions that keep the game "full priced" while old editions could be upgraded was a great concept, newcomers get everything additional content for the same price old players paid, while old players can upgrade for cheap, was a good thing. People hated CAPCOM for it for some reason, so yeah, season pass, be happy with it!), a great new cinematic singleplayer story mode has arrived for completely free (be sure to add and download it, it's free DLC, and may require activation in your library, right click on game, properties, DLCs tab, "check"). Because of the #RISE - pun intended - of the game's reputation with the added story mode, more and more players buy in or return to SFV on PC, that combined with the option to crossplay with PS4 players actually made a healthy, growing online scene. This is the good stuff.
NEGATIVE (changes didn't happen):
Keyboard support is still a piece of sh.t. If you want to play on a keyboard because you don't want to buy a controller for this game, you have to use a 3rd party program called AutoHotKey and write a script in it to be able to remap your keys to your liking. I offer help with that, if you need. If you have a X360 controller for Windows, it will run flawlessly with this game, but otherwise controller compatbility issues mainly concerning those with arcade sticks, still remain unfixed. It it outrageous knowing the game is PC/PS4 exclusive, and even PS4 controller compatibility issues arise while X360 controller works. Arcade mode is still missing, for those who are interested in it for some reason (I'm not), you should know. It's beyond my understanding why CAPCOM didn't add this yet, everything is there and functioning.
Ultimately, I changed the review because I was interested in the - by the way goofy and cringeworthy - story mode, finally got my AutoHotKey script working the way I wanted it so I can finally control the game the same way I played SFIV for 7 years, then I got stuck here after the story, digged myself to the depths of characters I love from this universe (previous games, anime), went online, found tons of people to play with and before I knew I was having tons of fun, finding challange in learning to play SF hardcore again with the changes after SFIV being the challange itself to overcome. And that's how from my 2 hours under 5 months playtime became over 30 in less than a week.
For those who are all about online competition, wanting to better themselves at something, finding challange in learning and turning the tide instead of getting frustrated because the game doesn't give you "omg you are the coolest dude ever have all this sh.t feel like a most hardcore player you are my hero" enouragements even if you don't deserve it yet, who are frustrated of being dragged down by others in team based games such as Overwatch / MOBAs, Street Fighter V and it's 1v1 face to face fight is for you. For the more casual, you have a long story mode to play through (4 hours), tons of training, trials, demonstrations, high accessability, but still missing arcade mode. You have to understand, this game is all about pure PvP, everything you need to train vs AI (that you can deeply customize to traing specific situations) is there however. Some technical issues are still present such as lack of native support for keyboard customization and some controller compatibility problems with noname stuff and some arcade sticks, but that's where it ends, otherwise it is an excellent PC port compared to Mortal Kombat series especially. If you have lag issues, be sure to set matchmaking to 5 star connection players only, and it's flawless. Was the IV generation better as a hardcore fighting game? Oh boy sure it was, sure it still is. However CAPCOM is promoting the living sh.t out of the V generation, adds content to it, the fighting game community moved over, the tournaments moved over, everything in the f.g.c. is about SFV and will stay that way for years to come, with about a week or two break when Injustice 2 gets out, because that's how much it takes for the f.g.c. to abandon it. Happend with every Netherrealm game for a good reason and the next won't be different for a good reason. Street Fighter however FAR dominates among the fighting games for generations now regarding 90% of the f.g.c. 's interests, and for a good reason. SFV after some hiccups, can proudly keep running with the flame SFIV passed on.

This game's made me lose faith in game critics, I've tried hard to see what the appeal is. I'll try and break it down to see if I'm missing something:
So we have a game mechanic that involves you controlling a character from a third person view using point and click interactions to interact with the environment. Doesn't seem too original to me, I've played many many games that use that same mechanic, to me it's boring to others it might be new.
So what else do we have; the storyline; post-apocalyptic. Trying to rebuild the world. There was a war. Again it's not really original enough for me, fair enough if you've not heard that story before then it might be intriguing, not for me though.
The sound - music is nice I wouldn't class it as critically acclaimed but fits the mood of the game and is varied enough to not bore me. The narration for me is probably the nicest feature, it makes the game a lot more immersive, the voice acting spot on.
Graphic assets; they look OK, they have their own style and feel, environment feels slightly dream-like not sure how that connects with any of the other aspects of the game though.
Can't think of much more to assess, am I missing something? My conclusion is that we have an over-used game mechanic combined with an over-used story but with a half decent soundtrack and a novel way of narrating a computer game. Problem is you can't rate a game on the narrator it's like reviewing a restaurant based on the quality of the plates.

Have been beta testing this since the first private beta build, and it is an absolute must-have for any serious game artist. Marmoset's Toolbag has always been the go-to for real time rendering, particularly for game assets, and 3 is no exception.
Since Toolbag 2, several key features have been added on top of core and lighting improvements, particularly:
- Animation support
- Real time global illumination
- Texture baking (one of the best bakers I've used to date, too)
- Massively improved lighting and general rendering quality
- Handles high poly models, particularly Zbrush sculpts with ease
And as Marmoset has a great track record about adding features to their tools in post-launch updates, it will only get better over time.

Highlands plays a lot like Risk, but has some really interesting elements to it that balance the gameplay and difficulty out.  In Risk, and Civilization, once you gain the upper hand the game is as good as won, and it's an unmotivated steamrolling of whatever's left in the game, which can really drag on.  In Highlands, taking a slower paced strategy can actually work against you, as every few turns there are respawns that get higher over time.  The third chapter in particular I had to restart because I wasn't aggressive enough at the beginning, and got boxed in and overwhelmed.  The resource management is pretty basic, but works well and plays a vital role to your success.  I felt like some abilities were slightly overpowered, but then on the last stage I realize it would have been impossible without them.  I think great attention was given to the overall balance of the game.
It falls a bit short on the story, and overall length.  It's about 15 hours total.  It lacks any kind of customization beyond a limited set of equipable items, which even on the weapon side is a one size fits all selection.  Level ups are important, but  adding a character attribute to advance each level would have added a ton of replayability to the game.
In summary, if you are looking for a quick, easy to learn, addictive turn based strategy game, this is an easy choice.  It has that Civilization feel of "one more turn" and the difficulty scales really well as you advance in the game.  I personally recommend doing the "Challenging" difficulty level if you are big into strategy games, which is the level I selected,

Still, it's a hugely enjoyable game in its present state and I heartily recommend it.

I fell in love with FPS with Doom 2. I played a lot the shareware of Doom. I've Doom Collector's Edition. I've Doom for GBA. I've played Doom 3 and RoE back then. Why do you think I owned that now? Because it contains old Doom for Win7. And because  now, I don't have to switch to flashling. And because there is a new mission. And... I'm a Doom fangirl. Nothing is better than Doom (and Half-Life).
Anyway, Doom 3 BFG Edition is composed of:
- Ultimate Doom
- Doom II
- Doom 3
- Doom 3: Resurrection of Evil
- The Lost Mission
Ultimate Doom is the original Doom with an episode added later. It means graphics from the 90', no jump button, mythic soundtrack. The only difference is that achievements were added. Not a lot though. You're a Marine sent on Mars after an altercation with your commanding officer. Too bad, you're the last one of the security still alive after something going wrong on Phobos...
Doom II is the sequel of Doom. After beating the demons, you returned on Earth. Unfortunately for you, it seems that Hell preceded you. It's up to you to save mankind! But as for Ultimate Doom, it's the same graphics, new soundtracks, the famous double-barreled shotgun and new enemies.
Doom 3 is a sort of reboot of Doom. You're sent on Mars to replace someone and well, it's the day someone decided that Hell will invade Mars. The graphics are those of mid-2000, with a nice soundtrack, the good old weapons with new designs. But this new version has a major difference: the flashlight is mounted on the weapon, which means that you loose a little of the ambiance where you had to switch from a weapon to a flashlight.
Doom 3: RoE is set two years after the loss of Mars City. A new signal has been picked up and Elizabeth McNeil's team return to check it. Too bad, the bad man from Doom 3 is back and you, as a new Marine, must defeat him. RoE introducted the principle of energy cells to transfer, a new artifact with special powers, the return of the double-barrelled gun and the introduction of the Grabber, sort of Gravity Gun. From the original RoE, the main difference is mainly set in Hell: you have a whole portion cut.
The Lost Mission is merely a sort of cut levels from Doom. It's just a nice bonus.
If you want a collection of Doom games, go for it. Because nothing is more fun to see the evolution and collect PDA, listening to them to get codes or reading them to get a good idea of the story, at least, for Doom 3. Because for Doom or Doom II, it's just a question of I shoot-I load-I find a key-I open the last door.

As you can tell I have put a lot of time into this game, and because of that I feel compelled to voice my opinion.
Now to start out I never really got into Terraria, to me it felt pointless. You can only walk so far left or right to adventure, only to have to walk back to your house to survive the night. Never really grasped me, but then came Starbound.
Starbound takes the same idea as Terraria, 2D side-scrolling world, you can dig, build and craft till' your heart is content. The beauty of Starbound is, when you've finally got tired of the world you're on, you can leave! Just beam up to your ship, and select a new planet! New adventure, new landscape, new dungeons etc.
Some of you may have your finger ready to click the buy button, but before you do I want to also let you in on something; it's not finished. I say this because it's very important you understand the level that this game is at, and where it needs to be to be complete.
First and foremost in my opinion is the progression, the system isn't even close to finished. At this point it's "Hello Welcome to Starbound, here's some basic supplies, now you're our interstellar b**ch and you're going to run all over retrieving the dumbest items we can think of".
When I first started I was like OKAY! My body is ready! But not anymore, I haven't actually sat down and delved back into SB for about 6 - 8 months. I do watch the dev's posts everyday (yes daily updates as to what is going on) and that's encouraging but watching those also shows how slowly stuff moves along.
The other system that isn't even close to done yet in my opinion is the combat, currently its when monster A hits player B, then do damage. That isn't an ideal system because it leaves you to kiting, jumping and then attack and that's basically it. If a monster gets to close, or basically close enough to inflict damage, it can be impossible to get away from them so you can return damage. Due to it being on-touch damage as soon as they touch you again, more damage, before you know it you've lost all your credits or items (depending on the difficulty you chose). You can't get them back because that monster is still there, waiting to touch you to death..
This for me ruined SB in a way I never expected because combat is such a crucial part of this game. Monsters drop stuff, and they also help you complete stuff, so not running into any monsters is pretty much impossible.
I know you're probably saying to yourself "But Soul, you recommended the game!" Yes I do recommend the game, and I do because I believe it will get better. I know the dev's aren't done and due to that I can only hope the systems I don't like in the game get altered. I know for a fact per the developer that they're going to re-implement hunger and temperatures but I haven't heard anything about the damage on touch.
All this is to say, if you can overcome the mishaps the game has because of it's level of incompleteness and really trial and error that the dev's have been doing, then buy it. If you can't overcome these things then wait. Starbound is a GREAT game, but it's just not done, and to hell with the people complaining about development time! You can't rush perfection!

It's the final round in a best of three set, the background npc's are going wild as the tension of the match rises. You stare down your opponent. A handsomely bearded man with muscles that ripple throughout the ages. HIs name is Ryu..... or in this case [Insertedgynamehere]. As both your healthbars close towards the endpoint you feel a rush of ecstasy as flashbacks rush your mind of the match thus far: Reacting to jump ins, landing combos and making clutch grabs. A sudden sweeping kick catches him offguard. A crush counter! A new mechanic in SFV, locking him down preventing a quick get up. In other words the perfect opportunity! You quickly runover to his laying body. One more blow to finish the match. As you consider grabbing to close off the game a quick glimpse of his previous wakeup shoryuken hits you.
In the final few frames of his get up animation you dash back............ A correct read. His shoryuken wiffs.... A quick dash and grab closes of this intense game and short sweet rivalry. A few moments later a notification pops up. You grin in anticpation as you accept your rivals friend request and demand of a rematch.....
This moment can be captured in any fighting decent fighting game. When the hype of a match rises after finding an opponent of your level and grinding a match against them. Pushing yourself to the limit of your ability and exceeding what is there is what makes fighting games fun. So time to actually start the review of this particular game Street fighter 5
-------REVIEW STARTS HERE------
Previously to a casual audience I would have said no. And I have said no to several friends in buying street fighter 5. However that was in it's pre-June update state. As of the June update it has become a fully fledged fighting game with all the functions it lacked on release: A fully animated cinematic story mode, fully functioning store and trials for each individual character. However that's not to say it has finished in its improvements and street fighter still has to build atop what it already has to truly become where it should have been in it's glory on release day.
--Pros--
-A fully animated story mode
-A cast of very diverse characters (Design wise)
-A set of characters that have very different playstyles (All very fun to play)
-A well flushed out lab (training mode)
-Possibly the easiest to get into iteration of street fighter yet (I think this is a good thing)
-Beautiful animations
-Dlc characters can be unlocked via in-game points (Fight money)
-Fight money is pretty much hand-fed to begin with via the character storys and general story
-The core of the game (mechanics) are incredibly well done smooth and work very well
-Capcom released character specific tutorial videos (On youtube)
-More DLC characters to come (I'm waiting for you Juri)
--Cons--
-No arcade mode
-Cannot do a single seperate match against a CPU
-Questionable way to give out colours via the survival mode
-Fight money is hard to come by past the previously mentioned story modes (Forces you to pick and choose and spend wisely or you will be grinding for a long time)
-Lack of punishment for ragequitters as far as I'm aware (However they are supposedly cracking down and banning them)
-Connection (For the most part my matches are quite nice when I say this I mean if I set the connection to 4-5 only why is it still occasionally giving me someone with a 2 bar connection to me?)
-Location (This is more of a personal one which has improved lately but for whatver reason I rarely play people from the UK or even Europe. I've probably played more Americans and Asians than I have people from Europe this can lead to connection issues but again has been improving)
--Anything I missed--
-Tutorial (Pretty generic stuff some conversation between Ken and Ryu that's about it)
-Stats (I'm not sure if it's just me I feel like it's not implemented properly as of yet)
-Access to replays of anyone you like (Pretty neat)
-Misguiding names (I mean a small thing IMO but something like your favourite character being designated as your "use for matches" character)
--Final words--
So if your wondering why I used an anecdote to start off my review it was because I wanted to capture something and share what every game should be striving to do. Be fun. In the end what were games made to be? Fun. Fun for me is being able to tryhard and have a good match. I mean I lose all the time and I've been on tilt way more than once being serious about this game. But in tanking all those losses I've become better at the game and when I hit the sweet sensation of victory BANG it's all there. The rush that makes me love this game :)
In the end it's up to you if you still want to play and buy the game. From my perspective Street FIghter 5 is an awesome game with a lot to offer (Now with the update) to both casuals and tryhards like myself. You can do whatever. You want to just play the game for the cutscenes and storymode? Sure play it and skip all the matches that come with the storymode. You want to become an elitist pro in the top 100 players? Sure hit up ranked and become an online warrior. You just like learning combos and making your character look awesome? Go for it training mode is for you. What I'm trying to say is despite all the crap it's been given (which it deserved) on release day I feel like it's redeemed itself (albeit roughly 4-5 months later) and missing out just because of those reviews is a waste. I still do reccomend waiting for a sale or something though :) Money is sparse nowadays.
PS. Sorry for how long this was

released in 1998 for the PlayStation (just way uglier and devoid of personality), the game is bereft of a soul. Its main strength comes from its humour which, to be fair, is largely hit or miss (mostly miss). Its inspirations are clear but none of them are treated with respect. I recognised at least two or three puzzles directly copied from
. H. P. Lovecraft's works serve mostly as a thematic concept for the visual design of the monsters and the story itself (which is then all thrown out the window at the end anyway). Other segments in the game - where you are forced to switch from a bird's-eye-view to first-person - come across as an unnavigable dime a dozen "white mouldy corridor walking simulator" rendition of
(if

All this coupled with the fact that there exists no option for saving your game and that it does not feature a decent checkpoint system, and you're condemned to prolong your exposure to this game by retrying an entire level from scratch if you mess up.
Nevertheless, there are certainly segments in the game that show the developers' potential for creating a far better game than
ever could be. It  has some jokes that actually hit well, sometimes features interesting puzzle designs and has moments where there are some clever bits of storytelling through its environment. Unfortunately, it is all bogged down by its own nature. It is a disorganised, repulsive, mean-spirited and (at best) a barely subpar mess.

After over 100 hours put into the game, I think I'm ready to review Street Fighter V. To preface this, I am a Street Fighter fan, and after the relative success they enjoyed from past iterations, I was ready and willing to spring for both the base game and the season pass at launch. During the game's initial forays, I found I was disappointed. The character story was lacking, battle lounges had no capacity for more than 2 players, as well as the lack of communication between players (you can only rely on pre-determined phrases you select from a menu). On top of this, there are issues with 8 frames of input lag, as well as the fact that you have to unlock colors via Survival Mode, which sounds simple on the surface, but it entails grinding through all difficulty levels (10 on easy, 30 on normal, and 50 on hard). If you lose, you have to start completely over. To further add to the grind, you have to do this for each costume you wish to unlock colors for. Fortunately, there have been some kind souls that have alleviated the process substantially.
As it stands now, more characters have been released (bringing the roster from the original 16 to 20), with two more on the way hopefully next month as of this writing. They have also released a statement saying they are considering other avenues for unlocking colors, and they've at least showed they've started listening. As for the gameplay itself, as I've stated before, it is well known that there are 8 frames of input lag, but the combat and controls are all comfortable and easier to learn. The training mode is adequate and the trials provide a decent jumping point for learning about a character. Of course, to get in-depth about a character, their frame data, and specific match-up knowledge, it's best to turn to
or other resources.
The addition of a fully fleshed-out story mode, titled "A Shadow Falls", is a entertaining 3-hour foray into the Street Fighter universe, even if it's a little canned and full of anime tropes. If nothing else, it's a good source of Fight Money. Unfortunately, in terms of garnering a new audience, I feel that was too little, too late. Had Capcom had released the story DLC on day one, they would've captured a new generation of Street Fighter enthusiasts.
All in all, I recommend the game. Despite several issues, Capcom has gotten around to addressing some of the major issues the community has expressed, and things have started looking up. At it's core, Street Fighter V is a solid game that continues to retain the mechanics that swept the gaming world so many years ago. With its excellent soundtrack, solid mechanics, and easy to pick up gameplay (that is hard to master), it is sure to not disappoint.

Well, this wasn't what I expected. BA (Blackbay Asylum) is exactly what I needed at a recent time of personal horror/adventure-craving. It's not easy finding many horror games that are this scary while focusing on puzzles. Yes, BA is at its core an adventure/puzzle game. It's even comparable to Sherlock Holmes The Awakened in a few ways: puzzle-heavy game with Lovecraftian horror and Cthulhu story.
PROS: Considering that most of the game is in top-down perspective, the creep factor is still huge as you wonder what you're going to come across at every corner. I say "most" because a few parts of this game are in first-person. Amazingly the game brilliantly combines the two gameplay styles together without difficulty. I have to admit that Chapter 3 (in its 1st person) was a level I won't forget anytime soon; this area frightened me so much I had to take minor breaks. While I don't need breathers while replaying (knowing now what to expect) I will say the level includes some horrific/bizarre imagery and edge-of-your-seat sound. You'll find more quality and depth in this one mission than the entirety of most other horror games! I also love the protagonist's endless un-PC comments whenever he interacts with something he cannot pick up. If you aren't easily offended, you'll get more than a few laughs. There are some good challenging puzzles which ocassionally required a walkthrough, but otherwise make you feel good as you accomplish them.
CONS: Given the chapter count, you would think during the first few levels that the game is lengthy. Unfortunately it's not. Surprisingly while some chapters are long, some are ridiculously short in comparison. If you know what to do, one of them can even be completed in less than 30 seconds! The second half of the game isn't as engaging either. From the 1st Chapter your character lawnmowers a mad cook, later followed by the horrifying 3rd. These left me wondering, could the game get any more compelling and strange? Not necessarily, but I certainly wouldn't expect it to be less! As you delve closer to the Cthulhu-mystery the game loses a lot of the shock and style that it opens up with. I liked the final boss "battle" but the concluding cutscene, though interesting, was brief and made little sense. It almost seemed very anti-climatic, and this doesn't look the kind of game that aches for a sequel.
Overall, I enjoyed the game a lot and it's well worth a purchase. I do think there's a slight missed opportunity here though. As a Cthulhu-inspired story it had a lot of potential, and the game's first half makes you believe it will reach it. Though it never ceases to be fun, I did feel a bit let down towards the end with the lack of horrifying build-up. Maybe I was expecting too much, but when the first few levels really displayed something special I would hope the game persisted from that. Still, if you're looking for some challenging puzzles filled with memorable and horrific moments then BA might be the right choice!

Blackbay Asylum is a top-down/first person puzzle/horror game set at the eponymous Blackbay Asylum, which is located off the coast of Innsmouth, Massachusetts. For those who are unfamiliar, Innsmouth is a fictional city known for it’s relation to the HP Lovecraft mythos. In here, you play as Doug, a large and heavily muscled man who recently incarcerated at Blackbay for being a mass murdering sociopath.
Gameplay in Blackbay Asylum generally consists of moving Doug through the level, collecting the equipment and knowledge to solve each puzzle as it pops up. Speaking of the game as a whole, the puzzler aspect is much stronger than the horror one. Although the first few chapters left me unimpressed, (if you can make sense of it then you can get through the first level within 10 minutes) it was probably designed that way to bring people into the game a lot more. The puzzles in the first level aren’t too difficult and they get you really immersed in the game and also makes you feel more intelligent than when you started. And it doesn’t take long for them to get genuinely tricky. Some of them have fairly simple gimmicks to work out before you can progress, but for the most part they’re cerebral enough to keep the old noggin’ working. Just like any good puzzler, the challenges you’re faced by start off fairly simple but ramp up the difficult as you go on.
Characters in the game are rare to come by; a lot of the other people that you see in the game are dead, dying or will soon be dead (either by monsters hands or by you) but the people you do come across aren’t overly well written. For instance you come across a man who is hiding in a dumpster in the first level who sounds insane, ironically, and some of the things he says just seem a bit too wild even for an insane asylum. Also a receptionist at the front desk who is working and on her cell phone the whole time doesn’t seem to care when a giant man covered in blood walks from Isolation into the lobby which is a bit odd. That being said, it’s worth reminding you that
is indeed a horror game. While the dialogue and descriptions are exceedingly silly, every aspect of the game is eerie.
So, I’d played through the first two chapters of the game and then I landed in Chapter 3. The third Chapter of BBA is almost flawless. It is genuine horror, perfectly executed. The camera moves from being a top down puzzle adventure game to a first person perspective and it’s at this point where you start to notice the graphics of the game, allowing you to see more of the surrounding environment more than before. From the top down perspective the graphics don’t really seem to great however once you start looking through Doug’s eyes you notice some smaller things in the game. And this was a great way to use the shift in perspective because there are things that you can only see through Doug’s eyes at this point such as items on the middle shelf or a piece of information written on a notice board. While in this first-person section, there were times when I had to stop playing for a few minutes, and just breath. I don’t mind admitting that I got genuinely spooked by the atmosphere it managed to create.
Whether you should play this game is determined by your tastes as a gamer. If you’re on the older side and looking to play as many adventure games as you can or don’t like puzzles, horror games, or any horror games that don’t take themselves seriously, I can’t say I’d recommend BlackBay Asylum. As for me, I think that Blackbay Asylum is a welcome addition to my Steam library and hearkens back to the days of top down action adventure, with a touch of horror, and some first person puzzle games which is terrific.

+However there should still be a way for people to resurrect such as bringing back the ammy.

What it falls down on:

+This means that people can get bored and only people who can stand for nonsensical repetition can play for thousands of hours and still have fun

A case of paradise found, or paradise lost?
I've played all Burnout games since Point of Impact, except Dominator. Paradise seemed just as exciting as previous titles in the series to begin with, but by the end it became an exercise in anger management. Having completed it on the PS3 I thought coming back to it on PC was going to be a cakewalk. If only.
Enjoying Paradise depends on a lot of ifs. Where you are at in the game, how much you intend to play, and how easily things annoy you, for starters.
The game dumps you on a map and basically says 'Enjoy!', leaving you to discover everything it offers for yourself. Perhaps the first and biggest wonder you'll notice is the miraculous lack of people - even the random cars you see on the road are all empty. Even your own car. Compared to games like GTA this is a bit of a sore point for me - having someone to run over and some voice-acting to laugh at would have been a nice addition. The only voice there is to listen to (besides the soundtrack / music) is DJ Atomica, who never ceases to bring you down with some disparaging remark when you lose an event. Sometimes he's ok, but the game would have been better off without his five pence of 'try harder' and 'the route you choose' bull.
If driving around in Robot City isn't a problem for you then you might like this title. There is a big garage of awesome looking cars to unlock, and the freedom of having a huge map fully unlocked already means you can pick and choose which roads to use in races and events. Occasionally it can get confusing, but the option is there to check an event's route before you start it, so you can take your time deciding how best to navigate the roads to get to where you need to as fast and effortlessly as possible.
Collectibles include challenges (both offline and online - online lists challenges for each of 2 players through to 8 players); smashes (which are construction fences that often fence off short-cuts); billboards (for smashing through as well); and super jumps. Just finding all of these can be a chore.
In addition, each road has a fastest lap record to beat, and a crash mode record to beat. Some roads are little, others are huge. Crash mode isn't quite the same as previous games though, where you get a specific set-up and have a bunch of buses all packed together in the distance. Instead, while driving you can start crash mode at the touch of a button (but careful not to start it in the middle of a race). The goal here is to rack up a big $$$ of carnage, hitting traffic, buses, signs, anything with a $$$ painted over it. The event stops when your boost bar empties, but is filled regularly as long as you keep hitting things. This is one of the more fun aspects of the game, but it can be frustrating too, as all too often the crash traffic will spawn on roads you can never possibly reach, sometimes you'll see traffic spawn in the distance only to de-spawn before it reaches you (possibly because too much traffic is spawning on other roads), and traffic has an awful habit of avoiding your bouncing wreck trying to aim for them. Overall it's fun, but I get the feeling it needs a patch or something.
Event types are colour-coded on the map, thankfully, as there are over a hundred and finding what you want can be problematic. They are broken down into races, burning routes (car-specific race against the clock), stunt runs, road rages (using your car to take out other cars within a time limit), and marked man (which is the biggest pile of doo-doo since Jurassic Park).
The goal of the game is to keep unlocking new licences, ending with the Burnout Elite licence, requiring you to complete everything. Up until this last licence it is possible to avoid most events you don't like, but this last licence forces you into events you may hate. For me it was Marked Man - an event that is akin to a bull in a china shop, with you playing as the china. It seems to me too heavily reliant on dumb luck just to survive the longer distances - repair drive-thrus often being too few or too far away to be of any use. I see it as utterly preposterous and totally unnecessary. Sometimes all you can do is sit and watch in sheer disbelief as attack cars rain down on your humble car from every possible angle, sometimes t-boning you mere seconds after respawning, leaving you no room to escape at all. And to top it all off DJ Atomica will whine at you afterwards, saying you have no skill.
Apologies to my brother,
, and my family for all the foul language and violence when I started doing Marked Man.
It's a shame but I believe Marked Man events will be a game breaker for perfectionists looking to get 100%. It can be done, but you may find items around you will get broken in your rage. Lots of excessive cinematics in the menu and waiting for cars to drop in before you can choose them to drive make the game unnecessarily longer. The menu is messed up to begin with - you use F1 and F2 to navigate various menus and a web page - not to mention the fail webpage that still tries to load every time you start the game.
But the visuals are pretty good considering the game's age, and the soundtrack is pretty beast. If you're a racing fan, need more cars to play with and there's nothing better out there, then you'll get this despite the menu problems or stupid Marked Man. Due to all the enjoyment I've had I can't recommend against it, but it's pretty close. 50/50. Racing probably isn't for me.

Any vehicle can destroy you if your relative velocity is too great.
If ea would add in the preexisting campaign mode which uses what appears to be a primitive version of the open map (and therefore a lightweight addition) I would be willing to get that as a dlc, or even as its own game with updated physics, over this one

This game is getting older as we speak. The game is a classic and is really the best Burnout game in the series, I love this game personally and can play it for hours with its multiple missions and many different cars. The cars in this game... Well I love them really, starting the cars driving them at high speeds through the city and the hills. There are many DLCs ,which you know I hate, but there is a definate way to bypass that. The cars are all interesting and really fun to drive, the handling is very easy and you can definatley feel the freedom when you're driving.
Firstly the cars in this are awesome! You can get many styles of cars such as: Rage, stunt, street and that wierd turbo thing that only lets you recharge... The entire car system has many different styles of driving, the cars can be stock or the upgraded unlocked version of the original car. You can get mini cars, police cars and many more random types of new cars which can only be found on the origin store. The DLC for paradise island is only avalible for the console versions of this game but you can mod it into the game which adds buggys and a whole new island. The entire games map is massive compared to new games and its nicley detailed, the whole thing has events placed "at every intersection" as explained in the first part of the game which is true! Events on every intersection which can be played again but only to beat your score.
The map concludes of beaches, mountains and city scapes with loads of driving to do. I had some technical problems with the game trying to set up multiplayer, EA actually sent me a copy onto my Origin account which then worked. The games multiplayer consists of free drive, races, stunt runs and free races (which is where you set up your own races for your friends). I like playing with my friends because you can have a lot of fun seeing who can get the biggest air alltogether in a certain place or just driving for fun. Multiplayer does have a negative side to it though, its very anoying to setup with multiple game platforms Steam/Origin but I was the only one with this problem.
