First review, but I will make it short and brief.
On Thursday, I wanted to get Age of Empires II because I utterly love all types of RTS' and Turn Based. Well, I switched over to the store and saw Northgard. I was instantly hooked, and with a $20 price tag, I couldn't resist. I bought it, waited an hour for it to load, and then I played it. I went on for three hours straight during launch, probably longer, not sure. I seriously hope good things come to this place, it's a real good game.
Pros:
- Nothing is too complex for this simple game, a young person could sit down and instantly know how to play the game within moments.
- Combat is simple and easy. Right click an area with your troops and they'll go there and attack.
- Buildings are unique, along with tech trees for various clans.
- Game gives you a good understanding of areas you can explore and colonize. (Meaning what gives you good resources and what not.)
Cons:
- Combat is pretty bland, honestly. You just have warriors, no archers, shield men, raiders, etc. Would seriously love to see more of it.
- Clan balances are kinda bad. The Wolf Clan starts off with increased attack, and if they get alot of lore, they can just spam into their military line and boost up even more damage. Where as the Goat Clan seems to be about survival and holding out.
- Some bugs that are pretty insane. I was sitting at the Helheim portal for 12 months and built a tower to defend it while my Warchief was off defending against the Goat Clan, but the thing fell and I lost the area. I turn back and I see twenty Valkire spawned. After a few more moments, my swamp next to it is under attack by ten of them. After I lose it I turn back and see that there are fourty one Valkire. Fourty One! And they will continue to endlessly spawn.
Overrall, the game is pretty dang fun. I will continue to play the hell out of it when I have the chance.
However, some misc things are, and I'd love to see the dev put them in are.
- Time. I know it's an RTS, but I'd love to slow down my game so I can organize my troops and peasents.
- Bigger warning icons above the map. I had almost my entire clan die due to sickness and I didn't even notice because I was too focused on the game.
Edit - Another thing I'd love is larger maps and more options to increase or decrease enemy spawn, more farm land, more forests, more dens, etc.
Edit 2 - The dev has fixed the Helheim spawning glitch, yay!

Highlands is a turn-based strategy set on a series of floating islands. The royal family in this world apparently have quite a set of cojones, as they are on the front lines with their troops the entire time. You can recruit new fodder in taverns littered around the map. There are a multitude of classes available, leaders capture resource points, engineers/mechanics can craft weapons and armor as well as fortifying your points on the map. Combatants are the meatshields, and academics are used to keep the meat on their feet.
Enemy robots and warlords will consistently advance on your position. Luckily your enemies can only move through your areas one at a time, but they do spawn friends after a set amount of turns (depending on the difficulty) which helps to keep the pressure on. There have been multiple situations where I screwed around for far too long capturing points only to be forced into combat with an almost insurmountable force at the end of the map. How did I overcome? Molotovs. Lots and lots of molotovs.
Trying to keep a decent pace while not missing out on crucial resources is indeed a delicate dance, and as with most dances, I fail pretty miserably. Leadership is a resource used to recruit new troops, food is used as upkeep for your troops as well as keeping your characters healed, finally scrap is used in every sort of crafting imaginable. Gearing up your troops with weapons and armor increases their fighting ability, but all the skill in the world won’t save your characters from the ever-looming threat of permadeath.
Random events ensure no game plays out the same, but the story will remain the same. While the events are cool, this along with some flowery writing and amazing visuals don’t really motivate me to give the game a second playthrough. I’m supremely glad I got to experience it, and won’t hesitate to call it another kickstarter success story, but I don’t think I’ll be sitting down to trek through it again, at least for a little while. Fantastic first game by Burrito Studio, we at IGB can’t wait to see what is next.

I was a Kickstarter backer for this game, but I honestly didn't think I would enjoy playing it myself. Turn-based strategy games are not usually my thing. So I was pleasantly surprised to find that I enjoy playing this very much.
The hand-drawn art is gorgeous (although it's hard to read the white text that appears over it and I wish they had given the text a black lining). I also like the intro that plays when you start a game, but I do not like that there doesn't seem to be a way to skip past it or to skip the tutorial aspects during the first chapter. This is a game that I'll want to play multiple times. I do not need a reminder of what each character type can do.
At the same time, the game leaves out important information at times. If an item that you have found or crafted isn't equipped at the end of the level, you lose it. They don't tell you this until after the end of the first level. So I lost a couple items. Nbd though.
Some people have expressed frustration with enemy characters spawning too quickly. The AI can be aggressive and that was overwhelming at first, but that's not an inherently bad feature (I mean, overwhelming enemies is the whole point of Castle Panic, and that's a great game). It's just part of the strategy. Just because enemies are spawning does not mean that you have to defeat all enemies to beat a level. Just a thought. And I have found that it's best to take things sloooowly. Take a few turns to build up your defenses before moving on to the next sector. Stock up on resources and don't be afraid to use your milita skill.
Like the description says, this game is easy to learn, but hard to master. You can choose your level of gameplay, which is cool, because I like to use casual gameplay first and work my way to the top.
Oh, and I have to say this: I hate the royal family! They are so obnoxious. Half the time when they run into people they accuse those people of treason. Stop being a bag of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ royal family.
Overall, this is a game totally worth buying and it is one of the few games I can say is worth the price (although it never hurts to wait for a sale or a bundle!).

All in all, I'd have to pass on this one.  If you have the chance to purchase this at $5 or so then I'd give it a whirl.
Where to start?  It's an interesting concept, using a mental asylum as the backdrop.  A serial killer who's the protagonist.  Find your way out of the asylum and figure out what's going on.
It's a concept that has been done before, and better -- Asylum I & II (Med Systems Software) in the 1980s, Sanitarium in the 1990s (available at various websites).  Radio Shack had a ghetto version of the asylum thriller called "Bedlam", it wasn't that good.
The view is from above, and is basically a pixel hunt and a challenge of paying attention.  It's gruesome at times, inappropriately funny at others, sometimes just plain obscure.  Some of the puzzles are easy, some more complicated.
I think that the main reason I would recommend against this game is the lack of a save feature.  You have to start at the beginning of a chapter each time you play.  This gets tedious.  Would it really have been that hard to add a save option?
The whole testosterone-fueled, inappropriately humorous game was played out by Duke Nuke'em.  The humor in this game isn't really so juvenile as it is unnecessary.  It adds nothing to the experience.  Much of the humor is merely recycled cliches in one way or another.
So, if I look at all the moments of my life as being precious and if I want to make sure that I don't waste those moments, I have to say no about this game.  All in all, it isn't that bad.  It just isn't that good.

This isn't one of those fancy simulation racing games where you go around a track a few times trying to avoid bumping the other cars. In this game you have an entire city and then some to explore at your leisure and grinding your opponent's car into a wall is how you win. There's races, stunts, marked man and road rage events as well as an impressive selection of sexy stylish cars to unlock.
The visuals and graphics are nicely done with each area of Paradise City offering something cool to look at it. Just driving around is fun in itself as the sensation of speed is intense and the transitions between day and night are gorgeous. Something that might disappoint people though is that all the cars are driverless and there are no pedestrians or even people to be found anywhere. It's a little weird but I can understand the decision why they were omitted. This game would've been a blood bath.
On the audio side the engine sounds, screeching tires and various crash effects are great. The soundtrack is a good mixture of rock, pop, alternative and there's a lot of tracks. The ability to add your own to the rotation is sadly missing though.
If there are any real letdowns it's that the bike portion of the game feels tacked on with only a small handful of bikes and events to do. A shame too as the physics and handling of the bikes feel really nice. Some Road Rash-style events would've been awesome. Driving at night is also a mixed bag. Not because of how dark it is but because a lot of places you'd expect to be illuminated are missing lighting. The buildings downtown are a glaring example. They would've been awesome lit up at night but instead look like someone forgot to pay the electricity bill.
The online multiplayer is unsurprisingly dead with the log on screen broken and prone to crashing the game. Also a big thumbs down to EA/Criterion for pulling the plug on the in-game store and withholding any DLC that came out afterwards (no Big Surf Island). That's just cheap. Even with all those setbacks though this is a still highly entertaining racing game worth owning. A lot of bang for your buck.

I'm not gonna lie: I went into Blackbay Asylum expecting to loathe it. Seeing some of the early gameplay and the casual racism and sexism thrown around was not exactly winning me over, never mind the visuals. However, I found out I'd picked it up somewhere along the line, probably in a bundle, and figured I'd give it a shot. Blackbay Asylum, while problematic, actually delivers quite the gameplay experience.
As quite the physical specimen and not quite the mental specimen of an asylum patient, you're given a surprise opportunity to escape Blackbay and quickly learn a lot of strange things have been going on. Between terrible things happening to other inmates/patients and walls suddenly being covered with blood and/or weird fleshy masses, things ramp up quickly in Blackbay Asylum.
Puzzle-solving and combat are fairly well balanced in the game, with the latter not coming up too often, but feeling just difficult enough when it does. The former, however, suffers from a lot of solution-integral items or spots to investigate proving much more difficult to spot visually than they really needed to be. I recommend falling back on the time-honored tradition of repeatedly investigating every little thing to make sure you don't miss such items, as frustration is easy to come by when you do. At least the puzzles are interesting despite their roughness, and the results of solving many of them is entertaining, to say the least.
What really surprised me is how the plot, about halfway through, takes a shift for an even darker, clearly Lovecraftian vibe, though this is telegraphed early on by Blackbay's geographical location. The nods to and influence from tales of old gods is very clear, and woven in more and more expertly as the later stages carry on. It feels a lot like the game's writer worked from beginning to end rather than stringing together plot points, and got progressively better at writing as they went on. It's not perfect, by any means, but it definitely improves upon the usual first impressions.
Long story short, if you can get over the offensive bits and the visuals, consider picking Blackbay Asylum up. Much like its Lovecraftian inspiration, it's clearly got problematic elements, but it's still worthwhile.

I LOVE games that open with a dumb little disclaimer. It either means they don't actually take themselves seriously, or they take themselves SO seriously that you shouldn't bother to. Blackbay Asylum is the former sort, mashing top-down and first-person adventure gaming together with a liberal sprinkling of incredibly silly design. There's a lot of humor to be found here... which clashes more and more with the game itself the further in you get.
You play as... um... I think his name is Doug? I'm not entirely sure because it's never consistent, but he's a 6'8" mass murderer with a teddy bear and a soft side. My take is that you're not really supposed to sympathize with or revile him, just laugh along with him. And that's easy, because he has a ton of genuinely funny lines while examining the many hotspots of the asylum. I knew we were going to get along fine when he found someone ripped in half and shoved into a bookshelf, and said "That's why I don't read."
Most of the game is played from a top-down perspective, with you leading Doug around the grim halls to examine things, collect items, solve puzzles, and maybe figure out why demons have ripped everyone else to pieces. The puzzles are generally very clear and well thought-out, though the top-down perspective can make it very hard to spot key elements on walls, or odd objects on tables or floors. I had a tricky time locating a puzzle box in one office because it looked like a tablecloth. Of course, if you just click on everything it'll be less of an issue, which you should to get more of Doug's musings.
While the tone of the text is firmly tongue-in-cheek, the aesthetic is not and only gets darker. Flayed bodies are everywhere, and the demons get creepier and more startling the further in you get. The third chapter actually shifts things to first-person and ups the spooks pretty hard, with some corpse jumpscares, a lantern segment, and a gauntlet of horrors. Bear in mind that this all comes immediately after being eaten and pooped out of a giant monster. It starts to get weirdly whiplashy, alternating between goofy lines from Doug and Unity horror tropes.
There's a certain trashy charm to Blackbay Asylum, not quite as fully endearing as something like Splatter, but probably unique enough to keep you on board if you know what to expect. For a fighting game that was supposedly meant to focus on online gaming, Street Fighter 5 has failed to reach this goal. That however is still no excuse for this garbage they've given us. Even after forwarding all the ports, deactivating my firewall and antivirus, I still get constantly disconnected from the servers. Sometimes it takes only 2 minutes, sometimes it takes 10 minutes. And the problem is not in my router - I rarely (once in 2 hours, if at all) get disconnected while playing on my PS4.
And don't even get me started on the online roll back netcode that gives you 8 frames of input lag - 8 FRAMES!!
I originally stopped playing SF5 within the first four days, tired of the bad connectivity and constant server disconnects. The idea that you can earn fight money in the game that allows you to buy in-game content, such as characters, skins and levels was a neat idea. Crapcom is seemingly really eager to become the new KONAMI.

Playing Sleeping Dogs reminds me of sitting around watching stuff like Infernal Affairs with my friend a decade ago. It's a great idea for the setting and basic themes of a game, and they really nailed the feel and tone of it in a lot of ways. The writing gets a little iffy sometimes with too many characters and a lot of them not really developed much or seen more than once or twice, but most of the time it does a pretty good job with the standard cops and triads and conflicted loyalties story, and it's reflected in the gameplay to some extent too by you doing missions for both sides.
Speaking of gameplay, I see what they're going for with the mix of "I know kung fu" brawling with hordes of bad dudes and "I know John Woo" slow motion gun fights, but a rather decent melee combo system in an open world game is waaaay more interesting than yet another game with bullet time. It doesn't help that Saints Row 3 has permanently ruined all other open world games for me when it comes to stuff like that with the sheer absurdity of what I could get away with, but at least the brawling is kind of fun, even if it's really easy to completely avoid all damage. It loses some of its charm whenever it makes you shoot people.
Something that stuck out as kind of weird to me was that they were quite thorough with being relatively authentic to the setting in some areas, using a decent amount of Cantonese in the dialogue, for example, and generally casting ethnically appropriate voice actors for various roles, some of the music was really out of place. As great as Chali 2na and Dream Theater are, they really don't feel appropriate as the soundtrack for a Hong Kong gangster movie. The songs in the karaoke minigame were the worst offenders though. That was a great opportunity for some Asian pop music, and instead it was all stuff that was popular in the US over 20 years ago.
Anyway, I enjoyed it enough to play through all the story/mission-containing DLC and do all the optional crap in the game, so I must've been having a pretty good time. It's no Saints Row game, but I certainly liked it more than any of the GTAs if I had to compare it to other similar stuff.

Let me start off by saying that the artwork for this game is simply extraordinary. I was skeptical at first reading about the whole "castles in the sky" theme, but after seeing the hand-drawn backgrounds and maps I was instantly transported to the Highlands. Pairing that with the superb background music made for a very good first impression.
In terms of game-play, let me split it into two parts:
- pre-update 1.1
-post-update 1.1
In
, there were many instances where the combat felt slightly unrealistic. For example, a 22 HP character could be out-damaged by a 4 HP swarm bot (pretty much a low-level grunt). Combat itself lacked variety, as it was simply a game of numbers with a lot of luck involved. Think a D&D and Risk hybrid. There were a few areas that needed improvement in hindsight, but didn't affect the game TOO much. The storyline itself is your typical strategy game type of story; just enough to motivate you to complete a level, but not deep enough to be praised. Overall, it was a game that may have been ready to exit Early-Access, but definitely needed some more work.
In
, nearly all of the problems I mentioned above were addressed, with most of them fixed completely. Combat has been diversified, with smarter AI, combat abilities such as double strike, as well as strategic abilities outside of combat. The field kit is a nice addition, providing that extra health boost in tight situations. The narrower damage range means that the minimum damage output of all units is more reliable, and more realistic. What may have been slightly too ridiculous (like the swarm bot mentioned above; D&D + Risk) is now a fun twist on the classic territory strategy game. With added tooltips, something that I didn't necessarily feel was lacking, the game has moved to a point where I personally feel is definitely ready for all strategy-loving Steam users to enjoy.
In closing, I'd like to note that Burrito Studios added another update on June 10th, with even more bug fixes and tooltips. This kind of dedication speaks to the work ethic of not only the studio but the developers as well.

First review, but I will make it short and brief.
On Thursday, I wanted to get Age of Empires II because I utterly love all types of RTS' and Turn Based. Well, I switched over to the store and saw Northgard. I was instantly hooked, and with a $20 price tag, I couldn't resist. I bought it, waited an hour for it to load, and then I played it. I went on for three hours straight during launch, probably longer, not sure. I seriously hope good things come to this place, it's a real good game.
Pros:
- Nothing is too complex for this simple game, a young person could sit down and instantly know how to play the game within moments.
- Combat is simple and easy. Right click an area with your troops and they'll go there and attack.
- Buildings are unique, along with tech trees for various clans.
- Game gives you a good understanding of areas you can explore and colonize. (Meaning what gives you good resources and what not.)
Cons:
- Combat is pretty bland, honestly. You just have warriors, no archers, shield men, raiders, etc. Would seriously love to see more of it.
- Clan balances are kinda bad. The Wolf Clan starts off with increased attack, and if they get alot of lore, they can just spam into their military line and boost up even more damage. Where as the Goat Clan seems to be about survival and holding out.
- Some bugs that are pretty insane. I was sitting at the Helheim portal for 12 months and built a tower to defend it while my Warchief was off defending against the Goat Clan, but the thing fell and I lost the area. A surprising little strategy gem. This is a turn-based strategy game that owes more to abstract wargames than it does to the likes of Final Fantasy Tactics or King's Bounty, complete with somewhat esoteric game mechanics, abstraction of combat, and emphasis on supply lines and areas of control. But where I usually find the gameplay of grand war games to be inaccessible at best, Highlands' mechanics are clean and simple to understand, and within a couple of chapters I found myself adroitly maneuvering my units toward victory.
The good:
The art is gorgeous, hand-drawn cel-style, and while the character portraits and chapter interstitials aren't animated, they don't really need to be: the art stands well enough on its own.
The game mechanics are unique, but not obtuse. I found them easy to understand and manipulate, and I really enjoyed the feeling of mastering a new and unfamiliar system by the end of the game. If you enjoy learning systems, this will scratch that itch.
On the Challenging difficulty (second-hardest out of four), the game is--apropriately enough--challenging, but not frustrating. I rarely felt like I was being handed a victory, and the objectives and parameters of each of the game's seven chapters mix it up enough that I kept having to devise new strategies.
The game moves at a very fast clip. The only downtime you'll ever really experience is when you're contemplating your next turn. Menus are smooth and fast, though I did find that the item/equip menu was a little clunky. Animations are fast, clean, and descriptive, and the game tells you everything you need to know and doesn't dilly-dally about it.
The meh:
The music is okay, but nothing exceptional. It's mostly inoffensive, light, airy background music. It fit the theme and accompanied the game well, but I don't think I'll be humming it months from now.
There is a fair amount of RNG in this game, as the outcome of combat is determined by a dice roll modified by the combatants' relative combat strength. The game's tutorial does a good job of instructing you on how to gain the edge in combat, but you may well run into situations where you have to rely on an against-the-odds roll in your favor to proceed. The game is generous with autosaves, but you may end up save-scumming a few battles if you're particularly unlucky.
The writing is servicable at best. It gets the job done, but it's mostly exposition dumps and the characters never develop much personality. The copy editing is rather poor, too; time and again I saw missing punctuation and bad sentence structure. The developers would have been wise to hire a line editor to mark up their script beforehand. The pacing is also awkward. In short, don't play the game for its writing or story.
Conclusion:
Despite its flaws, I really enjoyed the time I spent with the game. I thought it was just the right length, it provided just the right challenge, and was engrossing enough that the hours flew by while I was playing. I would recommend this game to anyone with an eye for strategy games, especially anyone who is interested in learning new systems.

In addittion, the guys have added some nice extra features including extra craftable consumables, extra character abilities, and extra enemy abilities. The Campaign and Multiplayer options are grayed out at the moment so they are still to come.
This game is clearly worth the investment and already worth the money I paid for it; it ticks all the boxes for that slightly chilled strategy game with no hair pulling frustration and lots of smiling moments.

If you're a fan of 2d side scrollers and played them before, Starbound is definitely one of the heavies of this particular genre league. The game focuses on a creative universe where you design everything from your main protagonist, to the spaceship he/she/it starts their adventure on. Each step along the way is as exciting as the last and there is a clear defining objective tree to follow so you know you won't get stuck along the journey.
Now I've been an avid fan of Starbound for some time now, from its first early days of development to where it is at present. Gotta say that being apart of Starbound's journey and seeing the new additions to the game have been very rewarding for me. My two close friends and I have enjoyed the game from when it was in its infancy to how it has turned out to be now.
The game is extremely fun to play solo but also gives the great option of being able to play with your mates. There is a feeling of teamwork and acheivement as you plan and take down one of the many crazy boss fights in the game. With the explorable universe you will know straight away that each planet is never the same, with a bunch of new creatures to fight or with a brand new element to take advantage of.
Terraria fans haven't strayed too far away from home with this game as both titles share many similar features. This is most likely because half of the development team for Starbound also came over from Terraria and have brought upon the same attitudes to the sci-fi scroller. A title that sells well for the simplistic gamer who just wants to jump into the game and for the gaming professor that wishes to spend as many hours into the game trying to break it. I assure you, if you're a fan of this type of genre you won't be dissapointed by adding this to your Steam library even in its current state.

Don't be fooled by the graphics, which might appear too simplistic to some people, this game is great! Actually, the crude style of the graphics and the alternating shifts from 2D to 3D perspective complement the weird story quite well. This is also no 2D/3D shooter/action game at all, but rather a strange but great mixture of adventure and puzzle game. There are only very few points in the game where timing is a bit important, the rest is definitely more brains than reflexes. Some puzzles are quite hard, but ultimately easy to figure out. There is no dedicated user save function, but in the larger levels, checkpoints are set automatically to which you return should you die. The game has auto-save after each chapter, with each chapter lasting between 3 and 15 minutes (in my playthrough at least).
All in all, a great Lovecraft-ian horror adventure/puzzle game that I enjoyed very very much!

I'm not a huge fan of the Street Fighter series. In fact the whole "releasing Street Fighter 4 four times" thing kinda put me away from the series. However, I wanted to get into a fighting game on PC and since Mortal Kombat X on PC pretty much got the shaft, I thought I'd give this a try. What I can say so far about this game is that it works, not only that, but it works pretty well.
I've seen other people complaining that the game is buggy and that things don't work or that they can't get this game to start, but honestly, I've never experienced any of that. The game starts without any problems, I haven't had to do any extra configuring or had to download some user made patch or whatever. The online works, the only time i've had a laggy game was my first one, but everyone after that was very smooth with no problems. There isn't an Arcade Mode, which is alittle disappointing, but there are short stories for each character (not sure about the DLC characters) and from what I can tell, beating these VERY SHORT story campaigns is how you unlock that character's Alternate costume. Most of the story for each character is depicted with voice acting over a "dynamic" picture with a few fights in between. There is also the newly released free Story mode DLC, which is a nice plus. The DLC adds a general story to the game which apparently bridges the gap between the Street Fighter III and Street Fighter 4 (I think, you might want to look that up yourself). Unlike the character story mode, the general story mode features full on cutscenes  instead of the dynamic pictures. While the story is not incredibly interesting, you do get the chance to see the characters we all know and love interact with each other instead of just beating the hell out of each other (I'm still feeling the burn from Marvel vs Capcom 3).
The fighting is pretty smooth from what I can tell. Again, I'm not a super big street fighter fan boy, and although I didn't play that much of Super Street Fighter 4, Street Fighter V's fighting does feel better in my opinion, but I think something like this should be decided by your own preference. The game does give you a tutorial when you first start which isn't super in-depth, but it isn't bare bones, and if you haven't played Street Fighter games before I strongly encourage you to not skip the tutorial.
Now to talk about the graphics. before I get into it, I should mention my Rig is nothing special.. in fact I think at this point in time its pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥ I have a Lenovo Y510p Laptop.. yes LAPTOP.. it has a Geforce GT 755m, 8 GB of RAM, i7-4700MQ CPU @ 2.4 GHz and have Windows 10. I'm not a computer buff, but from what I could gather, these aren't exactly "top of the line" specs. When I first started playing, the game ran pretty slowly, the settings were defaulted to 1080 and everything put on medium. With a little tampering I was able to get this game to run very smoothly while still looking pretty good, I did have to drop the resolution to 720, but honestly I don't care about that, I know that there are some people out there that shiver at the thought of playing their games at anything under 1080, but for me, the game still looks great, I have textures on Max and everything else on medium settings and I still get smooth gameplay. If your specs are worse than mine but you still feel like you might want this game, there is a launch option for "low spec" rigs, although I'm not sure what that does exactly or how the game will look, you might want to find a video demonstration on that.
In conclusion, this game had a very rocky start when it first came out, there's no denying that. However, after the updates and all that I think this game has gotten substantially better. I've experienced no bugs, graphics look pretty decent, and my online experience has been pretty damn fun. However, this is Capcom we are talking about, these are the guys that killed Mega Man but thought it would be a good idea to release Umbrella Corps, I understand if you still feel worried about buying this game. If you don't feel like paying the $60, you should wait for a sale to come around, this past Summer Sale it was about $40 I think. If you have a PS4, you could go to game stop to buy a used copy, which I believe is roughly $30 to $35, you'll still get the same player base as PC thanks to the Cross Platform play with Steam and PSN, the only thing you'll be missing out on is mods, some of which are pretty cool (and pretty naughty if you catch my meaning).

I saw the Jim Sterling video about the trailer of this game. He probably made fun of it because the game looks terrible. And let's be honest, the graphics of this game are pretty awful. Animations are pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥too.
However, the idea behind the game interested me so much that I bought the game. And it was very entertaining from start to finish!
I'm usually not the puzzle-kind-of-guy, but the puzzles in this game were pretty understandable and fun to solve. The rest of the gameplay is your typical run around and discover what items to pick up and how to use them.
The best part about this game is the story. Being inspired by H.P. Lovecraft, there are very interesting (and disturbing) things that you find out about Black Bay Asylum. I'm not gonna spoil it, but it was an exciting time I had with the game, and every new unlocked part of the game made me more interested to find out what's happening next.
Another very fun thing about this game is the protagonist. Playing a psychopath opens some interesting ways to solve some puzzles. Also, Doug has funny lines even for some very mundane things, which keeps the game interesting, even if you are just running around clicking on random stuff.
Two major flaws that I want to mention:
1. I don't like how some puzzles can actually kill you if you fail. This happens only 2-3 times in the game, but I don't like to re-do stuff, just because I didn't do it in the arbitrary way the dev wants me to.
2. There are no save-games in this game. So if you start a chapter, you should make sure you complete it in one sitting, because the game only saves whatever chapter you have unlocked.
But even those flaws (while being a bit of annoying) did not lower the fun I had while playing.
Overall I can recommend this game to anyone who is interested in the obscure story and doesn't care if the game looks like from the early PS1 era.

When Supergiant Games released
in August 2011, probably they themselves probably won't have dreamt of the enormous critical acclaim their debut title would get. Seldom has an independent developer hit the gaming scene with such an original and beautiful game as in this case.
When I started
for the first time, I immediately got the feeling I was in for a special treat. Few games begins as arrestingly as this one, with the whiskey- and smoke-weathered voice of the "narrator" immediately setting the scene. This narrative aspect proved crucial in the way
drawed me into its world. It seemed like every step I made or every action I tried, could be met with some commentary. This feeling that the story develops "on the spot" is further enhanced by the fact that the world literally materialised under my feet as I ventured further out. This world is painted in bright and gorgeous colours with a teint all of their own:
would be immediately recognizable just by looking at the colour-pallette.
The story by itself proved interesting enough to keep me playing, wanting to discover step-by-step how things would develop with the Bastion and the protagonists. Gameplay-wise,
is not as innovative as in its storytelling or visuals, but it takes a well-tried formula into perfection. At its core, it is an action-rpg (light), preferably to be played with an xbox 360 controller (as are so many games the past years!). Controls are perfectly laid out and very intuitive: after a couple of hours I played it as if I had done so for several years. As the game progresses, more weapons and special abilities are unlocked, all with their distinctive characteristics. Weapons can be upgraded in five stages each, and liquids add some punch to the main-characters possibilities. Several other elements complement this core gameplay so that there is always enough variety to keep things interested. I even signed up immediately for the "new game plus" mode after completing the game a first time, looking forward to more unlocks of different sorts.
Another department where
truly shines, is its soudtrack. Seldom has ingame-music helped me so much in getting "into" the game, as it captures the mood of every level to perfection. Combined with the unique grain of the narrator's voice, this develops into a great listening experience. The developers also did a wonderful jobs in the myriad of smaller sounds present in the game: every weapon for example has a unique "ring" to it, from the zippy sound of the Breaker's Bow to the rusty clack of the Musket. There really is no weak link in this game. Everything is extremely well thought-off, and even better implemented. It's a must-play for everyone who loves pc gaming.

Bastion is an enthralling game with beautiful artwork and a wonderful soundtrack. I was hooked from the first cut-scene introducing you to the story and felt compelled to investigate further.
It is a challenging game, in that it is not difficult, but you really have to pay attention. What I mean is that, you need to understand your weapons and the weaknesses of enemies to figure out the best methods to clear an area. Fortunately, there is a natural progression designed into the game that will certainly help you with this.
Some may say that it is short, but there are challenges and mini-games that could prolong it for you. There is also a type of new game plus that lets you re-explore the story with your already unlocked abilities/weapons from the start. Alas, I concede that it is short by most standards of gaming, but a real quality experience.
On a personal note, I found gameplay better using a gamepad than the mouse and keyboard. I typically try to stick to mouse and keyboard on PC as much as possible, but some games just go better with other input devices
To conclude, it is a fun game that will require you to think a bit, but don’t be afraid to pick it up and try it out.

Ah... Sanctum 2. A fun, and somewhat addicting game.
Combining an FPS and Tower Defense game is pretty fun and interesting in concept. Luckily this game does manage to deliver that. Sanctum 2 definitely isn't the best game out there, but there is an enjoyment factor for those who like some pretty fast paced action, with the addition of actually being able to be strategic with the proper placement of tower bases, and towers themselves. Since you can only have a total of 15 actual towers to assist you in combat you need to plan carefully on where you put them.
In your inventory you can only have a total of 4 different tower types in your inventory, so choose wisely on which one you choose as some can have certain advantages over others. This means you definitely have some choice in strategy as some different tower types will just be all around decent (like the Focus Laser or just "Focus"), while others are flat out useful like the Range and Amp Towers.
Aside from Towers you have Tower Bases which are what you use as walls in this game. Enemies can't walk over them, but a few can jump over the tower bases, or fly over them completely. These are what you use to funnel enemies down a path to make them have a harder time getting to your Core which you must defend. They are also what you place your towers on. Each round you will usually get 1-5 tower bases depending on the map or so until a certain round is reached. This is always dependant on what map you play on from my experience.
Okay now aside from the Towers, there are also perks. Perks are what they are, things that help you. These can range from giving you additional damage,  slowing down enemies with every shot, healing your core a certain amount after each round, or even giving you a little robot buddy and even the ability to dodge attacks. I like this as it can be a great help, and in multiplayer games you can have perks that can go well with your teammates perks to help your team survive longer.
Now there are 4 different characters (5 in total if you count Tsygan)
These characters are:
Skye Autumn who can double jump, deals more damage per hit you deal on an enemy, and is armed with an Assault Rifle as her main weapon. She is the easiest to use, and is one of my favorites.
Sweet Autumn who has better aerial control, armed with a rocket launcher as her default weapon, and every shot of hers can set enemies on fire allowing her to be useful for support.
SimO who is the sniper of the group. He has higher critical hit damage than the others, and is armed with a strong sniper rifle. He also has more accuracy by default when compared to the other characters, allowing him to be incredibly useful for attack Soakers, and Bobble Heads.
Haigen Hawkins who is the Point Man. Like SimO his mobility is... basic. Simple jump, walk, and sprint unless you have perks that can grant a character an extra jump and stuff. He is armed with a shotgun which can be charge to fire a full clip in a single shot. He does more damage the closer he is to an enemy, and he does have more health. Allowing him to survive a bit longer than the others.
In the DLC you get Tsygan who is pretty useful in crowds (in my opinion.) I like her a lot. She is armed with a Crossbow which has a scope, and can be charged for more power. She also moves a bit faster than the others which is nice. Aside from that her special ability is that the last clip in any magazine of any weapon she has deals extra damage. If you have on shot in your Crossbow, fully charge it, then strike an enemy's weak point with it you will deal some pretty nasty damage. With her Crossbow you can easily provide support fire from a distance, yet you can still do well in close range which is really nice. She is DLC though so that kind of sucks.
Now the graphics in the game are pretty good I must say. I find myself hooked when I play, and I don't ever really get tired of the graphics if I play for hours which is kind of rare for me. On top of that the music is REALLY nice, and reminds me of the Metroid Prime games, and a bit of Halo. In fact I find this game more entertaining than Halo.
The difficulty of the game is quite fair in all honesty, but can get pretty tough on later stages. Yet with how the game is if you do lose you can learn from your mistakes and try out a different tower layout and all.  Even then you can turn the difficulty down to easy if you are new, or just want a more casual experience. If you were to play with friends the difficulty will be automatically upped to make things quite challenging even with another player with you, and in my opinion... this game is better with friends you can trust.
Overall this game contains fun gameplay, a unique concept that I myself haven't seen before, great music, great combat, great weapons, perks, and towers. The enemies aren't all too bad either, and I find it really.
I give it a 7/10. It definitely isn't the perfect game, but if you like FPS games, Tower Defenses games, or both then this is the game for you!

Highlands is a deceptively simple looking strategy game.  I was drawn in by the gorgeous hand drawn art and the promise of a turn based strategy game with some rpg elements and I have not been disappointed.
The game puts you in charge of the Arislaan  family in a fight to reclaim their kingdom in the sky.  The clouds act as a fog of war and as you fight your way across the regions you gotta look out for both enemies and valuable resources that the regions have to offer.
You have four classes of characters; the combatant is a straight up fighter, the mechanics can build the very important fortifications, the leaders are needed to gain control of areas and finally the academic function as healers. There is a number of special skills that widen the scope of that, but those are the basic functions of the classes.
There are three basic resources; food  that is essential for survival and healing, leadership that allows you to purchase new heroes and finally scraps that you can use to craft items as well as other special stuff.
These simple mechanics make for some tough choices on the battlefield. When to advance. What regions to focus on and to get essential resources or  buildings (taverns to recruit new heroes or workshops to craft items) and so on. On top of that, death is permanent! So if  you loose any of the main characters they are really gone. So be careful.
Controls are simple and work well. The artwork is gorgeous like I said and the music also adds to the mood. So if you like stuff like the old Heroes of Might and Magic or Battle  Isles? Or maybe you enjoy some of the Japanese tactics games? Then this is for you! The combat system may seem simple, but don't be fooled, there is plenty of strategy to sink your teeth into here.
In conclusion, Highlands gives us some much needed turn based goodness. I highly recommend it.

The series that invented the first-person-shooter is still relevant eight years later and has influenced everything from BioShock to Dead Space. The culmination of the series in Doom 3 is not only a masterpiece in level design but a game that genuinely makes you feel under constant assault. It's immersion factor (via interaction with the environment, NPCs and an eReader) is a tact taken from Half-Life, but here the feeling of mankind going past ethical boundaries of science and munitions is played surprisingly tongue-in-cheek. If anything ID knew how to take simpler conceits and use it to play with it's audience rather than preach. For instance, you spend three levels hoofing it to a communication hub to send a distress message but are given the option to cancel. You send it anyway... And doom the Earth to demons. It's an aptly titled series because once the possession starts all hope is gone.

+ Each 'tile' feels uniquiely designed, and sets it aside from other titles of the genre that often settle for uniform tiles and grids
+ Absolutely incredible musical score; very melodic, and really pulls you into your chair
+ Random events keep one on one's toes, often doling out punishment instead of reward
+ One of the most important strategic elements involved is that of resource management; the game pulls this off successfully, despite there only being three essential resources to balance
+ Tutorial is well-woven into the early plot, and does an excellent job of introducing the game's mechanics
+ Hand-illustrated artwork is superb, particularly the storyboard pages that are use to advance the plot
+ Permanent death of one's characters is in effect; this does much to lend gravity to one's decisions, and it elicits a nervous reluctance to sacrifice your units (which will often be absolutely necessary)
+ There is actually a commendable amount of character development afoot; this is certainly refreshing for a strategy game
+ Forces must be properly utilized, not only in terms of proper dispersion and front line management, but also in using them to reorganize territories, post-liberation
+ The challenge builds substantially after the initial stage, getting the hook into newer players relatively early on
+ Disney-esque art style contrasts wonderfully with the dark tone pervading throughout
+ Class system is basic enough that one will pick it up quickly; the impact of its utilization is the critical component in your success on the battlefield, and is overall solid in its implementation
+ Equipment management, character stats, and the experience system are all par-for-the-course; nothing revolutionary, but it certainly adds to the depth of gameplay without feeling out of place
- Replenishment of enemy forces, while effective in creating a sense of urgency, can be horribly unforgiving on larger maps
- Unit lists expand awkwardly when attempting to select from the stack; feels a bit odd, in that it can be hard to get the right number of characters within the cursor's selection box, as they move outward when passing over them
- New recruits have a small pool of models to draw from
- There is no skirmish or custom-battle mode; in fact, although the main campaign is very well-done, the game would be well-suited to host more in the way of game-modes in the future (until that is implemented, there is limited replayability)

A fun little gem. If you enjoy strategy games then consider letting your eyes linger a while longer.
Mechanics: Highlands is a very elegant, very sharp game. At its core is a very simple system of board control and area denial. To gain and hold territory you have four types of units:
By the end of the first map you've pretty much figured it all out, at which point your characters start gaining new abilities as they level up (crafting, ranged zone control, etc.) and you rush to figure out how to best employ them, because...
Map Design: They've done a great job with campaign progression. As you progress the maps become progressively more challenging as more elements and twists on gameplay are thrown in your path, forcing you to discard old strategies and incorporate those shiny new abilities that seemed excessive only one map ago. A less innovative game would have reused the same basic layout time and time again, and the mechanics would have suffered from it.
Art/Layout Design: The art is gorgeous, and more importantly it meshes very well with the visual information the game needs to present. There is never any excess data in your field of vision, you know everything you need to without cluttering up the screen with too many inputs. Concision is a virtue even in game design!
The Writing: There's no way around it. As addictive as the gameplay is and as beautiful the world they've created is, they really dropped the ball here. Every word out of any character's mouth is the most banal, generic action/fantasy trope they could get their hands on. Maybe you don't care about storytelling, in which case move on, but as some who reads every codex entry I can find in games I was quickly fast-forwarding through any cutscene because my stomach couldn't handle it. It isn't even properly proofread, as characters will overtly contradict earlier events.
And it's a shame. Bad storytelling isn't news, and I usually just ignore it. It's a shame because the world they created isn't just beautiful because of the artwork: the mechanics themselves tell a tale far grander than the writing ever aspires to. You're introduced to the royal family: the daughter of the duke, a burgeoning warrior who wants to be just like her dad. The duke arrives and is this towering figure, with a combat value so much higher that you can't help but believe him to be that archetype of the invincible father present in almost every child's mind. And yet... by the end of the game, the daughter has surpassed him, reached heights even he could not. That is a beautiful story, and not a single word is devoted to it. A tale told entire in numbers.
There are many moments like that in the game, and if they're intentional then I tip my hat to their creators. But given the state of the actual plot, I'm not holding my breath.
Randomness of Combat: Combat is essentially determined by stack size. The bigger your total combat value, the harder your troops hit the other guy's troops, and vice versa. Except that all of this is determined by a ridiculously bounded dice roll. It's not unusual to see a possible roll of 1-120, where anything above 60 will one-shot a Fighter. And since power is adjusted as the battle goes on, the first dice roll is infinitely more critical than any other.
Oh and if any of your main characters die at any time, it's game over. Reloading is never painful, it just brings you back right before the battle, but the whole thing just incentivizes you to reroll until the result is what you need it to be. Later in maps you have the resources to just buy enough disposable characters to eat those first few blows, but it isn't good design.
Luckily the emphasis of the game is in the board mechanics and not the combat, so this isn't a huge issue. But it is one you will notice.
Highlands has a few flaws (story, combat) but when talking about an indie game it's far more important to talk about niche: what does this game do well, and why will I enjoy playing it?
The strategy component of this game, the board control gameplay, is an incredible amount of fun. The mechanics fit seamlessly into one another and have obviously received a lot of care. If that's a game type you enjoy, then you will definitely want to play Highlands.
Note: If you have any experience with this type of game, I recommend playing on Hard. While that may have been what created the excessively random combat rolls (I did not play on normal difficulty so perhaps they are balanced around it), the scarcity of resources and relative strength of the enemy was perfect. Overcoming the challenges presented is the most satisfying part of this game, and you'd be doing yourself a disfavour if you made it easier.

Simplistic, yet challenging. That was my experience with the first 2 hours of this game. While not being bombarded by very original artwork and a pretty decent musical score that is. The mechanics are simple, with more powerful skills and items showing up deeper into this story driven Turn Based Strategy game.
The premise of the game is you lead a family of nobles, who rule a land high in the clouds called the Highlands, in a tale of loss and spider robots. Yeah, that's right, spider robots, that will overwhelm you should you allow them to respawn too quickly. The game is simple, everyone has a combat value that increases through skills and experience that gives you a higher chance surviving encounters. You allocate resources by improving sectors you captured from combat which can be used to heal your troops and to recruit more troops. Again, the game is simple... yet one false move can lead to you having to restart level, after level should you take too long to complete a chapter. However, the challenge is not a bad thing.
I'm also not embarrassed to say that I got my butt kicked by the Swarmbots on the second level. Definitely recommended.

I've been checking this game out for my Lets Play channel, and I'm really getting into it!
There is a lot of hidden depth here that slowly reveals itself as you go along.
The various different classes each learn new and interesting abilities as they level up, many of which REALLY change the face of the battlefield and the flow of the war!
Options such as using a Leader's ability Militia to safely lock down an enemy squad and prevent their movement, and whittle down their strength, with no danger to your own troops.
Or Bombardment, allowing a Mechanic to force squads in adjacent sectors to stop moving for a turn, at the cost of supplies.
Or Fortifying your sectors themselves with the Mechanics, so the foe has to waste multiple turns attacking it before they can finally take it over. Or just to protect friendly troops stationed there.
With every campaign map I discover new tricks and tactics. I'm impressed so far!
A potential downside though, is the game is already getting quite difficult! But many people will like that about it, I'm sure.
I strongly recommend watching some of the gameplay to get a feel for whether or not this game feels like it is right for you. Check out my playlist below, I'm working on a full playthrough!

When Supergiant Games released
in August 2011, probably they themselves probably won't have dreamt of the enormous critical acclaim their debut title would get. Seldom has an independent developer hit the gaming scene with such an original and beautiful game as in this case.
When I started
for the first time, I immediately got the feeling I was in for a special treat. Few games begins as arrestingly as this one, with the whiskey- and smoke-weathered voice of the "narrator" immediately setting the scene. This narrative aspect proved crucial in the way
drawed me into its world. It seemed like every step I made or every action I tried, could be met with some commentary. This feeling that the story develops "on the spot" is further enhanced by the fact that the world literally materialised under my feet as I ventured further out. This world is painted in bright and gorgeous colours with a teint all of their own:
would be immediately recognizable just by looking at the colour-pallette.
The story by itself proved interesting enough to keep me playing, wanting to discover step-by-step how things would develop with the Bastion and the protagonists. Gameplay-wise,
is not as innovative as in its storytelling or visuals, but it takes a well-tried formula into perfection. At its core, it is an action-rpg (light), preferably to be played with an xbox 360 controller (as are so many games the past years!). Controls are perfectly laid out and very intuitive: after a couple of hours I played it as if I had done so for several years. As the game progresses, more weapons and special abilities are unlocked, all with their distinctive characteristics. Weapons can be upgraded in five stages each, and liquids add some punch to the main-characters possibilities. Several other elements complement this core gameplay so that there is always enough variety to keep things interested. I even signed up immediately for the "new game plus" mode after completing the game a first time, looking forward to more unlocks of different sorts.
Another department where
truly shines, is its soudtrack. Seldom has ingame-music helped me so much in getting "into" the game, as it captures the mood of every level to perfection. Combined with the unique grain of the narrator's voice, this develops into a great listening experience. The developers also did a wonderful jobs in the myriad of smaller sounds present in the game: every weapon for example has a unique "ring" to it, from the zippy sound of the Breaker's Bow to the rusty clack of the Musket. There really is no weak link in this game. Everything is extremely well thought-off, and even better implemented. It's a must-play for everyone who loves pc gaming.

Bastion is an enthralling game with beautiful artwork and a wonderful soundtrack. I was hooked from the first cut-scene introducing you to the story and felt compelled to investigate further.
It is a challenging game, in that it is not difficult, but you really have to pay attention. What I mean is that, you need to understand your weapons and the weaknesses of enemies to figure out the best methods to clear an area. Fortunately, there is a natural progression designed into the game that will certainly help you with this.
Some may say that it is short, but there are challenges and mini-games that could prolong it for you. There is also a type of new game plus that lets you re-explore the story with your already unlocked abilities/weapons from the start. Alas, I concede that it is short by most standards of gaming, but a real quality experience.
On a personal note, I found gameplay better using a gamepad than the mouse and keyboard. I typically try to stick to mouse and keyboard on PC as much as possible, but some games just go better with other input devices
To conclude, it is a fun game that will require you to think a bit, but don’t be afraid to pick it up and try it out.

As you can tell I have put a lot of time into this game, and because of that I feel compelled to voice my opinion.
Now to start out I never really got into Terraria, to me it felt pointless. You can only walk so far left or right to adventure, only to have to walk back to your house to survive the night. Never really grasped me, but then came Starbound.
Starbound takes the same idea as Terraria, 2D side-scrolling world, you can dig, build and craft till' your heart is content. The beauty of Starbound is, when you've finally got tired of the world you're on, you can leave! Just beam up to your ship, and select a new planet! New adventure, new landscape, new dungeons etc.
Some of you may have your finger ready to click the buy button, but before you do I want to also let you in on something; it's not finished. I say this because it's very important you understand the level that this game is at, and where it needs to be to be complete.
First and foremost in my opinion is the progression, the system isn't even close to finished. At this point it's "Hello Welcome to Starbound, here's some basic supplies, now you're our interstellar b**ch and you're going to run all over retrieving the dumbest items we can think of".
When I first started I was like OKAY! My body is ready! But not anymore, I haven't actually sat down and delved back into SB for about 6 - 8 months. I do watch the dev's posts everyday (yes daily updates as to what is going on) and that's encouraging but watching those also shows how slowly stuff moves along.
The other system that isn't even close to done yet in my opinion is the combat, currently its when monster A hits player B, then do damage. That isn't an ideal system because it leaves you to kiting, jumping and then attack and that's basically it. If a monster gets to close, or basically close enough to inflict damage, it can be impossible to get away from them so you can return damage. Due to it being on-touch damage as soon as they touch you again, more damage, before you know it you've lost all your credits or items (depending on the difficulty you chose). You can't get them back because that monster is still there, waiting to touch you to death..
This for me ruined SB in a way I never expected because combat is such a crucial part of this game. Monsters drop stuff, and they also help you complete stuff, so not running into any monsters is pretty much impossible.
I know you're probably saying to yourself "But Soul, you recommended the game!" Yes I do recommend the game, and I do because I believe it will get better. I know the dev's aren't done and due to that I can only hope the systems I don't like in the game get altered. I know for a fact per the developer that they're going to re-implement hunger and temperatures but I haven't heard anything about the damage on touch.
All this is to say, if you can overcome the mishaps the game has because of it's level of incompleteness and really trial and error that the dev's have been doing, then buy it. If you can't overcome these things then wait. Starbound is a GREAT game, but it's just not done, and to hell with the people complaining about development time! You can't rush perfection!

This game is a fun, creative, and addicting experience that will have you sitting on the edge of your seat, shooting enemies and upgrading towers for hours on end. I have played for over 30 hours so far, and have just started playing the DLCs. I would estimate that this game probably holds around well over 70 hours of gameplay (with DLCs). Not only that, but it is some amazing gameplay. You place tower bases which are platforms that are used to maze enemies throughout the battlefield, giving you more time for you to kill the enemies. There are upgradeable towers that you can place on top of the tower bases which shoot enemies for you. As for your character, there are around 40 unlockable, unique, and really cool weapons to use for your character with a primary fire, and a special secondary fire (such as a cluster bomb, an EMP effect, etc). The enemies come in long waves that must be strategically adapted to. The game is moderately challenging, however it is pretty easy without using any feats of strength (game options that increase XP gain and do things like increase enemy health, make enemies faster, etc). Multiplayer is very fun too. For each person that joins the game, the enemies get much stronger, but each person also gets their own income to place towers so that the team can defeat the enemy. The more people in your server, the more difficult it becomes.
As for the DLCs, each one provides a very substantial amount of extra gameplay, more enemies to fight, perks, weapons, etc. The complete pack comes with 4 map packs which, combined, provide you more gameplay than the actual main quest itself. That is very impressive, and i highly suggest that all people (fans of tower defence or not) should buy the complete pack for this game. I absolutely promise you that you will not regret it.

This is THE final tower defense game, and it is also a pretty entertaining coop shooter.

As far as RTS goes this is very casual, though it focuses more on the survival aspects (managing food/wood consumption, dealing with winter, ect) - you won't likely see huge armies as troops are expensive and building "room" is scarse, largest army I built was 20 soldiers + warchief; I could have won the game LONG before obtaining this.
I don't see PVP being strong in this game as the soldiers are so powerful (1 soldier can easily take out 3 villagers) - so I can imagine a human player would constantly harass your undefended nodes (towers are too expensive to put in all nodes and would cripple you to do so any ways) so it would come down to whether or not the enemy can cripple you early with 1-2 soldiers than a long terms build and fight that you see from traditional RTS.
On the plus side, they have found a more balanced RTS in the sense of "coming back" - in most RTS games, if you lose your army, it is pretty much over since the enemy still have a force and is consistently adding to it. Due to the strict population control in the game, it would be difficult and costly to expand the army much while rebuilding an army simply costs gold (scarse early but easy to stockpile late into the game.)
TLDR: Expect a game that is fun for a bit since it is new and tries to be different in a cookie-cutter RTS genre; don't expect this to go competative.

The numbered Doom games (SORRY FINAL DOOM) in a convenient package. Doom 1 and 2 remain relatively unchanged other than being ports of the Xbox versions. There are minor sprite differences, like the icon on the health pickups being a pill instead of a health cross, but thats about it. However, because they are ports, Doom 2 includes a new chapter only available previously on the Xbox, which is nice.
Most of the changes are to Doom 3, for better or worse. A whole new campaign was added called the Lost Mission, which focuses on a member of Bravo Team, whom you see breifly getting ambushed by demons in Doom 3. Its short, but pretty fun. Gameplay wise a few things are different, the game is a bit brighter overall, you get way more ammo than before, and you can hold a gun and the flashlight at the same time. These changes don't bother me so much, but I could understand how they could for someone who appreciated Doom 3's focus on a more horror atmosphere. These changes make it feel a tad bit more like the original games, where its easier to just run and gun monsters down, rather than being more apprehensive.
Most of the other changes are on the technical side, more support for new monitors/resolutions, better textures, new graphics options, ect. Whatever changes they made to the engine apparently breaks mods made for vanilla Doom 3, so if you like to mod maybe the original version is a better choice. I will recommend this because its Doom, and I love Doom. Do I recommend this version specifically? No, there are definitely pros and cons to consider with the gameplay tweaks, so look into whats best for you and choose which version accordingly.

This game is, unfortunatly, far inferior to the much cheaper original, which was a simulation classic.
Let's start with what this game does right. It presents a complex economic simulation, customizable planes, interesting charecters and interesting mechanics.
So why did I rate this game negativly?
The original game did all that, only better. The simulation  and mechanics were almost exactly the same, the original game's charecters and sense of humor are far superior, (Airline Tycoon 2's comedy falls completly flat) and in my opinion the ability to buy real-world planes in the original was better.
The game suffers from graphics that lag greatly in the terminal, and look overly cartoony, and the music is terrble.
Normally, I do not mind DLC, and I think it is worthwhile to support the developers if it is farily priced. However, this game's DLC feels like they took some of the most interesting parts of the orginal (Cargo and last minute contracts) and made you pay more for it.
The BIGGEST PROBLEM with this game is the pacing. In the original Airline Tycoon you can easily make over 500,000 dollers from the begining of the game, and in a little over a week by your next plane, which makes it easier to buy the next plane. The pacing is helped by the fact you can skip the morning meeting, and there are no loading screens. On the other hand Airline Tycoon 2 is hampered by the fact that planes 3 or 4 times as expensive, and they make substantialy less money per day than in Airline tycoon deluxe. Compounded with the HORRIBLE LOADING TIMES, it can take HOURS to purchase another plane. This game moves at a glacial pace.
CONCLUSION; If you want an tycoon game in which you manage an airline, DO NOT CHOSE AIRLINE TYCOON 2. You should go with the much cheaper, original Airline Tycoon deluxe!

I really want to like this game, but I am finding it very difficult to. Let me see if I can explain why.
What I Like:
1) Game imagery and setting seems really cool.
2) Game mechanics are fairly straight forward.
3) Game reminds me a lot of The Banner Saga (search on steam if you haven't heard of).
4) Game is tactical and requires strategic placement of units, use of limited resources, and distribution of items.
What I dont like:
1) Difficulty - The game has two modes, hard and normal. I am playing the game on normal and finding that the mechanics are not very well balanced for a fun game. I am only on the second mission, but I am finding myself getting overwhelmingly "zerged" by the AI.
2) AI Mechanics - goes hand in had with my first point. AI continuously spawns new units every X amount of turns, cause them to snowball into ridiculously impossible opponents. You on the other hand have to wait for resources to generate at a set rate by capturing nodes. You can heal your army with food, which seems to be a scarce resource.
3) Crashing - I spent an hour or so on the second mission. After what felt like an hour long grind fest of fighting enemy after enemy, trying to advance on the map, the game simply crashed. I am reluctant to continue playing the game because I am worried about future crashing and aggrevation.

Doug, our protaganist, is the mouthpiece for the majority of the game and to be honest I thought his goofball one-liners were really at odd with who he is but whatever. The game doesn't take its self seriously so why should I?
The puzzles are pretty good. The first few are infantile but they get harder and more interesting. Sometimes you'll get stuck because you missed an item which is a common failing of Point-and-Clicks. But to be fair this is not a Point-and-Click, its a Move-and-Push-Space and Doug is one bigass cursor. So comparitivily it's a little easier to find things you missed.
My only solid complaint is the voice acting, it's terrible. Doug is mercifully mute but you meet NPCs whose voices are somehow both obnoxious and boring. I can't skip through their dialouge fast enough!
I still dont think its worth twenty dollars but it was a fine game for five.

This is a pretty niché title, and I strongly believe would only really be enjoyed by a select sort of gamer. Let's look at the basics. It's a very old school looking top down (and occasionally First Person) adventure title. Gory and silly humour, horror theme, and plenty of puzzles along the way. The puzzles are generally fair (only ever found 1 that the clues, or lack thereof, weren't good enough for me to understand), and the story is just silly enough to keep you interested throughout the campaign.
The bad, however, are fairly obvious things. Firstly, it's a very old school game. Meaning the gameplay is a little clunky, the action sequences can frustrate, and the graphics are notably dated. It's also a fairly short game. Almost all of the chapters can be completed within about 10-20 minutes. The only exceptions are longer because the actual gameplay takes longer (such as the first person sections, where the movement is quite annoyingly slow).
Those things aside though, I had fun with it, and for the price, I can't really argue with the length or gameplay quality. This is the kind of game that people who still revel in retro would find enjoyable. You have to push past the annoyances to get to the fun, but the fun is there.

The best way I can describe this game is like an RTS version of Civilazation
Going into a more detailed explaination of the gameplay:
Domination: destroy all enemies
Fame: Control a certain amount of zones, gather fame (this is done by colinizing zones, attacking enemies, organizing feasts, discovering lore), and have a building called the Altar of Kings.
Trade: Collecting a certain amount of krowns, having a certain amount stockpiled, and having a certain amount of active merchants.
Wisdom: Gain all blessings from the Gods and have a certain amount of active Lore masters.
Food: Villagers will gather by default, can also be gained from other sources such as hunting, gathering, fishing, and farming. Needed to feed your units and colinizing new zones.
Wood: Gathered by building a woodcutting lodge and having active woodcutters. Basic building material and also used for firewood to keep units warm in winter.
Krowns: Gathered by having merchants and can be pillaged when attacking enemies. Used to build certain structures, building upkeep, training members of your warband, and purchasing other resources if you have a marketplace.
Stone: Gathered by building a mine in a zone with a stone node and having active miners. Used for upgrading structes and building certain structure.
Iron: Gathered by having a mine in a zone with an iron node and having active miners. Used for upgrading unit productivity and warband damage.
Lore: Gathered by building a carved stone or finding a runestone and having villagers worship at it, your clan also produces some by default depending on the population. Used for upgrading knowledge on a tech tree. After certain amount of knowledge is gained you can choose more blessings from different gods.
Zones: Scouts have to explore different parts of the map called zones in order for you to see whats on them. Zones must be colonized using food before you can build on them. Colonizing takes a lot of food and each zone has different benefits or none at all so you kind of need to choose carefully. Some zones have deer and sheep for hunting, streams for fishing, iron and stone nodes, increased woodcutting benefits, NPC enemies to fight and provide additional fame if colonized, NPC structures such as rune stones and circles which provide additional lore if worshipped at, ship wrecks and ruins which your scouts can explore for a one time boost in resources. Also, each zone can only have a certain amount of buildings in them, the range I've seen for each zone is 1 to 5 buildings.
Seasons: Currently there is just a summer and winter season. Summer is business as usual and doesn't have any effects.
Winter reduces your miltary units damage when you fighting outside of one of your zones. It also reduces food production and increases firewood consumption.
Events: I've only ran into 3 different events so far, the first one is Rat Infestion, which causes you to lose food if it's not protected by silos. Earthquakes damage your structures and will destroy them if you dont have wood to repair them quickly enough. Draugr portals open up random portals around the map which spawn draugrs, these are enemy NPC's that will attack your structures and units.
Unit Control in this game isn't anything like Warcraft or Starcraft, it's a lot less intensive and the gameplay is more focused toward strategy than managing units. Control groups are basically just for military units only and you assign them by having specific Warband units. Currently there are 2 units that are used for assigning these groups and you can only have one of each. There is the Warchief and the Berserker. For resource gathering units there is a tab that shows you how many you have of a certain type and lets you cycle through or select all, but there are no hot keys to set these to a control group. It's not really a bad thing though because you don't really spend a lot of time managing these units.
